# APTRANSCO Transmission Line Inspection System — Project Reference

> **Purpose of this document.** A complete working reference for this codebase, written so that
> someone (or an AI assistant) who has never seen it can gain full understanding without opening
> a source file. Start a new session by reading this document.
>
> **Scope.** Two live projects — a Django web application (backend + admin panel + oversight
> dashboard + REST API) and a Flutter offline-first field app — plus one dead reference folder.
>
> **Reliability convention.** Every claim here was checked against the source code, not just the
> project's own `line_inspection/README.md`. Where the README and the code disagree, the code is
> reported and the discrepancy is called out explicitly. Statements that could not be verified
> from the repository (for example live row counts) are labelled as such.
>
> **Path convention.** All file references are relative to `transcoapps/`, the directory this
> document sits in — e.g. `line_inspection/models.py:129`.
>
> **Secrets.** No credential values are reproduced in this document. Where a secret exists, its
> variable name and location are given and the value is shown as `<redacted>`. Secrets found
> hardcoded in tracked source are reported as findings in §2.7.

## 1. What This System Is

### 1.1 One paragraph

This repository holds the **APTRANSCO Transmission Line Inspection System**: a Django 6.0 web
backend + admin panel + read-only oversight dashboard (`line_inspection/`), and an offline-first
Flutter field app (`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/`) that talks to it over a REST API.
Together they replace the paper "line inspection register" that APTRANSCO field engineers carry
into the field twice a year when they walk their transmission lines tower by tower. The backend
owns the GIS master data (towers, lines, substations synced from ArcGIS), a **database-backed,
admin-editable inspection checklist**, a three-tier authorization model built without
`django.contrib.auth`, and every inspection / defect-ticket record. The phone app downloads a
field engineer's assigned area, enforces a GPS proof-of-presence gate at each tower, drives a
data-driven questionnaire, queues submissions in a durable outbox, and syncs them idempotently
when signal returns. A third folder, `Aptransco_TIS-main/aptransco_backend/`, is a **dead donor
project kept only as an API-contract reference** — it is never imported, never run, and must not
be used.

### 1.2 The business problem

#### Who APTRANSCO is

**APTRANSCO** — the Transmission Corporation of Andhra Pradesh — is the state transmission utility
for Andhra Pradesh, India. It does not generate or retail electricity; it owns and operates the
**Extra High Tension (EHT) transmission network** that moves bulk power from generating stations to
distribution companies. In this codebase the network is restricted to three voltage classes, and
that restriction is hard-coded in the ArcGIS sync and in the model choices
(`line_inspection/models.py:41`):

| Voltage class | Meaning here |
|---|---|
| `132kV` | Lowest EHT tier synced. The only class where `Tower.span_km` is reliably populated (`line_inspection/models.py:144`). |
| `220kV` | Mid tier. |
| `400kV` | Highest tier synced. |

`management/commands/sync_gis_towers.py` imports "towers, lines, and substations (132kV/220kV/400kV
only)" — anything outside those three classes is out of scope for this system.

#### The physical assets, defined

Everything below is a term you will meet repeatedly in the code; each is defined once here.

| Term | Definition as this project uses it |
|---|---|
| **Transmission line** | A named point-to-point run of overhead conductor between two substations, e.g. a 220 kV line from substation A to substation B. Modelled as `Line` (`line_inspection/models.py:90`), keyed by `(source_layer, arcgis_object_id)`, carrying a GeoJSON `geometry` polyline. |
| **Tower** (also *structure*, *location*, *Loc No*) | One steel lattice or pole structure holding the conductors up. Modelled as `Tower` (`line_inspection/models.py:129`). Identified in the field by `tower_number` — the field engineer calls this the **Loc No** (location number), and the register prints it as such. |
| **Circuit** | One complete three-phase set of conductors. A single physical tower can carry **1, 2 or 4 circuits** (`Tower.circuit_count`, parsed to 1/2/4 from ArcGIS's `SCT`/`DCT`/`MCT` · `1C`/`2C`/`4C` text). SC = single circuit, DC = double circuit, MC = multi circuit (`Tower.circuit_type`). |
| **VT / virtual tower** | ArcGIS models each *additional* circuit on a shared physical tower as its own row, with `tower_number` beginning `VT`. These are **not separate structures** — they are the same steel, described once per circuit. `Tower.is_virtual=True` marks them (`line_inspection/models.py:155`). |
| **`structure_key`** | The glue for the above: a key assigned during `sync_gis_towers` by **coordinate proximity (nominally ~33 m; effectively ~11 m — see §4.14)** that groups one real tower plus all its co-located VT rows into a single *physical structure* (`line_inspection/models.py:156`). **Only real towers (`is_virtual=False`) are ever inspected or counted** — every jurisdiction / oversight / map / register / rollup queryset filters on it, and `_create_inspection` hard-rejects a VT tower (`line_inspection/api/views.py:451`). The register still *shows* VT columns, sourcing their cells from the co-located real tower, so an inspected structure reads "inspected" on every circuit it carries. |
| **CP / SP** | `Tower.cp_sp` (`line_inspection/models.py:137`) — the structure's role in the line, observed values `CP` / `SP` / `Boom`. CP and SP distinguish the tower's function at that point in the corridor (e.g. a cut-point / crossing structure vs a suspension-type structure); the code treats it as opaque master data promoted from ArcGIS, never as logic. |
| **Substation** | The node at each end of a line where voltage is transformed and lines are switched. Modelled as `Substation` (`line_inspection/models.py:210`), also ArcGIS-synced. Not inspected by this system — it is context for the line. |
| **Span** | The stretch of conductor between two consecutive towers. `Tower.span_km` records it (132 kV only). |
| **LILO** ("Loop In, Loop Out") | A line reorganisation: an existing line is cut at a tower and both cut ends are looped into a new substation, turning one line into two (or more) lines plus new "loop" towers. This is the single most disruptive event for tower identity, because ArcGIS handles it by **delete-and-recreate**, churning every `arcgis_object_id` on the affected corridor. See §1.3's note on why the system re-identifies survivors by coordinates. |

#### The organisational hierarchy

APTRANSCO's O&M (operations & maintenance) org is a strict four-level geography, and every GIS row
carries all four as plain text plus an optional FK (`Line`/`Tower` both have
`zone`/`circle`/`division`/`subdivision_name` + `subdivision` FK; see `line_inspection/models.py:99`
and `:172`):

| Level | Scope | Typical officer |
|---|---|---|
| **Zone** | Largest — a multi-district region. | CE / GM and above |
| **Circle** | A group of divisions. | SE (Superintending Engineer) |
| **Division** | A group of subdivisions. | EE / DE (Executive / Divisional Engineer) |
| **Subdivision** | Smallest O&M unit; owns a set of lines and their towers. Modelled as `Subdivision` (`line_inspection/models.py:29`) with `name` unique plus its `circle`/`division`/`zone`. | AEE / DEE / AE |

**Cadre** is the SAP-side term for an employee's grade/rank band. It arrives as `emp_sub_grp` on
`EmployeeCadreSnapshot`, synced from SAP, and the real observed codes are coarse: `AAE`/`AE` = AEE,
`ADE/AEE` = DEE, `DE/EE` = EE (one combined code, **not** two separate `DE` and `EE` values),
`SE`, and management = `CE`/`DIRECTOR`/`GM`/`JMD`/`CMD`. Because the codes are coarse, this project
deliberately makes the *viewing tier* functional rather than grade-based — `viewing.cadre_tier()`
returns `field_user` / `supervisor` / `admin`, and `emp_sub_grp` only drives display labels and the
management gate.

#### What an inspection physically is

Twice a year, an engineer (typically AEE/DEE cadre) physically walks or drives the length of an
assigned line and stops at every tower. There are two distinct cycles, and the code carries them
as `Inspection.inspection_type` (`line_inspection/models.py:60`):

| Cycle | Code value | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **Ground Patrolling** | `ground_patrol` | The routine, non-detailed patrol. Walk the line, look up, note anything obviously wrong — encroachment, a leaning tower, a broken insulator disc visible from the ground, missing danger boards, vegetation growing into the corridor. |
| **Pre-Monsoon Inspection (PMI)** | `pmi` | The detailed inspection done before the monsoon season, when storms, waterlogging and lightning make failures most likely and most expensive. Everything Ground Patrolling covers, done thoroughly, plus the items you only check when you intend to find problems: earthing, foundation/coping condition, anti-climbing devices, bolt tightness, paint, conductor and jumper condition, and so on. |

At each tower the engineer walks the checklist item by item, and for anything that is **not**
normal, records a defect, answers whatever follow-up questions that defect triggers ("how many
discs?", "which leg?", "what board type?"), assigns a severity, and — under the new system —
photographs it. The severity vocabulary is fixed at four levels plus a not-inspected sentinel
(`WORST_CHOICES`, `line_inspection/models.py:49`): `none` (never inspected) → `ok` → `minor` →
`major` → `critical`.

#### The paper register this replaces

The formal output of a patrol is the **line inspection register**: one large ruled sheet per line,
laid out as a matrix.

- **Columns** = every tower on that line, in walking order down the line.
- **Rows** = a metadata block (Date, Loc No, Tower type) followed by every checklist item, grouped
  by component category, ending with a free-text Remarks row.
- **Cells** = blank (not yet done) / `N/A` / `Not available` / `✓` (normal) / a defect name with
  its criticality. Positional items (an item that must be checked separately at, say, each of four
  legs or each phase) get one sub-cell per position.

The register is what a supervisor signs off and what an audit reads. It is *the* artefact, and the
software reproduces it exactly rather than inventing a new report format:
`line_inspection/register.py` builds the same matrix from `Inspection`/`ItemResult`/`DefectEntry`
rows, `dashboard_register.html` renders it for print, and `register_to_xlsx()` exports it. The
docstring is explicit that it "mirrors the physical field register". Two problems the paper version
had, which the digital one fixes: a tower with a VT circuit used to need its cells copied by hand
onto every circuit's register (now sourced automatically via `structure_key`), and defects
discovered on paper had no lifecycle — someone had to notice them and act. Now every recorded
defect **auto-raises a `DefectTicket`** with an open/closed state.

### 1.3 End to end: the happy path, narrated

The following is one complete round trip. File references point at where each step actually
happens.

**1. An Admin assigns work.** An Admin (an EE-cadre employee whose SAP position id has been granted
Admin rights) opens `/inspection/admin/assignments/` (`admin_views.role_assignments`). The screen
defaults its candidate list to the Admin's own reporting-hierarchy subordinates — SAP's
`REPORTING_MANAGER_ID` chain, cached in `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` — with a full-employee search as
fallback. The Admin grants the chosen field engineer either:

- a **`RoleAssignment`** — role `FIELD_INSPECTOR` over a whole `Subdivision` and/or a set of
  specific `Line`s (M2M), stamped with who assigned it; or
- a **`LineTowerAssignment`** — a *from-tower → to-tower stretch* of one line, picked from that
  line's tower schedule, for when two engineers share a long line. Membership is computed as the
  line's real towers whose `line_sequence` falls between the two boundary towers' sequences.
  Crucially the range stores the **boundary towers**, not raw sequence numbers, so re-running
  `build_tower_schedule` can never silently drift an assigned stretch.

**2. The engineer signs in on the phone.** The Flutter app's login screen
(`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/screens/line_inspection_login_screen.dart`) posts an
employee ID + password to `POST /inspection/api/auth/login/`. The backend verifies them against
APTRANSCO's legacy **checkCred** gateway — `services/checkcred_client.py`, an HTTP endpoint at
`<APTRANSCO_AUTH_URL>/checkCred` that the app calls with its *own* app-level HTTP Basic credentials
(distinct from the employee's password) — and on success mints a DB-backed, revocable
`MobileAuthToken`. The app stores it (`services/auth_store.dart`) and sends
`Authorization: Token <token>` on every subsequent request; a 401 means "session expired, re-login".

**3. The engineer downloads their area.** Before leaving signal, the engineer taps **Download my
area** on the Home tab. `services/offline/offline_download.dart` walks four phases —
`lines` → `towers` → `catalog` → `tiles` — pre-warming the local store with the lines and towers in
their jurisdiction, the current checklist catalog, and the map tiles covering them. Downloaded
tiles are **pinned**, i.e. excluded from the tile cache's 160 MB LRU eviction, so the area they
deliberately downloaded cannot be evicted by casual panning elsewhere.

**4. Standing at a tower.** In the field the Inspection tab
(`lib/screens/li_tabs/inspection_tab.dart`) takes a live GPS fix via `services/location_service.dart`
and lists the towers **within 50 m** as in-range, with everything else requiring an explicit
override.

**5. The GPS gate.** Presence is treated as the utmost criterion of a genuine field inspection —
you cannot patrol a line from the office. The radius is a single constant,
`PRESENCE_RADIUS_M = 50.0` (`line_inspection/models.py:73`), and the gate is enforced **twice**:
once in the app for UX, and again on the server, which never trusts a client-supplied distance. On
submit, `_create_inspection` recomputes the great-circle distance itself with
`_haversine_m(...)` against the tower's stored coordinates and stamps one of three flags
(`line_inspection/api/views.py:462-480`):

```python
gps_aware = lat is not None or lng is not None or bool(data.get('presence_flag'))
if gps_aware:
    if lat is not None and lng is not None and tower.latitude is not None and tower.longitude is not None:
        distance_m = _haversine_m(lat, lng, tower.latitude, tower.longitude)
    if lat is None or lng is None:            presence_flag = 'no_fix'
    elif distance_m is not None and distance_m <= PRESENCE_RADIUS_M:
        presence_flag = 'in_range'
    else:                                     presence_flag = 'out_of_range'
    if presence_flag != 'in_range' and not override_reason:
        raise ValidationError({'override_reason': '...presence is required.'})
```

`no_fix` and `out_of_range` are permitted — GPS genuinely fails under a 400 kV line, in a valley,
or in dense canopy — but only with a written `override_reason`, which is stored on the record and
therefore auditable. The legacy JSON create path, which sends no coordinates at all, is
deliberately exempt (`gps_aware` is False), so pre-Phase-4 clients keep working.

**6. Filling the data-driven checklist.** The questionnaire is **not hardcoded anywhere** — not in
Python, not in Dart. The app renders it from `GET /inspection/api/catalog/`: groups → items
(with positions, `pos_meta`, availability gating, `applicable_tower_types`) → defects (each with an
ordered `ask` chain) → follow-up questions (`choice` / `multichoice` / `number` / `text`) →
criticality rules. Those are exactly the `ChecklistItemGroup` / `ChecklistItem` / `Defect` /
`FollowUpQuestion` / `CriticalityRule` tables, first populated by
`manage.py seed_checklist_catalog` and editable thereafter through the Checklist Catalog admin
screen. The reason is stated plainly in `models.py:10`: the questionnaire "is not yet finalised and
will be revised after field engineers review the app" — putting it in code would mean an app
release per wording change. Every catalog edit bumps a singleton `CatalogVersion`, and each
`Inspection` records the `catalog_version` it was captured under, so a five-year-old record stays
interpretable against the catalog shape that produced it.

The UI is **exception-based**: every item starts at `normal` (or `na` / `not_provided`); the
inspector only touches the ones that are wrong.

**7. Marking a defect; criticality suggested.** Selecting a defect reveals its follow-up questions
one at a time. From the answers, the app suggests a criticality via
`lib/services/criticality_engine.dart`, which is a client-side mirror of the server's
`services/criticality.py`: the `CriticalityRule` rows for that defect are evaluated in priority
order, first match wins, falling back to `Defect.default_criticality`. The inspector may accept or
override it. **Both** values are sent — `suggested_criticality` and the inspector-confirmed
`criticality` — so the record shows what the rules said *and* what the human decided; the server
re-derives the suggestion itself rather than trusting the client's.

**8. The offline outbox.** Submitting does not require connectivity. The submission goes into a
durable, file-backed FIFO outbox (`lib/services/offline/outbox.dart`) with a retry cap of 8. The
`client_id` — a v4 UUID from `lib/utils/uuid.dart` — is generated once and **reused across every
retry** of the same inspection. A slim `SyncStatusBar` shows the queue depth and hides itself when
online and empty. Connectivity is judged not by the link layer but by an actual `GET /ping/`
(`lib/services/offline/connectivity_service.dart`), because a phone can be joined to corporate
Wi-Fi and still have no route to the backend.

**9. Sync.** When the backend is reachable, `lib/services/offline/sync_engine.dart` drains the
outbox. An inspection goes as `multipart/form-data` to `POST /inspection/api/line-inspections/`:
one text field **`payload`** holding the JSON, plus zero or more file parts named by each
`photo_key` (`photo_0`, `photo_1`, …):

```jsonc
// the `payload` text part
{ "tower_id": 1234, "inspector_employee_id": "01073093", "catalog_version": 17,
  "date": "2026-07-28", "remarks": "", "client_id": "9f8b7c6d-…",
  "inspector_lat": 16.51, "inspector_lng": 80.63, "gps_accuracy_m": 6.0,
  "presence_flag": "in_range", "override_reason": "",
  "items": [ { "item_id": 12, "position": "A", "status": "defect", "meta": {},
               "photo_key": "photo_0",
               "entries": [ { "defect_id": 41, "answers": {"discs": 3},
                              "criticality": "major", "suggested_criticality": "major",
                              "note": "", "photo_key": "photo_1" } ] } ] }
```

**10. The server writes it, atomically.** `_create_inspection` (`line_inspection/api/views.py:439`)
is the single core both the mobile multipart path and the legacy JSON path funnel through — it
resolves checklist items and defects by **numeric id OR slug key** precisely so one implementation
can serve both. In order it: rejects an unknown tower; rejects a **VT tower** with a message telling
you to inspect the real co-located one; enforces `jurisdiction.can_edit_tower`; applies the GPS
gate above; then inside one `transaction.atomic()` creates the `Inspection`, one `ItemResult` per
item (or per item+position), one `DefectEntry` per recorded defect, attaches any photos to the
respective `ImageField`s, rolls the worst criticality up onto `Inspection.worst_criticality`, and
**bulk-creates one `DefectTicket` per `DefectEntry`** with `status='open'` and
`source='human_inspection'`. Any unresolvable item or defect raises and the whole thing rolls back
— there is no half-saved inspection.

**11. Idempotency.** `Inspection.client_id` is unique and nullable. Replaying the same `client_id`
returns the existing record with **200**; a new one creates and returns **201**. This is what makes
the outbox safe: a timeout after the server already committed does not produce a duplicate
inspection or a duplicate ticket.

**12. The tower's status cache advances.** In the same transaction,
`status.bump_tower_cache(...)` updates the denormalized `Tower.last_inspection_at` /
`last_worst_criticality` / `last_inspection_type`. This exists purely for read performance: the map
and the rollups must colour and count on the order of 67 k towers, and a per-tower join back to
`Inspection` would not hold up. The cache is advanced only when a *newer* inspection lands, and it
is fully rebuildable from the source-of-truth `Inspection` table with
`manage.py warm_tower_status`.

**13. The ticket appears on a supervisor's dashboard.** The supervisor opens
`/inspection/dashboard/tickets/`. What they see is scoped by the **oversight** scope, not the
assignment scope — see the distinction in §1.2's glossary follow-on below. They can filter by
status, criticality, and `source` (`human_inspection` vs `drone_inspection`). The Map screen
(`/inspection/dashboard/map/`) shows their towers coloured by latest status; the Inspections screen
gives per-tower history, each inspection expandable into its item results, defect entries,
follow-up answers, notes and photos.

**14. The register and the rollups.** `/inspection/dashboard/register/` regenerates the per-line
register described in §1.2 — all towers as columns (real + VT, VT badged), checklist items as rows,
a Latest / Ground Patrolling / PMI cycle selector, Print, and an `.xlsx` download.
`/inspection/dashboard/reports/` gives management the zonal / circle / division rollups: inspected
vs pending, criticality breakdown, open tickets, human-vs-drone split.

**15. Ticket closure.** `POST /inspection/api/tickets/<id>/close/` closes a ticket. Closure is
allowed both for the assigned field User acting within their own jurisdiction **and** for any Admin
acting in oversight — the second half was a real bug found in Phase 2 verification, where checking
only the requester's own jurisdiction locked out the very Admins who had assigned that jurisdiction
to someone else.

#### Two scopes, kept deliberately apart

This distinction runs through the entire codebase and is worth stating before you read any view:

| | **Jurisdiction** (`line_inspection/jurisdiction.py`) | **Oversight** (`line_inspection/viewing.py`) |
|---|---|---|
| Question it answers | "What may this employee **edit / capture**?" | "What may this employee **see**?" |
| Source | The employee's own `RoleAssignment` + `LineTowerAssignment` rows only | The above, **unioned up the SAP reporting hierarchy** — every tower assigned to anyone beneath the viewer in the reporting tree |
| Key functions | `visible_lines()`, `visible_towers()`, `can_edit_tower()`, `range_tower_ids()` | `subordinate_snapshots()`, `oversight_lines()`, `oversight_towers()`, `cadre_tier()`, `is_management()`, `circuits_at()` |
| Used by | The REST write path (`_create_inspection`), ticket close as the assigned user | Every dashboard screen, the map API, the register, the rollups, mobile reads |
| Grants edit rights? | Yes | **Never.** A supervisor's wider view must not become a wider write. |

They are separate modules for exactly that reason, and `viewing.py`'s docstring says so outright.

### 1.4 Two live projects and one dead reference

| # | Path (relative to `transcoapps/`) | Status | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `.` — `manage.py`, `transcoapps/`, `line_inspection/` | **LIVE** | The Django 6.0 web app: REST API for the phone, custom admin panel, read-only oversight dashboard, all master-data syncs. This is the system of record. |
| 2 | `Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/` | **LIVE** | The Flutter field app (v1.1.0+2), re-homed in Phase 4 onto project #1's backend. Edited in place — it is not a fork or a copy. |
| 3 | `Aptransco_TIS-main/aptransco_backend/` | **DEAD — DO NOT USE** | The donor project's own Django backend. |

**On #3, unambiguously.** `Aptransco_TIS-main/aptransco_backend/` is a Django 5.2 + SQLite
backend that came bundled with the Flutter app when it was adopted. It contains *two* apps: a
legacy `inspections` app (flat SQLite table, free-text component/defect — the older
proof-of-concept), and a `line_inspection` app that is an **auth-less, `managed=False` DRF mirror**
of project #1's `clear`-schema tables. It exists in this checkout for one reason only: it documents
the exact HTTP contract the Flutter app was originally written against. **Nothing in the live
system imports it, runs it, migrates it or depends on it.** It has its own `manage.py`, its own
`settings.py`, its own `db.sqlite3` and its own `requirements.txt`, none of which are the live
ones. The project README states the rule directly (`line_inspection/README.md:536`): *"Do not reuse
the reference backend code or its legacy `inspections` app — it is the contract spec + client, not
a dependency."* Its sibling docs `Aptransco_TIS-main/README.md` and `Aptransco_TIS-main/project.md`
describe that donor system, not this one; treat them as historical. Detail on the donor is in
section 15.

**Serious footgun:** `Aptransco_TIS-main/aptransco_backend/line_inspection/` has the **same package
name** as the live app `line_inspection/`. A grep for a model or view name will hit both. Always
check which prefix a path carries before believing a search result.

### 1.5 Annotated directory tree

Root of everything is `C:/Users/Admin/Downloads/line_inspection-main/transcoapps/`. Paths in this
document are relative to that directory (where `Project.md` sits). Build artefacts

### 1.6 Technology stack

#### Project 1 — the web app (LIVE)

`requirements.txt` **does exist** at `requirements.txt` in the project root. It was added recently,
and its header names the exact install command. Any statement that the web app lacks a dependency
list is out of date. (`Aptransco_TIS-main/aptransco_backend/requirements.txt` is a *different*,
donor-project file and pins different versions — do not confuse them.) A virtualenv is also
provisioned at `.venv/` in Windows layout (`.venv/Scripts/python.exe`).

| Layer | Declared in `requirements.txt` | Actually installed in `.venv` | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python | — | **3.13.5** (CPython, MSC v.1943, 64-bit) | Runtime |
| Django | `Django>=6.0,<6.1` | **6.0.7** | `settings.py`'s generated header says "using Django 6.0.5" |
| DRF | `djangorestframework>=3.16` | **3.17.1** | `'rest_framework'` in `INSTALLED_APPS`; the whole `line_inspection/api/` package |
| DB driver | `psycopg[binary]>=3.2` | **3.3.4** (+ `psycopg-binary`) | `ENGINE = django.db.backends.postgresql` |
| Imaging | `Pillow>=11.0` | **12.3.0** | `ItemResult.photo` / `DefectEntry.photo` `ImageField`s |
| HTTP | `requests>=2.32` | **2.34.2** | Every client in `services/` — Keycloak, SAP, ArcGIS, checkCred |
| Excel | `openpyxl>=3.1` | **3.1.5** (+ `et_xmlfile`) | `register.py`'s `.xlsx` register export |
| Dataframes | `pandas>=2.2` | **3.0.5** (+ `numpy` 2.5.1, `python-dateutil`, `six`) | `import_sap_lines.py` reads the SAP Excel export |

Notable stack *choices*, not just versions:

- **Database: PostgreSQL, two aliases, one physical database.** `DATABASES['default']` and
  `DATABASES['line_inspection_db']` share identical credentials and differ only in
  `OPTIONS: {'options': '-c search_path=clear'}` (`transcoapps/settings.py:150-166`). Django's own
  tables (auth/admin/sessions/contenttypes) live in `public` on `default`; every `line_inspection`
  table lives in the `clear` schema and is routed there by `LineInspectionRouter`. The router also
  refuses to let any *other* app touch that alias, and blocks migrations in the wrong direction.
  **Consequence you will hit immediately:** migrations must name the database explicitly —
  `python manage.py migrate line_inspection --database=line_inspection_db`. A plain
  `migrate line_inspection` records the migration against `default` while the router skips the
  operations, so the `clear` schema silently never changes.
- **No `django.contrib.auth`, ever.** Identity is a bare SAP `employee_id` in `request.session`.
  Authorization is a bespoke three tiers: **Super Admin** (decides who is an Admin; bootstrapped by
  CLI because an empty permission table would lock everyone out) → **Admin** (EE cadre holding a
  position id granted in `FieldEECadrePosition`) → **User** (an employee with an active
  `RoleAssignment`).
- **No `django.contrib.admin`, ever.** The admin panel is hand-written server-rendered Django
  templates plus vanilla JS — no SPA, no build toolchain. `line_inspection/admin.py` is empty on
  purpose. (`django.contrib.admin` *is* still in `INSTALLED_APPS` and mounted at `/admin/` in
  `transcoapps/urls.py:23` — leftover project scaffolding, not used by this app.)
- **Front-end**: Django templates + vanilla JS + **Leaflet via CDN** for the maps. There is no
  npm, no bundler, no `package.json` anywhere in the web app.
- **Static/media**: `STATIC_ROOT` and `MEDIA_ROOT` point at `static/` and `media/` under the
  project root; **neither directory exists in this checkout yet** (`media/` is created on the first
  photo upload). `transcoapps/urls.py:37` serves `MEDIA_URL` from Django in development, with a
  comment saying production should front it with nginx instead.
- **Testing**: one test module, `line_inspection/tests/test_dashboard.py`. Its header warns that it
  **cannot run on SQLite** — the models are routed to the `line_inspection_db` Postgres connection
  and `status.py` uses Postgres `DISTINCT ON`, so a Postgres test database is required for that
  alias. Wiring that into CI is Phase 5 work.

### 1.7 Project status

Phases 1 through 4 are complete and were each verified end-to-end against the real `clear` schema
inside a rolled-back transaction (Phase 3: 31 checks; Phase 4: 43 checks; `flutter analyze` clean).
That covers the schema and syncs, the three-tier auth and admin panel, the SAP line import and
mapping, the REST API, the read-only oversight dashboard and register, and the mobile app with
login, GPS-gated capture and offline-first download/outbox/sync. **Phase 5 is open**: hardening,
a CI Postgres test database, drone-ticket ingestion (the `DefectTicket.source='drone_inspection'`
and `drone_metadata` fields are schema-only today — no ingestion pipeline exists), and
production-grade deployment settings. The full roadmap is section 15.

### 1.8 Path and naming traps

Four things will confuse you if nobody warns you.

1. **The wrapper directory.** In this checkout the tree is
   `C:/Users/Admin/Downloads/line_inspection-main/transcoapps/…` — that is, a wrapper folder named
   after the GitHub zip (`line_inspection-main`) containing the actual project root `transcoapps/`.
   There is **no** `line_inspection-main/line_inspection-main/` doubling in this checkout, despite
   descriptions elsewhere that mention one; verified by listing the parent, which contains only
   `.vscode/` and `transcoapps/`. If you are handed a path with a doubled segment, it is a stale
   reference to a differently-unzipped copy — the layout below `transcoapps/` is identical either
   way.
2. **`transcoapps/transcoapps/`.** Standard Django: the project root and the project *package* share
   a name. `transcoapps/settings.py` means the package; `transcoapps/` alone means the root.
3. **Two apps named `line_inspection`.** The live one at `line_inspection/`, and the dead donor
   mirror at `Aptransco_TIS-main/aptransco_backend/line_inspection/`. Always read the full path.
4. **The app is named for drones but is used by humans on foot.** `drone_inspection_app` is the
   donor's name, kept because Phase 4 edited the app in place rather than renaming/forking it.
   Everything in it today serves human ground patrolling and PMI; drone ingestion is Phase 5.

Also present at the project root and easy to mistake for something meaningful:
`Import-Module PSReadLine.txt`, a four-line PowerShell profile snippet someone saved into the repo
by accident. Nothing reads it.

### 1.9 Where the code and the README disagree

`line_inspection/README.md` is unusually good and mostly accurate, but it is documentation and the
code has moved. Every item below was checked against the source; **the code wins**.

| # | The README says | The code actually does | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | "None of these have hardcoded fallback secrets in code — they must be set in the environment" and, of `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET`, "Never hardcode … as a source default." (`line_inspection/README.md:352-356`) | `transcoapps/settings.py:217-220` hardcodes `KEYCLOAK_BASE_URL`, `KEYCLOAK_REALM`, `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID` **and a literal `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET`** with no `os.environ` lookup at all. The value is not reproduced here. | `transcoapps/settings.py:220` |
| 2 | (Nothing — the README's Login section describes checkCred as the only mechanism.) | A **local dev-login bypass** exists: `line_inspection/services/dev_login.py`, reached by a four-line delegation at the top of `checkcred_client.verify_credentials`. It skips checkCred entirely and signs in **any** `employee_id` present in `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` against one shared string. It is triple-gated — `settings.DEBUG` True **and** `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN == '1'` **and** a non-empty `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD` — logs a loud warning on first use, and `.env.local` currently has it **switched on** with the password `<set in .env.local>`. Not a production path, but it is live on this machine. | `line_inspection/services/dev_login.py:38`, `line_inspection/services/checkcred_client.py:49-53` |
| 3 | "Login: `/inspection/login/` -> redirects to Keycloak -> `/inspection/auth/callback/`" (`line_inspection/README.md:288`) | Stale — the same README corrects it 200 lines earlier. `auth.login_view` renders a real form and calls `checkcred_client.verify_credentials` directly; there is no `callback_view` and no `auth/callback/` route in `line_inspection/urls.py`. | `line_inspection/auth.py:27-41` |

Host/credentials come from `PG_NAME`/`PG_USER`/`PG_PASSWORD`/`PG_HOST`/`PG_PORT`, all optional and all defaulted. | `transcoapps/settings.py:152-156` |
| 6 | Identity is "resolved via Keycloak" (`line_inspection/README.md:33`, `models.py:14`, `jurisdiction.py:3`) | Keycloak is **dormant**. Web sessions come from checkCred (or the dev bypass); the phone uses a checkCred-issued `MobileAuthToken`. `KeycloakBearerAuthentication` is still registered third in `AUTH_CLASSES` but nothing issues it a token. The stale phrasing survives in several docstrings. | `line_inspection/api/views.py:43`, `line_inspection/auth.py:1-9` |
| 7 | The "App structure" tree lists neither `services/dev_login.py` nor the Phase 4 `MobileAuthToken` / `MobileTokenAuthentication` (`line_inspection/README.md:99-167`) | Both exist. `MobileAuthToken` is `models.py:700`; `MobileTokenAuthentication` is first in `AUTH_CLASSES` so a bad/revoked/expired token returns 401 rather than 403. The Changelog *does* describe them — only the structure tree is stale. | `line_inspection/models.py:700`, `line_inspection/api/authentication.py` |

Several docstrings still cite them as the source of the checklist and colour palette; treat those citations as historical. | `transcoapps/settings.py:87-93` |

Two further security findings in tracked source, reported without reproducing the values:

- `transcoapps/settings.py:44` — the Django `SECRET_KEY` is the literal
  `django-insecure-…` value generated by `startproject`, committed as-is, with `DEBUG = True` on
  line 47.
- `transcoapps/settings.py:154` — `PG_PASSWORD` has a hardcoded non-empty **fallback** password
  baked into the source as the `os.environ.get` default, so an unset environment silently uses it.

Environment variables read by the web app, with their purposes (values deliberately not
reproduced — real credentials live in `.env.local`, which is gitignored and must never be
committed):

| Variable | Read by | Purpose / default |
|---|---|---|
| `PG_NAME` / `PG_USER` / `PG_PASSWORD` / `PG_HOST` / `PG_PORT` | `transcoapps/settings.py:152` | Postgres connection for **both** aliases. All defaulted in source; see the finding above about the password default. |
| `EXTRA_ALLOWED_HOSTS` | `transcoapps/settings.py:65` | Comma-separated extra hostnames appended to `ALLOWED_HOSTS`, so a developer can add their current Wi-Fi IP for a phone on the same LAN without editing tracked source. Currently set to a private LAN address in `.env.local`. |
| `APTRANSCO_AUTH_URL` | `line_inspection/services/checkcred_client.py:14` | Base of the checkCred gateway; defaults to `https://qaserv.aptransco.co.in/qath`. `checkCred` / `forgotPass` / `savePass` hang off it. |
| `APTRANSCO_AUTH_USER` / `APTRANSCO_AUTH_PASS` | `line_inspection/services/checkcred_client.py:20` | The **gateway's own** HTTP Basic credentials, not any employee's. Empty in `.env.local` today, so every real login fails early with *"APTRANSCO_AUTH_USER / APTRANSCO_AUTH_PASS are not configured."* — which is precisely why the dev bypass was added. |
| `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN` | `line_inspection/services/dev_login.py:32` | `'1'` enables the checkCred bypass. Any other value (or unset) disables it. |
| `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD` | `line_inspection/services/dev_login.py:33` | The single shared string every dev login is compared against with `hmac.compare_digest`. `<set in .env.local>`. |
| `ARCGIS_USERNAME` / `ARCGIS_PASSWORD` | `line_inspection/services/arcgis_client.py` | ArcGIS portal credentials used by `sync_gis_towers`. |
| `SAP_RFC_BASE_URL` / `SAP_RFC_USER` / `SAP_RFC_PASSWORD` | `line_inspection/services/sap_client.py` | The SAP RFC adapter serving `ZHR_GET_EMP_CADER_DETAILS`. Base URL defaults to the HEC production adapter. |
| `SAP_HIERARCHY_ROOT_EMPLOYEE_ID` | `line_inspection/services/sap_client.py` | Employee id whose full reporting subtree is fetched (the org-tree root, e.g. CMD). Overridable per run with `--root-employee-id`. |
| `KEYCLOAK_BASE_URL` / `KEYCLOAK_REALM` / `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID` / `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET` | `line_inspection/services/keycloak_client.py` | Dormant. Realm is case-sensitive and is `APTRANSCO-EMP`. See finding #1 — these are hardcoded in `settings.py` rather than read from the environment. |

`.env.local` is loaded by `_load_local_env()` at the very top of `transcoapps/settings.py:20-39`,
before anything else runs. The rationale in its own docstring is worth repeating, because it
explains an unusual choice: it uses `os.environ.setdefault` from inside `settings.py` — rather than
a shell script you dot-source — precisely so the variables apply *however* the server is started,
whether from an integrated terminal, a fresh terminal that never sourced anything, an IDE Run
button, or a task runner. Real environment variables always win over the file.
## 2. Architecture, Ground Rules & Configuration

The web app is a single-app Django 6.0 project. The project package is `transcoapps/`
(`settings.py`, `urls.py`, `wsgi.py`, `asgi.py`) and the only installed first-party app is
`line_inspection/`. There is no service layer beyond `line_inspection/services/`, no Celery, no
Redis, no channels — everything is synchronous request/response plus a handful of
`manage.py` commands. What makes this project unusual is not its shape but its **constraints**:
it is a tenant inside somebody else's Postgres database, inside somebody else's Django project,
and it is forbidden from using two of Django's most-used contrib apps. Those constraints are
written down as ground rules and they explain nearly every structural decision below.

### 2.1 The four ground rules

`line_inspection/README.md:19` opens with a section headed *"Ground rules (do not violate these
without re-confirming with the user)"*. Four of them are architectural; the rest (ArcGIS as the
only master-data source, DB-backed checklist, SAP↔ArcGIS mapping as an ongoing effort) are
domain rules covered elsewhere in this document. Each rule is stated below with its **actual
enforcement mechanism in code**, and whether the code honours it.

#### Rule 1 — only the `clear` Postgres schema is touched

> *"Only the `clear` schema on the shared Postgres server (`10.96.76.172`) is read or written by
> this app. No other schema there (`telecom_cps`, `lines`, `gismaps`, `keycloak`, etc.) is
> touched."* — `line_inspection/README.md:21`

APTRANSCO runs one shared Postgres instance carrying several unrelated departmental datasets,
each in its own schema. `clear` is the schema allotted to this platform. Reading a neighbouring
schema would create an undeclared coupling to a dataset this team does not own and cannot
version; writing to one could corrupt another department's data.

**Enforcement** is a combination of three things, none of which is a database GRANT:

1. `transcoapps/settings.py:162` defines a second connection alias, `line_inspection_db`, whose
   only difference from `default` is `OPTIONS: {'options': '-c search_path=clear'}`. Because the
   `search_path` is set to exactly one schema (not `clear,public`), an unqualified table name on
   that connection can only ever resolve inside `clear`. A typo referencing a `public` table
   fails loudly instead of silently reading the wrong data.
2. `line_inspection/db_router.py` sends every `line_inspection` model to that alias and nothing
   else to it (see §2.3).
3. Every model in `line_inspection/models.py` is Django-managed with `db_table` names local to
   the app — there are no `managed=False` models pointing at `lines.infom`, `towr_master`, or
   `cond_master`. The README (`:42`) calls those legacy tables *"explicitly out of scope"*.

**Verified.** A grep of the app for other schema names finds nothing. The one caveat: the
enforcement is *by convention plus search_path*, not by database permissions — a developer who
writes `Model.objects.using('default')` or raw SQL with a schema-qualified name would bypass it
entirely. Nothing in the repo does.

> **Discrepancy (README vs. runtime config).** The README names the shared server as
> `10.96.76.172`, but `transcoapps/settings.py:155` defaults `PG_HOST` to `localhost` and
> `.env.local` leaves `PG_HOST` commented out. In this checkout the app therefore talks to a
> **local** Postgres holding a copy of the `clear` schema, not the shared server. The README's
> IP documents the production target, not the current default.

#### Rule 2 — no runtime dependency on any sibling app

> *"`line_inspection` must not depend on any other app in this Django project at runtime — not
> `gisapp`, not `gisdata`, nothing. Some server deployments won't even have those apps installed.
> Where gisapp already had working code we wanted (ArcGIS client, Keycloak OIDC flow), we
> **copied** it into `line_inspection/services/` rather than importing it — some duplication is
> the accepted tradeoff for deployment independence. If you fix a bug in
> `gisapp/arcgis_client.py`, port the fix by hand into `line_inspection/services/arcgis_client.py`
> too (and vice versa for Keycloak logic in `gisapp/views.py`)."* — `line_inspection/README.md:24`

The rationale is deployment topology, not purity. `transcoapps` is a multi-app corporate Django
project (`contacts`, `image_inventory`, `gisdata`, `gisapp`, `vendor`, `scada_data`,
`organisation_chart`). Different servers install different subsets. If `line_inspection` imported
`gisapp.arcgis_client`, then every host running the inspection platform would also have to carry
`gisapp` and all of `gisapp`'s own dependencies and settings. Copying ~400 lines of HTTP client
is cheaper than that coupling.

The **cost** is explicit and accepted: three copied modules must be kept in sync **by hand**.
This is a standing maintenance obligation, and it is the single most likely source of future
"why does the map work in gisapp but not here" bugs.

| Copied module | Donor | What it does | Sync obligation |
|---|---|---|---|
| `line_inspection/services/arcgis_client.py` | `gisapp/arcgis_client.py` | ArcGIS Portal token acquisition + cached token + paged feature queries | Port fixes by hand, both directions. Header says so at `:1-7` |
| `line_inspection/services/keycloak_client.py` | `gisapp/views.py` OIDC flow | Keycloak authorize URL / code exchange / refresh / userinfo, rewritten as plain functions returning dicts instead of DRF `Response`s, because both `auth.py` (plain Django) and the DRF bearer authenticator use it | Port fixes by hand. Header at `:1-8` |
| `line_inspection/services/checkcred_client.py` | the same service `gisapp/views.py::login_proxy` calls | checkCred / forgotPass / savePass gateway client | Fresh reimplementation, not a literal copy. Header at `:1-10` |
| `line_inspection/services/sap_client.py` | conceptually `contacts` | SAP `ZHR_GET_EMP_CADER_DETAILS` RFC client | Header at `:1-7` explicitly refuses to import from `contacts/models.py`, arguing those helpers belong to the org-chart feature and are not shared infrastructure |

**Verified.** No module under `line_inspection/` imports from any other app package. The sibling
apps are not even installed in this checkout — `INSTALLED_APPS` has them commented out
(`transcoapps/settings.py:87-93`) with the note `# not part of this checkout`, and
`transcoapps/urls.py:24-30` has their URL includes commented out the same way. The rule is
therefore load-bearing right now: if any import existed, the project would not boot.

#### Rule 3 — never `django.contrib.auth`

> *"No `django.contrib.auth`, ever. Identity is a bare SAP `employee_id` resolved via Keycloak,
> stored directly in Django's session framework (`request.session` — independent of
> `contrib.auth`). Authorization is our own three-tier model (see below), not Django
> permissions/groups."* — `line_inspection/README.md:33`

The reason: APTRANSCO employees already exist in SAP and in the corporate identity provider.
There is no local user table, no local password to manage, no signup. Creating shadow
`auth.User` rows would immediately raise "which one is authoritative?" and would tempt someone
to store a password hash for an employee whose password lives in SAP. So the app stores exactly
one thing in the session — the 8-digit zero-padded SAP `employee_id` — and derives every
authorization decision from `clear`-schema tables keyed on that id.

**Enforcement / verification at the app level:**

- `line_inspection/auth.py:36` — login is literally `request.session['employee_id'] = ...`.
  `django.contrib.sessions` is used; `django.contrib.auth` is not. The two are independent
  frameworks; sessions do not require auth.
- `line_inspection/auth.py:95-122` — the app ships its own `@login_required`,
  `@admin_required`, `@super_admin_required` decorators. The name `login_required` deliberately
  shadows Django's, so a careless `from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required`
  would be an obvious diff.
- `line_inspection/api/authentication.py:15-23` — DRF needs a `request.user` with
  `.is_authenticated`, so the app supplies a 4-line `SimpleIdentity` stand-in carrying
  `employee_id` and `pk`. All three DRF authenticators return it.
- No model in `line_inspection/models.py` has a FK to `settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL`; ownership is
  recorded as a plain `employee_id` `CharField` everywhere (`RoleAssignment.employee_id`,
  `SuperAdmin.employee_id`, `Inspection.inspector_employee_id`, …).

**Verified for the app. Not true of the project.** See §2.2.

#### Rule 4 — never `django.contrib.admin`

> *"No `django.contrib.admin`, ever. The custom admin panel (`auth.py` + `admin_views.py` +
> templates) is server-rendered Django templates + vanilla JS, matching this project's existing
> style (`contacts`/`gisapp`/`gisdata`) — no new frontend toolchain. The Phase 3 field-engineer
> dashboard will be built the same way."* — `line_inspection/README.md:37`

Two reasons, one technical and one organisational. Technical: `django.contrib.admin`'s
permission system is built on `auth.User`/`auth.Permission`, which Rule 3 forbids — you cannot
gate a `ModelAdmin` on "is this employee_id a Super Admin?" without fighting the framework.
Organisational: the surrounding project is all server-rendered templates plus vanilla JS, and
introducing React/Vue/a build step for one app would be a toolchain nobody else on the team
maintains.

**Enforcement** is by omission, plus one deliberately-empty file. `line_inspection/admin.py` in
its entirety:

```python
from django.contrib import admin

# Register your models here.
```

That is the untouched `startapp` stub. It is kept (rather than deleted) so that the absence of
registrations is *visible* — the README calls it out at `:132` as **"Deliberately empty — no
django-admin usage."** No `admin.site.register(...)` and no `@admin.register` decorator exists
anywhere under `line_inspection/`.

The replacement is the custom panel at `/inspection/admin/…` (`line_inspection/admin_views.py`,
20 KB of plain function views) and the read-only dashboard at `/inspection/dashboard/…`
(`line_inspection/dashboard_views.py`). **Verified.**

### 2.2 The apparent contradiction: contrib.auth and contrib.admin *are* installed

A reader who greps `settings.py` after reading the ground rules will immediately think the rules
are broken. They are not — but the situation needs precision.

`transcoapps/settings.py:79-94`:

```python
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    'django.contrib.admin',
    'django.contrib.auth',
    'django.contrib.contenttypes',
    'django.contrib.sessions',
    'django.contrib.messages',
    'django.contrib.staticfiles',
    'rest_framework',
    'line_inspection',
]
```

and `transcoapps/urls.py:23`: `path('admin/', admin.site.urls)`.

What this actually means:

| Observation | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| `django.contrib.auth` is in `INSTALLED_APPS` | Its **tables** (`auth_user`, `auth_group`, `auth_permission`) exist on the `default` connection, i.e. in the **`public`** schema. The router (§2.3) guarantees they can never be created in `clear`. `line_inspection` never imports, queries, or FK-references any of them. |
| `AuthenticationMiddleware` is in `MIDDLEWARE` (`:103`) | It sets `request.user` to `AnonymousUser` on every request (there are no `auth_user` rows to log in as). `line_inspection` views ignore `request.user` entirely and read `request.session['employee_id']` instead. |
| `django.contrib.auth.context_processors.auth` is a template context processor (`:118`) | It injects `user`/`perms` into templates. `line_inspection/templates/line_inspection/base.html` never references them — it branches on `session_employee_id` / `is_admin` / `is_super_admin` from the app's own context processor (§2.4). |
| `django.contrib.admin` is installed and `/admin/` is routed | Django's admin site is reachable, but it can only administer models registered with it. Since `line_inspection/admin.py` registers nothing, `/admin/` exposes only `auth` and (if any) other contrib models — and logging in requires an `auth_user` superuser that this app never creates. The inspection platform's data is **not** reachable from `/admin/`. |
| `AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS` is present (`:172-185`) | Pure `startproject` boilerplate. Nothing in this project ever calls `validate_password`, because no password is ever stored locally. Dead configuration. |

The honest one-line summary: **`django.contrib.auth`/`admin` are installed because
`django-admin startproject` put them there and because `contrib.admin` hard-depends on
`contrib.auth`, `contenttypes`, `sessions` and `messages`; the `line_inspection` app itself uses
none of them, and the router keeps their tables out of the `clear` schema.** The ground rules are
about the *app*, not the *project*.

This is nonetheless a real (if low-severity) loose end. Routing `/admin/` at all is unnecessary
surface area for an app that has nothing to administer there. Removing `path('admin/',
admin.site.urls)` and `'django.contrib.admin'` from `INSTALLED_APPS` would be safe today;
`contrib.auth` must stay only because `contrib.admin`'s and `messages`' machinery reference it,
and because `AuthenticationMiddleware`/the auth context processor are still wired in.

`django.contrib.sessions` is the one contrib app the platform genuinely **depends on** — it is
the storage for `request.session['employee_id']`. Note the consequence: **the session table
`django_session` lives in `public`, not in `clear`.** Web-panel login state is therefore stored
outside the app's own schema. That is unavoidable given the design and is not a rule violation
(the rule constrains what *this app's models* touch), but it is worth knowing when someone asks
"why do I need `migrate` on `default` too?"

### 2.3 Dual database / dual schema

#### The two aliases

```python
_POSTGRES = {
    'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.postgresql',
    'NAME': os.environ.get('PG_NAME', 'aptransco_ai_db'),
    'USER': os.environ.get('PG_USER', 'postgres'),
    'PASSWORD': os.environ.get('PG_PASSWORD', 'subhash'),
    'HOST': os.environ.get('PG_HOST', 'localhost'),
    'PORT': os.environ.get('PG_PORT', '5432'),
}

DATABASES = {
    'default': {**_POSTGRES},
    # The alias must stay in sync with line_inspection.db_router.DB_ALIAS.
    'line_inspection_db': {
        **_POSTGRES,
        'OPTIONS': {'options': '-c search_path=clear'},
    },
}
```
— `transcoapps/settings.py:150-166`

**Both aliases point at the same physical Postgres database** (`aptransco_ai_db` on the same
host, port, user and password). They are not two databases; they are two *connections* with two
different `search_path` settings:

| Alias | `search_path` | Resolves unqualified tables in | Holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| `default` | Postgres default for the role (typically `"$user", public`) | `public` | `django_migrations`, `django_session`, `django_content_type`, `auth_*`, `django_admin_log` |
| `line_inspection_db` | `clear` (only) | `clear` | Every `line_inspection` table: towers, lines, subdivisions, substations, the checklist catalog, cadre snapshots, role assignments, inspections, tickets, LILO lineage, mobile auth tokens |

The `-c search_path=clear` is passed through libpq's `options` parameter, so it is applied by the
server at connection setup — every statement on that connection, including Django's introspection
and `CREATE TABLE`, resolves against `clear` and nothing else.

Why two connections rather than schema-qualified `db_table` names (`'clear"."tower'`)? Because
schema-qualifying `db_table` is fragile (Django quotes it inconsistently across backends and
introspection breaks), while `search_path` is a first-class Postgres feature that also gives you
the *negative* guarantee: on that connection, `public` is not even on the path, so an accidental
reference to a `public` table raises `relation does not exist` instead of silently succeeding.

Note the two `DATABASES` aliases that used to exist and are gone: `employee_login_db` and
`image_inventory_db`, dropped along with the `contacts` / `image_inventory` apps
(`transcoapps/settings.py:146-148`).

#### The router

`transcoapps/settings.py:96` — `DATABASE_ROUTERS = ['line_inspection.db_router.LineInspectionRouter']`.

`line_inspection/db_router.py` in full (31 lines):

```python
"""Routes every line_inspection model to its own connection/schema
(line_inspection_db -> the `clear` schema on the shared Postgres server) and
keeps every other app off that connection."""

APP_LABEL = 'line_inspection'
DB_ALIAS = 'line_inspection_db'


class LineInspectionRouter:
    def db_for_read(self, model, **hints):
        if model._meta.app_label == APP_LABEL:
            return DB_ALIAS
        return None

    def db_for_write(self, model, **hints):
        if model._meta.app_label == APP_LABEL:
            return DB_ALIAS
        return None

    def allow_relation(self, obj1, obj2, **hints):
        labels = {obj1._meta.app_label, obj2._meta.app_label}
        if APP_LABEL in labels:
            return labels == {APP_LABEL}
        return None

    def allow_migrate(self, db, app_label, model_name=None, **hints):
        if app_label == APP_LABEL:
            return db == DB_ALIAS
        if db == DB_ALIAS:
            return False
        return None
```

| Method | Behaviour | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `db_for_read(model)` | `'line_inspection_db'` for this app's models, `None` otherwise | `None` means "no opinion" — Django falls through to the next router, then to `default`. So contrib apps keep using `default`/`public` with zero configuration. |
| `db_for_write(model)` | identical to `db_for_read` | Reads and writes must not diverge, or you would read a row from `clear` and write it back into `public`. |
| `allow_relation(obj1, obj2)` | If **either** object is a `line_inspection` model, the relation is allowed **only if both are** (`labels == {APP_LABEL}`). If neither is, `None` (no opinion). | The **isolation rule.** It makes a cross-schema relation — e.g. `Inspection.inspector = <auth.User>` — a hard error at the ORM level rather than a runtime SQL failure or, worse, a silently unenforced FK. This is the mechanical backstop for Rule 3: you *cannot* accidentally FK an inspection to a Django user. Note the check is on app labels, not connections, so it also blocks a relation to a future third app even if that app were somehow on the same alias. |
| `allow_migrate(db, app_label)` | `line_inspection` migrations run **only** on `line_inspection_db`; **no** other app's migrations may run on `line_inspection_db`; everything else is `None` (allowed by default). | Two-way fence. The first clause stops `clear` tables being created in `public`. The second clause is the important one: it guarantees `auth_user`, `django_session`, `django_content_type` etc. can **never** be created inside the `clear` schema, which would pollute a schema this team shares with other departments. |

#### The operational consequence you must not get wrong

Because `allow_migrate` returns `False` for `('default', 'line_inspection')`, running migrations
without naming the alias **appears to succeed and does nothing**:

```bash
# WRONG — records the migration in django_migrations on `default`,
# but the router skips every operation, so `clear` never changes.
python manage.py migrate line_inspection

# RIGHT — the only command that actually alters the `clear` schema.
python manage.py migrate line_inspection --database=line_inspection_db
```

`line_inspection/README.md:396-401` states this warning as a blockquote. The failure mode is
nasty: `django_migrations` on `default` now claims migration `0009` is applied, so a subsequent
correct run against `line_inspection_db`… still works (that alias has its own
`django_migrations` row set — but in `clear`, since the whole connection is scoped there), while
the bogus rows on `default` linger forever and confuse anyone auditing migration state.

> **Discrepancy (README wrong on a detail).** `line_inspection/README.md:399-401` says a plain
> `migrate line_inspection` *"records the migration against the default (sqlite) connection"*.
> The `default` connection is **not** sqlite — `transcoapps/settings.py:160` makes it the same
> PostgreSQL server as `line_inspection_db`, differing only in `search_path`. "sqlite" is a
> leftover from the donor project (`Aptransco_TIS-main/aptransco_backend`, whose `default` really
> is sqlite — see its `settings.py:118-131`, which uses `clear_db` /
> `search_path=clear,public` / `ClearDbRouter`). The *behaviour* the README warns about is
> correct; only the named backend is wrong.

A full first-time setup therefore needs **both**:

```bash
python manage.py migrate                                            # public: sessions, contenttypes, auth, admin
python manage.py migrate line_inspection --database=line_inspection_db   # clear: the platform
```

Migration files present in this checkout: `line_inspection/migrations/0001_initial.py` through
`0008_inspection_gps_accuracy_m_inspection_gps_distance_m_and_more.py` (eight, all additive after
`0001`).

The same reasoning applies to the tests. `line_inspection/tests/test_dashboard.py:4-11` records
that the suite needs a **Postgres** test database for the `line_inspection_db` alias (the status
helper uses Postgres `DISTINCT ON`), and that its `TestCase.databases` attribute must list both
connections so Django wraps transactions on each.

### 2.4 Request lifecycle

#### Entry points

`manage.py:9`, `transcoapps/wsgi.py:14` and `transcoapps/asgi.py:14` all
`os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'transcoapps.settings')`. `WSGI_APPLICATION =
'transcoapps.wsgi.application'` (`transcoapps/settings.py:126`). There is no ASGI-specific
configuration or async view in the app; `asgi.py` is the untouched stub.

#### Middleware

`transcoapps/settings.py:98-106` — stock `startproject` list, unmodified, no custom middleware:

| # | Middleware | Effect here |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware` | Security headers. With `DEBUG=True` and no `SECURE_*` settings configured, most of its protections (HSTS, SSL redirect) are inert. |
| 2 | `django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware` | **Load-bearing.** Provides `request.session`, which is the entire identity mechanism for the web panel. |
| 3 | `django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware` | `APPEND_SLASH` etc. Relevant because every URL in this project is declared with a trailing slash. |
| 4 | `django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware` | Protects the admin-panel and dashboard POST forms. Interacts with `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` for the ngrok origin. DRF endpoints called with a `Token`/`Bearer` header are CSRF-exempt by DRF's own rules; DRF's `SessionAuthentication` would enforce CSRF, but this app uses a custom `SessionEmployeeAuthentication` that does **not** (see §2.2 note and the API section). |
| 5 | `django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware` | Sets `request.user = AnonymousUser`. Ignored by every `line_inspection` view. Required by `contrib.admin`. |
| 6 | `django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware` | The Django messages framework, used by the custom admin-panel views for "saved"/"error" flashes. |
| 7 | `django.middleware.clickjacking.XFrameOptionsMiddleware` | `X-Frame-Options: DENY`. |

`ROOT_URLCONF = 'transcoapps.urls'` (`transcoapps/settings.py:108`).

#### The URL tree

```
transcoapps/urls.py                        (ROOT_URLCONF)
├── /admin/                                → django.contrib.admin.site.urls
│                                            (Django's own admin; registers NO line_inspection models)
├── /inspection/                           → include('line_inspection.urls')   [app_name='line_inspection']
│   ├── login/  forgot-password/  change-password/  logout/      → line_inspection/auth.py
│   ├── admin/                                                   → line_inspection/admin_views.py
│   │   ├── super/positions/[lookup/<position_id>/]
│   │   ├── assignments/[new/<employee_id>/]
│   │   ├── line/<line_id>/schedule/                (JSON)
│   │   ├── checklist/  + group|item|defect|followup|rule  new/<pk>/
│   │   ├── checklist/delete/<model_name>/<pk>/
│   │   ├── sap-mapping/
│   │   └── lilo/[<pk>/]
│   ├── dashboard/                                               → line_inspection/dashboard_views.py
│   │   ├── map/  tickets/  inspections/  register/  reports/
│   └── api/                                                     → include('line_inspection.api.urls')
│       └── (see table below)
└── /media/<path>                          → django.views.static.serve (DEBUG only)
```

Full prefix map:

| Prefix | Declared in | Handled by | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/admin/…` | `transcoapps/urls.py:23` | `django.contrib.admin` | **Not** the app's admin panel. Easy to confuse with the next row. |
| `/inspection/admin/…` | `line_inspection/urls.py:16-41` | `admin_views.py` | The app's *custom* admin panel. |
| `/inspection/dashboard/…` | `line_inspection/urls.py:44-48` | `dashboard_views.py` | Phase 3 read-only oversight dashboard. |
| `/inspection/api/…` | `line_inspection/urls.py:51` → `line_inspection/api/urls.py` | DRF class-based views | The mobile + browser JSON API. |
| `/inspection/login/`, `/logout/`, `/forgot-password/`, `/change-password/` | `line_inspection/urls.py:10-13` | `auth.py` | Session login; pre-login templates do not extend `base.html`. |
| `/media/…` | `transcoapps/urls.py:37` | `django.views.static.serve` | Dev only — see §2.5 on `MEDIA_URL`. |
| `/static/…` | implicit (`staticfiles` app, DEBUG) | `staticfiles` | `STATICFILES_DIRS` is empty (all entries commented out); app-level `static/` dirs still work via `APP_DIRS`-style discovery. |

The `line_inspection` URLconf sets `app_name = 'line_inspection'`
(`line_inspection/urls.py:5`), so every reverse is namespaced:
`reverse('line_inspection:admin-home')`, `{% url 'line_inspection:dashboard-map' %}`, etc. The
API URLconf (`line_inspection/api/urls.py`) is included *inside* that namespace, so its names are
also `line_inspection:api-catalog` and so on.

API routes, for completeness (`line_inspection/api/urls.py`, all under `/inspection/api/`):

| Path | View | Path | View |
|---|---|---|---|
| `health/` | `HealthView` | `map/lines/` | `MapLineListView` |
| `ping/` | `PingView` | `map/towers/` | `MapTowerListView` |
| `auth/login/` | `MobileLoginView` | `line-inspections/` | `LineInspectionSubmitView` |
| `auth/logout/` | `MobileLogoutView` | `line-inspections/list/` | `MobileInspectionListView` |
| `auth/me/` | `MobileMeView` | `line-inspections/<pk>/` | `MobileInspectionDetailView` |
| `auth/keycloak/exchange/` | `KeycloakExchangeView` | `inspections/` | `InspectionListView` |
| `auth/keycloak/refresh/` | `KeycloakRefreshView` | `inspections/create/` | `InspectionCreateView` |
| `catalog/` | `CatalogView` | `tickets/` | `DefectTicketListView` |
| `subdivisions/` | `SubdivisionListView` | `tickets/<pk>/close/` | `DefectTicketCloseView` |
| `lines/` | `LineListView` | `support-requests/` | `SupportRequestListCreateView` |
| `lines/<line_id>/towers/` | `LineTowerListView` | `support-requests/<pk>/resolve/` | `SupportRequestResolveView` |
| `towers/` | `TowerListView` | `dashboard/` | `MobileDashboardView` |
| `towers/<pk>/` | `TowerDetailView` | | |

Ordering note worth preserving: `line-inspections/list/` is declared **before**
`line-inspections/<int:pk>/` (`line_inspection/api/urls.py:32-33`) so the literal segment wins;
the comment at `:29-30` says so explicitly. (In practice `<int:pk>` would not match `list`
anyway, but the ordering documents intent.)

**No `REST_FRAMEWORK` settings dict exists in `settings.py`.** DRF therefore runs on its stock
defaults — which would be `SessionAuthentication` + `BasicAuthentication` and `AllowAny`. That
would be a security hole, except that **every** API view sets both attributes explicitly:
`line_inspection/api/views.py:43` defines
`AUTH_CLASSES = [MobileTokenAuthentication, SessionEmployeeAuthentication, KeycloakBearerAuthentication]`
and each view sets `authentication_classes = AUTH_CLASSES` + `permission_classes =
[IsAuthenticated]`, except the three deliberately-public ones (`HealthView`, `PingView`,
`MobileLoginView`) which set `authentication_classes = []` + `permission_classes = [AllowAny]`.
This works, but it is *opt-in security*: a new view added without those two lines silently
inherits DRF's permissive defaults. Adding an explicit `REST_FRAMEWORK` block with
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES = ['rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated']` would make the safe
case the default. **(Finding, Medium — see §2.7.)**

### 2.5 Template context processor

`transcoapps/settings.py:110-124` registers four context processors; the fourth,
`'line_inspection.context_processors.identity'`, is the app's own. It is registered globally
(rather than passed per-view) because *every* template in the app's `base.html` chrome — the
header, the nav tabs, the admin-only links — needs the current identity, and threading it through
20-odd views by hand would be pure boilerplate.

`line_inspection/context_processors.py` in full:

```python
from .auth import is_admin, is_super_admin
from . import viewing


def identity(request):
    employee_id = request.session.get('employee_id')
    if not employee_id:
        return {}
    return {
        'session_employee_id': employee_id,
        'session_display_name': request.session.get('display_name', employee_id),
        'is_admin': is_admin(employee_id),
        'is_super_admin': is_super_admin(employee_id),
        # Drives the Reports tab + all-tower rollup scope. Cheap (one indexed
        # snapshot lookup); the heavier tier/subtree walk stays in the views.
        'is_management': viewing.is_management(employee_id),
        'cadre_label': viewing.display_label(employee_id),
    }
```

| Key | Type | Source | Consumed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `session_employee_id` | `str` (8-digit zero-padded SAP id) | `request.session` | `base.html:51,56` — gates the whole logged-in chrome |
| `session_display_name` | `str`, falls back to the id | `request.session`, set at login from checkCred's `CNAME`/`NAME1` | `base.html:52` |
| `is_admin` | `bool` | `auth.is_admin()` — Super Admin, or an `EmployeeCadreSnapshot.position_id` present in `FieldEECadrePosition` | `base.html:63` (Reports tab) and admin-only nav |
| `is_super_admin` | `bool` | `auth.is_super_admin()` — a `SuperAdmin` row exists | `base.html:69,70` (Manage Admins, LILO links) |
| `is_management` | `bool` | `viewing.is_management()` — cadre `emp_sub_grp` in `{CE, DIRECTOR, GM, JMD, CMD}` (`line_inspection/viewing.py:33`) or super admin | `base.html:63` — gates the Reports/rollup tab |
| `cadre_label` | `str` | `viewing.display_label()` (`line_inspection/viewing.py:148`) | Header chrome — the human-readable cadre/designation |

Two design notes the comment makes explicit and that a reader should absorb:

- **Returning `{}` when there is no session** keeps every key genuinely absent for anonymous
  requests, so `{% if is_admin %}` in a template is false by absence rather than by an
  explicitly-injected `False`. It also avoids five DB queries on the login page.
- **Cost discipline.** `is_management` is included because it is one indexed lookup on
  `EmployeeCadreSnapshot`; the *expensive* work (`viewing.cadre_tier`, the reporting-subtree walk
  in `viewing.subordinate_snapshots`) is deliberately left in the views that need it. The comment
  at `:14-15` states this tradeoff. Since a context processor runs on **every** template render,
  anything added here is a per-page cost.

Note that `is_admin`, `is_super_admin`, `is_management` and `cadre_label` each hit the
`line_inspection_db` connection, so any authenticated page render costs ~4 small queries against
the `clear` schema before the view's own work begins. None of them is cached.

`ALLOWED_HOSTS` entry by entry (`transcoapps/settings.py:52-60`), with the reason from the comment
at `:49-51` ("*the reserved ngrok static domain (used by the drone_inspection_app over
LTE/internet), plus localhost and the LAN/hotspot ranges for the office/field HTTP fallback*"):

| Entry | Why |
|---|---|
| `mammal-calamari-create.ngrok-free.dev` | The reserved (static) ngrok domain for this backend — the phone's route in over LTE |
| `.ngrok-free.dev` | Leading-dot wildcard: **any** subdomain of `ngrok-free.dev`. This is what makes a mismatched tunnel name still work (§2.8) |
| `.ngrok-free.app` | Same, for ngrok's older TLD |
| `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]` | Local development |
| `192.168.137.1` | The default gateway IP of **Windows Mobile Hotspot** — the laptop's address when the phone is tethered to it, used for the plain-HTTP LAN fallback when a corporate firewall breaks TLS to ngrok |
| `$EXTRA_ALLOWED_HOSTS` | Appended at `:65`; in this checkout `.env.local` sets it to the laptop's current Wi-Fi IP |

**`MEDIA_URL` has no leading slash — is that a bug?** No, and the reason is subtle enough to be
worth spelling out. Django's `LazySettings.__getattr__`
(`.venv/Lib/site-packages/django/conf/__init__.py:82-83`) special-cases `MEDIA_URL` and
`STATIC_URL` and passes them through `_add_script_prefix()` (`:122-134`), which prepends
`get_script_prefix()` (default `'/'`) to any value that does not already start with `/`,
`http://` or `https://`. So `settings.MEDIA_URL` **reads back as `/media/`** at runtime even
though the file says `'media/'`. Consequences:

- `transcoapps/urls.py:37`'s `static(settings.MEDIA_URL, …)` receives `/media/` and
  `lstrip('/')`s it into the regex `^media/(?P<path>.*)$` — correct either way
  (`django/conf/urls/static.py`).
- `{{ r.photo.url }}` in `line_inspection/templates/line_inspection/dashboard_inspections.html:58,65`
  resolves to `/media/…` — correct.
- `line_inspection/api/serializers.py:9-18`'s `absolute_photo_url()` sidesteps the setting
  entirely and hardcodes `f'/media/{image_field.name}'`, then `request.build_absolute_uri(path)`.

> **Discrepancy (comment vs. framework behaviour).** The docstring at
> `line_inspection/api/serializers.py:10-13` justifies the hardcoded `/media/` by saying *"our
> MEDIA_URL has no leading slash"*. At runtime it does have one, because of
> `_add_script_prefix`. The hardcoding is harmless and the stated *outcome* (matching the Flutter
> client's `mediaUrl()`, which strips `/api` and appends `/media/<path>`) is right — but the
> stated *reason* is not. The real fragility is the opposite one: hardcoding `/media/` would
> break if the app were ever deployed under a `SCRIPT_NAME` subpath, which is precisely the case
> `_add_script_prefix` exists to handle.

**The four `KEYCLOAK_*` settings are dead.** `line_inspection/services/keycloak_client.py:16-21`
reads its configuration from `os.environ` directly, **not** from `django.conf.settings`. A grep
for `settings.KEYCLOAK` across the app returns nothing. So editing `settings.py:217-220` has no
effect on behaviour whatsoever — you must set the environment variables. This duplication is
itself a trap: someone rotating the Keycloak secret would very plausibly edit `settings.py` and
believe they were done.

(excluding `.venv/` and the donor project).

#### 2.6.1 The dev-login bypass (`LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN`)

A recent addition, absent from the README. `line_inspection/services/dev_login.py` is an offline
stand-in for the checkCred gateway. Its own docstring explains why it exists: checkCred is
*"unreachable from outside APTRANSCO's network and needs app-level gateway credentials
(`APTRANSCO_AUTH_USER` / `APTRANSCO_AUTH_PASS`) that are not in this checkout. That makes the web
admin panel and the Flutter app un-loggable-into on a developer machine."*

**What it does:** it resolves the submitted employee id against the locally-synced
`EmployeeCadreSnapshot` table and compares the submitted password against **one shared string**
from the environment. It does **not** verify anyone's real password. Any employee id present in
`EmployeeCadreSnapshot` signs in with that one string — including Super Admins.

**How it is gated.** Three independent conditions, all checked at call time in `is_enabled()`
(`dev_login.py:38-59`):

```python
if not getattr(settings, 'DEBUG', False):
    return False
if os.environ.get(ENV_FLAG, '') != '1':          # LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN
    return False
if not os.environ.get(ENV_PASSWORD, ''):         # LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD
    return False
```

**How it hooks in.** Four lines at the very top of the real verifier
(`line_inspection/services/checkcred_client.py:48-53`):

```python
# Local-development escape hatch. Inert unless DEBUG *and* both
# LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN / LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD are set --
# see services/dev_login.py. Delete these four lines to remove it.
from . import dev_login
if dev_login.is_enabled():
    return dev_login.verify(user_id, passwd)
```

Because it hooks `checkcred_client.verify_credentials`, it covers **both** the web login
(`line_inspection/auth.py:32`) and the mobile `POST /inspection/api/auth/login/` — meaning a dev
build of the Flutter app can obtain a real `MobileAuthToken` this way too.

Things the implementation gets right, worth noting as a model for similar escape hatches:

- Uses `hmac.compare_digest` for the comparison (`:76`) rather than `==`.
- Reproduces the real gateway's id normalization exactly — `user_id.zfill(8)` for numeric ids
  (`:81`) — with a comment explaining that everything downstream expects 8-digit zero-padded SAP
  ids, so a bypass that skipped padding would produce sessions that silently fail every lookup.
- Refuses ids not present in `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` (`:83-88`) rather than minting arbitrary
  identities.
- Logs a `WARNING` once per process when armed, and a `WARNING` on every sign-in
  (`:53-58`, `:90-91`).
- Marks the synthesized `empdata` payload with `'_source': 'dev_login'` (`:101`) so a downstream
  consumer can tell.
- Imports models lazily inside `verify()` (`:66-68`) because `checkcred_client` is imported
  during app-registry population, before models are ready.
- Documents its own removal procedure: delete the file plus the four-line delegation.

**Residual risk (Finding S5, High-in-context):** the whole thing collapses to one condition,
because `DEBUG = True` is hardcoded (`settings.py:47`) and `.env.local` in this checkout sets
`LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN=1` **and** a non-empty `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD`. So in this
checkout **the bypass is currently ARMED**, and any employee id in `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` can
sign in with one shared string. The `.env.local` comments concede the point directly: *"this is a
shared dev secret, not a real password check… It is set to the real employee password only so the
login screen feels normal while testing — it proves nothing about who is signing in."* Setting
the shared dev password to a **real** employee password is the sharpest edge here: it means a
real credential is sitting in a plaintext file whose only protection is a `.gitignore` that
**does not exist in this checkout** (see §2.6.2).

#### 2.6.2 `.env.local` and the `_load_local_env()` loader

`transcoapps/settings.py:20-39`:

```python
def _load_local_env():
    """Load BASE_DIR/.env.local (gitignored, never committed) into
    os.environ, if present. Runs here — the very first thing settings.py
    does — so it applies no matter how the server process gets started
    (integrated terminal, a separate terminal that never sourced anything,
    an IDE's Run/Debug button, a task runner, etc). Dot-sourcing a shell
    script only sets env vars in that one shell session; this doesn't have
    that gap."""
    env_file = BASE_DIR / '.env.local'
    if not env_file.exists():
        return
    for line in env_file.read_text(encoding='utf-8').splitlines():
        line = line.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith('#') or '=' not in line:
            continue
        key, _, value = line.partition('=')
        os.environ.setdefault(key.strip(), value.strip())


_load_local_env()
```

**Why it exists** (the docstring's own argument): the alternative — a `set-env.ps1` you
dot-source — only affects the one shell that sourced it. Launching via VS Code's Run button, a
second terminal, a scheduled task or a WSGI server would silently run with no configuration and
fail in confusing ways. Doing the load inside `settings.py`, before anything else, means the
configuration follows the *project*, not the *shell*. There is no `python-dotenv` dependency —
it is ~15 lines of hand-rolled parsing, consistent with the project's minimal-dependency stance
(`requirements.txt` lists only seven packages).

**Semantics and file format:**

| Aspect | Behaviour |
|---|---|
