| Location | `BASE_DIR/.env.local` — i.e. `transcoapps/.env.local`, beside `manage.py` |
| Missing file | Silent no-op (`return`) — the app still boots on its defaults |
| Comments | Lines whose first non-space character is `#` are skipped |
| Blank lines | Skipped |
| Lines without `=` | Skipped silently |
| Parsing | `line.partition('=')` — splits on the **first** `=`, so values may contain `=` |
| Whitespace | Both key and value are `.strip()`ped |
| Quoting | **None.** `FOO="bar"` sets `FOO` to the literal 5 characters `"bar"`. Do not quote values. |
| Escapes / multiline / variable interpolation | Not supported |
| Precedence | `os.environ.setdefault` — a **real** environment variable always wins over the file. So CI/production env vars are never clobbered by a stray local file. |
| Ordering | Called at `:39`, before `SECRET_KEY`/`ALLOWED_HOSTS`/`DATABASES` are evaluated, so every later `os.environ.get(...)` in `settings.py` sees the loaded values. Modules under `services/` read `os.environ` at **import** time, which happens after settings are loaded — so they see them too. |

**The file exists in this checkout** at `transcoapps/.env.local` (1,941 bytes). Its variables:
`APTRANSCO_AUTH_USER` (blank), `APTRANSCO_AUTH_PASS` (blank), `APTRANSCO_AUTH_URL` (commented
out), `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN=1`, `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD=<set in .env.local>`,
`EXTRA_ALLOWED_HOSTS=<the developer's current Wi-Fi IP>`, and the five `PG_*` variables all
commented out. Its own header comments are unusually good and double as documentation for the
gateway-vs-employee-credential distinction.

> **Caveat.** The docstring calls the file *"gitignored, never committed"*, but **there is no
> `.gitignore` anywhere in `transcoapps/`** — the only one in the tree is
> `Aptransco_TIS-main/.gitignore`, which governs the donor/Flutter subtree — and the checkout is
> not a git working tree at all (no `.git/` directory under
> `C:/Users/Admin/Downloads/line_inspection-main/`). The protection the comment claims is
> currently aspirational. Adding `.env.local` to a root `.gitignore` should be step one before
> this tree is ever committed. **(Finding S6.)**

### 2.7 Security issues

Each item below is real, present in the tree as read, and stated with file and line. No secret
value is reproduced here.

| # | Severity | Issue | Location |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | **Critical** | Live Keycloak client secret hardcoded — twice | `transcoapps/settings.py:220`, `line_inspection/services/keycloak_client.py:21` |
| S2 | **High** | `SECRET_KEY` hardcoded, `django-insecure-` prefixed | `transcoapps/settings.py:44` |
| S3 | **High** | `DEBUG = True` hardcoded with no env override | `transcoapps/settings.py:47` |
| S4 | **High** | Database password as a source-code fallback | `transcoapps/settings.py:154` (and donor `Aptransco_TIS-main/aptransco_backend/aptransco_backend/settings.py:120`) |
| S5 | **High (in this checkout)** | Dev-login bypass currently armed | `line_inspection/services/dev_login.py` + `.env.local` |
| S6 | **Medium** | `.env.local` holding real credentials, with no `.gitignore` protecting it | `transcoapps/.env.local` |
| S7 | **Medium** | DRF has no `REST_FRAMEWORK` defaults; security is opt-in per view | `transcoapps/settings.py` (absent), `line_inspection/api/views.py:43` |
| S8 | **Low** | `/admin/` routed to Django's admin site for an app that registers nothing there | `transcoapps/urls.py:23` |

#### S1 — hardcoded live Keycloak client secret (Critical)

`transcoapps/settings.py:220` assigns a real-looking 32-character Keycloak client secret to
`KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET` as a plain string literal. The identical string appears again as the
*default* of the environment lookup at `line_inspection/services/keycloak_client.py:21`.

This directly violates a rule the project wrote for itself. `line_inspection/README.md:352`:

> *"Never hardcode `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET` as a source default."*

and `line_inspection/README.md:355`:

> *"None of these have hardcoded fallback secrets in code — they must be set in the environment
> wherever these commands/the web app run."*

The `keycloak_client.py` occurrence is the more striking of the two, because the two comment
lines immediately above it say the opposite of what the next line does:

```python
# No hardcoded secret default on purpose — a real secret must never live in
# source. Set KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET in the environment before runserver.
KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET = os.environ.get('KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET', '<redacted — real secret in source>')
```

**Why it matters:** an OIDC *confidential client* secret is the credential that proves this
backend is the `clear` client to `keycloak.aptransco.co.in`. Anyone holding it can perform the
authorization-code exchange and the refresh-token grant as this application against the
`APTRANSCO-EMP` realm. The mitigating factor — and it is only partial — is that the Keycloak path
is **dormant**: `line_inspection/urls.py:8-9` notes the callback view was removed, and
`_require_client_secret()` (`keycloak_client.py:32-34`) is only reached via
`/inspection/api/auth/keycloak/{exchange,refresh}/`, which are still routed
(`line_inspection/api/urls.py:14-15`). Dormant does not mean unusable, and it does not
un-disclose the secret.

**What to do:** (1) treat the secret as compromised and **rotate it in the Keycloak admin
console**; (2) delete both literals — `settings.py:217-220` outright (they are dead, see §2.6a)
and the default at `keycloak_client.py:21`, replacing it with `os.environ.get('KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET', '')`
so `_require_client_secret()` does its job; (3) set the value in `.env.local` / the deployment
environment; (4) scrub it from git history if this tree is ever committed.

#### S2 — hardcoded `SECRET_KEY` (High)

`transcoapps/settings.py:44` — the `startproject`-generated `django-insecure-…` key, still
literal, under a comment that reads *"SECURITY WARNING: keep the secret key used in production
secret!"*.

**Why it matters:** `SECRET_KEY` signs session cookies and CSRF tokens. Since identity in this
app is *entirely* `request.session['employee_id']` with no password re-check, anyone who knows
the key can forge a signed session cookie asserting any employee id — including a Super Admin's —
and get full access to the admin panel. There is no second factor to stop them.

**What to do:** `SECRET_KEY = os.environ['DJANGO_SECRET_KEY']` (fail-fast, no default), value in
`.env.local` / the deployment environment. Note the donor project already does this properly —
`Aptransco_TIS-main/aptransco_backend/aptransco_backend/settings.py:28-31` reads
`DJANGO_SECRET_KEY` from the environment. The pattern is available for copying.

#### S3 — `DEBUG = True` hardcoded (High)

`transcoapps/settings.py:47`, with no environment override. Deploying this file as-is means:
full tracebacks with local variables (including the DB password) rendered to any visitor on an
unhandled exception; `django.db.connection.queries` accumulating unbounded; `ALLOWED_HOSTS`
checks still enforced (that part is fine) but `/media/` served by Django rather than nginx
(`transcoapps/urls.py:37`); and the dev-login bypass's first guard satisfied (S5).

**What to do:** `DEBUG = os.environ.get('DJANGO_DEBUG', 'true').strip().lower() not in ('false','0','no','off')`
— again, exactly what the donor already does at
`Aptransco_TIS-main/aptransco_backend/aptransco_backend/settings.py:33-35`.

#### S4 — database password as a source default (High)

`transcoapps/settings.py:154`: `'PASSWORD': os.environ.get('PG_PASSWORD', '<redacted>')`. The
fallback is a short lowercase word that reads like a person's name, i.e. a real chosen password
rather than a placeholder. The **same** fallback appears in the donor project at
`Aptransco_TIS-main/aptransco_backend/aptransco_backend/settings.py:120`
(`os.environ.get('CLEAR_DB_PASSWORD', <same value>)`), which strongly suggests it is the actual
password for the `postgres` role on the shared `aptransco_ai_db` instance and has simply been
copied forward.

**Why it matters:** the `postgres` superuser role with that password has access to *every* schema
on the shared server — `telecom_cps`, `lines`, `gismaps`, `keycloak` — i.e. Ground Rule 1's
entire blast radius, for other departments' data. Combined with S3, an unhandled exception page
would print the whole `DATABASES` dict.

**What to do:** remove both defaults (`os.environ['PG_PASSWORD']`, fail-fast); rotate the role's
password; and separately, stop connecting as `postgres` — create a dedicated role whose grants
cover only the `clear` schema, which would turn Ground Rule 1 from a convention into an
enforced permission.

#### S5 — dev-login bypass armed (High, in this checkout)

See §2.6.1 for the mechanism. The design of the guard is careful (three independent conditions,
constant-time compare, loud logging, documented removal), but all three conditions are satisfied
right now, and the `.env.local` comment states the shared password was set to a real employee's
password. **What to do:** set `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN=0` (or delete the two lines) the moment
`APTRANSCO_AUTH_USER`/`APTRANSCO_AUTH_PASS` are available; never let `DEBUG=True` and this flag
coexist on any host reachable beyond localhost — note that ngrok makes "reachable beyond
localhost" the *normal* state of this dev machine; and change the real employee password that was
reused as the shared dev string.

#### S6 — `.env.local` unprotected (Medium)

The file holds a real credential and the tree has no root `.gitignore` and no git repo (§2.6.2).
**What to do:** create `transcoapps/.gitignore` containing at minimum `.env.local`, `.venv/`,
`media/`, `static/`, `__pycache__/`, `*.pyc` **before** the first commit.

#### S7 — no DRF defaults (Medium)

There is no `REST_FRAMEWORK` dict in `settings.py`, so DRF's stock
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES = ['rest_framework.permissions.AllowAny']` applies to any view that
forgets to set `permission_classes`. Today every view sets it (`line_inspection/api/views.py`),
so nothing is exposed — but the safe outcome depends on per-view discipline rather than on
configuration. **What to do:** add

```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES': [
        'line_inspection.api.authentication.MobileTokenAuthentication',
        'line_inspection.api.authentication.SessionEmployeeAuthentication',
        'line_inspection.api.authentication.KeycloakBearerAuthentication',
    ],
    'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES': ['rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated'],
}
```

so that the three public views become the explicit exceptions (they already declare
`permission_classes = [AllowAny]`) instead of the protected views being the explicit rule.

#### S8 — `/admin/` mounted needlessly (Low)

`transcoapps/urls.py:23` routes Django's admin for an app that registers no models there
(Rule 4). It is not exploitable without an `auth_user` superuser, which nothing creates, but it
is free attack surface and an invitation to confuse `/admin/` with `/inspection/admin/`.
**What to do:** drop the route and `'django.contrib.admin'` from `INSTALLED_APPS`.

### 2.8 The ngrok tunnel arrangement

The Flutter field app runs on a phone that is usually **not** on the same network as the
developer's laptop. To make `runserver` reachable from LTE, the project uses an ngrok tunnel with
a **reserved static domain** — a fixed hostname, so the app can hardcode a default that keeps
working across restarts (a free ephemeral ngrok URL changes every time and would need a rebuild).

The command implied by `Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/services/api_service.dart:16-17`:

```bash
ngrok http 8000 --url=<reserved-domain>
```

The Flutter client resolves its base URL through **three layers, most specific first**
(`api_service.dart:19-38`):

1. an in-app override persisted in `SharedPreferences` (key `api_base_url_override`), settable
   from the Settings dialog on the Line Inspection screen — lets a field engineer flip between
   office/LAN and field/ngrok **without a rebuild**;
2. a compile-time `--dart-define=API_BASE_URL=…`;
3. the compile-time default at `api_service.dart:27-30`.

The escape hatch in layers 1 and 2 exists for a specific, well-documented failure: on APTRANSCO's
corporate Wi-Fi a FortiGate performs TLS interception, so HTTPS to ngrok fails with
`CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED: self signed certificate`
(`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/services/network_security.dart:11`), and the ngrok
host may also be DNS-sinkholed
(`.../lib/services/offline/connectivity_service.dart:12`). The workaround is to point the app at
`http://<laptop-lan-ip>:8000/inspection/api` over plain HTTP, which the firewall does not
inspect — which is exactly why `ALLOWED_HOSTS` carries `192.168.137.1` (Windows Mobile Hotspot
gateway) and why `EXTRA_ALLOWED_HOSTS` exists.

**The two ngrok names do not match:**

| Side | Host | Location |
|---|---|---|
| Backend `ALLOWED_HOSTS` / `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` | `mammal-calamari-create.ngrok-free.dev` | `transcoapps/settings.py:53` and `:71` |
| Flutter compile-time default | `mispacked-beamy-noelle.ngrok-free.dev` | `Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/services/api_service.dart:29` |

**Why it still works anyway:** `ALLOWED_HOSTS` contains the leading-dot wildcards
`.ngrok-free.dev` and `.ngrok-free.app` (`settings.py:54-55`), and `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS`
contains `https://*.ngrok-free.dev` / `https://*.ngrok-free.app` (`:72-73`). A leading dot in
`ALLOWED_HOSTS` matches the domain **and all its subdomains**, so *any* `*.ngrok-free.dev` host
header is accepted — including `mispacked-beamy-noelle`. The explicitly-named
`mammal-calamari-create` entry is therefore redundant with the wildcard immediately below it, and
purely documentary.

**One of the two names is stale.** `mispacked-beamy-noelle.ngrok-free.dev` is the **donor
project's** reserved domain — it appears in `Aptransco_TIS-main/project.md:409` and `:522`
(`ngrok http 8000 --url=mispacked-beamy-noelle.ngrok-free.dev`) as that project's tunnel, and the
Flutter app has simply never had its default updated after being re-homed onto this backend.
`mammal-calamari-create.ngrok-free.dev` is the one this backend's settings names. A build of the
Flutter app with no `--dart-define` and no in-app override will therefore try to reach the donor's
tunnel, which nobody is running — the app will appear offline until someone sets the override.
The fix is one line: update `defaultValue` in `api_service.dart:29`.

One further detail worth carrying: the Flutter base URL **must end in `/api`** by that client's
convention, but this backend serves the API under `/inspection/api/`. Hence the default is
`https://<host>/inspection/api` and the comment at `api_service.dart:24-26` telling anyone setting
an override to include the `/inspection` prefix. The client's `mediaUrl()` helper strips the
trailing `/api` and appends `/media/<path>` — which is why
`line_inspection/api/serializers.py:9-18` builds photo URLs as `<host>/media/<name>` rather than
`<host>/inspection/media/<name>`, matching `transcoapps/urls.py:37`'s root-level `/media/` mount.
## 3. Identity, Authentication & Authorization

This is the load-bearing spine of the platform. Every query in the web dashboard, every REST
response to the Flutter field app, and every admin screen resolves down to one string — a SAP
employee id — and then to a hand-rolled set of rules about what that string is allowed to see
and change. There is no Django `User` object anywhere in the system.

### 3.1 Why there is no `django.contrib.auth.User`

APTRANSCO already has a system of record for people: SAP HR. Every employee has an `EMP_ID`
(an 8-digit, zero-padded numeric string such as `01073093`), a position, an org unit, a cadre
sub-group, and a reporting manager. Passwords are held by a separate legacy gateway
(`checkCred`, section 3.3) and — eventually — by Keycloak (section 3.5). Creating a parallel
`auth_user` table would mean inventing a second identity namespace that must be kept in sync
with SAP forever, and it would tempt the code into storing passwords locally. So the app does
the opposite: **identity is the bare `employee_id` string, and nothing else.**

The module docstring at `line_inspection/auth.py:1-15` states the rule outright:

```python
"""Session-based identity for the admin panel / web dashboard — no
django.contrib.auth.User anywhere. Identity is a bare SAP employee_id,
stored directly in Django's session framework (independent of contrib.auth).
```

Consequences that ripple through the entire codebase — a reader will hit all four of these
within minutes of opening any file:

| Consequence | Where it shows up |
|---|---|
| **No `ForeignKey` to a user, anywhere.** Every model that needs to record a person stores a `CharField` instead. | `RoleAssignment.employee_id`, `RoleAssignment.assigned_by_employee_id` (`line_inspection/models.py:449,454`), `LineTowerAssignment.employee_id` (`:472`), `Inspection.inspector_employee_id`, `DefectTicket.raised_by_employee_id` / `closed_by_employee_id`, `SupportRequest.raised_by_employee_id` / `resolved_by_employee_id`, `MobileAuthToken.employee_id` (`:702`), `SuperAdmin.employee_id` (`:420`). |
| **No referential integrity on people.** Nothing stops a typo'd employee id being written. Correctness is enforced by only ever writing an id that came out of an authenticated session, plus the `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` lookup table (section 3.2). | `line_inspection/admin_views.py:150` writes `assignment.assigned_by_employee_id = request.session['employee_id']` — the session value, never client input. |
| **DRF needs a stand-in `request.user`.** DRF's `IsAuthenticated` permission just checks `request.user.is_authenticated`, so the app supplies a two-attribute duck-typed object. | `SimpleIdentity` in `line_inspection/api/authentication.py:15-23`. |
| **Permissions are hand-rolled.** There is no `user.has_perm`, no permission table, no groups. Three tiers are computed on demand from three small tables. | `is_admin` / `is_super_admin` in `line_inspection/auth.py:79-92`; the decorators at `:95-122`. |

`django.contrib.auth` **is** still in `INSTALLED_APPS` (`transcoapps/settings.py:81`) and
`AuthenticationMiddleware` is still in `MIDDLEWARE` (`:103`) — but only because
`django.contrib.admin` (also installed, `:80`) refuses to start without them. The `auth_user`
table exists in the `public` schema and is unused by this app; `line_inspection`'s own tables
live in the `clear` schema on a separate connection alias (`line_inspection/db_router.py`).
`django.contrib.auth.context_processors.auth` is still registered (`transcoapps/settings.py:118`),
so `{{ user }}` in a template resolves to `AnonymousUser` on every page — templates must use
`{{ session_employee_id }}` from `line_inspection/context_processors.py` instead.

> **Session storage note.** Because `LineInspectionRouter` only claims models whose
> `app_label == 'line_inspection'` (`line_inspection/db_router.py:11-18`), the `django_session`
> table is written to the `default` alias / `public` schema. Web sessions therefore live in a
> different schema from all inspection data.

### 3.2 `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` — the local mirror of SAP identity

An `employee_id` alone carries no attributes, so the app keeps a periodically-synced local copy
of SAP's cadre service. `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` (`line_inspection/models.py:389-411`) is
**never live-queried per request** — the docstring says so explicitly — because an HTTP call to
SAP on every permission check would be unacceptable.

| Field | Type | Purpose in the auth story |
|---|---|---|
| `employee_id` | `CharField(32)`, unique | The identity key. Zero-padded to 8 digits by the sync and by login normalisation. |
| `employee_name` | `CharField(255)` | Display name fallback. |
| `position_id` | `CharField(32)` | **The Admin hinge.** Matched against `FieldEECadrePosition.position_id` (section 3.9). |
| `position_text` | `CharField(255)` | e.g. `"EE/O&M/Kadapa"`. Used by the Admin-candidate filter (`icontains='O&M'`). |
| `org_unit_id` / `org_unit_text` | `CharField` | Org placement; display + rollups. |
| `emp_sub_grp` | `CharField(32)` | SAP cadre code, e.g. `DE/EE`, `AE`, `SE`, `CE`. Drives display labels and the *management* gate — **not** the Admin gate. |
| `emp_sub_grp_desc` | `CharField(255)` | Human text for the above. |
| `mobile`, `mail` | `CharField` | Contact only. |
| `reporting_manager_id` | `CharField(32)`, **indexed** | The edge of the reporting tree. The entire oversight scope (section 3.11) is a BFS over this column. |
| `reporting_manager_name` | `CharField(255)` | Display. |
| `synced_at` | `DateTimeField(auto_now=True)` | Sync freshness. |

Populated by `python manage.py sync_employee_cadre [--root-employee-id ...]`
(`line_inspection/management/commands/sync_employee_cadre.py`), which calls
`services/sap_client.get_employee_cadre_details()` and `update_or_create`s one row per
`EMP_ID` inside a single transaction. The command's docstring says it is meant to run hourly
via `run_sync_scheduler`. It is **additive-only** — it never deletes rows for employees that
disappear from SAP (it collects `seen_ids` but only uses the set for the success message).

`viewing.subordinate_snapshots` describes the table as "the ~1,830-row snapshot"
(`line_inspection/viewing.py:39`) — that figure is a code comment, not verified against a live
database here.

**Domain jargon — cadre.** In Indian public-sector utilities a *cadre* is a rank/grade class in
the technical service ladder. Ascending: AE / AAE (Assistant Engineer) → AEE (Assistant
Executive Engineer) → DEE (Deputy Executive Engineer) → EE (Executive Engineer) → SE
(Superintending Engineer) → CE (Chief Engineer) → GM / Director / JMD / CMD. SAP encodes these
in `emp_sub_grp`, but **coarsely and sometimes as combined codes** — `DE/EE` is one single code
value, not two. `line_inspection/viewing.py:25-29` maps codes to display labels:

```python
CADRE_LABELS = {
    'AAE': 'AEE', 'AE': 'AEE', 'ADE/AEE': 'DEE',
    'DE/EE': 'EE', 'SE': 'SE', 'CE': 'CE',
    'DIRECTOR': 'Director', 'GM': 'GM', 'JMD': 'JMD', 'CMD': 'CMD',
}
```

The comment above it is emphatic that this map is **display-only and NOT authoritative for
authorization** — precisely because the codes are coarse. Authorization derives from the
reporting tree plus who actually holds grant rows.

### 3.3 checkCred — the ACTIVE login mechanism

**Domain jargon — checkCred.** APTRANSCO's pre-existing, organisation-wide employee credential
gateway. It is a small JSON-over-HTTP service exposing three endpoints (`checkCred`,
`forgotPass`, `savePass`) that sit in front of the real employee password store. This app never
sees or stores an employee password; it forwards the pair to checkCred and trusts the verdict.

The client is `line_inspection/services/checkcred_client.py` — 97 lines, no class, four public
names. Its docstring records two deliberate decisions: (a) it is a *fresh, local* implementation
of the same call `gisapp/views.py:login_proxy` already makes, copied rather than imported,
because `line_inspection` must not depend on any other Django app in the project at runtime;
(b) the service's own credentials come from the environment only.

#### 3.3.1 Configuration

```python
CHECKCRED_BASE_URL = os.environ.get('APTRANSCO_AUTH_URL', 'https://qaserv.aptransco.co.in/qath').rstrip('/')
CHECKCRED_URL         = f'{CHECKCRED_BASE_URL}/checkCred'
FORGOT_PASSWORD_URL   = f'{CHECKCRED_BASE_URL}/forgotPass'
SAVE_PASSWORD_URL     = f'{CHECKCRED_BASE_URL}/savePass'
CHECKCRED_USER = os.environ.get('APTRANSCO_AUTH_USER', '')
CHECKCRED_PASS = os.environ.get('APTRANSCO_AUTH_PASS', '')
```
(`line_inspection/services/checkcred_client.py:14-20`)

| Env var | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `APTRANSCO_AUTH_URL` | `https://qaserv.aptransco.co.in/qath` | Base URL; all three endpoints hang off it. Note `qaserv` — this default points at the **QA** host. Trailing slash stripped. |
| `APTRANSCO_AUTH_USER` | `''` (empty) | **App-level** HTTP Basic username for the gateway itself. |
| `APTRANSCO_AUTH_PASS` | `''` (empty) | **App-level** HTTP Basic password for the gateway itself. |

**The two-credential distinction is the single most confusing thing about this client and must
be internalised.** There are *two independent* credential pairs in every login:

1. `APTRANSCO_AUTH_USER` / `APTRANSCO_AUTH_PASS` — identify *this Django application* to the
   gateway, sent as HTTP Basic Auth on the connection (`auth=(...)` in `requests.post`). Same
   for every login, every employee. Configured once per deployment.
2. `user_id` / `passwd` — the *employee's own* SAP id and password, sent in the JSON **body**.
   These are what actually get verified.

Module-level constants are read **at import time**, so changing these env vars requires a
process restart. (Contrast with `dev_login.is_enabled()`, section 3.4, which reads at call time
and documents why.)

Values are read from real environment variables or from `.env.local`, which
`_load_local_env()` in `transcoapps/settings.py:20-39` loads with `os.environ.setdefault` —
so a real environment variable always **wins** over the file.

#### 3.3.2 The three operations

| Function | HTTP call | Request body | Returns / raises |
|---|---|---|---|
| `verify_credentials(user_id, passwd)` | `POST {base}/checkCred`, Basic-auth'd, `timeout=20` | `{"user_id": ..., "passwd": ...}` | `{'employee_id', 'display_name', 'empdata'}` on success; `CheckCredError` otherwise |
| `forgot_password(user_id)` | `POST {base}/forgotPass` | `{"user_id": ...}` | Whatever JSON the gateway returns (passed through raw); `CheckCredError` on transport/parse failure or empty id |
| `save_password(user_id, passwd, oldpass)` | `POST {base}/savePass` | `{"user_id": ..., "passwd": <new>, "oldpass": <current>}` | Raw gateway JSON; `CheckCredError` if any of the three is empty |

All three funnel through one helper:

```python
def _post(url, payload, timeout=20):
    _require_credentials()
    try:
        response = requests.post(
            url, json=payload, auth=(CHECKCRED_USER, CHECKCRED_PASS), timeout=timeout,
        )
        return response.json()
    except requests.RequestException as exc:
        raise CheckCredError(f'Auth service unreachable: {exc}') from exc
    except ValueError as exc:
        raise CheckCredError('Auth service returned an invalid response.') from exc
```
(`line_inspection/services/checkcred_client.py:32-42`)

Behavioural details worth knowing:

- `_require_credentials()` (`:27-29`) short-circuits **before any network call** if either app-level
  credential is blank, raising `CheckCredError('APTRANSCO_AUTH_USER / APTRANSCO_AUTH_PASS are
  not configured.')`. This is why an unconfigured checkout fails login instantly with a
  configuration message rather than an "invalid password" message.
- `response.json()` is called **without checking the HTTP status code**. A 500 that returns a
  JSON error body is parsed and flows into `verify_credentials`'s validity test rather than
  raising. A non-JSON body raises `ValueError`, which is converted to
  `CheckCredError('Auth service returned an invalid response.')`.
- `CheckCredError` (`:23-24`) is a bare `Exception` subclass. Its message is **rendered directly
  to the user** by `login_view` (`line_inspection/auth.py:34`) and returned to the mobile client
  as `{"error": str(exc)}` (`line_inspection/api/views.py:101`), so messages are written to be
  user-safe. Note the gateway-unreachable message interpolates the raw `requests` exception,
  which can leak the internal hostname to the login page.

#### 3.3.3 `verify_credentials` in detail

```python
result = _post(CHECKCRED_URL, {'user_id': user_id, 'passwd': passwd})

message = str(result.get('message', '')).lower()
empdata = result.get('empdata')
is_valid = ('valid' in message and 'invalid' not in message) and isinstance(empdata, dict)
if not is_valid:
    raise CheckCredError(result.get('message') or 'Invalid credentials.')
```
(`line_inspection/services/checkcred_client.py:60-66`)

The gateway signals success with a free-text `message` — the client treats a response as valid
only if the lower-cased message **contains `"valid"` and does not contain `"invalid"`**, *and*
`empdata` is a dict. This substring dance exists because the upstream service has no status
field; the `'invalid' not in message` clause is what stops `"Invalid credentials"` from matching
on the substring `valid`. It is fragile by nature — a future gateway message like
`"credentials could not be validated"` would be read as success (it contains `valid` and not
`invalid`) — but the extra `isinstance(empdata, dict)` requirement is the backstop.

Display name is taken from SAP's `CNAME`, falling back to `NAME1`, falling back to `''`
(`:68`).

**The `zfill(8)` normalisation is present and is important** (`:70-77`):

```python
# SAP employee ids are zero-padded to 8 digits everywhere else in this app
# (EmployeeCadreSnapshot/SuperAdmin/RoleAssignment) — checkCred's response
# (or whatever the user typed) may drop a leading zero, e.g. "1073093"
# instead of "01073093", which would silently fail every downstream
# employee_id lookup. Normalize here, once, at the point identity enters
# the session.
employee_id = str(result.get('user_id') or user_id).strip()
if employee_id.isdigit():
    employee_id = employee_id.zfill(8)
```

The *why* matters more than the *what*: because employee ids are plain strings compared with
`=`, a missing leading zero would not error — it would silently return "no rows", i.e. the user
would log in successfully and then appear to have no admin rights, no assignments and no
towers. Normalising once, at the single point identity enters the system, is what keeps that
class of bug out of the other 20 files. Note the guard: only ids that are **entirely digits**
are padded, so a non-numeric id passes through untouched.

The gateway's own `user_id` in the response takes precedence over what the user typed; the
typed value is the fallback.

Returned shape:

```python
{'employee_id': '01073093', 'display_name': 'SOME NAME', 'empdata': { ...full SAP record... }}
```

`empdata` is **not** persisted anywhere — `login_view` and `MobileLoginView` both ignore it. It
is returned only so a future caller could use it.

### 3.4 The local dev-login bypass (`services/dev_login.py`)

A recent addition, **not mentioned anywhere in `line_inspection/README.md`**. It exists because
checkCred is unreachable from outside APTRANSCO's network and the gateway Basic-auth pair is not
in this checkout, which would otherwise make both the web panel and the Flutter app impossible
to sign into on a developer laptop.

The hook is four lines at the very top of `verify_credentials`
(`line_inspection/services/checkcred_client.py:48-53`):

```python
# Local-development escape hatch. Inert unless DEBUG *and* both
# LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN / LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD are set --
# see services/dev_login.py. Delete these four lines to remove it.
from . import dev_login
if dev_login.is_enabled():
    return dev_login.verify(user_id, passwd)
```

Because it sits inside `verify_credentials`, it covers **both** login paths at once — the web
session login and `POST /api/auth/login/` (which mints a real `MobileAuthToken`). `forgot_password`
and `save_password` are *not* intercepted and still hit the real gateway.

**Three independent guards**, all of which must hold (`line_inspection/services/dev_login.py:38-59`):

| # | Guard | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `settings.DEBUG is True` | `getattr(settings, 'DEBUG', False)` |
| 2 | `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN == '1'` | exact string compare against the env var |
| 3 | `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD` non-empty | env var |

`is_enabled()` imports `django.conf.settings` **inside the function** and reads the env vars at
call time, "so toggling the env var takes effect on the next server start without any
import-order subtlety". The first time it returns True it emits a one-shot
`logger.warning('DEV LOGIN ACTIVE - checkCred is bypassed and passwords are NOT verified...')`,
guarded by a module-level `_warned` flag.

`verify(user_id, passwd)` (`:62-103`) honours the same contract as the real function:

1. Rejects empty id or password.
2. Compares the submitted password against `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD` using
   `hmac.compare_digest` (constant-time — a small correctness nicety even in a dev stub).
   **One shared string for everybody.**
3. Applies the identical `zfill(8)` normalisation, with a comment pointing at the real
   implementation so the two can't drift.
4. Looks the id up in `EmployeeCadreSnapshot`. If absent, raises
   `CheckCredError('No cadre snapshot for employee <id>. Dev login can only sign in employees
   already synced into EmployeeCadreSnapshot.')` — so the reachable identity set is exactly the
   synced snapshot table.
5. Logs a second warning naming the employee, then returns a synthetic identity dict whose
   `empdata` is `{'CNAME': ..., 'NAME1': ..., '_source': 'dev_login'}` — only the two keys
   anything downstream reads, plus a provenance marker.

Its own docstring states the security position plainly: *"It DOES NOT verify anyone's real
password... Never treat a session created this way as proof of identity."*

The current `.env.local` in this checkout has it **switched on**:

| Variable in `.env.local` | Value | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `APTRANSCO_AUTH_USER` | *(empty)* | Real gateway unusable |
| `APTRANSCO_AUTH_PASS` | *(empty)* | Real gateway unusable |
| `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN` | `1` | Bypass armed |
| `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD` | `<set in .env.local>` | Shared sign-in string |

Combined with `DEBUG = True` (`transcoapps/settings.py:47`), **this checkout currently signs in
any employee present in `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` with one shared password and no real
verification.** The `.env.local` comments acknowledge this and mark the block "TEMPORARY -
remove once the gateway pair above works". The removal recipe is: delete `services/dev_login.py`
and the four-line delegation, or simply set `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN=0`.

### 3.5 Keycloak — fully built, DORMANT

**Domain jargon — Keycloak / OIDC.** Keycloak is Red Hat's open-source identity provider;
OIDC (OpenID Connect) is the OAuth2-based protocol it speaks. The intended future flow is the
standard authorization-code flow: browser → Keycloak login page → redirect back with a `code` →
server exchanges `code` for tokens → server reads the employee id out of the token claims.

`line_inspection/services/keycloak_client.py` (174 lines) is complete and never wired into a
live route for browser login. Its docstring explains it was *"deliberately copied rather than
imported"* from `gisapp/views.py` for the same no-cross-app-dependency reason as checkCred, and
reshaped into plain functions returning dicts (not DRF `Response` objects) so it could serve
both a plain Django session view and DRF auth.

#### 3.5.1 Configuration and the realm gotcha

| Constant | Env var | Default in code |
|---|---|---|
| `KEYCLOAK_BASE_URL` | `KEYCLOAK_BASE_URL` | `https://keycloak.aptransco.co.in` |
| `KEYCLOAK_REALM` | `KEYCLOAK_REALM` | `APTRANSCO-EMP` |
| `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID` | `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID` | `clear` |
| `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET` | `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET` | **a real secret is hardcoded as the default — see finding F1 below** |

Derived URLs (`line_inspection/services/keycloak_client.py:22-24`):
`{base}/realms/{realm}/protocol/openid-connect/{auth,token,userinfo}`.

**The realm-name gotcha.** The realm segment is embedded in every URL and is **case-sensitive**.
`line_inspection/README.md:352` records the hard-won fact: *"Realm is case-sensitive — the real
realm is `APTRANSCO-EMP`, confirmed live; `aptransco-realm` does not exist."* The changelog
(`README.md:653-656`) adds that a wrong realm name was one of the two things that broke the
original Keycloak attempt — hitting a nonexistent realm yields a 404 that reads like a generic
Keycloak error rather than "you spelled the realm wrong".

`KEYCLOAK_EMPLOYEE_ID_CLAIMS = ('employee_id', 'emp_id', 'empid', 'preferred_username', 'user_id')`
(`:25`) — the ordered list of token claims searched for an employee id; the first non-empty one
wins. The breadth exists because the realm's claim mapping was never nailed down.

#### 3.5.2 Public surface

| Function | Signature | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `get_authorize_url` | `(redirect_uri, state='') -> str` | Builds `{auth_url}?client_id&redirect_uri&response_type=code&scope=openid profile email[&state]`. Pure string building, no network. |
| `exchange_code` | `(code, redirect_uri) -> dict` | `grant_type=authorization_code` token POST, then resolves an identity. |
| `refresh` | `(refresh_token) -> dict` | `grant_type=refresh_token` token POST, same resolution. |
| `resolve_bearer_token` | `(access_token) -> {'employee_id','name','display_name'}` | **No code exchange.** Calls `/userinfo` with the token and extracts identity. This is the one function the DRF layer actually calls. |
| `KeycloakClientError` | `Exception` | Single failure type for all of the above. |

Private helpers: `_require_client_secret()` (raises if the secret is blank);
`_decode_jwt_payload(token)` — base64url-decodes the JWT **payload without verifying the
signature** (acceptable only because it is merged *under* the verified `/userinfo` response,
see below); `_fetch_userinfo(access_token)` — `GET /userinfo` with `raise_for_status()`,
`timeout=15`; `_extract_identity(claims)` — the claim search plus a `"Name - 01073093"`
`display_name`; `_session_from_token_response(token_data)`; `_post_token_request(grant_params)`.

The claim-merge order is the security-relevant line (`:103`):

```python
claims = {**id_token_claims, **_fetch_userinfo(access_token)}
```

`/userinfo` claims (fetched over TLS from Keycloak, therefore trustworthy) are merged **on top
of** the unverified locally-decoded `id_token` claims, so the server-fetched values always win.

`_session_from_token_response` raises `KeycloakClientError('Keycloak did not return an access
token.')` if `access_token` is absent, and `'Employee ID was not present in the Keycloak login
response.'` if no configured claim yields an id. On success it returns
`{employee_id, name, display_name, access_token, refresh_token, expires_in, refresh_expires_in,
token_type}`.

`_post_token_request` sends `client_id` + `client_secret` + the grant params as form data
(`timeout=20`) and, on a non-2xx, raises with `error_description` → `error` → a generic message.

#### 3.5.3 What IS wired up, and what is not

Wired: `KeycloakBearerAuthentication` (section 3.8) and two unauthenticated pass-through
endpoints, `POST /api/auth/keycloak/exchange/` and `POST /api/auth/keycloak/refresh/`
(`line_inspection/api/views.py:141-167`, routed at `line_inspection/api/urls.py:14-15`). Both
validate that their required field is present (400 if not) and convert `KeycloakClientError`
into a 401. Nothing in the Flutter app calls them.

Not wired: **there is no browser login path through Keycloak.** `line_inspection/auth.py`
contains no `callback_view`; `line_inspection/urls.py:10` points `login/` at
`auth.login_view`, which renders a local form.

#### 3.5.4 Why it is deferred, and the exact recipe to re-enable

The blocker is *not* code. `line_inspection/README.md:58-63` and the changelog at `:653-661`:
the Keycloak client's registered **"Valid Redirect URIs"** must be changed in the Keycloak
admin console, which the team does not have access to. Live diagnostics found two separate
problems: the realm name in use was wrong (`aptransco-realm` doesn't exist; the real one is
`APTRANSCO-EMP`), and even after correcting it Keycloak still rejected the redirect URI. Rather
than block Phase 2, the team switched the active mechanism to checkCred and left the Keycloak
code untouched and ready.

The README's re-enable recipe (`line_inspection/README.md:78-83`), verbatim in substance:

1. Get the app's redirect URI registered under **Valid Redirect URIs** for client `clear` in
   realm `APTRANSCO-EMP` in the Keycloak admin console.
2. Add back a thin `callback_view` in `line_inspection/auth.py` (~15 lines of glue; only the
   glue was removed, `keycloak_client.py` itself was never touched):
   - a view that redirects to `keycloak_client.get_authorize_url(redirect_uri, state)`,
   - a callback view that calls `keycloak_client.exchange_code(code, redirect_uri)` and sets
     `request.session['employee_id']` / `['display_name']` from the returned dict.
3. Re-point `login_view` (or the `login/` URL) at the redirect, and add the callback route.

A fourth step the README does not mention but the code demands: **apply the `zfill(8)`
normalisation** to the Keycloak-derived `employee_id`. `keycloak_client._extract_identity` does
`str(value).strip()` and nothing more (`:78`), so an id arriving without its leading zero would
silently fail every downstream lookup — the exact bug `checkcred_client` guards against.

> **Stale comment.** `line_inspection/urls.py:9` says *"Keycloak (auth.callback_view) is dormant"*,
> naming a function that no longer exists in `auth.py`.

### 3.6 The web session

`line_inspection/auth.py:27-41` — `login_view`:

```python
if request.method == 'POST':
    user_id = request.POST.get('user_id', '')
    passwd = request.POST.get('passwd', '')
    try:
        identity = checkcred_client.verify_credentials(user_id, passwd)
    except CheckCredError as exc:
        return render(request, 'line_inspection/login.html', {'error': str(exc), 'user_id': user_id})

    request.session['employee_id'] = identity['employee_id']
    request.session['display_name'] = identity['display_name'] or identity['employee_id']
    next_url = request.POST.get('next') or request.GET.get('next') or reverse('line_inspection:admin-home')
    return redirect(next_url)
```

The whole session contract is those two keys. Django's session framework is used **directly** —
no `django.contrib.auth.login()`, no `_auth_user_id`, no session-fixation rotation (`login()`
normally calls `cycle_key()`; this code does not, so the pre-login session key survives
authentication).

| Session key | Set by | Read by |
|---|---|---|
| `employee_id` | `login_view` (`auth.py:36`) | `login_required` / `admin_required` / `super_admin_required`; every admin and dashboard view; `SessionEmployeeAuthentication`; `context_processors.identity` |
| `display_name` | `login_view` (`auth.py:37`), falling back to the id | Templates via `context_processors.identity` |

On failure the template is re-rendered with `error` and the typed `user_id` preserved; **the
session is never touched** on a failed login.

`logout_view` (`:74-76`) is `request.session.flush()` then redirect to `login` — `flush()`
deletes the server-side session row *and* rotates the cookie to a new empty session, which is
stronger than clearing the two keys.

`forgot_password_view` (`:44-53`) posts the id to `forgot_password()` and always shows the same
non-committal string on success — *"If that employee id is registered, password-reset
instructions have been sent."* — a deliberate anti-enumeration message that does not confirm
whether the id exists. On `CheckCredError` it shows `f'Error: {exc}'`, which does leak
configuration/transport detail.

`change_password_view` (`:56-71`) compares `passwd` against `confirm` locally (the only
client-side-equivalent check performed server-side) and otherwise delegates to
`save_password(user_id, passwd, oldpass)`. Note it takes `user_id` as a form field and requires
`oldpass` — it is reachable **without being logged in** (no decorator), which is safe only
because the old password is required and checkCred does the real verification.

Templates — all three are standalone, self-contained HTML documents (they do **not** extend
`base.html`), single-card, inline `<style>`, and all carry `{% csrf_token %}`:

| Template | Fields (`name=`) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `line_inspection/templates/line_inspection/login.html` | `next` (hidden), `user_id`, `passwd` | Shows `{{ error }}` in a red box; links to Forgot password. |
| `.../forgot_password.html` | `user_id` | Shows `{{ result }}`; links back to sign-in and to Change password. |
| `.../change_password.html` | `user_id`, `oldpass`, `passwd`, `confirm` | Colours the result box red via `{% if 'Error' in result %}` — a string sniff on the message text. |

`line_inspection/context_processors.py` turns the session into template variables on **every**
render (registered at `transcoapps/settings.py:120`):

```python
def identity(request):
    employee_id = request.session.get('employee_id')
    if not employee_id:
        return {}
    return {'session_employee_id': ..., 'session_display_name': ..., 'is_admin': ...,
            'is_super_admin': ..., 'is_management': ..., 'cadre_label': ...}
```

Returning `{}` for anonymous requests means templates can use `{% if session_employee_id %}`.
The comment notes `is_management` is deliberately included because it is *"cheap (one indexed
snapshot lookup)"* while the heavier tier/subtree walk stays in the views — but `is_admin` and
`is_super_admin` each run a query too, so a logged-in page render costs ~3–4 extra small
queries. There is no caching or memoisation of these calls anywhere.

### 3.7 The mobile token — `MobileAuthToken`

Phase 4 (the Flutter field app) needs an auth credential that survives app restarts, works
without cookies, and can be revoked centrally. `MobileAuthToken`
(`line_inspection/models.py:700-729`) is a hand-rolled DRF-`Token`-style model.

| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `key` | `CharField(64)`, `unique=True`, `db_index=True` | The bearer string itself. |
| `employee_id` | `CharField(32)`, `db_index=True` | Comment: *"already zfill(8) from checkcred"*. |
| `display_name` | `CharField(255)`, blank | Cached at issue time so `/auth/me/` need not re-hit SAP. |
| `created_at` | `DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)` | |
| `last_used_at` | `DateTimeField(null=True, blank=True)` | Throttled write — section 3.8. |
| `expires_at` | `DateTimeField(null=True, blank=True, default=_default_token_expiry)` | Nullable = never expires; the default is now + 30 days. |
| `is_active` | `BooleanField(default=True)` | Revocation flag. |
| `revoked_at` | `DateTimeField(null=True, blank=True)` | Audit stamp. |

`Meta.indexes = [Index(fields=['employee_id', 'is_active'])]` — for "all live tokens for this
employee" queries.

```python
def _default_token_expiry():
    # Long-lived on purpose — field engineers may stay offline for days between
    # syncs. Revocation is explicit (logout) or by expiry, not by a short TTL.
    return timezone.now() + timedelta(days=30)
```
(`line_inspection/models.py:694-697`)

The 30-day life is a deliberate trade-off against the operating reality: a lineman walking a
transmission corridor may be out of coverage for days, and an expired token in the field means
an inspection that cannot be submitted. Security is bought back with **explicit revocability**
(a DB flag the server controls) rather than a short TTL — a stolen token can be killed
server-side at any moment, which a stateless JWT could not offer.

Methods:

| Member | Implementation | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `generate_key()` | `@staticmethod`, `secrets.token_urlsafe(48)` | 48 random bytes → ~64 URL-safe chars, ~384 bits of entropy. Cryptographically secure (`secrets`, not `random`). The 64-char field is exactly sized for it. |
| `is_valid` | `@property`: `False` if `not is_active`; else `not (expires_at and expires_at < now)` | A `NULL` `expires_at` is treated as never-expiring. **Not actually used by the DRF auth class**, which re-implements the same two checks inline so it can raise distinct messages. |
| `revoke()` | sets `is_active=False`, `revoked_at=now`, `save(update_fields=[...])` | Rows are kept, never deleted — the audit trail survives. |

#### 3.7.1 The three mobile auth endpoints

| Endpoint | View | Auth | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POST /inspection/api/auth/login/` | `MobileLoginView` (`api/views.py:91-110`) | `authentication_classes = []`, `AllowAny` | Reads `user_id` / `passwd` from `request.data`, calls `checkcred_client.verify_credentials`; on `CheckCredError` returns **401** `{"error": "..."}`; on success creates a fresh `MobileAuthToken` and returns **201** with the identity profile + `token` + `display_name`. |
| `POST /inspection/api/auth/logout/` | `MobileLogoutView` (`:113-120`) | `AUTH_CLASSES`, `IsAuthenticated` | `if isinstance(request.auth, MobileAuthToken): request.auth.revoke()`. Always returns `{"ok": true}`. A session- or Keycloak-authenticated caller therefore gets a successful no-op. |
| `GET /inspection/api/auth/me/` | `MobileMeView` (`:123-132`) | `AUTH_CLASSES`, `IsAuthenticated` | Re-hydrates identity/role on app launch from a stored token; overrides `display_name` with the token's cached copy when the caller used a token. |

The response body of login and `/auth/me/` is built by one shared helper so the two can never
drift (`line_inspection/api/views.py:56-66`):

```python
def _identity_profile(employee_id):
    return {
        'employee_id': employee_id,
        'is_admin': auth.is_admin(employee_id),
        'is_super_admin': auth.is_super_admin(employee_id),
        'cadre': viewing.display_label(employee_id),
        'tier': viewing.cadre_tier(employee_id),
        'is_management': viewing.is_management(employee_id),
    }
```

Login additionally adds `token` and `display_name`. Example success body:

```json
{"employee_id": "01073093", "is_admin": true, "is_super_admin": false,
 "cadre": "EE", "tier": "admin", "is_management": false,
 "token": "<64-char url-safe string>", "display_name": "SOME NAME"}
```

The `is_admin` / `is_management` / `tier` values are advisory **UI hints** for the app — every
endpoint re-derives authority server-side. `LiSession` in the Flutter app is explicit about this:
*"Server-side jurisdiction is authoritative regardless."*
(`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/models/li_session.dart:15`).

Client side: `AuthStore` (`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/services/auth_store.dart`)
persists the session JSON in `SharedPreferences` under key `li_session_v1`, loads it once at
startup, and exposes `authHeaders()` returning `{'Authorization': 'Token $t'}` merged into every
request. `LineInspectionApi.login` (`.../lib/services/line_inspection_api.dart:56-71`) accepts
200 **or** 201, maps 401 to a `LoginFailedException` carrying the server's `error` string, and
`logout()` is best-effort (`.../:76-82`) — it always clears locally even if the revoke call fails.
A `_guard` helper converts any 401 on a later call into `UnauthorizedException`, which the app
treats as "session expired → re-login".

Operational gaps worth flagging: `MobileLoginView` has **no rate limiting or lockout**, and each
login creates a **new** token without revoking prior ones, so tokens accumulate per employee.
Nothing prunes expired rows.

### 3.8 The DRF authentication layer

`line_inspection/api/authentication.py` defines one stand-in identity object and three
authentication classes. Its docstring restates the constraint: *"there is no
django.contrib.auth.User anywhere in this app, so request.user is a small stand-in object rather
than a real model instance."*

```python
class SimpleIdentity:
    is_authenticated = True

    def __init__(self, employee_id):
        self.employee_id = employee_id
        self.pk = employee_id

    def __str__(self):
        return self.employee_id
```

Just enough surface for DRF: `is_authenticated` (what `IsAuthenticated` checks), `pk` (what DRF's
throttling and some generic machinery look for), and `__str__` for logs. Views then read
`request.user.employee_id` — a pattern repeated ~20 times in `api/views.py`.

| Class | Trigger | Success → `(user, auth)` | Failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SessionEmployeeAuthentication` | `request.session['employee_id']` present | `(SimpleIdentity(employee_id), None)` | Returns `None` (declines) if the session key is absent — never raises. |
| `MobileTokenAuthentication` | `Authorization: Token <key>` | `(SimpleIdentity(token.employee_id), token)` — **`request.auth` is the `MobileAuthToken` instance** | Declines (`None`) if the header is missing/not `token ` or the key is empty; raises `AuthenticationFailed('Invalid or revoked token.')` for unknown/inactive, `AuthenticationFailed('Token expired — please sign in again.')` for expired. |
| `KeycloakBearerAuthentication` | `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` | `(SimpleIdentity(identity['employee_id']), token_string)` | Declines if not `bearer `/empty; converts `KeycloakClientError` into `AuthenticationFailed(str(exc))`. |

#### 3.8.1 `Token` vs `Bearer` — why all three coexist

This is the design point the code comments call out (`api/authentication.py:36-40`):

```python
"""For the Phase 4 Flutter field app: a DB-backed, revocable token issued by
the checkCred login endpoint. Uses the `Token` scheme (NOT `Bearer`, which
KeycloakBearerAuthentication owns) so the two coexist regardless of order —
each declines a header that isn't its scheme."""
```

Both token classes read the same `Authorization` header, so they must be distinguishable. By
giving the mobile token the `Token` scheme and leaving `Bearer` to Keycloak, each class can
cheaply inspect the scheme prefix (case-insensitively: `header.lower().startswith('token ')` /
`'bearer '`) and return `None` — "not mine" — for anything else. DRF then walks to the next
class. Session auth reads no header at all. The result: **any of the three can authenticate a
request, order is irrelevant for correctness, and no class can ever mis-parse another's
credential.** Had the mobile token also used `Bearer`, every mobile request would have been
shipped off to Keycloak's `/userinfo` first.

Note the offsets are hardcoded to the scheme lengths: `header[6:]` for `Token ` and `header[7:]`
for `Bearer `, then `.strip()`.

#### 3.8.2 `AUTH_CLASSES` order and the 401-vs-403 reasoning

`line_inspection/api/views.py:37-43`:

```python
# The mobile `Token` class is first so DRF's 401-vs-403 decision uses its
# `authenticate_header` ('Token') — a bad/revoked/expired token then returns
# 401 (which the app treats as "session expired → re-login") rather than 403.
# Each class declines a header that isn't its scheme, so they still coexist:
# a browser request with only a session cookie falls through to the session
# class, and a Keycloak `Bearer` token to the Keycloak class.
AUTH_CLASSES = [MobileTokenAuthentication, SessionEmployeeAuthentication, KeycloakBearerAuthentication]
```

The mechanism behind the comment: when DRF raises `NotAuthenticated`/`AuthenticationFailed`, it
calls `APIView.get_authenticate_header(request)`, which is
`self.authentication_classes[0]().authenticate_header(request)` — **the first class only**. If
that returns a string, DRF emits **401** with a `WWW-Authenticate` header; if it returns `None`,
DRF converts the response to **403**. `BaseAuthentication.authenticate_header` returns `None` by
default, and neither `SessionEmployeeAuthentication` nor `KeycloakBearerAuthentication` overrides
it. Only `MobileTokenAuthentication` does:

```python
def authenticate_header(self, request):
    return 'Token'
```
(`line_inspection/api/authentication.py:67-68`)

So putting it first is what makes an expired/revoked mobile token produce a 401 instead of a
403 — and the Flutter client keys its "re-login" behaviour purely off the 401 status code
(`_guard` in `line_inspection_api.dart`). Reordering `AUTH_CLASSES` would silently turn every
expired-token response into a 403 and strand the app.

`AUTH_CLASSES` is applied to **every** authenticated API view (18 of them, `api/views.py`), each
paired with `permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]`. The four unauthenticated views set
`authentication_classes = []` + `AllowAny`: `HealthView`, `PingView`, `MobileLoginView`,
`KeycloakExchangeView`/`KeycloakRefreshView`. `transcoapps/settings.py` has no `REST_FRAMEWORK`
block at all, so a view that forgot to set these would silently fall back to DRF's defaults
(`SessionAuthentication` + `BasicAuthentication` against the unused `auth_user` table) — every
view sets them explicitly today.

#### 3.8.3 The `_touch_after` throttle

```python
keyword = 'token'
# Only bother touching last_used_at when it's this stale, so a busy client
# doesn't write a row to the clear schema on every single request.
_touch_after = timedelta(minutes=5)
...
now = timezone.now()
if token.last_used_at is None or (now - token.last_used_at) > self._touch_after:
    token.last_used_at = now
    token.save(update_fields=['last_used_at'])
```
(`line_inspection/api/authentication.py:42-63`)

`last_used_at` exists for operational visibility ("is this token still in use?"), which needs
minute-scale precision at best. Writing it on every request would turn every read-only GET into
a read **plus a write** against the `clear` schema — a real cost when the field app polls, and a
source of row-lock contention on a hot token. The 5-minute staleness window keeps the signal
useful while making the write rate essentially negligible. `update_fields=['last_used_at']`
keeps it to a single-column UPDATE. (`keyword = 'token'` is declared for DRF-convention parity
but the code does the prefix test with a literal rather than reading it.)

Also note the ordering inside `authenticate`: revocation/expiry are checked **before** the touch,
so an invalid token never causes a write.

### 3.9 The three-tier authorization model

Three tiers, three completely different determination mechanisms — this is the part most likely
to be misremembered.

```
Super Admin  ─ a row in SuperAdmin keyed by employee_id       ─ CLI bootstrap
     │  (superset of Admin)
Admin        ─ your position_id appears in FieldEECadrePosition ─ granted by a Super Admin
     │
User         ─ an active RoleAssignment / LineTowerAssignment   ─ granted by an Admin
```

#### 3.9.1 Super Admin

- **Membership:** a row in `SuperAdmin` with your `employee_id`
  (`line_inspection/models.py:414-425`: `employee_id` unique, `granted_at` auto, `notes` text).
  `is_super_admin(employee_id)` is literally
  `SuperAdmin.objects.filter(employee_id=employee_id).exists()` (`line_inspection/auth.py:91-92`).
- **A person, not a position.** Unlike Admin, this is granted to a specific individual.
- **Bootstrap:** `python manage.py grant_super_admin --employee-id <id> [--notes "..."]`
  (`line_inspection/management/commands/grant_super_admin.py`). It is a `get_or_create`, hence
  idempotent, and prints either "Granted…" or "…is already a Super Admin."
- **Why a CLI escape hatch is necessary:** the docstring says it — *"an empty SuperAdmin table
  would otherwise lock everyone out of the admin panel (nobody could grant the first one through
  the UI)"*. The Manage Admins screen is itself `@super_admin_required`, so bootstrapping through
  the web UI is a chicken-and-egg impossibility. Shell access is the out-of-band root of trust.
  The README's worked example is `python manage.py grant_super_admin --employee-id 01073093`
  (`line_inspection/README.md:377`) — note the leading zero, matching the `zfill(8)` convention.
- **Note:** the command does **not** apply `zfill(8)`; it uses the argument verbatim after
  `.strip()`. A bootstrap typed without the leading zero would create a row that never matches a
  logged-in identity. There is also no `revoke_super_admin` command — removal means deleting the
  row directly.
- **Unlocks:** everything Admin unlocks, **plus** the Manage Admins screen
  (`/inspection/admin/super/positions/`), the SAP position-lookup JSON endpoint, the LILO screens
  (`/inspection/admin/lilo/`, `@super_admin_required` at `admin_views.py:415,440`), the LILO churn
  badge on the admin home (`admin_views.py:47-48`), and unconditional `is_management` (rollups /
  all-tower scope) via `viewing.is_management` (`viewing.py:142-143`).
- **A Super Admin can grant another Super Admin** — but only in the sense described in the model
  docstring; in practice new Super Admins are added via the CLI, since no UI form for
  `SuperAdmin` rows exists in `admin_views.py`. **The model docstring at `models.py:414-419`
  overstates what the UI provides.**

#### 3.9.2 Admin — a *position* is granted, not a person

This is the design subtlety that trips up every new reader.

`FieldEECadrePosition` (`line_inspection/models.py:428-440`) holds `position_id` (unique),
`position_text`, `notes`, `created_at`. A row means: *whoever currently holds SAP position
`position_id` is an Admin.*

The link back to a human is made at check time (`line_inspection/auth.py:79-88`):

```python
def is_admin(employee_id):
    """True if employee_id currently holds a position_id that's been
    granted Admin (FieldEECadrePosition) rights, or is a Super Admin —
    Super Admin is a superset of Admin, not a separate/unrelated tier."""
    if is_super_admin(employee_id):
        return True
    snapshot = EmployeeCadreSnapshot.objects.filter(employee_id=employee_id).first()
    if not snapshot or not snapshot.position_id:
        return False
    return FieldEECadrePosition.objects.filter(position_id=snapshot.position_id).exists()
```

Chain: `employee_id` → `EmployeeCadreSnapshot.position_id` → `FieldEECadrePosition.position_id`.

**Why grant a position rather than a person?** Because in a utility the *post* carries the
authority, not the individual. When an EE is transferred, SAP reassigns the position to the
successor; the next `sync_employee_cadre` run updates `EmployeeCadreSnapshot.position_id`, and
Admin rights follow the chair automatically — the outgoing officer loses them and the incoming
one gains them, with **no action in this app at all**. The corollary is that an Admin's rights
can change without anyone touching this system, and that a stale snapshot means stale
authority.

Two failure modes fall straight out of the implementation:
- An employee with **no** `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` row can never be an Admin (only a Super Admin).
- An employee whose snapshot has a blank `position_id` can never be an Admin.

**Candidate surfacing on the Manage Admins screen** (`line_inspection/admin_views.py:80-96`):

```python
# The exact candidate filter the user specified: DE/EE cadre + O&M postings.
# Real synced data uses the single combined code "DE/EE" (confirmed against
# the live sync, not two separate "DE"/"EE" values).
candidates_qs = (
    EmployeeCadreSnapshot.objects
    .filter(emp_sub_grp='DE/EE', position_text__icontains='O&M')
    .exclude(position_id='')
    .order_by('position_text')
)
```

Two filters, both essential:
- `emp_sub_grp='DE/EE'` — **exact match on one combined SAP code**. It is *not* `DE` or `EE`; it
  is the literal five-character string `DE/EE`. The comment records that this was confirmed
  against the live sync. Anyone "fixing" this to `emp_sub_grp__in=['DE','EE']` would empty the
  candidate list.
- `position_text__icontains='O&M'` — **O&M** = *Operation & Maintenance*, the field wing that
  actually walks lines, as opposed to Construction, Civil, Design, SCADA, etc. Not every EE is a
  field engineer; the rationale is spelled out in the model docstring (`models.py:429-433`).

The results are deduplicated **by position** into `seen_positions` (`admin_views.py:89-96`),
carrying `position_id`, `position_text`, a `sample_employee` name (the current holder, shown only
so a Super Admin can recognise the post), and a `granted` boolean.

The screen (`manage_admins`, `@super_admin_required`, `admin_views.py:56-103`) handles three POST
actions:

| `action` | Effect |
|---|---|
| `grant` | `FieldEECadrePosition.objects.get_or_create(position_id=..., defaults={'position_text': ...})` |
| `revoke` | `FieldEECadrePosition.objects.filter(position_id=...).delete()` — a **hard delete**, no audit row |
| `add_manual` | Saves `FieldEECadrePositionForm` (fields `position_id`, `position_text`, `notes`) — the fallback for a position that the DE/EE + O&M filter did not surface |

`position_text` is rendered `readonly` in the manual form and auto-filled by JS calling
`GET /inspection/admin/super/positions/lookup/<position_id>/` → `lookup_position`
(`@super_admin_required`, `admin_views.py:106-115`), which asks SAP live via
`sap_client.get_employee_by_position_id`. Rationale in the docstring: *"posid/postext are
interlinked in SAP, so an Admin only needs to type the position id"*.

**What Admin unlocks:** Roles & Jurisdiction (`/inspection/admin/assignments/`), the Checklist
Catalog editor, the SAP↔ArcGIS line mapping screen — and, in the API, the ability to close **any**
ticket in oversight rather than only tickets on towers they personally hold jurisdiction over
(`line_inspection/api/views.py:716-720`).

#### 3.9.3 User

A **User** is simply an employee with at least one active grant row. There is no "User" table
and no flag.

`RoleAssignment` (`line_inspection/models.py:448-462`):

| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `employee_id` | `CharField(32)` | The assignee. |
| `role` | `CharField(32)`, choices | `ROLE_CHOICES = [('FIELD_INSPECTOR', 'Field Inspector')]` — exactly one role exists today; `admin_views.py:149` hardcodes it on create. |
| `subdivision` | FK `Subdivision`, `PROTECT`, nullable | Grants **every** line in that subdivision. |
| `lines` | M2M `Line` | Grants specific lines. |
| `assigned_by_employee_id` | `CharField(32)` | Audit — set from the session, never from the form. |
| `assigned_at` | auto-add | |
| `is_active` | `BooleanField(default=True)` | Revocation is a soft flag; the screen's `deactivate` action sets it `False`, never deletes. |

`Meta.indexes = [Index(fields=['employee_id', 'is_active'])]` — the exact predicate every
jurisdiction query uses.

`LineTowerAssignment` (`:465-488`) complements it with a from-tower→to-tower **stretch** of a
line, for when a whole line is not one person's. Boundaries are stored as `Tower` FKs (not raw
indices) *"so rebuilding the schedule can't drift an assigned stretch"*.

Granting happens on `role_assignments` (`@admin_required`, `admin_views.py:141-207`) with four
POST actions: `create`, `deactivate`, `create_range`, `deactivate_range`. Candidate employees
default to the Admin's **reporting-hierarchy subordinates**
(`viewing.subordinate_snapshots`, via `_subordinates`) with a name/id search fallback capped at
50 rows — so an Admin's natural working set is their own org subtree, but the search escape
hatch means the UI does **not** hard-restrict an Admin to assigning only their own subordinates.
`create_range` validates that both boundary towers belong to the chosen line before saving.

#### 3.9.4 `is_admin` / `is_super_admin` semantics

- **Super Admin is a strict superset of Admin.** `is_admin()` returns `True` for any Super Admin
  *before* looking at positions (`auth.py:83-84`), and the docstring states it: *"Super Admin is
  a superset of Admin, not a separate/unrelated tier."* Consequence: a Super Admin never needs an
  `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` row or a granted position to reach the Admin screens.
- **Admin is not a superset of User.** Being an Admin grants *no* jurisdiction. An Admin with no
  `RoleAssignment` of their own has an empty `jurisdiction.visible_towers` and cannot submit an
  inspection anywhere — though `viewing.cadre_tier` still reports `'admin'` and they can close
  tickets via the `is_admin` bypass.
- Neither function is cached; each call is 1–2 indexed queries. They are called from the
  decorators, the context processor (every page), `_identity_profile`, `viewing.cadre_tier`,
  `viewing.is_management`, and `DefectTicketCloseView`.

### 3.10 The three view decorators

Hand-written in `line_inspection/auth.py:95-122`. **They shadow the names of Django's own
`django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required` etc. and are entirely unrelated to them** — they
know nothing about `request.user`, `LOGIN_URL`, or `PermissionDenied`. Views import them as
`from . import auth` and apply them as `@auth.login_required` (`admin_views.py`,
`dashboard_views.py`), which keeps the distinction visible at the call site.

```python
def login_required(view_func):
    @wraps(view_func)
    def wrapper(request, *args, **kwargs):
        if not request.session.get('employee_id'):
            login_url = reverse('line_inspection:login') + f'?next={request.path}'
            return redirect(login_url)
        return view_func(request, *args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper


def admin_required(view_func):
    @login_required
    @wraps(view_func)
    def wrapper(request, *args, **kwargs):
        if not is_admin(request.session['employee_id']):
            return HttpResponseForbidden('This section is restricted to Admins (EE cadre with an assigned field position).')
        return view_func(request, *args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper


def super_admin_required(view_func):
    @login_required
    @wraps(view_func)
    def wrapper(request, *args, **kwargs):
        if not is_super_admin(request.session['employee_id']):
            return HttpResponseForbidden('This section is restricted to Super Admins.')
        return view_func(request, *args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper
```

| Decorator | Anonymous | Insufficient tier | Response body on denial |
|---|---|---|---|
| `login_required` | 302 → `/inspection/login/?next=<path>` | n/a | — |
| `admin_required` | 302 (via the stacked `login_required`) | 403 | `This section is restricted to Admins (EE cadre with an assigned field position).` |
| `super_admin_required` | 302 | 403 | `This section is restricted to Super Admins.` |

Details:

- **The `?next=` redirect.** `login_required` appends `?next={request.path}` so that after a
  successful sign-in `login_view` sends the user back where they were aiming
  (`auth.py:38` reads `POST['next']` first, then `GET['next']`, then falls back to
  `reverse('line_inspection:admin-home')`). `login.html` carries it through the POST as a hidden
  input. Two caveats: `request.path` **excludes the query string**, so `?tower=42` is lost across
  a login bounce; and the value is not URL-encoded.
- **The tier decorators stack `@login_required` internally** — `admin_required` is
  `login_required(wraps(view_func)(wrapper))` — so a session check always runs *before*
  `request.session['employee_id']` is dereferenced with a bare `[...]` (which would otherwise
  `KeyError`). That is why the inner functions can index the session directly.
- **403 bodies are plain text**, produced by `HttpResponseForbidden`, not a styled template. A
  denied Admin sees an unstyled sentence, not the app chrome.
- `@wraps` preserves `__name__`/`__doc__` so `reverse()` and error pages name the real view.

Beyond the decorators, two views do their own inline gating:
`dashboard_views.py:230-231` restricts `/inspection/dashboard/reports/` with
`if not (is_mgmt or auth.is_admin(employee_id)): return HttpResponseForbidden('The management
reports are restricted to admins and management cadre.')`, and `dashboard_views.py:154` returns
`HttpResponseForbidden('That line is outside your jurisdiction.')` for an out-of-scope register
line. `line_inspection/tests/test_dashboard.py` asserts both of these 403s
(`:124`, `:187`, `:383`) by hand-building a session: `s = c.session; s['employee_id'] = eid; s.save()`.

### 3.11 Jurisdiction (edit) vs oversight (read) — the critical distinction

Two scope systems exist, deliberately kept in two separate modules, and confusing them is the
easiest way to introduce a privilege-escalation bug.

| | **Jurisdiction** (`line_inspection/jurisdiction.py`) | **Oversight** (`line_inspection/viewing.py`) |
|---|---|---|
| Question answered | "What may this employee **capture / edit**?" | "What may this employee **see**?" |
| Derived from | *Only* that employee's own active `RoleAssignment` + `LineTowerAssignment` rows | The union of the grants held by the employee **and everyone below them in the reporting tree** |
| Key functions | `visible_lines`, `visible_towers`, `range_tower_ids`, `can_edit_tower` | `subordinate_snapshots`, `visible_employee_ids`, `oversight_lines`, `oversight_towers`, `cadre_tier`, `is_management`, `circuits_at` |
| Used by | The write path: `_create_inspection` (`api/views.py:453`), ticket close | Every dashboard screen, all read API endpoints, the map |

**The invariant, stated in the source.** `jurisdiction.py:8-11`:

> *"The reporting-hierarchy-widened **oversight** (read) scope for the Phase 3 dashboard lives in
> viewing.py and is built on top of `_lines_for_assignments` below — never by widening these
> functions."*

and `viewing.py:4-8`:

> *"jurisdiction.visible_*/can_edit_tower is the *edit/capture* authority the REST API write path
> relies on and must stay scoped to an employee's own RoleAssignments. viewing.* is *read-only*
> oversight — a supervisor sees every tower assigned to Users beneath them in the reporting
> hierarchy, but that never grants edit rights."*

**A wider view NEVER grants edit rights.** The two modules share exactly one function —
`jurisdiction._lines_for_assignments(assignments)` — which turns a *set of assignment rows* into
lines. `viewing.oversight_lines` calls it with the subtree's rows; `jurisdiction.visible_lines`
calls it with one employee's rows. The widening happens in *which rows are passed in*, never
inside the edit-path functions.

**Worked example.** Take AEE Rao, EE Kumar (Rao's reporting manager), and SE Nair (Kumar's
manager). Only Rao holds a `RoleAssignment` — the Kadapa subdivision.

| Person | `jurisdiction.visible_towers` (may inspect) | `viewing.oversight_towers` (may see) | `cadre_tier` |
|---|---|---|---|
| AEE Rao | all Kadapa towers | all Kadapa towers (self is included in `visible_employee_ids`, so a leaf User's oversight equals their jurisdiction exactly — `viewing.py:64`) | `field_user` |
| EE Kumar | **∅ — nothing** | all Kadapa towers (Rao is a subordinate) | `supervisor` |
| SE Nair | **∅ — nothing** | all Kadapa towers plus every other subordinate's | `supervisor` |

If Kumar `POST`s an inspection for a Kadapa tower, `_create_inspection` calls
`jurisdiction.can_edit_tower('KUMAR', tower)` → no active `RoleAssignment` → `PermissionDenied:
"You don't have jurisdiction over this tower."` (`api/views.py:453-454`) — **even though the
tower is plainly visible on Kumar's own dashboard.** That asymmetry is intentional: it preserves
accountability (the person who signed the inspection is the person assigned to the asset) while
still giving supervisors full visibility. If Kumar becomes an Admin, that changes *ticket
closing* (the `is_admin` bypass at `api/views.py:719`) but still **not** inspection capture.

Full implementation — the BFS over `reporting_manager_id`, the tower-range union, `circuits_at`,
and the map bbox invariant — is section 6.

### 3.12 Auth decision table

Assumes the web dashboard and API as they stand. "Oversight scope" = own grants ∪ all
subordinates' grants; "own jurisdiction" = own grants only.

| Actor | Login screens | `/inspection/admin/` home | Dashboard map / tickets / inspections / register | `/inspection/dashboard/reports/` | Roles & Jurisdiction, Checklist, SAP mapping | Manage Admins, LILO | API reads | Submit an inspection | Close a ticket |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Anonymous** | yes (login, forgot-password, change-password are all ungated) | 302 → login | 302 → login | 302 → login | 302 → login | 302 → login | 401 (`/health/`, `/ping/`, `/auth/login/`, the two Keycloak endpoints are open) | no | no |
| **Logged-in employee, no assignment, not Admin** | — | yes (counts are global, not scoped) | yes, but **empty** — no lines/towers in scope | 403 | 403 | 403 | 200 with empty result sets | no (`can_edit_tower` false) | no |
| **User (has an active `RoleAssignment` / range)** | — | yes | own towers (+ subordinates' if any) | 403 | 403 | 403 | oversight-scoped | **yes**, on towers in own jurisdiction, subject to the 50 m GPS presence gate | only on towers in own jurisdiction |
| **Admin (granted `FieldEECadrePosition`)** | — | yes | oversight scope | **yes** (`is_admin` branch, `dashboard_views.py:230`) | **yes** | 403 | oversight-scoped | only where they personally hold a `RoleAssignment` — Admin grants **no** capture rights | **any** ticket (`is_admin` bypass) |
| **Super Admin (`SuperAdmin` row)** | — | yes, plus the LILO churn badge | **all** active lines and towers — `is_management` is forced `True`, and `oversight_lines`/`oversight_towers` honour it, so the map, tickets, inspections, register and rollups all cover the whole estate with no `RoleAssignment` needed | yes | yes | **yes** | all-tower / all-line | same as Admin — no implicit capture rights | any ticket |
| **Management cadre (`emp_sub_grp` ∈ `{CE, DIRECTOR, GM, JMD, CMD}`)** | — | yes | **all** active lines and towers (`is_management`), not just their subtree | **yes** (`is_management` branch) | 403 unless also an Admin | 403 unless also a Super Admin | all-tower / all-line; `SubdivisionListView` returns **all** subdivisions (`api/views.py:213-218`) | no, unless separately assigned | **any** ticket — `oversees_tower` widens with `oversight_towers` |

### 3.13 Findings and README discrepancies

**F1 — Hardcoded Keycloak client secret, contradicting the comment directly above it.**
`line_inspection/services/keycloak_client.py:19-21` reads:

```python
# No hardcoded secret default on purpose — a real secret must never live in
# source. Set KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET in the environment before runserver.
KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET = os.environ.get('KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET', '<redacted — a real 32-char secret is in the source>')
```

The default value is a real-looking 32-character secret. The same secret is also assigned as a
plain module-level setting at `transcoapps/settings.py:220`, alongside `KEYCLOAK_BASE_URL`,
`KEYCLOAK_REALM` and `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID` (`:217-219`) — note that those four settings are
**never read by any code**; the client reads `os.environ` directly, so the settings block is
dead weight that only serves to leak the secret. `line_inspection/README.md:352` explicitly
instructs *"Never hardcode `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET` as a source default"* and `:355` claims
*"None of these have hardcoded fallback secrets in code"* — **both statements are false against
the current code.** The secret should be rotated in Keycloak and both occurrences removed.

**F2 — Other secrets in tracked source.** `transcoapps/settings.py:44` contains a
`django-insecure-…` `SECRET_KEY` literal (a `startproject` default, but it signs session
cookies — sessions are the entire web auth mechanism, so anyone with this key can forge a
session for any `employee_id`). `transcoapps/settings.py:154` supplies a real-looking Postgres
password as the `PG_PASSWORD` default. `DEBUG = True` is hardcoded at `:47`.

**F3 — Dev login is active in this checkout and is undocumented in the README.**
`DEBUG=True` + `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN=1` + a set `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD` means any
employee id in `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` signs in with one shared string, on both the web panel and
the mobile API (which mints a real 30-day `MobileAuthToken`). The guards are well-designed —
`DEBUG` is a hard prerequisite — but `DEBUG` is itself hardcoded `True`, so the only real gate is
the env flag. `line_inspection/README.md` does not mention `services/dev_login.py` at all.

**F4 — README: "Login: `/inspection/login/` -> redirects to Keycloak -> `/inspection/auth/callback/`"**
(`line_inspection/README.md:288`). **Stale — the code does not do this.** `login_view` renders a
local form and calls checkCred; there is no `callback_view` and no `auth/callback/` route. The
same stale reference appears in the comment at `line_inspection/urls.py:9`. The README's own
