"Login" section (`:56-83`) is correct; only the Admin-panel section was not updated.

**F5 — README: "Two DRF authentication classes"** (`line_inspection/README.md:325-328`,
naming only `SessionEmployeeAuthentication` and `KeycloakBearerAuthentication`). **There are
three**, and the third — `MobileTokenAuthentication` — is the one actually used in production by
the field app. The README's changelog (`:544`) does describe it, so this is an un-updated section
rather than a wholesale omission. The API endpoint table at `:330-345` likewise omits
`/auth/login/`, `/auth/logout/`, `/auth/me/` and `/ping/`.

**F6 — `SupportRequestResolveView` performs no authorization check.**
`line_inspection/api/views.py:780-793`: any authenticated employee can `POST
/api/support-requests/<pk>/resolve/` for **any** support request id — there is no `is_admin`
test and no scope test, unlike the sibling `DefectTicketCloseView` which does check
(`:719-720`). `line_inspection/README.md:344` states *"Resolve is Admin-oversight, same as
ticket-close"*. **The code does not implement that.** (The *list* queryset at `:746-758` is
correctly scoped — only the resolve action is unguarded.)

**F7 — Unvalidated `next=` redirect.** `line_inspection/auth.py:38` passes a user-supplied
`next` straight to `redirect()` with no `url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme()` check (Django's
built-in `LoginView` does this check). `/inspection/login/?next=https://evil.example/` will
redirect off-site after a successful login — a classic open-redirect / phishing aid.

**F8 — No CSRF enforcement on session-authenticated API writes.**
`SessionEmployeeAuthentication` subclasses `BaseAuthentication`, not DRF's `SessionAuthentication`,
so it never calls `enforce_csrf`. DRF's `APIView` is `csrf_exempt` at the Django level, so a
cookie-authenticated `POST /inspection/api/...` from another origin is not CSRF-checked. In
practice Django's default `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE = 'Lax'` blocks cross-site POST cookies, so
this is defence-in-depth rather than an open hole today — but the protection is absent by
construction, and `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` includes wildcard ngrok domains
(`transcoapps/settings.py:70-74`). The HTML form views are unaffected (they use `{% csrf_token %}`
and normal middleware).

**F9 — No session hardening.** `login_view` does not rotate the session key on login (no
`cycle_key()`), so a session-fixation attacker who plants a session id before login keeps a
valid session after it. `transcoapps/settings.py` sets none of `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE`,
`SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY` (defaults `True`, so this one is fine), `SESSION_COOKIE_AGE`, or
`SESSION_EXPIRE_AT_BROWSER_CLOSE` — web sessions therefore last Django's default two weeks over
plain HTTP if the deployment is not TLS-terminated.

**F10 — Small consistency gaps.** `MobileAuthToken.is_valid` is defined but unused (the auth
class re-implements it inline). `grant_super_admin` does not `zfill(8)` its argument while
login normalisation does. `MobileTokenAuthentication.keyword = 'token'` is declared but the
prefix test uses a string literal. Login has no rate limiting on either the web or mobile path,
and mobile tokens accumulate per login with no pruning of expired rows.
## 4. Data Model — Part 1: GIS Master Data

Everything in this section lives in `line_inspection/models.py` lines 25–239, under the banner
comment *"1. GIS master data (synced from ArcGIS — see management/commands/sync_gis_towers.py)"*.
These five models — `Subdivision`, `SapLine`, `Line`, `Tower`, `Substation` — are the **reference
data** of the system: the physical grid as APTRANSCO's GIS department records it, mirrored into the
app's own Postgres tables so that every other feature (jurisdiction, inspection capture, the
register, rollups, the mobile app) can join against a stable local primary key instead of hitting a
remote ArcGIS FeatureServer per request.

All of these tables live in the `clear` schema of a shared production Postgres server, reached
through the `line_inspection_db` alias whose connection sets `-c search_path=clear`
(`transcoapps/settings.py:164`) and is selected by `LineInspectionRouter` in
`line_inspection/db_router.py`. The module docstring at `line_inspection/models.py:1-17` states the
rule plainly: no other schema on that server is read or written by this app.

### 4.0 Domain vocabulary used throughout this section

Define these once; the rest of the document assumes them.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **ArcGIS / FeatureServer** | Esri's REST GIS platform. APTRANSCO publishes its grid as feature layers at `https://gis.aptransco.gov.in/server/rest/services/AP_Grid_Map/...` (layer catalogue in `line_inspection/services/arcgis_client.py:80-125`). Each *feature* is a geometry plus a flat `properties` dict. |
| **Layer id / `source_layer`** | This app's short alias for one FeatureServer layer, e.g. `towers-132kv`, `lines-220kv`, `substations-400kv`. Only the 132/220/400 kV EHT (Extra-High-Tension) layers are synced (`sync_gis_towers.py:34-36`). |
| **OBJECTID / `arcgis_object_id`** | ArcGIS's own row id inside a layer. Unique **within** a layer only — hence the composite natural key described in §4.6. |
| **VT / virtual tower** | A row in an ArcGIS tower layer whose `tower_number` begins with `VT`. It is not a second physical mast; it is the *other electrical circuit* strung on a structure that already has a real tower row. See §4.8. |
| **Physical structure** | The actual steel mast in the field. One structure = one real tower row + zero or more co-located VT rows, grouped by `Tower.structure_key`. |
| **LILO** | *Line-In Line-Out.* A network reorganisation in which an existing line is cut at a tower and both cut ends are looped into a new substation, turning one line into two (or more). Physically the towers stay where they are, but ArcGIS re-issues new OBJECTIDs and new line names. This is the single biggest source of churn in the GIS master data and it is why several design decisions here look over-cautious. |
| **Tap line** | A branch off an existing line. Like a LILO it produces a *branched* corridor, where a single "order along the line" is ambiguous (§4.9). |
| **SAP / functional location** | SAP is APTRANSCO's enterprise asset/HR system. A *functional location* is SAP's hierarchical asset code for a line. SAP and ArcGIS are two independent registries of the same lines with no shared identifier — bridging them is what `SapLine` + `Line.sap_line` exist for (§4.7). |
| **PMI** | *Pre-Monsoon Inspection* — the detailed half of the twice-yearly inspection cycle; the other half is *Ground Patrolling* (routine, non-detailed). |
| **Cadre** | An employee's SAP grade/designation band (`AE`, `ADE/AEE`, `DE/EE`, `SE`, `CE` …). Used for display labels and the management-report gate, never as the authorization primitive. |
| **checkCred** | The upstream APTRANSCO credential-verification service used to authenticate an `employee_id`. Referenced here only because a dev bypass can skip it; identity and authorization are covered elsewhere in this document. |
| **Jurisdiction vs oversight** | *Jurisdiction* (`line_inspection/jurisdiction.py`) = the employee's **own** `RoleAssignment` scope; it is the write/capture authority. *Oversight* (`line_inspection/viewing.py`) = the read-only, reporting-hierarchy-widened superset. Both filter `is_virtual=False`; see §4.8.3. |
| **CP / SP / Boom** | The three observed values of `Tower.cp_sp` — see §4.11.1, including an explicit note that the repository never expands the abbreviation. |

### 4.1 `Subdivision`

**Purpose.** The APTRANSCO field-organisation unit that owns a stretch of grid. The administrative
hierarchy is Zone → Circle → Division → Subdivision, and every ArcGIS feature (tower, line,
substation) carries those four names as plain text attributes. `Subdivision` promotes the innermost
level to a real table so it can be a foreign key, because subdivision is the unit that
`RoleAssignment.subdivision` grants jurisdiction over — without a real row there would be nothing to
point a jurisdiction grant at.

**Where rows come from.** Nothing imports subdivisions directly. They are created as a *side effect*
of `sync_gis_towers`, by the `SubdivisionCache` helper (`sync_gis_towers.py:142-165`), which does a
`get_or_create(name=…)` the first time each distinct subdivision name is seen on any feature. The
cache exists because there are only a handful of distinct names across tens of thousands of features
and a naive `get_or_create` per feature would issue one query per row.

**Lifecycle.** Create-only. There is no `is_active` flag, no natural ArcGIS key, and — importantly —
`circle`/`division`/`zone` are passed in `defaults={...}`, which Django applies **only on creation**.
If ArcGIS later corrects a subdivision's parent circle, the local `Subdivision` row keeps the stale
value forever. The per-feature `Line.circle` / `Tower.circle` text columns *are* refreshed each sync,
so the two can disagree; the rollup views (`dashboard_views.py`) roll up on the denormalized text
columns on `Tower`, not on `Subdivision`, so this staleness does not currently affect reports.

| Field | Django type | Meaning | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `BigAutoField` (implicit PK) | Surrogate PK | auto |
| `name` | `CharField(max_length=255, unique=True)` | Subdivision name exactly as ArcGIS spells it | ArcGIS feature property `subdivision`, falling back to the upstream misspelling `subdivison` (`sync_gis_towers.py:150`) |
| `circle` | `CharField(max_length=255, blank=True)` | Parent Circle | ArcGIS `circle`, captured at first sight only |
| `division` | `CharField(max_length=255, blank=True)` | Parent Division | ArcGIS `division`, captured at first sight only |
| `zone` | `CharField(max_length=255, blank=True)` | Parent Zone | ArcGIS `zone`, captured at first sight only |
| `created_at` | `DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)` | Row creation timestamp | computed |
| `updated_at` | `DateTimeField(auto_now=True)` | Last `save()` timestamp | computed |

**Meta.** None declared — no `constraints`, no `indexes`, no `ordering`. The only index beyond the PK
is the implicit unique index Postgres creates for `name unique=True`, which is exactly the index
`SubdivisionCache` and the subdivision pickers need.

**Relationships out.** None.

**Relationships in.**

| From | Field | `on_delete` | `related_name` | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Line` | `subdivision` | `SET_NULL` | `lines` | GIS master data: losing the subdivision must not delete a line. |
| `Tower` | `subdivision` | `SET_NULL` | `towers` | Same. |
| `Substation` | `subdivision` | `SET_NULL` | `substations` | Same. |
| `RoleAssignment` | `subdivision` | `PROTECT` | `role_assignments` (`models.py:451`) | An authorization grant must never be silently voided by a master-data delete — deleting a subdivision that someone has jurisdiction over is an error, not a cascade. |
| `SupportRequest` | `subdivision` | `PROTECT` | `support_requests` (`models.py:620`) | Same reasoning: a support ticket's routing context must not vanish. |

The `SET_NULL` / `PROTECT` split is the recurring pattern in this schema: **GIS-derived pointers are
`SET_NULL`** (master data is disposable, the app degrades to the denormalized `*_name` text column),
**human-authored pointers are `PROTECT`** (an operator's decision must never be destroyed by a data
refresh). In practice neither fires, because §4.6's soft-delete policy means these rows are never
`DELETE`d at all.

### 4.2 `SapLine`

**Purpose.** A verbatim mirror of one row of APTRANSCO's SAP line master data. It exists so that the
app can eventually reconcile the GIS view of the network with the enterprise-asset view — SAP is
where work orders, maintenance history and financial asset records live, and it identifies a line by
a *functional location* code that appears nowhere in ArcGIS. `SapLine` holds the SAP side of that
bridge; `Line.sap_line` (§4.7) holds the bridge itself.

**Where rows come from.** `python manage.py import_sap_lines [--file <path>]`
(`line_inspection/management/commands/import_sap_lines.py`), which reads an Excel export with pandas.
The default path is `settings.BASE_DIR / 'EHT LINES SAP DATA 06.07.2026.XLSX'`
(`import_sap_lines.py:17`) — a hardcoded dated filename, so a newer export must be passed with
`--file` or the constant edited. The command hard-requires the two columns
`Functional Location` and `Description of functional location` and raises `CommandError` otherwise.

**Lifecycle.** `update_or_create` keyed on `functional_location`, so re-running with a newer export
refreshes descriptions in place and adds new codes; it never deletes. The command's own docstring is
emphatic that **importing creates no mapping by itself** — this is raw SAP data only.

| Field | Django type | Meaning | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `BigAutoField` (implicit PK) | Surrogate PK | auto |
| `functional_location` | `CharField(max_length=64, unique=True)` | SAP functional-location code — the natural key of the SAP row | Excel column `Functional Location`, `.strip()`ed; blank rows skipped |
| `description` | `CharField(max_length=255, blank=True)` | SAP's human description of the line | Excel column `Description of functional location`, `.strip()`ed |
| `voltage` | `CharField(max_length=16, blank=True)` | Voltage class, e.g. `132kV`. **Deliberately not `choices=VOLTAGE_CHOICES`** — this is raw SAP text and may contain classes the ArcGIS enum does not model (comment at `models.py:82`) | Computed: regex `(\d+)\s*KV` (`import_sap_lines.py:18`) applied first to `functional_location`, then to `description`; `''` if neither matches |
| `raw_row` | `JSONField(default=dict, blank=True)` | The entire spreadsheet row as `{column: value}`, with `NaN` normalised to `None` | Computed from the pandas row (`import_sap_lines.py:52`) |
| `imported_at` | `DateTimeField(auto_now=True)` | Last time this row was written by an import | computed |

**Meta.** None. The only non-PK index is the implicit unique index on `functional_location`.

**Relationships out.** None.

**Relationships in.** `Line.sap_line` — a `OneToOneField` with `on_delete=SET_NULL`,
`related_name='line'` (singular). Reverse access is therefore `sap_line.line`, returning a single
`Line` or raising `Line.DoesNotExist`. **This is a behavioural change from migration `0002`, where
`related_name` was `'lines'` (plural, a manager).** Any code or template still writing
`sap_line.lines.all()` would break; a grep of the tree finds none.

### 4.3 `Line`

**Purpose.** One transmission line (a named 132/220/400 kV circuit corridor) as ArcGIS records it,
including its polyline geometry. `Line` is the pivot of the whole application: jurisdiction is
granted per line or per subdivision-of-lines (`RoleAssignment`), towers hang off lines, the tower
schedule is computed *along* a line's geometry, the register is rendered per line, and the map's
line layer is `Line.geometry` straight out of this table.

**Where rows come from.** `python manage.py sync_gis_towers` (`_sync_lines`,
`sync_gis_towers.py:223-261`), which pulls the three layers `lines-132kv`, `lines-220kv`,
`lines-400kv` with `outFields='*'`.

**Lifecycle.** Upserted per sync via `bulk_create(update_conflicts=True, unique_fields=['source_layer','arcgis_object_id'])`
in 1,000-row chunks. Rows no longer returned upstream are flipped to `is_active=False` (never
deleted) at `sync_gis_towers.py:257-261`. The README states 1,212 lines were loaded in Phase 1
(unverified against a live DB).

| Field | Django type | Meaning | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `BigAutoField` (implicit PK) | Surrogate PK. Stable across ArcGIS churn; every FK in the app points here | auto |
| `source_layer` | `CharField(max_length=64)` | Which ArcGIS layer this row came from, e.g. `lines-220kv`. Also the voltage discriminator | computed from the loop variable `layer_id` |
| `arcgis_object_id` | `CharField(max_length=64)` | ArcGIS `OBJECTID`, stringified | ArcGIS `OBJECTID` / `objectid` (case-insensitive lookup) |
| `name` | `CharField(max_length=255, blank=True)` | Line name as ArcGIS spells it, e.g. `220KV VIJAYAWADA - GUNADALA CKT-1` | ArcGIS `line_name` |
| `voltage` | `CharField(max_length=16, choices=VOLTAGE_CHOICES)` | `132kV` / `220kV` / `400kV`. Not null-able and has no default — sync always sets it | Computed from the layer id: `VOLTAGE_BY_LAYER` splits `lines-220kv` → `220kV` (`sync_gis_towers.py:38-41`) |
| `line_length` | `CharField(max_length=64, blank=True)` | Route length as ArcGIS reports it. **Stored as text, not a number**, because the upstream values are not consistently numeric | ArcGIS `line_length`, `str()`-cast |
| `circuit_type` | `CharField(max_length=255, blank=True)` | `SC` / `DC` / `MC` etc. at line level | ArcGIS `circuit_type`, `str()`-cast |
| `date_of_commissioning` | `CharField(max_length=64, blank=True)` | Commissioning date. Text for the same reason as `line_length` | ArcGIS `date_of_commissioning`, `str()`-cast (note: unlike `Tower`, this is **not** passed through `normalize_arcgis_date`) |
| `zone` | `CharField(max_length=255, blank=True)` | Zone name, denormalized | ArcGIS `zone` |
| `circle` | `CharField(max_length=255, blank=True)` | Circle name, denormalized | ArcGIS `circle` |
| `division` | `CharField(max_length=255, blank=True)` | Division name, denormalized | ArcGIS `division` |
| `subdivision_name` | `CharField(max_length=255, blank=True)` | Subdivision name, denormalized (survives even if the FK is nulled) | ArcGIS `subdivision`/`subdivison` |
| `subdivision` | `FK(Subdivision, SET_NULL, null, blank, related_name='lines')` | Resolved subdivision row | `SubdivisionCache.get_or_create` |
| `sap_line` | `OneToOneField(SapLine, SET_NULL, null, blank, related_name='line')` | The SAP functional location this line corresponds to | `map_sap_lines` auto-match or the mapping admin page — **never** the GIS sync (`sap_line` is absent from `_sync_lines`'s `update_fields`, so a re-sync cannot clobber a mapping) |
| `geometry` | `JSONField(null=True, blank=True)` | Raw GeoJSON geometry (`LineString` or `MultiLineString`) | ArcGIS feature `geometry`, stored verbatim |
| `raw_properties` | `JSONField(default=dict, blank=True)` | **Every** ArcGIS attribute for this feature, untouched | ArcGIS feature `properties` |
| `is_active` | `BooleanField(default=True)` | Soft-delete flag; `False` = no longer present upstream | computed by the sync |
| `first_synced_at` | `DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)` | When this row was first created locally | computed |
| `last_synced_at` | `DateTimeField(auto_now=True)` | Last write. Also explicitly set by the deactivation `update()` | computed |

**Meta.**

| Kind | Name | Fields | Which query it serves |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `UniqueConstraint` | `uniq_line_source_object` | `(source_layer, arcgis_object_id)` | The upsert target of `bulk_create(update_conflicts=True, unique_fields=[...])`. Without it the sync could not do a conflict-based upsert at all, and re-running would duplicate every line. |
| `Index` | auto-named `line_inspec_name_a4a733_idx` | `(name)` | The SAP-mapping admin page's `Line.objects.filter(name__icontains=q).order_by('name')` (`admin_views.py:388-391`) and every `order_by('name')` line picker. Note a B-tree on `name` accelerates the `ORDER BY` and prefix matches, not the `icontains` scan itself. |

**Relationships out.** `subdivision` (`SET_NULL`), `sap_line` (`SET_NULL`, one-to-one).

**Relationships in.**

| From | Field | `on_delete` | `related_name` | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Tower` | `line` | `SET_NULL` | `towers` | A tower whose line row disappears is still a physical tower with inspection history; orphaning it into `line=NULL` is strictly better than deleting it. |
| `RoleAssignment` | `lines` (M2M) | n/a | `role_assignments` (`models.py:452`) | Explicit per-line jurisdiction grants. |
| `LineTowerAssignment` | `line` | `CASCADE` | `tower_ranges` (`models.py:473`) | A from/to stretch is meaningless without its line, so it is the one place a cascade is correct. |
| `LiloEvent` | `old_line` | `PROTECT` | `lilo_events_as_old` (`models.py:649`) | LILO lineage is an audit record; deleting the pre-LILO line would destroy the provenance. |
| `LiloEvent` | `new_lines` (M2M) | n/a | `lilo_events_as_new` (`models.py:650`) | The post-LILO line(s). |

### 4.4 `Tower`

**Purpose.** The single most important table in the system: one row per ArcGIS tower feature. It is
the unit of inspection (`Inspection.tower`), the unit of defect tracking (`DefectTicket.tower`), the
unit of map rendering, and — after the Data-Foundation expansion — also carries the **tower asset
master** (conductor, circuit and commissioning attributes promoted out of ArcGIS, §4.11), the
**virtual-tower/physical-structure model** (§4.8), the **tower schedule** (§4.9) and the
**denormalized inspection-status cache** (§4.10).

A deliberate design decision recorded in the README: **one indexed `Tower` table** was chosen over
three per-voltage tables, because ~113k rows (including VT) is small for Postgres and a single table
keeps `Inspection.tower` / `DefectTicket.tower` as ordinary foreign keys instead of a polymorphic
mess.

**Where rows come from.** `sync_gis_towers._sync_towers` (`sync_gis_towers.py:263-338`), pulling
`towers-132kv`, `towers-220kv`, `towers-400kv` with `outFields='*'`. Row counts from the README
(unverified against a live DB): 67,128 towers in Phase 1 before VT rows were imported, ~113k
including VT afterwards.

**Lifecycle.** Chunked upsert on `(source_layer, arcgis_object_id)`; missing rows soft-deleted to
`is_active=False`; `insulator_type`/`type_of_earthing` deliberately excluded from `update_fields` so
manual data survives (§4.11.2); LILO churn handled separately and only on demand by
`services/lilo_matching.py` + `manage.py lilo_reconcile` / `detect_tower_churn`, never by the routine
sync.

#### 4.4.1 Complete field table

| Field | Django type | Meaning | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `BigAutoField` (implicit PK) | Surrogate PK. **The durable identity of a physical tower** — LILO reconcile revives a survivor in place under its existing PK precisely so `Inspection`/`DefectTicket` history is preserved | auto |
| `source_layer` | `CharField(max_length=64)` | `towers-132kv` / `towers-220kv` / `towers-400kv` | loop variable |
| `arcgis_object_id` | `CharField(max_length=64)` | ArcGIS `OBJECTID`, stringified. **Not stable across a LILO** | ArcGIS `OBJECTID`/`objectid` |
| `tower_number` | `CharField(max_length=64, blank=True)` | Location number on the line, e.g. `42`, `12/1`, `VT 42`, `Boom`. `.strip()`ed at sync time (`sync_gis_towers.py:298`) — a leading/trailing space would otherwise break the `VT` prefix test and the numeric sort | ArcGIS `tower_number` |
| `tower_type` | `CharField(max_length=64, blank=True)` | Structural type. Comment at `models.py:133` warns these are *real domain values, not assumed* — observed values look like `"Boom"`, **not** the placeholder `DA/DB/DC/DD` codes the checklist catalog was seeded with | ArcGIS `tower_type` |
| `voltage` | `CharField(max_length=16, choices=VOLTAGE_CHOICES)` | `132kV`/`220kV`/`400kV` | derived from `source_layer` |

| `circuit_type` | `CharField(max_length=32, blank=True)` | `SC` / `DC` / `MC` / `DC/SC` | ArcGIS `circuit_type` |

| `relay_setting_length_in_km` | `CharField(max_length=32, blank=True)` | Protection relay's configured line length. Text, because upstream values are not consistently numeric | ArcGIS `relay_setting_length_in_km`, `str()`-cast |
| `span_km` | `FloatField(null=True, blank=True)` | Span to the next tower, km. Only reliably populated on 132 kV — §4.11.1 | ArcGIS `span_km` via `_to_float` |

| `insulator_type` | `CharField(max_length=128, blank=True)` | Insulator description — **manually maintained**, §4.11.2 | manual only; sync never writes it |

| `is_virtual` | `BooleanField(default=False)` | `True` for a VT row (§4.8) | Computed: `tower_number.upper().startswith('VT')` (`sync_gis_towers.py:316`) |
| `structure_key` | `CharField(max_length=64, blank=True)` | Groups a real tower and its co-located VT rows into one physical structure. Format `"{voltage}:{lat:.5f}:{lng:.5f}"` | Computed by `_assign_structure_keys` (§4.8.2) |
| `line_sequence` | `PositiveIntegerField(null=True, blank=True)` | 1-based ordered position of this tower along its line (the "tower schedule") | Computed by `build_tower_schedule` / `schedule.assign_line_sequence` (§4.9) |
| `line_offset_m` | `FloatField(null=True, blank=True)` | Perpendicular distance in metres from the tower to `Line.geometry`; a QA / branch-detection signal | Computed by the same, rounded to 2 dp; `None` when the geometry fallback was used |
| `line_name` | `CharField(max_length=255, blank=True)` | Line name **as text**, exactly as ArcGIS returned it. Kept even when the FK resolves, so a tower is still identifiable when `line` is NULL | ArcGIS `line_name` |
| `line` | `FK(Line, SET_NULL, null, blank, related_name='towers')` | Resolved line row | Computed: `line_lookup[(line_name, voltage)]` — an in-memory dict built once per run (`sync_gis_towers.py:265`) |
| `latitude` | `FloatField(null=True, blank=True)` | WGS-84 latitude | GeoJSON `geometry.coordinates[1]` if the feature is a Point, else the ArcGIS `latitude` attribute; `_to_float`-coerced |
| `longitude` | `FloatField(null=True, blank=True)` | WGS-84 longitude | GeoJSON `geometry.coordinates[0]`, else ArcGIS `longitude` |
| `zone` / `circle` / `division` / `subdivision_name` | `CharField(max_length=255, blank=True)` ×4 | Denormalized administrative hierarchy — these four are what the management rollups group by | ArcGIS `zone`/`circle`/`division`/`subdivision`\|`subdivison` |
| `subdivision` | `FK(Subdivision, SET_NULL, null, blank, related_name='towers')` | Resolved subdivision row | `SubdivisionCache` |
| `geometry` | `JSONField(null=True, blank=True)` | Raw GeoJSON Point | ArcGIS feature `geometry` |
| `raw_properties` | `JSONField(default=dict, blank=True)` | Every ArcGIS attribute for this feature | ArcGIS feature `properties` |
| `is_active` | `BooleanField(default=True)` | Soft-delete flag | sync |
| `first_synced_at` | `DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)` | First local creation | computed |
| `last_synced_at` | `DateTimeField(auto_now=True)` | Last write | computed |
| `last_inspection_at` | `DateTimeField(null=True, blank=True)` | Status cache — timestamp of the newest inspection (§4.10) | Written by `status.bump_tower_cache` / `warm_tower_status` |
| `last_worst_criticality` | `CharField(max_length=16, choices=WORST_CHOICES, default='none')` | Status cache — worst criticality of that inspection; `'none'` = never inspected | same |
| `last_inspection_type` | `CharField(max_length=16, choices=INSPECTION_TYPE_CHOICES, null=True, blank=True)` | Status cache — which cycle that inspection belonged to; NULL = unknown/legacy | same |

Two sync-time caveats worth knowing, both visible in the code and neither documented in the README:

1. `line_lookup` is built from `Line.objects.all()` — **including inactive lines** — and is keyed on
   `(name, voltage)`. If two `Line` rows share a name and voltage (which duplicate ArcGIS entries or
   a stale soft-deleted row can produce), the *last one iterated wins* and towers may be linked to a
   deactivated line. `_sync_lines` runs before `_sync_towers` in the same invocation, so the lookup
   at least reflects the current sync's line rows.
2. `date_of_commissioning` is normalised for towers but not for lines (`sync_gis_towers.py:248` vs
   `:315`), so the same logical attribute can be formatted differently on the two tables.

**Out:** `line` → `Line` (`SET_NULL`, `related_name='towers'`), `subdivision` → `Subdivision`
(`SET_NULL`, `related_name='towers'`).

| From | Field | `on_delete` | `related_name` | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Inspection` | `tower` | `PROTECT` | `inspections` (`models.py:500`) | An inspection is a legal field record. Deleting the tower it refers to must be impossible, not cascading. This is the single strongest reason towers are soft-deleted. |
| `DefectTicket` | `tower` | `PROTECT` | `tickets` (`models.py:584`) | Same — an open defect ticket must never be silently destroyed. |
| `LineTowerAssignment` | `from_tower` | `PROTECT` | `range_starts` (`models.py:474`) | The boundary towers *are* the assignment; deleting one would silently redefine somebody's work stretch. |
| `LineTowerAssignment` | `to_tower` | `PROTECT` | `range_ends` (`models.py:475`) | Same. |

| `LiloTowerRemap` | `surviving_tower` | `PROTECT` | `lilo_remaps` (`models.py:674`) | The remap row's whole purpose is to record which tower survived; that pointer must hold. |

### 4.5 `Substation`

**Purpose.** A 132/220/400 kV substation as a point feature. Present for map context and future
line-endpoint modelling.

**Where rows come from.** `sync_gis_towers._sync_substations` (`sync_gis_towers.py:340-380`). A
quirk worth knowing: **all three substation layer aliases point at the same FeatureServer layer 13**
(`arcgis_client.py:103-105`); they are separated by
`filter_substation_features_by_voltage()` inside `fetch_all_features`, which matches a voltage code
in the feature's `voltage` attribute — and the ArcGIS service stores 220 kV substations with the code
**`"200"`**, not `"220"` (`arcgis_client.py:311-317`). Without that mapping the 220 kV substation
sync would return nothing.

**Lifecycle.** Same upsert-and-soft-delete cycle as `Line`/`Tower`. The README reports 384
substations loaded in Phase 1 (unverified against a live DB).

**Honest status note:** a grep of the entire app finds `Substation` referenced *only* in
`models.py` and `sync_gis_towers.py`. Nothing reads it — no view, no serializer, no template, no
management report. It is populated master data awaiting a consumer, not a live feature.

### 4.6 Deep dive — the `(source_layer, arcgis_object_id)` natural key, soft delete, and `raw_properties`

#### 4.6.1 Why the key is composite

ArcGIS `OBJECTID` is unique *within a layer*, not across layers. Tower #1 exists in
`towers-132kv`, `towers-220kv` **and** `towers-400kv` simultaneously and they are three different
physical towers. So the natural key must be the pair. Every one of the four ArcGIS-backed models
therefore declares:

```python
class Meta:
    constraints = [
        models.UniqueConstraint(fields=['source_layer', 'arcgis_object_id'],
                                name='uniq_tower_source_object'),
    ]
```

This is not decorative. It is the `unique_fields=` argument that makes the batched upsert work:

```python
model.objects.using('line_inspection_db').bulk_create(
    batch, update_conflicts=True,
    unique_fields=['source_layer', 'arcgis_object_id'],
    update_fields=update_fields,
)
```
— `sync_gis_towers.py:214-216`. Postgres turns that into `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (source_layer,
arcgis_object_id) DO UPDATE SET …`, which requires a real unique index on exactly those columns.

Just as important is what the key is *not*: it is **not** the primary key. The PK stays a surrogate
`BigAutoField`. ArcGIS re-issues OBJECTIDs when a line is redrawn (a LILO), so an OBJECTID-keyed PK
would mean a LILO destroys and recreates every tower on the corridor — annihilating its inspection
history. Instead `services/lilo_matching.py` re-identifies survivors by *coordinates* (a physical
tower keeps its coordinates through a LILO; thresholds `AUTO_EXACT_M = 5.0`,
`AUTO_NUMBER_M = 60.0` with a matching tower number, `CANDIDATE_M = 250.0` for manual review) and
revives the existing row **under its existing PK**, rewriting only `arcgis_object_id`.

#### 4.6.2 Why nothing is ever hard-deleted

Each sync collects the set of OBJECTIDs it actually saw per layer and then, instead of deleting the
rest:

```python
stale = Tower.objects.filter(source_layer=layer_id, is_active=True) \
                     .exclude(arcgis_object_id__in=seen_ids[layer_id])
count = stale.update(is_active=False, last_synced_at=now)
```
— `sync_gis_towers.py:334-338` (identical shape for `Line` and `Substation`).

The reason is stated in the sync's module docstring at `sync_gis_towers.py:10-11` and repeated in
`models.py`: `Inspection.tower` and `DefectTicket.tower` are `on_delete=PROTECT`, and
`LineTowerAssignment.from_tower`/`to_tower` are too. A hard delete would either raise
`ProtectedError` mid-sync (breaking the whole run because ArcGIS dropped one feature) or, with a
looser `on_delete`, orphan or destroy legally significant field records. Soft delete makes an
upstream disappearance a *non-event* for the sync: the row stays, history stays intact, and every
read path simply filters `is_active=True`.

There is a real consequence the codebase takes seriously: a soft-deleted tower that still carries
inspection history is "stranded". `manage.py detect_tower_churn` exists purely to flag those — it
finds deactivated towers with inspection history or active range assignments that have an *active*
co-located twin within `CHURN_M = 30.0` metres, i.e. a probable undeclared LILO or road-works shift
where the history should be migrated rather than left behind. It is read-only and never run by the
routine sync.

#### 4.6.3 The `raw_properties` policy

Every ArcGIS-backed model carries `raw_properties = models.JSONField(default=dict, blank=True)` and
the sync writes the feature's *entire* `properties` dict into it, while separately promoting a
handful of attributes to real typed columns.

The rationale, from the sync docstring (`sync_gis_towers.py:8-9`) and the model comment
(`models.py:113`, `models.py:179`): **promotion is for querying, preservation is for truth.** Adding
a promoted column later is a cheap additive migration *if the data was already captured*; it is a
full re-sync of ~113k features against a production GIS server if it was not. Migration `0004` is
exactly that scenario paying off — nine tower-master columns and two manual ones were added in one
additive migration and could be backfilled straight out of `raw_properties`.

Two supporting details make the policy work:

- The sync always calls `fetch_all_features(..., extra_params={'outFields': '*'})`
  (`sync_gis_towers.py:203`), which **overrides** the curated per-layer field list in
  `get_arcgis_layer_fields()`. That curated list exists only because some fields are missing from
  some layers and requesting them makes ArcGIS reject the whole query with a generic 400 — the
  comment at `arcgis_client.py:141-147` documents that `location_number` was removed upstream, and
  that `insulator_type`/`type_of_earthing`/`span_km` exist only on `towers-132kv`. With `'*'` the
  sync sidesteps the problem entirely and still captures whatever each layer happens to have.
- `apply_domain_descriptions()` and `normalize_feature_dates()` run inside `fetch_all_features`
  before the sync ever sees the properties, so `raw_properties` holds *decoded* ArcGIS coded-domain
  values (human-readable descriptions), not raw numeric domain codes.

### 4.7 Deep dive — `Line.sap_line`, the SAP↔ArcGIS bridge

#### 4.7.1 It is a `OneToOneField`, and the README is out of date

Current code (`models.py:110`):

```python
sap_line = models.OneToOneField(SapLine, on_delete=models.SET_NULL,
                                null=True, blank=True, related_name='line')
```

The field's history across migrations:

| Migration | Definition | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0001_initial` | `sap_line_id = CharField(max_length=64, null=True, blank=True)` | A bare text column — no relation at all. |
| `0002` | drops `sap_line_id`; adds `sap_line = ForeignKey(SapLine, SET_NULL, null, blank, related_name='lines')` | Becomes a real FK. Many lines could point at one `SapLine`. |
| `0005` | `AlterField` → `ForeignKey(..., unique=True)` | Enforces one-to-one at the DB level. |
| `0006` | `AlterField` → `OneToOneField(..., related_name='line')` | **Semantics unchanged** — `OneToOneField` *is* `ForeignKey(unique=True)` in Django. The change clears Django's system-check warning **`fields.W342`** ("Setting `unique=True` on a `ForeignKey` has the same effect as using a `OneToOneField`"). It also flips `related_name` from plural to singular, which is the only behavioural difference: reverse access is now `sap_line.line` (an object) rather than `sap_line.lines` (a manager). |

> **README discrepancy.** `line_inspection/README.md:178-186` still describes this field as
> "FK to `SapLine` … **`unique=True`** enforces a one-to-one SAP↔ArcGIS line mapping". The code has
> been a `OneToOneField` since migration `0006`. The *meaning* the README conveys is correct; the
> type name and the reverse accessor name are stale.

#### 4.7.2 Why a nullable unique column is exactly the right constraint

Postgres unique indexes treat `NULL`s as distinct from one another, so a nullable unique column
permits **unlimited unmapped rows** while still forbidding two rows from claiming the same value.
That is precisely the required semantics:

- Most lines are unmapped. The README reports 1,167 SAP lines imported and only 302 of 1,212 ArcGIS
  lines auto-matched at high confidence (unverified against a live DB) — the remaining ~910 sit at
  `sap_line = NULL` indefinitely, which the constraint happily allows.
- Double-mapping is a data-integrity error. Two ArcGIS lines pointing at one SAP functional location
  would mean the enterprise system cannot tell which physical corridor a work order belongs to.

The admin UI is written around that guarantee rather than duplicating the check in Python:

```python
line.sap_line_id = request.POST.get('sap_line_id') or None
try:
    # Atomic so a unique-violation rolls back cleanly instead of
    # leaving the connection in an aborted-transaction state.
    with transaction.atomic(using='line_inspection_db'):
        line.save(update_fields=['sap_line'])
except IntegrityError:
    messages.error(request, 'That SAP line is already mapped to another ArcGIS line — clear the existing mapping first.')
```
— `admin_views.py:372-381`. The `transaction.atomic` wrapper is not incidental: in Postgres an
`IntegrityError` aborts the surrounding transaction, and without a savepoint every subsequent query
on that connection fails with "current transaction is aborted".

The auto-matcher enforces the same invariant optimistically: `map_sap_lines` pre-computes
`claimed_sap_line_ids` and excludes already-claimed `SapLine`s from the candidate pool
(`map_sap_lines.py:23,28,40`), so it can never propose a duplicate.

Matching itself is name-similarity scoring shared by the command and the admin page
(`services/sap_matching.py`, one implementation so the two can never disagree): tokenise both names,
drop noise tokens (`LINE`, `KV`, `DC`, `SC`, `CKT`, `TAP`, …) and tokens shorter than 3 characters,
hard-zero the score on a voltage mismatch, compute a Jaccard index, then multiply by `0.3` when both
names carry an explicit circuit number and the numbers differ ("almost certainly the wrong circuit of
a duplicated route"). `HIGH_CONFIDENCE_JACCARD = 0.75`, tuned up from an initial 0.5 after
spot-checking caught false positives.

Minor inconsistency in the admin page's counters: `unmatched_count` filters `is_active=True` but
`matched_count` does not (`admin_views.py:404-405`), so the two need not sum to the active line
count.

#### 4.7.3 Why the surrogate `id` stays the PK

Making the SAP functional location the primary key of `Line` would be superficially attractive — it
is the enterprise-wide identifier. The code comment at `models.py:107-109` and the README both reject
it, and the reasoning is worth internalising because it generalises to the whole schema:

1. **SAP codes get corrected.** A functional location is human-maintained data; typos are fixed and
   hierarchies are restructured. A primary key must never change.
2. **Lines get LILO-split.** One line becomes two, and neither successor cleanly inherits the
   predecessor's SAP code. A natural PK cannot express "this row is the continuation of that row".
3. **A mutable PK cascades.** `Line.id` is referenced by `Tower.line` across ~113k tower rows, by the
   `RoleAssignment.lines` M2M join table, by `LineTowerAssignment.line`, and by both
   `LiloEvent.old_line` and the `LiloEvent.new_lines` M2M. An `UPDATE` of a PK propagates through
   every one of those (Django would have to rewrite them; Postgres would have to re-check every FK),
   turning a clerical correction in SAP into a multi-table rewrite on a shared production server.

The general rule this expresses: **externally-owned identifiers are natural keys stored beside the
PK, never the PK itself.** The same rule produces `(source_layer, arcgis_object_id)` as a unique
constraint rather than a PK in §4.6.

### 4.8 Deep dive — virtual towers and physical structures

#### 4.8.1 What a VT row is, and why it exists

A single steel structure can carry more than one three-phase circuit — a double-circuit (DC) tower
carries two, a multi-circuit (MC) tower up to four. ArcGIS does not model that as one feature with a
multiplicity attribute. Instead it emits **one feature per circuit**: the first circuit gets a normal
tower row, and each additional circuit gets a separate, *co-located* row whose `tower_number` is
prefixed `VT` (e.g. `VT 42` sitting at the same coordinates as tower `42`). Those extra rows are what
this codebase calls **virtual towers**.

Earlier phases of this app simply discarded them — `get_layer_where_clause()` used to filter
`tower_number NOT LIKE 'VT%'`. The Data-Foundation step reversed that decision, and the function now
documents why (`arcgis_client.py:298-306`):

```python
def get_layer_where_clause(layer_id):
    """...
    Tower layers now include VT (virtual) towers: a VT row is the second/other
    circuit of a multi-circuit line sharing the same physical structure as a
    real tower (co-located). Field crews need to know every circuit strung on a
    structure, so we no longer drop `tower_number LIKE 'VT%'`. ...
    """
    return '1=1'
```

The operational need is concrete: an inspector standing at a tower must know *every* circuit passing
overhead — a defect on the second circuit's insulator string is on the same structure they are
looking at, and a shutdown plan depends on which circuits are affected. Dropping VT rows made those
circuits invisible.

`Tower.is_virtual` is set purely lexically at sync time:

```python
is_virtual=tower_number.upper().startswith('VT'),
```
— `sync_gis_towers.py:316`, where `tower_number` has already been `.strip()`ed at line 298. The strip
matters: a leading space in the upstream data would make the prefix test fail and silently promote a
VT row to a real, inspectable tower.

#### 4.8.2 `structure_key` — grouping by coordinate proximity

`structure_key` is the identifier of the *physical structure*, shared by a real tower and all its
co-located VT rows. It is assigned by `_assign_structure_keys()`
(`sync_gis_towers.py:99-139`), which runs once per voltage layer over all that layer's parsed
features, **before** anything is written to the database.

The key format is a canonical coordinate string:

```python
def _canonical_key(voltage, lat, lng):
    return f'{voltage}:{lat:.5f}:{lng:.5f}'
```
— e.g. `132kV:16.55571:81.54668`. Voltage is part of the key so that a 132 kV and a 220 kV line
crossing at nearly the same point are never merged into one "structure".

The algorithm has two passes:

1. **Real towers seed the structures.** Every non-virtual tower with coordinates gets
   `structure_key = _canonical_key(voltage, its own lat, its own lng)` and is inserted into a spatial
   hash `grid` keyed by `(round(lat, 4), round(lng, 4))` — a ~11 m bucket (`_CELL = 4`).
2. **VT towers snap to the nearest real tower.** For each VT row the code scans the 3×3 block of grid
   cells around its own cell and picks the nearest seeded real tower within the threshold. A VT with
   no real tower in range — an **orphan VT** — falls back to keying on its own coordinates, so it
   forms a structure of one rather than being left blank.

The threshold, verified in code at `sync_gis_towers.py:104`:

```python
_CELL = 4                        # rounding decimals for the spatial grid (~11 m)
_MATCH_THRESHOLD2 = 0.0003 ** 2  # ~33 m, squared (degrees)
```

`0.0003°` of latitude is `0.0003 × 110,574 ≈ 33.2 m`; at Andhra Pradesh's ~16° N latitude `0.0003°`
of longitude is `0.0003 × 111,320 × cos(16°) ≈ 32.1 m`. So the README's "~33 m" is accurate as a
description of the constant. Note the comparison itself is done in **squared degrees**
(`d2 = (clat-lat)**2 + (clng-lng)**2`), not metres, so the match region is a circle in degree space —
very slightly elliptical when measured in metres. For matching towers metres apart this is immaterial.

> **Finding (code vs. its own comment / the README): the effective search radius is narrower than
> the stated threshold.** The candidate scan only visits `dlat, dlng ∈ (-1, 0, 1)` cells of size
> `10**-4°` (`sync_gis_towers.py:122,132-134`), i.e. it looks at most ±0.0001° away, while
> `_MATCH_THRESHOLD2` permits matches out to 0.0003°. Two points more than one grid cell apart can
> land in cells that differ by 2 or 3 and will never be compared. Matching is therefore *guaranteed*
> only within ~0.0001° (≈11 m) and merely *possible* out to ~33 m depending on where the rounding
> falls. Since genuine VT rows are emitted at (near-)identical coordinates to their real tower, this
> does not appear to bite in practice — the unit test at
> `line_inspection/tests/test_dashboard.py:397-408` uses exactly-co-located points — but a VT
> displaced by 15–30 m would silently become an orphan structure. Widening the neighbourhood to ±3
> cells (or enlarging `_CELL`) would make behaviour match the documented threshold.

`structure_key` is written by the sync and *is* in `update_fields`, so it is recomputed every run. It
is stable as long as coordinates are stable — which is the same durability assumption the LILO
matcher relies on.

#### 4.8.3 THE INVARIANT: only `is_virtual=False` towers are inspected or counted

A VT row is an informational mirror. It has no independent physical existence, so inspecting it would
double-count the structure, and its "inspection" would be indistinguishable from the real tower's.
The invariant is therefore: **only real towers are ever inspected, assigned, counted or coloured.**

Every enforcement point found by grepping `is_virtual` across the app:

| # | Location | What it does | Category |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `line_inspection/api/views.py:451` | `if tower.is_virtual: raise ValidationError({'tower': 'Virtual (VT) towers are not inspected — inspect the real co-located tower.'})` inside `_create_inspection` | **Write gate** — the last line of defence; every inspection, web or mobile, goes through here |
| 2 | `line_inspection/jurisdiction.py:85` | `visible_towers()` returns `Tower.objects.filter(scope, is_active=True, is_virtual=False)` | Edit/capture scope |
| 3 | `line_inspection/jurisdiction.py:68` | `range_tower_ids()` expands a from/to stretch with `is_virtual=False` | Edit/capture scope |
| 4 | `line_inspection/viewing.py:90` | `oversight_towers()` filters `is_active=True, is_virtual=False` | Read/oversight scope — feeds the map, tickets, inspections list, rollups and the mobile dashboard |
| 5 | `line_inspection/api/views.py:296` | `MapLineListView` per-line tower rollup counts `is_active=True, is_virtual=False` | Counting |
| 6 | `line_inspection/api/views.py:810` | `MobileDashboardView` management path: `Tower.objects.filter(is_active=True, is_virtual=False)` | Counting |
| 7 | `line_inspection/dashboard_views.py:240` | `rollup_view` management path: `Tower.objects.filter(is_active=True, is_virtual=False)` | Counting |
| 8 | `line_inspection/schedule.py:127` | `line_schedule(line, include_virtual=False)` drops VT rows | Optional filter |
| 9 | `line_inspection/register.py:97` | Resolves a VT column's inspection from the co-located **real** tower (`structure_key` + `is_virtual=False`) | Read-through, not exclusion |
| 10 | `line_inspection/sync_gis_towers.py:316` | Sets the flag in the first place | Origin |

Points 5–7 are the *management/all-towers* code paths that bypass `oversight_towers()`; they repeat
the filter explicitly rather than inherit it, which is why the invariant survives even when the
oversight scope is skipped.

Two places intentionally do **not** exclude VT rows, and both are correct:

- `viewing.circuits_at(tower)` (`viewing.py:96-110`) deliberately gathers *all* co-located rows —
  real and virtual — to answer "which circuits run through this structure?", surfaced by
  `GET /inspection/api/towers/<id>/` and the map pop-up. Excluding VT would defeat its purpose.
- `register.build_register()` (`register.py:80-120`) includes VT rows **as columns** so the digital
  register mirrors the paper one circuit-for-circuit, but sources each VT column's cells from the
  co-located real tower's inspection via `structure_key`. The template badges them: 
  `{% if h.is_virtual %}<span class="crit-chip">VT</span>{% endif %}`
  (`line_inspection/templates/line_inspection/dashboard_register.html:76`). The consequence is
  intended — **an inspected structure reads as inspected on every circuit passing through it.**

Test coverage for the invariant lives in `line_inspection/tests/test_dashboard.py`:
`TowerStructureTests.test_scopes_exclude_vt` asserts both `viewing.oversight_towers` and
`jurisdiction.visible_towers` return only the real tower;
`test_circuits_at_returns_all_colocated_lines` asserts `circuits_at` returns both circuits; and
`test_structure_linking_by_colocation` exercises `_assign_structure_keys` directly with a co-located
pair plus an orphan.

### 4.9 Deep dive — the tower schedule (`line_sequence`, `line_offset_m`)

#### 4.9.1 What they mean

`Tower.line_sequence` is the tower's **1-based ordinal position walking along its line from one end to
the other** — the "tower schedule" in field parlance, the order in which a patrolling crew encounters
towers. It is what makes "towers 12 through 40 of this line" a meaningful, machine-checkable phrase.
`Tower.line_offset_m` is the **perpendicular distance in metres from the tower to the line's
polyline**; it is a quality signal, not an ordering input. A large offset means either bad
coordinates or a tower that belongs to a branch of the corridor rather than the main run.

Both are NULL until `build_tower_schedule` has run. Both are recomputed, never incrementally patched.

#### 4.9.2 How `build_tower_schedule` assigns them

The command (`line_inspection/management/commands/build_tower_schedule.py`) iterates active lines and
delegates the actual work to `line_inspection/schedule.py:compute_line_order(line)`, so the same logic
is reused by the LILO reconcile's per-line `assign_line_sequence()`.

The primary method is **geometric projection**: take the line's GeoJSON `LineString` (or flatten a
`MultiLineString`), convert every vertex and the tower's lat/lng into local metres with an
equirectangular approximation about the line's first vertex, then for each polyline segment compute
the closest point and the cumulative distance *along* the line to it. The tower's sort key is that
along-distance; the perpendicular distance to the closest point becomes `line_offset_m`
(`schedule.py:53-77`).

```python
_M_PER_DEG_LAT = 110_574.0
_M_PER_DEG_LON_EQ = 111_320.0

def _to_xy(lon, lat, cos_lat0):
    return (lon * _M_PER_DEG_LON_EQ * cos_lat0, lat * _M_PER_DEG_LAT)
```

The module docstring is explicit that this is deliberately **pure Python with no PostGIS**: "an
equirectangular metres approximation about the line's first vertex is plenty accurate for *ordering*
towers along a ~kilometres-long corridor." Avoiding a PostGIS dependency on a shared production
server was worth more than sub-metre accuracy the use case does not need.

The **fallback** is a numeric-prefix sort on `tower_number`
(`schedule.tower_sort_key`: leading integer first by value, then the rest lexicographically, with
non-numeric labels like `Boom` sorted to the tail). It is used when either condition holds
(`schedule.py:89-91`):

- the line has fewer than 2 usable geometry vertices (missing or degenerate geometry), **or**
- the line is **branched**, detected as *any duplicate `tower_number` among its active towers*:
  ```python
  dup = any(c > 1 for c in Counter(t.tower_number for t in towers if t.tower_number).values())
  use_geometry = len(verts) >= 2 and not dup
  ```

Duplicate tower numbers are the signature of a Tap or LILO corridor: two physical branches each
numbered from 1, so a single linear "distance along the line" ordering is genuinely ambiguous and
projection would interleave the two branches nonsensically. The `tower_number` sort at least produces
a stable, human-recognisable order.

Towers that have a line but no coordinates are appended after the projected ones, sorted by
`tower_sort_key`, with `line_offset_m = None` (`schedule.py:102-103`). In the fallback path *all*
offsets are `None`.

The command reports the split at the end — `"{geom_lines} lines ordered by geometry, {fallback_lines}
by tower_number fallback"` — and writes with `bulk_update` in 1,000-row batches inside
`transaction.atomic(using='line_inspection_db')`. It is idempotent and re-runnable, which matters
because it must be re-run after every `sync_gis_towers` that changed tower membership.

Reading it back is `schedule.line_schedule(line, include_virtual=True)`, which orders by
`F('line_sequence').asc(nulls_last=True), 'tower_number', 'id'` — so an un-scheduled line still
renders in a sensible order rather than by insertion order.

#### 4.9.3 Why `LineTowerAssignment` stores boundary *towers*, not sequence numbers

`LineTowerAssignment` (`models.py:471-475`) is the "this employee patrols towers 12→40 of line X"
grant, for when a single line is shared between crews. The obvious implementation would store
`from_sequence = 12, to_sequence = 40`. The code deliberately does not:

```python
line       = models.ForeignKey(Line,  on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='tower_ranges')
from_tower = models.ForeignKey(Tower, on_delete=models.PROTECT, related_name='range_starts')
to_tower   = models.ForeignKey(Tower, on_delete=models.PROTECT, related_name='range_ends')
```

The reasoning, stated at `models.py:161-162`: **a schedule rebuild must not be able to drift an
assigned stretch.** `line_sequence` is a derived, recomputed value. If ArcGIS adds three towers at
the start of a corridor, or a line flips direction, or the branch-detection heuristic switches a line
from geometry mode to fallback mode, every sequence number shifts — and a stretch stored as
`12→40` would silently now cover a *different set of physical towers*, quietly changing who is
authorized to inspect what. Stored as boundary towers, the assignment always means the same two steel
structures and everything between them, whatever the numbering happens to be today.

Membership is resolved at read time by `jurisdiction.range_tower_ids()`
(`jurisdiction.py:51-73`), which looks up the two boundary towers' *current* sequences, sorts them
(so from/to order does not matter), and selects the real towers in between:

```python
f_seq, t_seq = r.from_tower.line_sequence, r.to_tower.line_sequence
if f_seq is not None and t_seq is not None:
    lo, hi = sorted((f_seq, t_seq))
    ids.update(Tower.objects.filter(
        line_id=r.line_id, is_active=True, is_virtual=False,
        line_sequence__gte=lo, line_sequence__lte=hi,
    ).values_list('id', flat=True))
else:
    ids.update({r.from_tower_id, r.to_tower_id})   # schedule not built yet
```

The `else` branch is the fail-safe: if the schedule has not been built for those towers,
the range degrades to *just the two boundary towers* rather than silently expanding to the whole
line. Failing closed is the right default for an authorization primitive. This is also why the
`(line, line_sequence)` composite index exists — this query runs on every jurisdiction check.

### 4.10 Deep dive — the tower status cache (`last_inspection_at`, `last_worst_criticality`, `last_inspection_type`)

#### 4.10.1 What is denormalized, and why

The three `last_*` columns cache the answer to "what is this tower's most recent inspection, and how
bad was it?" — a question the map, the rollups and the mobile dashboard ask about **every tower in
scope, on every page load**.

Computing it honestly means a latest-per-tower lookup against `Inspection`. `status.py` does have
that query, and it is well-optimised (a single Postgres `DISTINCT ON` over the
`(tower, saved_at)` index):

```python
rows = (qs.order_by('tower_id', '-saved_at', '-id')
          .distinct('tower_id')
          .values_list('tower_id', 'worst_criticality'))
```
— `status.latest_inspection_status()`, `status.py:39-43`. But `oversight_towers()` for a senior
manager can be ~67k rows, and colouring a map or summing a rollup would mean shipping 67k ids into
that query on every request. The cache lets the hot paths read the answer straight off the `Tower`
row — `dashboard_views.rollup_view` and `api.views.MobileDashboardView` aggregate with plain
`Count(..., filter=Q(last_worst_criticality='critical'))`, and `MapTowerListView` selects
`last_worst_criticality` as just another column in the GeoJSON `values()` — **with no `Inspection`
join at all**. The `(last_inspection_at)` index serves the `inspected` counts.

The columns are stated to be **rebuildable from `Inspection` at any time** (`models.py:188`), which is
what makes the denormalization safe: `Inspection` remains the source of truth, and the cache is
disposable.

| Column | Type | Caches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `last_inspection_at` | `DateTimeField(null=True, blank=True)` | `Inspection.saved_at` of the newest inspection. NULL ⇒ never inspected. |
| `last_worst_criticality` | `CharField(max_length=16, choices=WORST_CHOICES, default='none')` | That inspection's `worst_criticality`. `'none'` ⇒ never inspected — note it defaults to a *value*, not NULL, so counting queries never need `COALESCE`. |
| `last_inspection_type` | `CharField(max_length=16, choices=INSPECTION_TYPE_CHOICES, null=True, blank=True)` | That inspection's cycle. NULL ⇒ unknown (pre-Phase-4 rows never stamped one). |

#### 4.10.2 Where the cache is written

**Hot path.** `api.views._create_inspection` calls, as the last statement inside the same
`transaction.atomic()` block that created the `Inspection`, its `ItemResult`s, its `DefectEntry`s and
its auto-raised `DefectTicket`s:

```python
# Phase 3: advance the tower's denormalized status cache in the same
# transaction so the map/rollups reflect this inspection immediately.
tower_status.bump_tower_cache(tower, now, inspection.worst_criticality, inspection.inspection_type)
```
— `api/views.py:542-544`. Being inside the transaction is the point: either the inspection and the
cache both land, or neither does. There is no window in which the map disagrees with the data.

`bump_tower_cache` itself (`status.py:67-77`) contains the one non-obvious rule:

```python
def bump_tower_cache(tower, saved_at, worst_criticality, inspection_type):
    if tower.last_inspection_at and saved_at and saved_at < tower.last_inspection_at:
        return
    tower.last_inspection_at = saved_at
    tower.last_worst_criticality = worst_criticality
    tower.last_inspection_type = inspection_type
    tower.save(update_fields=['last_inspection_at', 'last_worst_criticality', 'last_inspection_type'])
```

**The cache only ever advances.** This matters because the Flutter field app captures offline and
syncs later: an inspection performed on Monday can arrive after one performed on Tuesday. Without the
guard, a late-arriving older inspection would regress the tower's colour and criticality. Note the
comparison is against `saved_at` — the server-side `timezone.now()` at submission time
(`api/views.py:482,491`) — not the inspector-entered `date`. `update_fields` keeps the write to three
columns, so a concurrent sync updating GIS attributes on the same row does not lose them.

**Bulk path.** `python manage.py warm_tower_status`
(`line_inspection/management/commands/warm_tower_status.py`) rebuilds the cache from scratch:
collect every distinct `tower_id` that has an inspection, run one `DISTINCT ON (tower_id)` ordered by
`-saved_at, -id`, then `bulk_update` in batches of 500.

```python
latest = (Inspection.objects.filter(tower_id__in=tower_ids)
          .order_by('tower_id', '-saved_at', '-id')
          .distinct('tower_id')
          .values('tower_id', 'saved_at', 'worst_criticality', 'inspection_type'))
```

Run it after deploying migration `0003`, and any time the cache is suspected stale. It is idempotent.
Two properties to be aware of: it only touches towers that *have* inspections (a tower whose
inspections were all deleted keeps a stale cache), and unlike `bump_tower_cache` it **overwrites
unconditionally** — which is correct, because it is computing the true latest rather than merging in
one new record.

#### 4.10.3 When the cache is deliberately bypassed

The cache stores the latest inspection of *any* type. When a caller needs the latest of a **specific
cycle** — "show me PMI status only" — the cache cannot answer, and the code falls back to the live
query. `MapTowerListView` (`api/views.py:344-357`) does exactly that: when an `inspection_type` query
parameter is present it caps the tower set at `MAX_MAP_TOWERS`, calls
`tower_status.latest_inspection_status(capped_ids, inspection_type=…)`, and colours from that result
instead. `register.build_register()` similarly uses `status.latest_inspections(..., inspection_type)`.
This is the intended division of labour: **cache for the default view, live `DISTINCT ON` for
cycle-filtered views**, with the tower cap keeping the live query bounded.

### 4.11 Deep dive — tower master columns

#### 4.11.1 Promoted from ArcGIS

Nine columns added by migration `0004` (additive-only), all written by the sync.

| Column | Domain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `cp_sp` | The structure's role, with observed values **`CP`**, **`SP`** and **`Boom`**. **The repository never expands the abbreviation** — `models.py:137` says only "CP / SP / Boom (structure role)" and the README repeats "(CP/SP/Boom role)". Do not guess an expansion from this document. What the code *does* tell us is that `Boom` is functionally different from the other two: `_parse_circuit_count` returns `None` for anything containing `BOOM` or `GANTRY`, with the comment "terminal structures, not line circuits" — i.e. a Boom is a substation-entry/gantry structure that terminates conductors rather than a line tower carrying circuits through. `schedule.tower_sort_key` likewise sorts non-numeric labels such as `Boom` to the tail of a line. |
| `tower_ckts_conductor` | A free-text descriptor combining circuit configuration and conductor, e.g. `DCT, 2C, ACFR Panther` — read as "double-circuit tower, 2 circuits, ACFR Panther conductor". It is the most reliable single source for circuit count, which is why the parser reads it first. |
| `circuit_type` | Coarse configuration: `SC` (single-circuit), `DC` (double-circuit), `MC` (multi-circuit), and mixed values such as `DC/SC` where a corridor changes configuration. Used as the parser's fallback. |
| `circuit_count` | **Computed, not fetched.** The integer number of three-phase circuits on the structure: 1, 2 or 4. |
| `conductor_type` | The conductor product name, e.g. `ACSR Panther`, `ACSR Moose`, `ACFR Panther`. Determines the conductor's rated capacity and its inspection failure modes. |
| `no_of_conductors_per_phase` | **Bundle size.** On higher-voltage lines each electrical phase is carried by several physically separate sub-conductors held apart by spacers, to reduce corona loss and reactance. A value of 2 means "twin bundle" — two conductors per phase, six conductors per circuit. This is **orthogonal to `circuit_count`**: a DC tower with a twin bundle is `circuit_count=2, no_of_conductors_per_phase=2` and carries 2 × 3 × 2 = 12 conductors. The model comment flags the confusion explicitly (`models.py:142`), because "2C" and "2 conductors per phase" read almost identically in the source data. |
| `relay_setting_length_in_km` | The line length configured into the distance-protection relay at the substation. Can legitimately differ from the surveyed route length; kept as text because upstream values are not consistently numeric. |
| `span_km` | Distance to the adjacent tower. **Only reliably populated on 132 kV.** The concrete reason is in `arcgis_client.py:141-147`: `span`/`span_km` "aren't reliable across layers, so requesting them would 400 the 220/400kV queries" — the field is simply absent from the 220 kV and 400 kV tower layers' schemas. Because the sync fetches with `outFields='*'`, the column is populated wherever the source layer actually carries it and stays NULL elsewhere. Treat a NULL `span_km` on a 220/400 kV tower as "not available upstream", never as "zero span". |
| `date_of_commissioning` | When the structure was energised — the base for age-related deterioration expectations. Passed through `normalize_arcgis_date()`, which converts ArcGIS's epoch-milliseconds representation to a `YYYY-MM-DD` string; stored as text because upstream formats are inconsistent. |

The circuit-count parser, verbatim (`sync_gis_towers.py:75-96`):

```python
def _parse_circuit_count(tower_ckts_conductor, circuit_type):
    text = (tower_ckts_conductor or '').upper()
    if 'BOOM' in text or 'GANTRY' in text:   # terminal structures, not line circuits
        return None
    if '4C' in text or 'MCT' in text: return 4
    if '2C' in text or 'DCT' in text: return 2
    if '1C' in text or 'SCT' in text: return 1
    ct = (circuit_type or '').upper()
    if 'MC' in ct: return 4
    if 'DC' in ct: return 2
    if 'SC' in ct: return 1
    return None
```

Order matters: the descriptive string is checked before the coarse `circuit_type`, and the
Boom/Gantry check comes first so a terminal structure is never assigned a circuit count. Note the
fallback's substring test means `'MC/DC'` yields 4 (MC is checked first) — a case pinned by
`test_dashboard.py:394`. All nine columns are surfaced by `GET /inspection/api/towers/<id>/`
(`api/views.py:396-410`), which backs the map pop-up.

#### 4.11.2 Manually maintained: `insulator_type` and `type_of_earthing`

```python
# Manually maintained — empty/absent in ArcGIS, so never written by the sync.
insulator_type = models.CharField(max_length=128, blank=True)
type_of_earthing = models.CharField(max_length=128, blank=True)
```
— `models.py:147-149`.

These two attributes matter for inspection (insulator string type determines which checklist items
apply; earthing arrangement determines what an earth-resistance reading should be) but ArcGIS does
not carry usable values: per `arcgis_client.py:142-144` they "exist only on `towers-132kv` (and are
empty)". So the app models them as **local, human-owned data on a table otherwise owned by the sync**.

Protecting them requires one specific discipline, called out in a comment right above the list
(`sync_gis_towers.py:267-276`):

```python
# NOTE: insulator_type / type_of_earthing are deliberately NOT in update_fields —
# they are manually maintained (empty/absent in ArcGIS) and must survive re-syncs.
update_fields = [
    'tower_number', 'tower_type', 'voltage', 'line_name', 'line', 'latitude', 'longitude',
    'cp_sp', 'tower_ckts_conductor', 'circuit_type', 'circuit_count', 'conductor_type',
    ...
]
```

Because the sync upserts with `bulk_create(update_conflicts=True, update_fields=update_fields)`,
Postgres's `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET` touches **only the listed columns**. Any column omitted from
that list keeps its existing value. That is the whole protection mechanism, and it is fragile in a
specific way: the `Tower(...)` constructor at `sync_gis_towers.py:302-321` never sets these two
fields, so on an **insert** they are written as `''` (the field default) — correct for a new tower —
but if either name were ever added to `update_fields` without also being populated from ArcGIS, every
manually entered value in the system would be blanked on the next sync. The same omission protects
`line_sequence`, `line_offset_m` and the three `last_*` cache columns, which are likewise absent from
`update_fields`.

> **Gap worth recording.** These two columns are declared manually maintained, and
> `GET /inspection/api/towers/<id>/` reads them back (`api/views.py:402`) — but a grep across
> `*.py`, `*.html` and `*.dart` finds **no admin screen, form, API endpoint or management command
> that writes them**. Today the only way to populate `insulator_type` / `type_of_earthing` is a
> direct DB update or a `manage.py shell` session. The schema and the read path are ready; the
> capture UI does not exist yet. The README's phrasing ("manually maintained") describes the intent
> accurately but could be read as implying a UI exists.

### 4.12 The module-level choice constants

Four choice lists and one numeric constant are defined in this part of the file, between
`Subdivision` and `SapLine` (`models.py:41-73`).

**`VOLTAGE_CHOICES`** (`models.py:41-45`) — used by `Line.voltage`, `Tower.voltage`,
`Substation.voltage`.

| Value | Label |
| --- | --- |
| `132kV` | 132kV |
| `220kV` | 220kV |
| `400kV` | 400kV |

Only these three EHT classes are in scope. The values are produced mechanically from the layer alias
by `VOLTAGE_BY_LAYER` (`sync_gis_towers.py:38-41`: `'towers-220kv'.rsplit('-',1)[1].replace('kv','kV')`),
so the string form is load-bearing — changing a label here without changing the derivation would
break every sync write. Note `SapLine.voltage` deliberately does **not** use this enum, because raw
SAP text may contain classes outside it.

**`WORST_CHOICES`** (`models.py:49-55`) — the criticality ladder, worst-case status of a tower or an
inspection.

| Value | Label | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `none` | Not inspected | Sentinel, not a severity. Distinguishes "never inspected" from "inspected and fine". |
| `ok` | Normal | Inspected, no defects. |
| `minor` | Minor | Defect(s), lowest severity. |
| `major` | Major | Defect(s), elevated severity. |
| `critical` | Critical | Defect(s), highest severity. |

**Why it is declared this high up in the file** — the comment at `models.py:47-48` answers directly:

```python
# Worst-case status of a tower/inspection. Defined here (not further down) so
# the Tower denormalized status cache can reference it. 'none' == never inspected.
```

`WORST_CHOICES` logically belongs with the transactional inspection models in section 4 of
`models.py` — `Inspection.worst_criticality`, `DefectEntry.criticality`, `DefectTicket.criticality`
all use it (or its three-value sibling for defect rows, which excludes `none`/`ok`). But
`Tower.last_worst_criticality` at `models.py:190` also references it, and Python evaluates a module
top to bottom: a name used in a class body at line 190 must already be bound. Denormalizing the
criticality onto `Tower` forced the constant upward. The ordering of the list is also meaningful —
`services/criticality.py:worst_of()` reduces a set of criticalities to the worst one, and the
dashboard's `status.STATUS_COLORS` maps these exact keys to the POC's colour codes
(`none` `#898781`, `ok` `#0ca30c`, `minor` `#fab219`, `major` `#ec835a`, `critical` `#d03b3b`) so
that map markers, legend and rollup bars cannot drift apart.

**`INSPECTION_TYPE_CHOICES`** (`models.py:60-63`) — the twice-yearly inspection cycle.

| Value | Label | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ground_patrol` | Ground Patrolling | The routine, non-detailed walk of the line. |
| `pmi` | Pre-Monsoon Inspection | The detailed inspection carried out before the monsoon season, when weather-driven failure risk peaks. |

The comment at `models.py:57-59` records the migration strategy: the field is **nullable everywhere**
because the Flutter app (Phase 4) is what starts stamping it, and pre-existing rows must stay NULL
(meaning *unknown*, not *neither*). Every cycle-aware query therefore treats NULL as "counts toward
the latest-of-any-type view but matches no specific cycle filter" — see
`status.latest_inspection_status(tower_ids, inspection_type=None)`.

**`PRESENCE_FLAG_CHOICES`** (`models.py:68-72`) — Phase 4 GPS proof-of-presence outcome, stamped on
each `Inspection`. Declared in this block but consumed by the transactional models.

| Value | Label | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `in_range` | In range (<=50 m) | Server-recomputed distance from the submitted fix to `Tower.latitude/longitude` was within the radius. |
| `out_of_range` | Out of range (overridden) | A fix was supplied but exceeded the radius; the submit required a written `override_reason`. |
| `no_fix` | No GPS fix (overridden) | No usable fix; likewise requires an `override_reason`. |

**`PRESENCE_RADIUS_M = 50.0`** (`models.py:73`) — the gate radius in metres. The rationale at
`models.py:65-67`: "Presence is the utmost criterion for field inspection: the mobile app enforces a
50 m gate with an audited override, and the server records which case applied." The server never
trusts a client-supplied distance — `_create_inspection` recomputes it with `_haversine_m()` against
the tower's stored coordinates (`api/views.py:465-479`) and rejects an out-of-range or no-fix submit
that carries no `override_reason`. Legacy JSON submits that send no coordinates and no
`presence_flag` are `gps_aware = False` and exempt from the gate, with `presence_flag = ''`.

Note this 50 m presence radius is a **different constant for a different purpose** from the ~33 m
`_MATCH_THRESHOLD2` co-location radius in §4.8.2 and the 5/60/250/30 m LILO thresholds in
`services/lilo_matching.py`. They are not interchangeable and none is derived from another.
