### 4.14 Summary of README-vs-code discrepancies found in this section

| # | README says | Code says | Where |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `Line.sap_line` is a `ForeignKey` with `unique=True` | It is a `OneToOneField` since migration `0006`, with `related_name='line'` (singular), not `'lines'` | `README.md:178-181` vs `models.py:110`, `migrations/0006_…py:34-38` |
| 2 | VT rows are grouped "by coordinate proximity, ~33 m" | The constant is ~33 m, but the spatial-grid neighbourhood scanned is only ±1 cell of `10**-4°` (≈11 m), so matching is guaranteed only to ~11 m and merely possible out to 33 m | `README.md:200-202` vs `sync_gis_towers.py:103-139` |
| 3 | `insulator_type` / `type_of_earthing` are "manually maintained" | Correct that the sync never writes them, but **no** admin screen, form, API endpoint or command writes them either — direct DB access is currently the only way | `README.md:212-213` vs grep across `*.py`/`*.html`/`*.dart` |
| 4 | Row counts: 67,128 towers / 1,212 lines / 384 substations, ~113k towers incl. VT, 302/1,212 lines mapped, 1,167 SAP lines | Not verifiable from the repository — these are README assertions against a live DB and are reproduced here as such | `README.md:405-416`, `:629` |
## 5. Data Model — Part 2: Checklist Catalog, Cadre & Roles

This section covers sections 2 and 3 of `line_inspection/models.py` (lines 242–488): the
**checklist catalog** (the questionnaire a field inspector fills in at a tower) and the
**cadre / role / jurisdiction** tables (who an employee is, and what they are allowed to
inspect). Section 4 of this document covered the GIS master data (`Subdivision`, `SapLine`,
`Line`, `Tower`, `Substation`); the transactional inspection tables (`Inspection`,
`ItemResult`, `DefectEntry`, `DefectTicket`) are covered later.

### 5.1 Where these tables live

Every model in `line_inspection/models.py` — including all eleven described here — is routed
by `line_inspection/db_router.py` to the `line_inspection_db` connection, which points at the
`clear` schema of the shared APTRANSCO Postgres server. The router is absolute in both
directions:

```python
# line_inspection/db_router.py:26
def allow_migrate(self, db, app_label, model_name=None, **hints):
    if app_label == APP_LABEL:
        return db == DB_ALIAS      # our models ONLY migrate onto line_inspection_db
    if db == DB_ALIAS:
        return False               # no other app may create tables in `clear`
    return None
```

No model in this section declares `Meta.db_table`, so all table names are Django defaults:
`line_inspection_catalogversion`, `line_inspection_checklistitemgroup`,
`line_inspection_checklistitem`, `line_inspection_defect`,
`line_inspection_followupquestion`, `line_inspection_criticalityrule`,
`line_inspection_employeecadresnapshot`, `line_inspection_superadmin`,
`line_inspection_fieldeecadreposition`, `line_inspection_roleassignment`
(+ the `..._lines` M2M through table), `line_inspection_linetowerassignment`.

All primary keys are the implicit `BigAutoField id` (see
`line_inspection/migrations/0001_initial.py`); none of these models uses a natural key as its
PK, deliberately — see §5.6 and §5.11 for the reasoning in each case.

---

### 5.2 The core design decision: the questionnaire is data, not code

The single most important thing to understand about the catalog is stated in the module
docstring of `line_inspection/models.py:10`:

> *Checklist catalog — DB-backed and editable, not hardcoded Python, since the questionnaire
> is not yet finalised and will be revised after field engineers review the app.*

and restated in `line_inspection/README.md:47`:

> *The checklist (items/defects/follow-up questions/criticality thresholds) is DB-backed and
> editable, not hardcoded Python — it is not finalised and field engineers will request
> changes after reviewing the app.*

The rationale is operational, not aesthetic. APTRANSCO's transmission-line inspection
proforma is a living document owned by field engineering, not by the software team. Hardcoding
the 25 items / 75 defects / 22 follow-up questions in Python would mean every wording tweak,
every new defect type, every recalibrated criticality threshold becomes a code change → a
review → a deployment window on a government-network server. Instead the entire questionnaire
is six ordinary database tables edited through a purpose-built admin screen, and the mobile app
downloads it as JSON from `GET /inspection/api/catalog/`.

**The operational rule that follows** (`line_inspection/README.md:49`):

> *Edit it via the checklist editor admin screen, not by hand-editing
> `seed_checklist_catalog.py` after the first run.*

`line_inspection/management/commands/seed_checklist_catalog.py` is a **one-time bootstrap**,
not a source of truth. Its own docstring (line 7) says: *"This is a one-time/idempotent data
migration, not a permanent code dependency — the catalog rows this creates are meant to be
edited afterwards."* Re-running it after a live edit is destructive in two specific ways:

| Re-run effect | Mechanism | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Overwrites edited item/defect/group text and flags | `update_or_create(key=..., defaults={...})` at `seed_checklist_catalog.py:261`, `:279`, `:254` | Any Admin edit to a *seeded* key (label, positions, `applicable_tower_types`, `na_reason`, gating flags, `ask`, `default_criticality`) silently reverts |
| **Deletes all criticality rules on every seeded defect** | `CriticalityRule.objects.filter(defect=defect).delete()` at `seed_checklist_catalog.py:290`, executed before re-creating only the rules hardcoded in the file | Admin-authored rules on seeded defects are destroyed with no warning |

Rows *added* through the editor with new keys survive a re-run (nothing deletes unknown keys),
but rows with seeded keys are clobbered. Treat `seed_checklist_catalog` as first-run-only.

> **Discrepancy with the seed file's own docstring.** `seed_checklist_catalog.py:4` says it was
> *"Ported from the two POC iterations (transcoapps/gisdata/clearpoc.html and the newer
> transcoapps/poc_v2.html…)"*. Neither file exists in this checkout — the only top-level
> directories under `transcoapps/` are `Aptransco_TIS-main/`, `line_inspection/` and
> `transcoapps/`. The POC HTML prototypes are gone; the comment is a historical reference only.

---

### 5.3 `CatalogVersion` — the singleton stamp

```python
# line_inspection/models.py:248
class CatalogVersion(models.Model):
    """Singleton counter bumped whenever any catalog table below changes, and
    stamped onto each Inspection so historical records stay traceable to the
    catalog shape that produced them."""
    version = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=1)
    updated_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)

    @classmethod
    def current(cls):
        obj, _ = cls.objects.get_or_create(pk=1)
        return obj.version

    @classmethod
    def bump(cls):
        obj, _ = cls.objects.get_or_create(pk=1)
        obj.version += 1
        obj.save(update_fields=['version', 'updated_at'])
        return obj.version
```

| Field | Type | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | BigAutoField (PK) | auto | Always **1** in practice — see the singleton pattern below |
| `version` | PositiveIntegerField | `1` | Monotonically increasing counter |
| `updated_at` | DateTimeField(`auto_now=True`) | now on every save | Served to the mobile app as the catalog's `updated_at` |

#### The `pk=1 get_or_create` singleton pattern

There is no database-level uniqueness making this a singleton; it is enforced *by convention*
in code. Both classmethods call `cls.objects.get_or_create(pk=1)`, so:

- The **first** call anywhere in the system (a page render, an API request, a test) creates row
  `id=1` with `version=1`. There is no migration data-seed and no `AppConfig.ready()` hook — the
  row springs into existence on first read.
- Every subsequent call resolves the same row. Nothing else in the codebase ever creates a
  `CatalogVersion` with a different pk, so the table has exactly one row.
- `CatalogVersion.objects.filter(pk=1).first()` in `line_inspection/api/views.py:180` reads the
  row directly (to expose `updated_at`) rather than going through `current()`, and tolerates
  `None` if it somehow does not exist yet.

Two consequences worth knowing:

1. **`current()` performs a write on a read path.** `get_or_create` opens a transaction and may
   INSERT. In practice it INSERTs once, forever, but the call is not read-only and would fail
   against a read-only replica. Callers include `admin_views.admin_home` (`admin_views.py:44`),
   `admin_views.checklist_editor` (`:250`), the REST catalog endpoint
   (`line_inspection/api/views.py:182`) and the inspection write path (`:488`).
2. **`bump()` is a read-modify-write, not an atomic increment.** It does
   `obj.version += 1; obj.save(...)` rather than `F('version') + 1`. Two Admins saving catalog
   edits in the same instant can both read version *N* and both write *N+1*, losing one bump.
   Harmless in practice (a version number that lags by one is still monotonic and still changes
   on edit) and there is at most a handful of Admins, but it is not concurrency-safe.

#### Why the version is stamped onto every `Inspection`

`Inspection.catalog_version` (`line_inspection/models.py:502`, a non-null
`PositiveIntegerField`) records the catalog version in force when the inspection was captured.
This exists because the catalog is *mutable*. An inspection recorded in March against
"11. Insulators → disc_broken → critical if discCount ≥ 2" is a permanent legal/engineering
record. If in June an engineer changes that threshold to 3, or renames the defect, or deletes
it, the March record must still be interpretable. Stamping the version means:

- Anyone auditing a historical inspection knows exactly which catalog generation produced it.
- The tickets raised by that inspection **also** snapshot the human-readable text
  (`DefectTicket.item_label`, `DefectTicket.defect_label` at `models.py:587` and `:590`) so
  they stay readable independently of the current catalog wording.
- The mobile app sends its cached `catalog_version` back on submit; the server accepts it, and
  only falls back to `CatalogVersion.current()` when the client omitted it
  (`line_inspection/api/views.py:488`: `catalog_version=data.get('catalog_version') or CatalogVersion.current()`).
  This is correct: an offline inspector who cached the catalog three days ago genuinely
  captured against that older shape, and the record should say so.

Every mutating path in the checklist editor calls `CatalogVersion.bump()` — group save
(`admin_views.py:266`), item save (`:285`), defect save (`:305`), follow-up-question save
(`:323`), rule save (`:339`), and any delete (`:355`). `seed_checklist_catalog` bumps once at
the end of its run (`seed_checklist_catalog.py:302`). Nothing else bumps it. The version is
therefore an accurate "has the questionnaire changed?" signal for the mobile app's cache
invalidation.

---

### 5.4 The catalog tree

```
CatalogVersion  (singleton, pk=1 — a stamp, not part of the tree)
      │  version N is copied onto every Inspection
      ▼
ChecklistItemGroup ─── key, label, sort_order                       (5 rows seeded)
      │  1..N   (ChecklistItem.group, on_delete=PROTECT)
      ▼
ChecklistItem ──────── key, sno, label, sort_order,                (25 rows seeded)
      │                positions[], pos_meta{},
      │                is_availability_gated,
      │                is_position_availability_gated,
      │                applicable_tower_types[], na_reason
      │  1..N   (Defect.item, on_delete=PROTECT)
      ▼
Defect ─────────────── key, label, sort_order,                     (75 rows seeded)
      │                ask[]  ──────────────────┐  (list of slugs,
      │                default_criticality      │   NOT a FK)
      │  1..N   (CriticalityRule.defect,        │
      │          on_delete=CASCADE)             │
      ▼                                         ▼
CriticalityRule ────── follow_up_key ─────► FollowUpQuestion       (16 rules,
                       operator                key, question_text,   22 questions)
                       threshold_value         answer_type,
                       resulting_criticality   options[], unit,
                       priority                placeholder
                          (matched by slug string, NOT a FK)
```

Two edges in this tree are **string references, not foreign keys**: `Defect.ask` (a JSON list
of `FollowUpQuestion.key` slugs) and `CriticalityRule.follow_up_key` (a `CharField`). This is
deliberate — it keeps the JSON payload the mobile app receives flat and self-describing, and it
lets an Admin type a key into a text box in the editor rather than picking from a dropdown of
FK objects. The cost is **no referential integrity**: deleting a `FollowUpQuestion` leaves
every `ask` list that mentioned it pointing at nothing, and no validation anywhere catches it.
Verified against the seed data, the references are all currently sound: all 22 follow-up
questions are referenced by at least one `ask`, every key in every `ask` list resolves, and
every `CriticalityRule.follow_up_key` is both a real question and present in its own defect's
`ask` list. Nothing enforces that this stays true.

Seeded catalog shape, computed from `seed_checklist_catalog.py` (matches the counts in
`line_inspection/README.md:217`):

| Group `key` | Label | Items | Defects |
|---|---|---|---|
| `civil` | Coping & foundation | 1 | 3 |
| `tower` | Tower parts | 6 | 15 |
| `hardware` | Suspension / tension hardware | 8 | 26 |
| `conductor` | Conductor & accessories | 5 | 16 |
| `earthing` | Earthing | 5 | 15 |
| **Total** | | **25** | **75** |

Plus 22 `FollowUpQuestion` rows (11 `choice`, 9 `number`, 1 `multichoice`, 1 `text`) and 16
`CriticalityRule` rows.

> **README nuance.** `line_inspection/README.md:217` describes the items as *"`ChecklistItem`
> (25, `sno` 4–28 + Remarks at 29)"*. The `sno` range 4–28 is exactly right (verified: the 25
> seeded `sno` values are the contiguous integers 4…28). **There is no ChecklistItem with
> `sno` 29** — "Remarks at 29" refers to the free-text `Inspection.remarks` field
> (`models.py:507`), which the paper proforma and the POC numbered as row 29 but which is a
> column on the inspection, not a catalog row. Numbers 1–3 are likewise header fields on the
> paper form (line, tower number, date), not checklist items.

---

### 5.5 `ChecklistItemGroup`

The top-level accordion sections of the questionnaire. `models.py:268`.

| Field | Type | Constraints / default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | BigAutoField | PK | |
| `key` | SlugField(64) | **unique** | Stable machine identifier (`civil`, `tower`, `hardware`, `conductor`, `earthing`). Serialized to mobile as the item's `group_key` so the Flutter client can bucket items without relying on ids. |
| `label` | CharField(255) | — | Human heading, e.g. "Suspension / tension hardware" |
| `sort_order` | PositiveIntegerField | `0` | Display order |

`Meta.ordering = ['sort_order']` — so `ChecklistItemGroup.objects.all()` is always in form
order without the caller sorting. `__str__` returns the label.

`key` is unique but is **not** the primary key. Same reasoning as elsewhere in this schema:
a slug is a human-chosen natural key and humans rename things; making it the PK would cascade a
rename through every FK. The surrogate `id` absorbs that.

The group is referenced by `ChecklistItem.group` with **`on_delete=PROTECT`**
(`models.py:281`). Rationale: a group is pure taxonomy, and silently deleting 8 hardware items
because someone tidied up a heading would destroy questionnaire content. PROTECT forces the
Admin to empty the group first. **Consequence:** the editor's delete endpoint
(`admin_views.checklist_delete`, `admin_views.py:346`) calls
`model.objects.filter(pk=pk).delete()` with no `try/except`, so deleting a non-empty group
raises an unhandled `ProtectedError` → HTTP 500 rather than a friendly message. Same for
deleting an item that still has defects.

---

### 5.6 `ChecklistItem`

One numbered row of the inspection proforma. `models.py:280`.

| Field | Type | Constraints / default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | BigAutoField | PK | The mobile payload references items by this numeric id (`item_id`), the JSON API by `key` — `_resolve_item()` in `line_inspection/api/views.py` accepts both |
| `group` | FK → `ChecklistItemGroup` | **`on_delete=PROTECT`**, `related_name='items'` | Owning section |
| `key` | SlugField(64) | **unique** | e.g. `insulators`, `susp_hw`, `earthpit` |
| `sno` | PositiveIntegerField | required | The serial number printed on the paper proforma (4–28). Not unique, not enforced against `sort_order` |
| `label` | CharField(255) | — | e.g. "Suspension hardware (clamps & fittings)" |
| `sort_order` | PositiveIntegerField | `0` | Display order **within the whole catalog** — the seeder writes the item's global index `i`, not its index inside the group |
| `positions` | JSONField(list) | `[]` | Ordered position labels; `[]` = not positional. See §5.6.1 |
| `pos_meta` | JSONField | `null=True, blank=True` | Optional extra per-position dropdown spec. See §5.6.2 |
| `is_availability_gated` | BooleanField | `False` | Item-level "is this fitting even present?" gate. See §5.6.3 |
| `is_position_availability_gated` | BooleanField | `False` | Per-position availability gate. See §5.6.3 |
| `applicable_tower_types` | JSONField(list) | `[]` | N/A gate by tower type; `[]`/null = applies to every tower. See §5.6.4 |
| `na_reason` | CharField(255) | `''` | Text shown to the inspector when the item is auto-N/A, e.g. "Only on tension (CP) towers — DB, DC, DD" |

`Meta.ordering = ['sort_order']`. `__str__` returns `"{sno}. {label}"`.

No unique constraint pairs `(group, sno)` or `(group, sort_order)`; nothing prevents two items
sharing an `sno`. `key` alone is the uniqueness guarantee.

#### 5.6.1 What "positional" means

Most defects on a transmission tower are not properties of the tower as a whole — they are
properties of a particular **conductor position** on it. A double-circuit tower carries three
phase conductors per circuit, strung at three vertical levels on the cross-arms, plus an earth
wire at the peak. An inspector who finds a broken insulator disc must record *which level*.

`positions` is that list. In the seed data exactly two shapes exist:

```python
# line_inspection/management/commands/seed_checklist_catalog.py:19
POS3   = ['Top', 'Middle', 'Bottom']
POS3EW = ['Top', 'Middle', 'Bottom', 'Earth wire']
```

An item with a non-empty `positions` renders as N independent sub-rows in the mobile form, each
with its own status (`normal` / `defect` / optionally `not_provided`), its own defect entries
and its own photo. On the server this becomes N `ItemResult` rows differing only in
`ItemResult.position` — which is why the uniqueness constraint on results is the triple
`(inspection, item, position)` (`models.py:550`), and why non-positional items store
`position=''` (`models.py:543`).

The 12 positional items in the seed:

| Item `key` | Label | Positions |
|---|---|---|
| `insulators` | Insulators | Top, Middle, Bottom (+ `pos_meta`) |
| `susp_hw` | Suspension hardware (clamps & fittings) | Top, Middle, Bottom |
| `tens_hw` | Tension hardware (dead-end & PG clamps) | Top, Middle, Bottom |
| `wpins` | W Pins and split pins (cotter pins) | Top, Middle, Bottom |
| `dampers` | Vibration dampers | Top, Middle, Bottom, **Earth wire** |
| `horns` | Arcing horns | Top, Middle, Bottom |
| `armour` | Armour rods | Top, Middle, Bottom |
| `birdguards` | Bird guards | Top, Middle, Bottom |
| `conductor` | Conductor | Top, Middle, Bottom |
| `midspan` | Mid span joints | Top, Middle, Bottom |
| `sleeves` | Repair sleeves | Top, Middle, Bottom |
| `jumpers` | Jumper, terminal dead end joints | Top, Middle, Bottom |

`dampers` is the only item using the four-slot list: vibration dampers are fitted to the earth
wire as well as to the three phase conductors, so "Earth wire" is a genuine fourth inspection
position for that item alone.

In the checklist editor the list is edited as a comma-separated string and split back into a
list by `ChecklistItemForm.clean_positions()` (`line_inspection/forms.py:67`), with the widget
placeholder *"Top,Middle,Bottom (comma-separated, blank = not positional)"*.

#### 5.6.2 `pos_meta` — the extra per-position dropdown

`pos_meta` attaches **one additional attribute select to each position row**. It is a free-form
JSON object; the shape the client understands is documented in the model comment
(`models.py:289`) and parsed by `PosMeta.fromJson` in
`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/models/inspection_catalog.dart:122`:

| JSON key | Meaning | Client field |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | The key under which the chosen value is stored in `ItemResult.meta` | `PosMeta.id` |
| `label` | Human label for the dropdown | `PosMeta.label` |
| `options` | List of allowed strings | `PosMeta.options` |
| `default` | Pre-selected value when the form is built | `PosMeta.defaultValue` |

Exactly one seeded item uses it — `insulators`:

```python
# line_inspection/management/commands/seed_checklist_catalog.py:21
INSULATOR_META = {
    'id': 'insType', 'label': 'Type of insulator',
    'options': ['Normal Disc', 'Fog Disc', 'SRC', 'Glass'], 'default': 'Normal Disc',
}
```

**Why it exists.** The insulator string type is not a defect and not a fixed property of the
tower in ArcGIS (`Tower.insulator_type` is one of the manually-maintained, usually-empty
fields). It varies *per position* on the same tower — a line may have fog-type discs on the
bottom phase where pollution deposits worst and normal discs above. So the inspector records it
alongside the condition, per position. It ends up in `ItemResult.meta`, whose model comment
gives precisely this example: `# e.g. {"insType": "Fog Disc"}` (`models.py:545`).

Client behaviour: `_buildDrafts()` in
`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/screens/line_inspection_form_screen.dart:89`
pre-seeds each position slot's `meta[posMeta.id]` with `posMeta.defaultValue`, and `_posRow`
(`:658`) renders it as a `DropdownButton` inline on the position row, to the right of the
position label. `pos_meta` is only rendered on positional items — a non-positional item with a
`pos_meta` would have nowhere to draw it.

> **Editor gap.** `pos_meta` is **not** in `ChecklistItemForm.Meta.fields`
> (`line_inspection/forms.py:54`). An Admin can edit `positions`, both gating flags,
> `applicable_tower_types` and `na_reason` through the UI, but **cannot create or change a
> `pos_meta` dropdown** without direct DB access or a shell. This is a real limitation of the
> "no code deploy needed" claim, and it is not mentioned in the README.

#### 5.6.3 The two availability-gating flags

These two booleans answer a question that is distinct from "is it defective?": **is the fitting
fitted at all?** Bird guards, anti-climbing devices, mid-span joints and repair sleeves are not
present on every tower or every span. Recording "Normal" for a bird guard that was never
installed is a false record; recording "Defect" is worse. Hence a third status,
`not_provided` — one of the four `ITEM_STATUS_CHOICES` (`models.py:532`: `na`, `not_provided`,
`normal`, `defect`).

| Flag | Scope | Effect on the mobile form |
|---|---|---|
| `is_availability_gated` | Whole item | The item's header row becomes an availability toggle. For a **non-positional** item it renders a 3-way segmented control **Not available / Normal / Defect** (`line_inspection_form_screen.dart:608`). For a **positional** item it renders a 2-way **Not available / Available** master switch (`:598`); choosing "Not available" collapses and resets all its position rows (`:116`). The item's draft **starts at `not_provided`** (`:80`) — the safe default is "assume absent until the inspector confirms presence". |
| `is_position_availability_gated` | Each position independently | No item-level toggle; instead **each** position row gets an extra "Not available" option prepended to its segmented control (`:681`), and each position's draft **starts at `not_provided`** (`:88`, `:119`). Used where the fitting may exist at one level and not another. |

Seeded usage:

| Item | `is_availability_gated` | `is_position_availability_gated` | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `anti_climb` (Anti-climbing device) | ✔ | | Not fitted on every tower |
| `birdguards` (Bird guards) | ✔ | | Fitted selectively; also tower-type gated |
| `earthpit` (Earth pit and counter poise earthing) | ✔ | | Not every tower has a counterpoise |
| `midspan` (Mid span joints) | | ✔ | A mid-span joint exists in some spans and phases, not others |
| `sleeves` (Repair sleeves) | | ✔ | Repair sleeves are added ad-hoc where a conductor was previously repaired |

`birdguards` is the only item that is both availability-gated **and** tower-type gated —
suspension towers only, and even then only if guards were actually fitted. Nothing in the
model prevents setting both flags on one item; the client's `_buildDrafts` would then start the
item at `not_provided` *and* every position at `not_provided`, and the item-level 2-way switch
takes precedence in rendering (the `hasPositions && isAvailabilityGated` branch at `:598` is
checked before the `isPositionAvailabilityGated` branch at `:681` fires per row). No seeded item
does this.

Both flags are plain checkboxes in the editor (`forms.py:56`), so an Admin can retro-fit
availability gating onto any item without a deploy.

#### 5.6.4 `applicable_tower_types`, `applies_to()`, and the known unfixed gap

Some checklist items are physically meaningful only on one *kind* of tower. The two kinds that
matter are:

- **SP / suspension tower** — the conductor passes *through*, hanging from a vertical
  I-string. Suspension hardware, armour rods and bird guards live here.
- **CP / tension (dead-end) tower** — the conductor *terminates* on the tower and is
  electrically bridged around it by a **jumper**. Tension hardware, PG clamps and jumper/dead-end
  joints live here.

(The abbreviations CP/SP also appear as `Tower.cp_sp` in the GIS master data, §4.)

Asking an inspector about armour rods on a tension tower is noise, so the item is marked
**N/A** and rendered greyed out with the `na_reason` text instead of a status control
(`line_inspection_form_screen.dart:591`).

The gate is a JSON list on the item:

```python
# line_inspection/models.py:294
# tower_type values this item applies to, e.g. ["DA"]; [] / null = applies to all tower types.
# Data-driven on purpose: editing this list changes N/A logic without a code change.
applicable_tower_types = models.JSONField(default=list, blank=True)
```

and the model helper is a two-line exact-membership test:

```python
# line_inspection/models.py:305
def applies_to(self, tower_type):
    if not self.applicable_tower_types:
        return True                                  # empty list = universal
    return tower_type in self.applicable_tower_types  # exact string membership
```

Semantics: **empty list means "applies to everything"**, not "applies to nothing". A falsy
check (`not self.applicable_tower_types`) so `[]`, `None` and a missing value all mean
universal. Otherwise plain, case-sensitive, exact `in` on the list.

**`applies_to()` has no callers anywhere in the server codebase.** A repository-wide search
finds only its definition at `models.py:305`. The N/A decision is made **entirely on the
client**: the field is serialized out by `ChecklistItemSerializer`
(`line_inspection/api/serializers.py:50`) and evaluated by
`CriticalityEngine.itemApplies()` in
`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/services/criticality_engine.dart:97`. The server
does not reject an `ItemResult` for an item that does not apply to that tower; it stores
whatever the client sends. So `applies_to()` is dead-but-correct reference code documenting the
intended semantics.

##### The known, unfixed gap

The seed hardcodes POC-era placeholder tower-type codes:

```python
# line_inspection/management/commands/seed_checklist_catalog.py:25
SP_TYPES  = ['DA']
CP_TYPES  = ['DB', 'DC', 'DD']
SP_REASON = 'Only on suspension (SP) towers'
CP_REASON = 'Only on tension (CP) towers — DB, DC, DD'
```

| Item | `applicable_tower_types` | `na_reason` |
|---|---|---|
| `susp_hw` | `['DA']` | Only on suspension (SP) towers |
| `armour` | `['DA']` | Only on suspension (SP) towers |
| `birdguards` | `['DA']` | Only on suspension (SP) towers |
| `tens_hw` | `['DB', 'DC', 'DD']` | Only on tension (CP) towers — DB, DC, DD |
| `jumpers` | `['DB', 'DC', 'DD']` | Only on tension (CP) towers — DB, DC, DD |

But **real `Tower.tower_type` values synced from ArcGIS do not look like this.** The model
comment on the GIS side is explicit that the values are *"real domain values, not assumed"*
(`models.py:133`), and `line_inspection/README.md:221` states the gap outright:

> ***Known gap, not yet fixed:** still seeded with the POC's placeholder `DA/DB/DC/DD` codes,
> but real ArcGIS `Tower.tower_type` values look like `"Boom"`.*

The remediation path was built and is available: the checklist editor's item form replaces the
free-text field with **checkboxes populated from the tower types actually observed in the
database**:

```python
# line_inspection/admin_views.py:255
def _tower_type_choices():
    return sorted({t for t in Tower.objects.values_list('tower_type', flat=True).distinct() if t})
```

```python
# line_inspection/forms.py:50
applicable_tower_types = forms.MultipleChoiceField(required=False, widget=forms.CheckboxSelectMultiple)
...
def __init__(self, *args, tower_type_choices=(), **kwargs):
    super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
    self.fields['applicable_tower_types'].choices = [(t, t) for t in tower_type_choices]
```

So an Admin opening "edit item → Suspension hardware" sees a checkbox per real tower type in
their data and can correct the gate with no code change and no deploy — exactly the payoff the
DB-backed design was built for. **Nobody has done it.** The seeded placeholder codes are still
what is in the database.

##### The client's defensive workaround

Because the gate is wrong, a naive exact-match would mark five items N/A on essentially every
real tower — silently making them un-inspectable. The Flutter client therefore does **not**
implement `applies_to()`'s exact-match semantics. It implements a deliberately permissive
prefix match with a fail-open default:

```dart
// Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/services/criticality_engine.dart:97
static bool itemApplies(ChecklistItem item, String towerType) {
  final types = item.applicableTowerTypes;
  if (types.isEmpty) return true;
  final tt = towerType.toUpperCase().trim();
  for (final code in types) {
    if (tt.startsWith(code.toUpperCase())) return true;   // "DA+0".startsWith("DA")
  }
  final gateIsDSeries = types.every((c) => c.toUpperCase().startsWith('D'));
  final towerIsDSeries = tt.startsWith('D');
  if (gateIsDSeries && towerIsDSeries) return false;      // genuinely out of scope
  return true;                                            // fail open
}
```

Its own doc comment (`criticality_engine.dart:86`) explains the reasoning: real tower types
carry a body-extension suffix (`DA+0`, `DB+3`) so matching must be by prefix; and *"a tower that
is NOT in the gated (D-series) family at all — `A+0`, `P+0`, `S+0`, `Boom`, … — is treated as
applicable rather than forced to N/A, so no item is ever silently un-inspectable on the bulk of
real towers"*, with a `NOTE` that *"this gating scheme needs confirmation against APTRANSCO
tower nomenclature; it is intentionally permissive until then."*

**This is a genuine server/client semantic divergence** that no document states: `applies_to()`
on the server is exact-match and case-sensitive; `itemApplies()` on the client is
prefix-match, case-insensitive, and fail-open. Only the client's version runs. If a future
server-side validation ever starts calling `applies_to()`, it will disagree with what the app
allowed the inspector to submit.

### 5.7 `Defect`

The specific fault an inspector can report against a checklist item. `models.py:318`.

| Field | Type | Constraints / default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | BigAutoField | PK | Mobile submits `defect_id`; JSON API submits the `key` |
| `item` | FK → `ChecklistItem` | **`on_delete=PROTECT`**, `related_name='defects'` | Owning item |
| `key` | SlugField(64) | **not globally unique** — unique per item via constraint | e.g. `disc_broken`, `bolts_missing` |
| `label` | CharField(255) | — | Text shown in the defect picker |
| `sort_order` | PositiveIntegerField | `0` | Order within the item |
| `ask` | JSONField(list) | `[]` | **Ordered** list of `FollowUpQuestion.key` slugs to ask when this defect is selected |
| `default_criticality` | CharField(16), `choices=CRITICALITY_CHOICES` | **required, no default** | Fallback severity when no `CriticalityRule` matches |

```python
class Meta:
    ordering = ['sort_order']
    constraints = [
        models.UniqueConstraint(fields=['item', 'key'], name='uniq_defect_item_key'),
    ]
```

`__str__` returns `"{item.key}:{defect.key}"` — the composite that is actually unique.

`CRITICALITY_CHOICES` (`models.py:311`) is `minor` / `major` / `critical` — note this is
**three** values, deliberately *not* the five-value `WORST_CHOICES` (`none`, `ok`, `minor`,
`major`, `critical`) used for rolled-up tower/inspection status. A `Defect` by definition is at
least minor; `ok` and `none` are states of a *tower*, not of a defect.

#### `Defect.ask` — the ordered follow-up list

When the inspector selects a defect, the form does not just record "broken". It asks the
follow-up questions named in `ask`, **in list order**, and stores the responses in
`DefectEntry.answers` as `{followUpKey: scalar | [scalar,…]}` (`models.py:560`). Example from
the seed:

```python
{'key': 'members_missing', 'label': 'Members missing (theft)',
 'ask': ['memberType', 'towerLoc', 'count'], 'default_criticality': 'major', ...}
```

→ the inspector is asked, in order: *Which type of member?* → *Where on the tower is it?* →
*How many are affected?* Answers land as
`{"memberType": "Main leg / corner member", "towerLoc": "Leg member", "count": 2}`.

`ask` may be empty (`[]`) — e.g. `paint_faded`, `creepers`, `flashover_marks` — meaning the
defect is fully described by its label and needs no qualification.

The ordering matters because the questions are a triage funnel: identify the component, then
its location, then the magnitude. Order is preserved as a JSON list rather than derived from a
sort column precisely so the Admin can reorder by retyping the comma-separated string
(`DefectForm.clean_ask`, `forms.py:81`).

#### `on_delete` rationale in the catalog

| Relationship | on_delete | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `ChecklistItem.group` → group | **PROTECT** | A group is a container; deleting it must not take its items with it |
| `Defect.item` → item | **PROTECT** | Same — deleting an item must not silently discard its defect vocabulary |
| `CriticalityRule.defect` → defect | **CASCADE** | A rule has no meaning apart from its defect; it is a property of it, not an independent record. Deleting the defect *should* take its rules |
| `ItemResult.item` → item (§ inspections) | **PROTECT** | Historical inspection data must never be destroyed by a catalog edit |
| `DefectEntry.defect` → defect | **PROTECT** | Same |
| `DefectTicket.item` / `.defect` | **PROTECT** | Same, plus tickets are operational work orders |

The net effect: **once a defect has ever been recorded in the field, it can no longer be
deleted from the catalog** — PROTECT from `DefectEntry`/`DefectTicket` blocks it. This is the
correct behaviour for an audit-bearing system (the alternative would orphan or destroy
inspection history), but it means the editor's "delete" button becomes a 500 error on any
catalog row that has been used. The practical workaround is to edit the label or move it to
the bottom via `sort_order`, not to delete.

---

### 5.8 `FollowUpQuestion`

A reusable question, shared across defects. `models.py:344`.

| Field | Type | Constraints / default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | BigAutoField | PK | |
| `key` | SlugField(64) | **unique** | The slug used in `Defect.ask` and `CriticalityRule.follow_up_key`, and the key in `DefectEntry.answers` |
| `question_text` | CharField(500) | — | The prompt, e.g. "How many discs are affected?" |
| `answer_type` | CharField(16), `choices=ANSWER_TYPE_CHOICES` | required | `choice` / `multichoice` / `number` / `text` |
| `options` | JSONField(list) | `[]` | Allowed values — **only** for `choice`/`multichoice` |
| `unit` | CharField(32) | `''` | Unit suffix — **only** for `number`, e.g. `m`, `discs`, `strands`, `Ω`, `nos` |
| `placeholder` | CharField(255) | `''` | Input hint — **only** for `text` |

No `Meta` — no ordering, no constraints beyond `key` uniqueness. `__str__` returns the key.

Questions are **global, not owned by a defect**. That is the point: `span` ("In which span?"),
`count`, `locationText` and `leg` are asked by many different defects across many items.
Defining them once and referencing by key means changing "How many are affected?" to a clearer
wording updates it everywhere at once.

#### How the three auxiliary fields map to the four answer types

| `answer_type` | `options` | `unit` | `placeholder` | Stored answer shape | Seeded count |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `choice` | **used** — one must be picked | ignored | ignored | a single string from `options` | 11 |
| `multichoice` | **used** — zero or more picked | ignored | ignored | a **list** of strings from `options` | 1 |
| `number` | ignored | **used** — rendered as a suffix next to the numeric field | ignored | a number (may arrive as a numeric string) | 9 |
| `text` | ignored | ignored | **used** — greyed hint text in the empty field | a free string | 1 |

Nothing enforces this mapping — the model allows a `number` question with `options`, and the
editor's `FollowUpQuestionForm` (`forms.py:85`) exposes all three fields for every type with
only the help text *"Comma-separated options (for choice/multichoice only)"* as guidance. It is
a convention.

Complete seeded question catalog:

| `key` | Type | Question | `options` / `unit` / `placeholder` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `leg` | choice | Which leg / footing? | Leg A · Leg B · Leg C · Leg D · More than one leg |
| `span` | choice | In which span? | Back span (towards previous tower) · Forward span (towards next tower) |
| `towerLoc` | choice | Where on the tower is it? | Below waist level · Above waist level · Cross-arm · Cage / boom · Peak · Leg member |
| `memberType` | choice | Which type of member? | Main leg / corner member · Bracing / redundant member · Cross-arm member · Peak member |
| `boltType` | choice | Which bolts are affected? | Member bolts & nuts · Step bolts · Both |
| `clampPart` | choice | Which part is missing? | Bolt / nut · Keeper / retaining clip · Cotter pin · Clamp body · PG clamp |
| `hornEnd` | choice | Which horn is affected? | Line-side horn · Tower-side horn · Both |
| `boardType` | **multichoice** | Which board / plate? (select all that apply) | Danger board · Number plate · Phase plate · Circuit plate |
| `paintExtent` | choice | Extent of rusting / paint failure? | Isolated spots · Less than 25% of members · 25% – 50% of members · More than 50% of members |
| `crackExtent` | choice | How severe is the damage? | Just crack observed · Major structural crack / broken |
| `erosion` | choice | How much of the revetment is affected? | Less than 25% · 25% – 50% · More than 50% / washed out |
| `treeKind` | choice | What kind of growth? | Fast-growing trees (eucalyptus, casuarina…) · Slow-growing trees · Bamboo · Creepers on tower · Crop / bushes |
| `count` | number | How many are affected? | unit `nos` |
| `discCount` | number | How many discs are affected? | unit `discs` |
| `strandCount` | number | How many strands are cut / damaged? | unit `strands` |
| `distance` | number | Approximate distance from the tower? | unit `m` |
| `clearance` | number | Measured / estimated clearance from conductor? | unit `m` |
| `jumperClr` | number | Measured clearance of jumper to tower body? | unit `m` |
| `resistance` | number | Measured tower-footing resistance? | unit `Ω` |
| `exposedLen` | number | Length of counterpoise exposed / missing? | unit `m` |
| `theftHeight` | number | Up to what height from ground is it missing? | unit `m` |
| `locationText` | **text** | Describe the exact location | placeholder "e.g. B-phase cross-arm tip · 40 m into forward span…" |

`boardType` (multichoice) was added by the second POC iteration and is the only question that
produces a **list-valued** answer — which is exactly what the `contains_any` / `contains_all`
operators exist to test (§5.9), though no seeded rule uses them yet.

### 5.9 `CriticalityRule`

```python
# line_inspection/models.py:366
class CriticalityRule(models.Model):
    """Data-driven replacement for the POC's hardcoded critRule() JS
    functions — e.g. "if discCount >= 2 -> critical". Evaluated in ascending
    `priority` order; the first matching rule wins, else Defect.default_criticality
    applies."""
    defect = models.ForeignKey(Defect, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='criticality_rules')
    follow_up_key = models.CharField(max_length=64)
    operator = models.CharField(max_length=16, choices=CRITICALITY_OPERATOR_CHOICES)
    threshold_value = models.JSONField()
    resulting_criticality = models.CharField(max_length=16, choices=CRITICALITY_CHOICES)
    priority = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=0)

    class Meta:
        ordering = ['priority']
```

| Field | Type | Constraints / default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | BigAutoField | PK | |
| `defect` | FK → `Defect` | **`on_delete=CASCADE`**, `related_name='criticality_rules'` | The defect this rule escalates/de-escalates |
| `follow_up_key` | CharField(64) | required, **no FK** | Which answer to test — a `FollowUpQuestion.key` |
| `operator` | CharField(16) | `choices=CRITICALITY_OPERATOR_CHOICES` | See operator table below |
| `threshold_value` | **JSONField**, no default | **required** | Polymorphic — number, string, or list depending on the operator and the question's answer type |
| `resulting_criticality` | CharField(16) | `choices=CRITICALITY_CHOICES` (`minor`/`major`/`critical`) | The severity to assign when this rule matches |
| `priority` | PositiveIntegerField | `0` | **Lower runs first.** `Meta.ordering = ['priority']` |

`__str__` renders the rule as a readable sentence:
`"{item.key}:{defect.key}: {follow_up_key} {operator} {threshold_value} -> {resulting_criticality}"`.

#### Why the rules are data

`models.py:367` is explicit: this is the *"data-driven replacement for the POC's hardcoded
`critRule()` JS functions"*. In the HTML proof-of-concept, "2 or more broken discs is critical"
was a JavaScript function. Criticality thresholds are precisely the part of the questionnaire
most likely to be argued over and recalibrated by engineering, so they are the part that most
needs to be editable without a deploy.

#### `threshold_value` polymorphism

`threshold_value` is a bare `JSONField()` with **no default and no null**, so it is required on
every rule. It holds whatever JSON scalar or array the operator needs:

| Operator | Expected `threshold_value` JSON | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `gte`, `lte` | number | `2`, `1.5`, `20` |
| `eq` | usually a string; may be any JSON scalar | `"Main leg / corner member"` |
| `in` | list (a bare scalar is auto-wrapped) | `["Bamboo", "Creepers on tower"]` |
| `contains_any` | list | `["Danger board", "Phase plate"]` |
| `contains_all` | list | `["Danger board", "Number plate"]` |

The editor exposes it as a raw JSON text input with the help text
*"A plain number or string, e.g. 2 or \"Main leg / corner member\" (JSON — quote text values)."*
(`line_inspection/forms.py:100`). An Admin who types `2` gets the JSON number 2; who types
`Main leg` unquoted gets a JSON parse error from the form field.

#### Every operator, with implemented semantics

Implemented in `line_inspection/services/criticality.py:16`:

| Code | Display | Server semantics (`_rule_matches`) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gte` | `>=` | `float(value) >= float(threshold)` after `_coerce_for_compare` | Non-numeric answer → coercion returns `None` → no match (never crashes) |
| `lte` | `<=` | `float(value) <= float(threshold)` after `_coerce_for_compare` | Same |
| `eq` | `==` | **strict Python `value == threshold`, no coercion** | `2 == "2"` is False. Type-sensitive |
| `in` | `in` | `value in threshold` (threshold wrapped in a list if it is not one) | Tests whether the *scalar answer* is one of a set |
| `contains_any` | contains any of | `bool(set(values) & set(threshold or []))` — answer wrapped in a list if scalar | For multichoice answers: matches if **at least one** selected option is in the threshold set |
| `contains_all` | contains all of | `set(threshold or []).issubset(set(values))` | Matches if **every** threshold option was selected |
| *(anything else)* | — | `return False` | Unknown operators never match |

The numeric coercion helper:

```python
# line_inspection/services/criticality.py:7
def _coerce_for_compare(value, threshold):
    if isinstance(threshold, (int, float)) and not isinstance(threshold, bool):
        try:
            return float(value)
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            return None
    return value
```

Coercion is driven by the **threshold's** type, not the answer's — so a numeric threshold pulls
a string answer (`"3"`, which is how a JSON payload from a text input often arrives) into
`float`. The `not isinstance(threshold, bool)` guard exists because in Python `bool` is a
subclass of `int`; without it, a boolean threshold would be treated as numeric.

Before any operator runs, there is a universal precondition:

```python
value = answers.get(rule.follow_up_key)
if value is None:
    return False
```

A rule whose question was **not answered** never matches. It does not error and does not
escalate. Note `''` (empty string) is *not* `None`, so an empty text answer still reaches the
operator — harmless for `gte`/`lte` (coercion fails → no match) but an `eq` rule with an empty
threshold would match.

#### Evaluation: first match wins

```python
# line_inspection/services/criticality.py:41
def suggest_criticality(defect, answers):
    for rule in defect.criticality_rules.all():
        if _rule_matches(rule, answers):
            return rule.resulting_criticality
    return defect.default_criticality
```

`defect.criticality_rules.all()` inherits `Meta.ordering = ['priority']`, so iteration is in
ascending priority. **The first rule that matches returns immediately** — remaining rules are
never evaluated. If none match, `Defect.default_criticality` is the answer. There is no
"highest severity wins" logic and no accumulation; ordering is entirely the Admin's
responsibility via `priority`.

The critical corollary: **the narrowest / most severe condition must have the lowest priority
number.** Two overlapping thresholds ordered wrongly produce a silently wrong severity — see
worked example 2.

Where it is called: `line_inspection/api/views.py:522`, inside the atomic nested create:

```python
answers = entry_data.get('answers', {})
suggested = suggest_criticality(defect, answers)
final = entry_data.get('criticality') or suggested
entry = DefectEntry.objects.create(
    item_result=item_result, defect=defect, answers=answers,
    suggested_criticality=suggested, criticality=final, note=..., )
```

Both values are persisted: `DefectEntry.suggested_criticality` is what the rules computed
**server-side** (recomputed, never trusted from the client), and `DefectEntry.criticality` is
the inspector's override if they supplied one, else the suggestion. Storing both gives a clean
audit trail of every case where a human disagreed with the rule engine. The `or` means a
falsy/absent client value falls through to the suggestion, so `criticality` is always populated.
The per-entry `criticality` values then feed `worst_of()` (`criticality.py:51`) to compute
`Inspection.worst_criticality`, which in turn advances the denormalized `Tower` status cache.

#### Worked example 1 — `high_resistance` (two numeric thresholds, ordering critical)

Seeded on item `earthpit` (sno 28, "Earth pit and counter poise earthing"), from
`seed_checklist_catalog.py:224`:

```python
{'key': 'high_resistance', 'label': 'High footing resistance',
 'ask': ['resistance'], 'default_criticality': 'minor',
 'rules': [
     {'follow_up_key': 'resistance', 'operator': 'gte', 'threshold_value': 20,
      'resulting_criticality': 'critical', 'priority': 0},
     {'follow_up_key': 'resistance', 'operator': 'gte', 'threshold_value': 10,
      'resulting_criticality': 'major',    'priority': 1},
 ]},
```

Domain meaning: tower-footing resistance is measured in ohms; higher means a worse earth path
and a higher lightning-flashover risk. The engineering bands are roughly <10 Ω acceptable,
10–20 Ω needs attention, ≥20 Ω urgent.

Trace with `answers = {"resistance": 14}`:

1. `defect.criticality_rules.all()` yields the priority-0 rule first (`gte 20 → critical`).
2. `value = answers.get('resistance')` → `14`. Not `None`, so evaluation proceeds.
3. Operator `gte`: `_coerce_for_compare(14, 20)` — threshold is an `int` and not a `bool`, so
   `float(14)` → `14.0`. Test `14.0 >= float(20)` → **False**. No match.
4. Next rule, priority 1 (`gte 10 → major`). `14.0 >= 10.0` → **True**. Match.
5. Return `'major'` immediately. → `suggested_criticality = 'major'`.

Other inputs against the same rule set:

| `resistance` answer | Priority-0 (`≥20`) | Priority-1 (`≥10`) | Result | Path |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `25` | match | (not reached) | `critical` | first rule wins |
| `20` | match (inclusive `>=`) | (not reached) | `critical` | boundary is inclusive |
| `14` | no | match | `major` | second rule |
| `10` | no | match | `major` | boundary inclusive |
| `4` | no | no | `minor` | `Defect.default_criticality` |
| `"14"` (string from a text input) | no | match — coerced by `_coerce_for_compare` | `major` | string→float coercion |
| `"n/a"` | no (coercion → `None`) | no | `minor` | fails safe to the default |
| *(question unanswered)* | no (`value is None`) | no | `minor` | fails safe to the default |

Note the priority ordering is load-bearing: swap the two priorities and a 25 Ω reading would
match `≥10` first and be reported as `major`, permanently under-rating an urgent defect. The
same trap exists in `tree_infringing` (`seed_checklist_catalog.py:193`), where
`clearance lte 4 → critical` (priority 0) must precede `clearance lte 6 → major` (priority 1);
reversed, a 3 m clearance to a live conductor would be filed as `major`.

#### Worked example 2 — `members_missing` (mixed operators, categorical + numeric)

Seeded on item `members` (sno 6, "Tower members"), from `seed_checklist_catalog.py:92`:

```python
{'key': 'members_missing', 'label': 'Members missing (theft)',
 'ask': ['memberType', 'towerLoc', 'count'], 'default_criticality': 'major',
 'rules': [
     {'follow_up_key': 'memberType', 'operator': 'eq',
      'threshold_value': 'Main leg / corner member',
      'resulting_criticality': 'critical', 'priority': 0},
     {'follow_up_key': 'count', 'operator': 'gte', 'threshold_value': 6,
      'resulting_criticality': 'critical', 'priority': 1},
 ]},
```

Domain meaning: steel members stolen from a tower. A missing *main leg / corner* member is
structurally critical regardless of how many; otherwise, six or more missing bracing members is
critical by accumulation. Anything less is `major` (the default) — never merely `minor`,
because theft of steel from a live tower is always serious.

Trace with `answers = {"memberType": "Bracing / redundant member", "towerLoc": "Below waist level", "count": 7}`:

1. Priority-0 rule: `value = answers['memberType']` → `"Bracing / redundant member"`. Operator
   `eq`: strict `"Bracing / redundant member" == "Main leg / corner member"` → **False**.
   (Note `eq` does *no* coercion — this is an exact string comparison against the exact option
   text stored in `FollowUpQuestion.options`, which is why the threshold must be typed
   byte-for-byte identically, spaces and slashes included.)
2. Priority-1 rule: `value = answers['count']` → `7`. Operator `gte`, threshold `6` is numeric →
   `float(7) >= float(6)` → **True**. Match.
3. Return `'critical'`.

Same defect, other inputs:

| `memberType` | `count` | Priority-0 (`eq` main leg) | Priority-1 (`≥6`) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Main leg / corner member` | `1` | match | (not reached) | `critical` |
| `Bracing / redundant member` | `7` | no | match | `critical` |
| `Bracing / redundant member` | `2` | no | no | `major` (default) |
| `Cross-arm member` | *(unanswered)* | no | no (`value is None`) | `major` (default) |
| `main leg / corner member` (lower-case) | `1` | **no** — `eq` is case-sensitive | no | `major` ⚠︎ |

That last row is the practical hazard of string-`eq`: the threshold text must match the option
text exactly. Since the answer comes from a dropdown populated by `FollowUpQuestion.options`,
this holds automatically as long as the Admin does not edit the option wording without also
editing the rule threshold — a coupling nothing in the schema enforces.

#### Which operators are actually used

Across the 16 seeded rules only three operators appear: `gte` ×8, `eq` ×4, `lte` ×4. **`in`,
`contains_any` and `contains_all` are implemented and selectable in the editor but unused by
any seeded rule.** They exist for future rules over the `boardType` multichoice question and
over categorical sets (e.g. "critical if `treeKind` in `[Bamboo, Fast-growing trees]`"). All 16
seeded rules, in full:

| Item | Defect | Rule (priority) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `coping` | `coping_cracked` | `crackExtent eq "Major structural crack / broken"` (0) | major |
| `coping` | `revet_eroded` | `erosion eq "Less than 25%"` (0) | minor (*de-escalation* from default `major`) |
| `members` | `members_missing` | `memberType eq "Main leg / corner member"` (0) | critical |
| `members` | `members_missing` | `count gte 6` (1) | critical |
| `bolts` | `bolts_missing` | `count gte 10` (0) | major |
| `painting` | `paint_rusted` | `paintExtent eq "More than 50% of members"` (0) | major |
| `insulators` | `disc_broken` | `discCount gte 2` (0) | critical |
| `wpins` | `wpin_missing` | `count gte 3` (0) | critical |
| `conductor` | `strands_cut` | `strandCount gte 3` (0) | critical |
| `conductor` | `sag_abnormal` | `clearance lte 6` (0) | critical |
| `jumpers` | `jumper_clearance` | `jumperClr lte 1.5` (0) | critical |
| `trees` | `tree_infringing` | `clearance lte 4` (0) | critical |
| `trees` | `tree_infringing` | `clearance lte 6` (1) | major |
| `earthwire` | `ew_strands` | `strandCount gte 3` (0) | critical |
| `earthpit` | `high_resistance` | `resistance gte 20` (0) | critical |
| `earthpit` | `high_resistance` | `resistance gte 10` (1) | major |

`revet_eroded` is the only **de-escalating** rule in the set (default `major`, downgraded to
`minor` when less than 25% of the revetment is affected) — proof that the mechanism is not
escalation-only.

#### Server / client rule-engine divergence (undocumented)

The mobile app re-implements the engine locally so it can colour a defect's severity *offline,
before submit* — `CriticalityEngine.suggestedCriticality` in
`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/services/criticality_engine.dart:38`. Its
behaviour is **not identical** to `services/criticality.py`:

| Aspect | Server (`services/criticality.py`) | Client (`criticality_engine.dart`) |
|---|---|---|
| Supported operators | `gte`, `lte`, `eq`, `in`, `contains_any`, `contains_all` | `eq`, `neq`, `gte`, `lte`, `gt`, `lt` |
| `in` / `contains_any` / `contains_all` | implemented | **not implemented** — fall to `default: return false` |
| `neq` / `gt` / `lt` | **not implemented** and not in `CRITICALITY_OPERATOR_CHOICES` — a rule using them is unsaveable via the editor and would never match | implemented |
| `eq` comparison | strict Python `==`, type-sensitive | `a.toString() == b.toString()` — **string-coerced**, so `2` matches `"2"` |
| Rule ordering | DB `Meta.ordering = ['priority']` | client-side `..sort((a,b) => a.priority.compareTo(b.priority))` |
| Rules→defect matching | FK (`defect.criticality_rules`) | by **`defect_key` string** from the flattened top-level `criticality_rules[]` (`MobileCriticalityRuleSerializer`, `api/serializers.py:54`) |
| Skip condition | `value is None` | `!answers.containsKey(key)` **or** `v == null` **or** `v == ''` |

Practical impact today is nil — the 16 seeded rules use only `eq`/`gte`/`lte` with matching
types, and the **server value is authoritative** (it recomputes `suggested_criticality` on
submit regardless of what the client displayed). But the moment an Admin adds a
`contains_any` rule through the editor, the mobile app will show the wrong severity in the form
while the server records the right one. This divergence is not noted anywhere in the README.

A second latent issue: because `Defect.key` is unique only **per item**
(`uniq_defect_item_key`), but the mobile catalog matches rules to defects by `defect_key`
alone, two defects on *different* items sharing a key would cross-apply each other's rules on
the client. Verified: all 75 seeded defect keys are globally unique today, so it does not bite —
but the schema permits the collision and nothing warns an Admin who creates one.

### 5.10 Operating the catalog: the editor screens

`admin_views.checklist_editor` (`line_inspection/admin_views.py:244`, `@auth.admin_required`)
renders the whole tree in one page via
`ChecklistItemGroup.objects.prefetch_related('items__defects__criticality_rules')`, plus the
flat follow-up-question list and the current catalog version. The template
(`line_inspection/templates/line_inspection/checklist_editor.html`) leads with the rationale
verbatim:

> *"Editable — this questionnaire is not finalised. Editing anything here bumps the catalog
> version so past inspections stay traceable to the shape they were recorded under."*

| View | URL name | Model | Form | Bumps version |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `checklist_editor` | `checklist-editor` | (read-only tree) | — | no |
| `checklist_item_group_form` | `checklist-group-new` / `-edit` | `ChecklistItemGroup` | `ChecklistItemGroupForm` | yes |
| `checklist_item_form` | `checklist-item-new` / `-edit` | `ChecklistItem` | `ChecklistItemForm` (+ live tower-type checkboxes) | yes |
| `defect_form` | `checklist-defect-new` / `-edit` | `Defect` | `DefectForm` | yes |
| `followup_question_form` | `checklist-followup-new` / `-edit` | `FollowUpQuestion` | `FollowUpQuestionForm` | yes |
| `criticality_rule_form` | `checklist-rule-new` / `-edit` | `CriticalityRule` | `CriticalityRuleForm` | yes |
| `checklist_delete` | `checklist-delete` | any of the five (`model_map`) | POST only | yes |

The three JSON-list fields are edited as comma-separated text and re-split on save —
`ChecklistItemForm.clean_positions` (`forms.py:67`), `DefectForm.clean_ask` (`:81`),
`FollowUpQuestionForm.clean_options` (`:92`) — while `applicable_tower_types` uses the
live-populated `CheckboxSelectMultiple` described in §5.6.4. `pos_meta` is not editable (§5.6.2).

The catalog is **read-only over the REST API** — `line_inspection/api/serializers.py:22` says
so explicitly (*"edited via the admin panel, not the API"*). `CatalogView`
(`api/views.py:174`) is GET-only and requires authentication.

### 5.11 `EmployeeCadreSnapshot`

```python
# line_inspection/models.py:389
class EmployeeCadreSnapshot(models.Model):
    """Synced periodically from the live SAP employee-cadre-details service
    (see services/sap_client.py + management/commands/sync_employee_cadre.py).
    Never live-queried per request."""
```

This is the app's entire notion of "who works here". There is **no `django.contrib.auth.User`
anywhere in this project** (`models.py:13`); identity is a bare SAP `employee_id` string, and
everything the system knows about that person comes from this locally-cached table.

| Field | Type | Constraints | SAP source key (`sync_employee_cadre.py`) | HR meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | BigAutoField | PK | — | Surrogate |
| `employee_id` | CharField(32) | **unique** | `EMP_ID` | SAP personnel number (PERNR). Zero-padded to 8 digits by the login path (`zfill(8)`), so stored ids look like `00012345` |
| `employee_name` | CharField(255) | blank | `EMP_NAME` | Full name |
| `position_id` | CharField(32) | blank | `EMP_POSITION` ∥ `POSITION_ID` | **Position** = the SAP *chair*, not the person. A position (e.g. "AEE/O&M/Vijayawada") persists across the people who occupy it. This is the field authorization keys off (§5.13) |
| `position_text` | CharField(255) | blank | `EMP_POS_TEXT` ∥ `POSITION_TEXT` | Human description of that chair, e.g. "…O&M…". Interlinked with `position_id` in SAP |
| `org_unit_id` | CharField(32) | blank | `ORG_UNIT_ID` | **Org unit** = the *department/office box* the position hangs in (a division, a circle office). Distinct from the position: many positions sit in one org unit |
| `org_unit_text` | CharField(255) | blank | `ORG_UNIT_TEXT` ∥ `WORKING_LOC_DES` | Org-unit name / working location description |
| `emp_sub_grp` | CharField(32) | blank | `EMP_SUB_GROUP` ∥ `EMP_SUB_GRP` | **Employee subgroup** = the *pay-scale / cadre band* (`AAE`, `AE`, `ADE/AEE`, `DE/EE`, `SE`, `CE`, …). Property of the person's grade, not of their posting |
| `emp_sub_grp_desc` | CharField(255) | blank | `EMP_SUB_GRP_DESC` | Long form of the subgroup |
| `mobile` | CharField(32) | blank | `mobileno` ∥ `MOBILE` | Contact |
| `mail` | CharField(255) | blank | `mail` ∥ `MAIL` | Contact |
| `reporting_manager_id` | CharField(32) | blank, **indexed** | `REPORTING_MANAGER_ID` | The `employee_id` of this person's manager — the edge that makes the whole hierarchy possible |
| `reporting_manager_name` | CharField(255) | blank | `REPORTING_MANAGER_NAME` | Denormalized manager name, so a UI row can show it without a self-join |
| `synced_at` | DateTimeField(`auto_now=True`) | — | — | Set on every sync write; the freshness signal |

```python
class Meta:
    indexes = [models.Index(fields=['reporting_manager_id'])]   # line_inspec_reporti_ae06d7_idx
```

`__str__` → `"{employee_id} — {employee_name}"`.

**Position vs org unit vs employee subgroup** is the trio that trips people up. In SAP HR terms:
the *position* is the job slot; the *org unit* is the organisational box that slot lives in; the
*employee subgroup* is the person's pay-grade band. A single human has all three, and they vary
independently: two people in the same `emp_sub_grp` (`DE/EE`) can hold completely different
positions in different org units, and an org unit contains positions across several subgroups.
This app authorizes on **position_id** (§5.13) and displays **emp_sub_grp** (§5.11.2), and
never confuses the two.

#### 5.11.1 How it is synced, and why it is a snapshot

`line_inspection/management/commands/sync_employee_cadre.py` calls
`services/sap_client.get_employee_cadre_details()`, which POSTs to the SAP RESTAdapter RFC
endpoint `ZHR_GET_EMP_CADER_DETAILS` with `{"EMPLOYEE_ID": <root>}` and reads
`result['LT_OUT'][0]['item']`. The RFC returns the requested employee **plus their entire
reporting subtree**, so one call with the organisation's root employee id populates the whole
table (`sap_client.py:18`).

Configuration is environment-only — `sap_client.py:6` states *"Credentials/config come from
environment variables only; nothing is hardcoded"*:

| Env var | Default in code | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `SAP_RFC_BASE_URL` | a hardcoded internal APTRANSCO RESTAdapter URL (`sap_client.py:12`) | Base of the RFC gateway |
| `SAP_RFC_USER` | `''` | Basic-auth user — `<set in .env.local>` |
| `SAP_RFC_PASSWORD` | `''` | Basic-auth password — `<set in .env.local>` |
| `SAP_HIERARCHY_ROOT_EMPLOYEE_ID` | `''` (no default — *"there is no safe default to guess here"*) | The top-of-hierarchy employee whose subtree is fetched |

`_require_credentials()` raises `SapClientError` with an actionable message if user/password
are unset, and the command surfaces it as a `CommandError` rather than a traceback.

The write loop is a single `transaction.atomic()` doing `update_or_create` keyed on
`employee_id` (`sync_employee_cadre.py:36`), skipping rows with a blank `EMP_ID`.

**Why cached rather than live-queried.** Stated in three places (`models.py:392`,
`sync_employee_cadre.py:2`, `README.md:235`): *"Never live-queried per request."* The reasons
are all practical — the RFC is a slow cross-network POST to a government SAP gateway with a
60-second timeout; it returns the *whole organisation* per call, so per-request use would be
absurd; and authorization decisions (`is_admin`, the subordinate walk, the role-assignment
candidate list) happen on every page render. A stale-by-an-hour local table is the right
trade-off. `run_sync_scheduler` refreshes it hourly by default
(`README.md:373`: `--cadre-interval-minutes 60`).

> **The sync never deletes.** `sync_employee_cadre.py:30` builds a `seen_ids` set but only uses
> it for the final count message — there is no `.exclude(employee_id__in=seen_ids).delete()`.
> Employees who leave APTRANSCO, or who fall outside the configured root's subtree, keep a stale
> row forever. Since `is_admin()` reads `position_id` from this table, a departed employee whose
> position is still on the Admin allow-list would still pass the Admin gate. Not called out in
> the README.

#### 5.11.2 The real cadre codes

`emp_sub_grp` values observed in the live synced data, mapped to their field-cadre display
labels in `line_inspection/viewing.py:25`:

```python
CADRE_LABELS = {
    'AAE': 'AEE', 'AE': 'AEE', 'ADE/AEE': 'DEE',
    'DE/EE': 'EE', 'SE': 'SE', 'CE': 'CE',
    'DIRECTOR': 'Director', 'GM': 'GM', 'JMD': 'JMD', 'CMD': 'CMD',
}
```

| Raw `emp_sub_grp` | Displayed as | Rank / meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `AAE` | **AEE** | Assistant Executive Engineer — the field inspector tier |
| `AE` | **AEE** | Assistant Engineer — also displayed as AEE |
| `ADE/AEE` | **DEE** | Deputy Executive Engineer |
| `DE/EE` | **EE** | Divisional Engineer / Executive Engineer — the Admin tier |
| `SE` | SE | Superintending Engineer |
| `CE` | CE | Chief Engineer — **management** |
| `DIRECTOR` | Director | Board-level — **management** |
| `GM` | GM | General Manager — **management** |
| `JMD` | JMD | Joint Managing Director — **management** |
| `CMD` | CMD | Chairman & Managing Director — **management** |

Two things a newcomer must internalise:

1. **`DE/EE` is one combined string, not two codes.** The literal characters `D`,`E`,`/`,`E`,`E`
   form a single `emp_sub_grp` value. So does `ADE/AEE`. Any code that tries to split on `/` or
   filter `emp_sub_grp__in=['DE','EE']` will match nothing. The Admin-candidate query gets this
   right and says so in a comment:

   ```python
   # line_inspection/admin_views.py:80
   # The exact candidate filter the user specified: DE/EE cadre + O&M postings.
   # Real synced data uses the single combined code "DE/EE" (confirmed against
   # the live sync, not two separate "DE"/"EE" values).
   candidates_qs = (EmployeeCadreSnapshot.objects
       .filter(emp_sub_grp='DE/EE', position_text__icontains='O&M')
       .exclude(position_id='').order_by('position_text'))
   ```

   Note also that two *different* codes (`AAE` and `AE`) both display as "AEE", so the mapping is
   many-to-one in both directions of confusion.

2. **Cadre codes are display-only and are never authoritative for authorization.**
   `viewing.py:22` is unambiguous: *"NOT authoritative for authorization."* The module docstring
   (`viewing.py:11`) explains why: *"Viewing tier is FUNCTIONAL, not grade-based: real SAP cadre
   codes are coarse/combined (e.g. 'DE/EE'), so authorization derives from the reporting tree +
   who actually holds RoleAssignments."* Knowing someone is graded `DE/EE` tells you nothing
   about whether they run a field division or sit in a design office. Authorization is therefore:

   | Decision | Actual authority | Not |
   |---|---|---|
   | Is this person an Admin? | `FieldEECadrePosition` contains their `position_id`, **or** they are a `SuperAdmin` (`auth.is_admin`, `auth.py:79`) | their cadre |
   | What can they inspect? | their own active `RoleAssignment`s + `LineTowerAssignment` ranges (`jurisdiction.py`) | their cadre |
   | What can they *see*? | the union over themselves + their reporting subtree (`viewing.oversight_*`) | their cadre |
   | Which display label? | `CADRE_LABELS[emp_sub_grp]`, falling back to the raw code (`viewing.display_label`) | — |
   | Do they get the zonal/circle rollups? | `emp_sub_grp in MANAGEMENT_SUBGRPS` = `{CE, DIRECTOR, GM, JMD, CMD}` — **the one place cadre does gate something**, plus Super Admin always (`viewing.is_management`, `viewing.py:139`) | — |

   `viewing.cadre_tier()` returns a *functional* tier (`admin` / `supervisor` / `field_user` /
   `none`) computed from who holds assignments, and its docstring notes it is *"Used only for map
   framing and the landing view; never to restrict a viewer below their own jurisdiction."*

#### 5.11.3 Why `reporting_manager_id` is the keystone

`reporting_manager_id` and `reporting_manager_name` were added in Phase 2 (migration
`0002_sapline_superadmin_remove_line_sap_line_id_and_more.py`, which also created the index
`line_inspec_reporti_ae06d7_idx`). They are what turn a flat employee list into a tree, and
that tree is what makes **oversight** possible at all.

The single implementation of the subtree walk is `viewing.subordinate_snapshots()`
(`viewing.py:36`): it loads every snapshot with a non-blank `reporting_manager_id` into an
in-memory `{manager_id: [employees]}` dict, then does a breadth-first expansion from the seed
employee, with a `seen` set so a cyclic or self-referential manager chain in the SAP data cannot
loop forever. The seed employee is **not** included in the result. The docstring notes it is a
*"Cheap in-memory walk over the ~1,830-row snapshot"* — that row count is the README/comment's
figure and is **unverified against a live DB from this checkout**.

The index on `reporting_manager_id` supports this: `subordinate_snapshots` currently does one
full scan with `.only(...)`, but the index makes any targeted "who reports to X" query O(log n),
and it is the column the walk is fundamentally organised around.

Two consumers, deliberately distinct:

- **`viewing.oversight_lines/oversight_towers`** — the read-only supervision scope. A viewer sees
  every line/tower assigned to anyone at or below them in the tree
  (`visible_employee_ids` = self + subordinates, `viewing.py:61`). Self is included *"so a leaf
  User's oversight scope equals their own jurisdiction exactly."*
- **`admin_views._subordinates`** (`admin_views.py:122`) — the role-assignment screen's default
  candidate list, so an Admin is first offered the people who actually report to them, with a
  full-employee name/id search as fallback. It explicitly delegates to
  `viewing.subordinate_snapshots` rather than re-implementing the walk.

#### 5.11.4 A second, development-only consumer

`line_inspection/services/dev_login.py` (recently added) resolves an employee id **against this
table** instead of calling the real checkCred credential gateway, so UI work can proceed on a
developer machine that cannot reach APTRANSCO's network. It never verifies a real password — it
compares the submitted password against one shared value from the environment using
`hmac.compare_digest`, then looks up the `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` row to obtain the display name:

```python
# line_inspection/services/dev_login.py:83
snapshot = EmployeeCadreSnapshot.objects.filter(employee_id=employee_id).first()
if snapshot is None:
    raise CheckCredError(f'No cadre snapshot for employee {employee_id}. Dev login can only '
                         f'sign in employees already synced into EmployeeCadreSnapshot.')
```

Three guards must **all** hold before it activates (`dev_login.is_enabled()`, `:38`):
`settings.DEBUG is True`, `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN == '1'`, and `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD`
non-empty (value `<set in .env.local>`). It matches the real gateway's `zfill(8)` id
normalisation so downstream lookups behave identically, and logs a `WARNING` on activation and
on every sign-in. Relevant here only because it means **any employee_id present in
`EmployeeCadreSnapshot` can be impersonated with one shared string when those three guards
hold** — the snapshot table is the dev-login user directory. The full auth story belongs to the
authentication section.

### 5.12 `SuperAdmin`

```python
# line_inspection/models.py:414
class SuperAdmin(models.Model):
    """A very small set of people who decide who counts as an Admin (grants/
    revokes FieldEECadrePosition). Seeded via `manage.py grant_super_admin`
    (CLI-only bootstrap, since an empty permissions table would otherwise
    lock everyone out); managed thereafter through the admin panel itself
    only in the sense that a Super Admin can grant another Super Admin."""
```

| Field | Type | Constraints | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | BigAutoField | PK | |
| `employee_id` | CharField(32) | **unique** | The SAP id granted Super Admin. **No FK to `EmployeeCadreSnapshot`** — a Super Admin can be granted before the cadre sync has ever run |
| `granted_at` | DateTimeField(`auto_now_add`) | — | Audit |
| `notes` | TextField | blank | Free-text justification |

No `Meta`. `__str__` → the employee id.

The **bootstrap problem** is the design driver, spelled out in
`management/commands/grant_super_admin.py:3`: *"Needed because an empty SuperAdmin table would
otherwise lock everyone out of the admin panel (nobody could grant the first one through the
UI)."* The command is idempotent (`get_or_create`) and CLI-only:

```
python manage.py grant_super_admin --employee-id 00012345 [--notes "..."]
```

Authorization semantics (`line_inspection/auth.py`): `is_super_admin(employee_id)` is a plain
existence check (`auth.py:91`), and **Super Admin is a strict superset of Admin** —
`is_admin()` returns `True` immediately for a Super Admin *"Super Admin is a superset of Admin,
not a separate/unrelated tier"* (`auth.py:82`). Screens gated `@super_admin_required`: Manage
Admins, the SAP position lookup endpoint, and the LILO screens.

Note the deliberate absence of a `revoked`/`is_active` flag: revocation is a row delete.

### 5.13 `FieldEECadrePosition`

```python
# line_inspection/models.py:428
class FieldEECadrePosition(models.Model):
    """Admin-curated allow-list of the specific EE position IDs authorized to
    assign inspection roles — not every EE is a field engineer. …"""
```

| Field | Type | Constraints | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | BigAutoField | PK | |
| `position_id` | CharField(32) | **unique** | The SAP **position** (chair) id that carries Admin rights |
| `position_text` | CharField(255) | blank | Description, auto-filled from SAP |
| `notes` | TextField | blank | Justification |
| `created_at` | DateTimeField(`auto_now_add`) | — | Audit |

`__str__` → `"{position_id} — {position_text}"`.

**Why the allow-list keys on position, not employee.** APTRANSCO staff transfer constantly. If
Admin rights were granted to *a person*, every transfer would require a permissions edit, and a
transferred-out engineer would retain rights over a division they no longer run. Granting to
the *position* means the rights follow the chair: `auth.is_admin()` reads the caller's **current**
`position_id` from the (hourly-refreshed) cadre snapshot and checks whether that position is on
the list:

```python
# line_inspection/auth.py:79
def is_admin(employee_id):
    if is_super_admin(employee_id):
        return True
    snapshot = EmployeeCadreSnapshot.objects.filter(employee_id=employee_id).first()
    if not snapshot or not snapshot.position_id:
        return False
    return FieldEECadrePosition.objects.filter(position_id=snapshot.position_id).exists()
```

A transfer therefore moves Admin rights automatically at the next cadre sync, with no
administrative action.

**Why an allow-list at all** rather than "every EE is an Admin": the docstring says it —
*"not every EE is a field engineer."* The `DE/EE` cadre includes design, projects, IT and
headquarters engineers who have no business assigning inspection jurisdiction. So the Super
Admin curates the subset.

**How candidates are surfaced** (`admin_views.manage_admins`, `admin_views.py:83`): the screen
lists distinct positions held by employees matching `emp_sub_grp='DE/EE'` **AND**
`position_text__icontains='O&M'` (Operation & Maintenance) with a non-blank `position_id`,
de-duplicated by position and annotated with a sample holder's name and whether it is already
granted. That is a heuristic shortlist, not a rule — the screen also offers a manual
"add by position id" fallback, whose `position_text` is auto-filled by a live SAP lookup
(`admin_views.lookup_position` → `sap_client.get_employee_by_position_id`, hitting the
`EMP_INFO_POS_ID` RFC) *"since posid/postext are interlinked in SAP"* so an Admin only types the
id (`admin_views.py:106`, `forms.py:15`).

Grant/revoke are `get_or_create` / `filter(...).delete()` at `admin_views.py:64` and `:69`.
