### 5.14 `RoleAssignment`

The primary jurisdiction grant. `models.py:448`.

| Field | Type | Constraints / default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | BigAutoField | PK | |
| `employee_id` | CharField(32) | **not unique, no FK** | Who is being assigned |
| `role` | CharField(32) | `choices=ROLE_CHOICES` | Today always `FIELD_INSPECTOR` |
| `subdivision` | FK → `Subdivision` | **`on_delete=PROTECT`**, `null=True, blank=True`, `related_name='role_assignments'` | Grants **every active line in that subdivision** |
| `lines` | M2M → `Line` | `blank=True`, `related_name='role_assignments'` | Grants **specific lines** |
| `assigned_by_employee_id` | CharField(32) | required | Audit: which Admin created this |
| `assigned_at` | DateTimeField(`auto_now_add`) | — | Audit |
| `is_active` | BooleanField | `True` | **Soft delete** — the UI never hard-deletes |

```python
class Meta:
    indexes = [models.Index(fields=['employee_id', 'is_active'])]  # line_inspec_employe_a3215e_idx
```

`__str__` → `"{employee_id}: {role}"`.

`ROLE_CHOICES` (`models.py:443`) has **exactly one value today**:

```python
ROLE_CHOICES = [
    ('FIELD_INSPECTOR', 'Field Inspector'),
]
```

The field exists as a `choices` CharField rather than being omitted because more roles are
anticipated (drone operator, contractor, reviewer). Today it carries no information — nothing
branches on it. `admin_views.role_assignments` hardcodes it on create
(`admin_views.py:149`: `assignment.role = 'FIELD_INSPECTOR'`) and it is not even in
`RoleAssignmentForm.Meta.fields` (`forms.py:27`), so an Admin never sees or chooses it.

**Subdivision OR lines OR both.** Both jurisdiction fields are optional, and
`jurisdiction._lines_for_assignments` unions them:

```python
# line_inspection/jurisdiction.py:39
query = Q(pk__in=[])                                  # matches nothing — the identity element
if subdivision_ids:
    query |= Q(subdivision_id__in=subdivision_ids)
if line_ids:
    query |= Q(pk__in=line_ids)
return Line.objects.filter(query, is_active=True).distinct()
```

The `Q(pk__in=[])` seed is a small but important idiom: it makes the OR-accumulation safe when
neither branch fires (an assignment with no subdivision and no lines grants nothing, rather than
everything). The function short-circuits to `Line.objects.none()` before that if the assignment
list is empty or carries no jurisdiction at all.

That helper is shared deliberately (`jurisdiction.py:21`): the same union logic serves
`jurisdiction.visible_lines` (a single employee's own scope) and `viewing.oversight_lines` (a
whole reporting subtree), *"so the union logic exists once."*

**`on_delete=PROTECT` on `subdivision`**: deleting a subdivision that still grants someone
jurisdiction would silently revoke it. PROTECT forces the operator to deal with the assignments
first. The `lines` M2M has no `on_delete` (M2M rows are removed with the line), but `Line`
deletion is not something the sync does — it soft-deletes with `is_active=False`, and
`_lines_for_assignments` filters `is_active=True`, so a decommissioned line drops out of
jurisdiction automatically without touching the assignment.

**Soft delete via `is_active`.** `admin_views.py:157` does
`RoleAssignment.objects.filter(pk=...).update(is_active=False)`. Every read path filters
`is_active=True`. The row survives as an audit record of who was assigned what, by whom, and
when. There is **no `deactivated_at` / `deactivated_by`** column, so the *revocation* event
itself is not audited — only the grant is. Not mentioned in the README.

**No uniqueness constraint.** Nothing prevents multiple active `RoleAssignment` rows for the same
employee; they simply union. That is intended (an engineer may hold one subdivision plus two
extra lines in a neighbouring one).

### 5.15 `LineTowerAssignment` — the from→to tower stretch

```python
# line_inspection/models.py:465
class LineTowerAssignment(models.Model):
    """A from-tower -> to-tower stretch of a line assigned to a User, for when a
    whole line isn't one person's. Complements RoleAssignment (whole-line/
    subdivision grants) — it does NOT replace it. Range membership is the line's
    towers whose line_sequence is between the two boundary towers' sequences;
    boundaries are stored as Towers (not raw indices) so rebuilding the schedule
    can't drift an assigned stretch. jurisdiction.py unions these in."""
```

| Field | Type | Constraints / default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | BigAutoField | PK | |
| `employee_id` | CharField(32) | no FK | Who gets the stretch |
| `line` | FK → `Line` | **`on_delete=CASCADE`**, `related_name='tower_ranges'` | The line the stretch is on |
| `from_tower` | FK → `Tower` | **`on_delete=PROTECT`**, `related_name='range_starts'` | One boundary |
| `to_tower` | FK → `Tower` | **`on_delete=PROTECT`**, `related_name='range_ends'` | The other boundary |
| `assigned_by_employee_id` | CharField(32) | required | Audit |
| `assigned_at` | DateTimeField(`auto_now_add`) | — | Audit |
| `is_active` | BooleanField | `True` | Soft delete |

```python
class Meta:
    indexes = [
        models.Index(fields=['employee_id', 'is_active']),  # line_inspec_employe_dfc14e_idx
        models.Index(fields=['line', 'is_active']),         # line_inspec_line_id_3adf08_idx
    ]
```

`__str__` → `"{employee_id}: {line_id} [{from_tower_id}..{to_tower_id}]"`. Added in migration
`0006_linetowerassignment_tower_line_offset_m_and_more.py`, alongside `Tower.line_sequence` /
`Tower.line_offset_m` — the same migration, because the range model is meaningless without the
tower schedule.

#### Why it exists

A 220 kV transmission line can run 80 km through three subdivisions. `RoleAssignment` grants a
**whole** line or a **whole** subdivision; there was no way to say "AEE Rao inspects towers 1–45,
AEE Reddy inspects 46–112 of the same line." Since lines are routinely shared between engineers
at subdivision boundaries, whole-line granularity either over-grants (both engineers see the
whole line and neither is accountable for a specific stretch) or under-grants (one engineer is
denied towers they are responsible for).

#### It complements, never replaces, `RoleAssignment`

The model docstring says it twice, and `jurisdiction.py` implements it as a **union**, never a
filter or an intersection:

```python
# line_inspection/jurisdiction.py:76
def visible_towers(employee_id):
    line_ids  = list(visible_lines(employee_id).values_list('id', flat=True))
    range_ids = range_tower_ids(employee_id)
    scope = Q(line_id__in=line_ids)
    if range_ids:
        scope |= Q(id__in=range_ids)          # UNION, not intersection
    return Tower.objects.filter(scope, is_active=True, is_virtual=False)
```

Consequences to be precise about:

- An employee with **only** ranges and no `RoleAssignment` still sees exactly their range towers.
- An employee with a whole-line `RoleAssignment` **plus** a range on that same line sees the
  whole line — the range does not narrow the grant. To genuinely restrict someone to a stretch,
  give them the range and **not** a `RoleAssignment` covering that line.
- The `if range_ids:` guard matters: without it, an empty `Q(id__in=set())` would still be
  OR-ed in harmlessly, but the guard avoids emitting a pointless `IN ()` clause.

The same union is applied in the write-authority check (`can_edit_tower`, `jurisdiction.py:88`)
and in the oversight read scope (`viewing.oversight_towers`, `viewing.py:79`), so a range
genuinely governs what a User may inspect — not just what they can see. Both filter
`is_virtual=False`: VT (virtual tower) rows are additional circuits strung on the same physical
structure and are never inspected in their own right.

#### How membership is computed

```python
# line_inspection/jurisdiction.py:51
def range_tower_ids(employee_ids):
    if isinstance(employee_ids, str):
        employee_ids = [employee_ids]
    ids = set()
    ranges = (LineTowerAssignment.objects
              .filter(employee_id__in=list(employee_ids), is_active=True)
              .select_related('from_tower', 'to_tower'))
    for r in ranges:
        f_seq, t_seq = r.from_tower.line_sequence, r.to_tower.line_sequence
        if f_seq is not None and t_seq is not None:
            lo, hi = sorted((f_seq, t_seq))
            ids.update(Tower.objects.filter(
                line_id=r.line_id, is_active=True, is_virtual=False,
                line_sequence__gte=lo, line_sequence__lte=hi,
            ).values_list('id', flat=True))
        else:
            ids.update({r.from_tower_id, r.to_tower_id})   # schedule not built yet
    return ids
```

Step by step:

1. Accepts a single id or an iterable — the same function serves one employee
   (`jurisdiction.visible_towers`) and a whole reporting subtree
   (`viewing.oversight_towers` passes `visible_employee_ids(...)`).
2. Boundary towers are resolved to their `Tower.line_sequence` — the ordered position along the
   line computed by `build_tower_schedule` / `line_inspection/schedule.py` (geometry projection
   onto the line's GeoJSON polyline, with a numeric-`tower_number` fallback for branched or
   geometry-less lines).
3. `sorted((f_seq, t_seq))` makes the range **direction-agnostic**: an Admin may pick the towers
   in either order and get the same stretch.
4. Membership is an inclusive `line_sequence BETWEEN lo AND hi` on **the same line**, active,
   real (non-virtual). Both boundary towers are inside their own range.
5. This query is supported by the `Tower` composite index `['line', 'line_sequence']`
   (`models.py:203`, created in the same migration 0006).

#### Why boundaries are Towers, not integers — and the fallback

Storing `from_sequence=12, to_sequence=45` would be simpler and would need no join. It was
rejected, and the reason is stated in three places (`models.py:161` on `Tower.line_sequence`,
`models.py:469` here, and `jurisdiction.py:54`): **`line_sequence` is a derived, rebuildable
value.** `build_tower_schedule` recomputes it whenever the schedule is rebuilt — after an ArcGIS
sync adds or removes towers, after a LILO reconcile, after a geometry fix. If a tower is
inserted mid-line, every downstream sequence number shifts by one, and a stretch stored as
`12..45` would silently slide onto a different set of towers. Storing FKs to the **boundary
towers themselves** means the stretch is defined by two physical structures; a renumbering moves
the numbers but the boundaries — and therefore the stretch — stay anchored to the same real
towers.

The **fallback** covers the case where the schedule has not been built for those towers yet
(`line_sequence` is `null=True` and starts NULL for every tower until
`build_tower_schedule` runs, and a newly-synced tower is NULL until the next rebuild). If either
boundary has a NULL sequence, "between" is undefined, so `range_tower_ids` degrades to
`{from_tower_id, to_tower_id}` — **just the two boundary towers**. This fails *closed*
(under-grant, not over-grant): the employee can still inspect the two towers explicitly named in
their assignment, and the intervening ones appear as soon as the schedule is built. No exception,
no empty result, no silent grant of the whole line.

#### How a range is created

On the **Roles & Jurisdiction** screen (`admin_views.role_assignments`, `action='create_range'`,
`admin_views.py:159`). The picker is driven by `admin_views.line_schedule_json`
(`admin_views.py:210`), which returns the line's **real** towers in schedule order
(`sched.line_schedule(line, include_virtual=False)`) as
`{id, tower_number, cp_sp, line_sequence}` — so the Admin picks from an ordered, human-readable
tower list rather than typing ids. Server-side validation confirms **both** boundary towers
belong to the selected line before creating the row:

```python
# line_inspection/admin_views.py:165
on_line = set(Tower.objects.filter(pk__in=[from_id, to_id], line_id=line_id).values_list('id', flat=True))
if {int(from_id), int(to_id)} <= on_line:
    LineTowerAssignment.objects.create(...)
else:
    messages.error(request, 'From/To towers must both belong to the selected line.')
```

Deactivation is the same soft-delete pattern (`action='deactivate_range'`, `admin_views.py:178`).

#### `on_delete` rationale

| FK | on_delete | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `line` | **CASCADE** | A range is defined *relative to* a line; if the `Line` row itself is truly deleted the range is meaningless. (In normal operation lines are soft-deleted via `is_active=False`, never row-deleted, so this rarely fires.) |
| `from_tower`, `to_tower` | **PROTECT** | Deleting a boundary tower would leave the stretch undefined — worse, it would silently change *which* towers someone is responsible for. PROTECT forces the operator to deactivate the range first. This is also what makes the LILO reconcile's "re-link surviving towers in place" strategy necessary: preserving tower PKs preserves range assignments |

No uniqueness constraint — an employee may hold several overlapping ranges on one line, and they
simply union.

```
        auth.is_admin() ▲                    ▲ auth.is_super_admin()
                        └────── superset ────┘

   ┌───────────────────────────────┐         ┌────────────────────────────────┐
   │  RoleAssignment               │         │  LineTowerAssignment           │
   │  employee_id  [INDEX+active]  │         │  employee_id  [INDEX+active]   │
   │  role = FIELD_INSPECTOR       │         │  line ──CASCADE──▶ Line        │
   │  subdivision ─PROTECT─▶ Sub'n │         │  from_tower ─PROTECT─▶ Tower   │
   │  lines  ◀── M2M ──▶ Line      │         │  to_tower   ─PROTECT─▶ Tower   │
   │  assigned_by / assigned_at    │         │  [INDEX line+active]           │
   │  is_active (soft delete)      │         │  is_active (soft delete)       │
   └───────────────┬───────────────┘         └───────────────┬────────────────┘
                   │                                          │
                   └──────────── UNION (never intersect) ──────┘
                                       │
                     jurisdiction.visible_towers / can_edit_tower   (own scope, write)
                     viewing.oversight_towers                       (subtree, read-only)
```

---

### 5.17 Findings and README discrepancies for this section

| # | Finding | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **"Remarks at 29" is not a ChecklistItem.** README describes items as *"25, `sno` 4–28 + Remarks at 29"*; the 25 seeded `sno` values are exactly 4…28 and there is no row 29. "Remarks" is `Inspection.remarks`, a free-text column. | `README.md:217` vs `seed_checklist_catalog.py` ITEMS; `models.py:507` |
| 2 | **`ChecklistItem.applies_to()` is dead code.** No server caller exists; N/A gating is decided entirely client-side, and the client's `itemApplies()` uses *different* semantics (prefix match, case-insensitive, fail-open) from the model's exact case-sensitive membership. Not documented anywhere. | `models.py:305` (no callers) vs `criticality_engine.dart:97` |
| 3 | **The `DA/DB/DC/DD` tower-type gate is still wrong**, as the README honestly admits — but the README does not mention that the client works around it with permissive prefix matching, i.e. the gate is currently near-inert rather than mis-firing. | `README.md:221`; `seed_checklist_catalog.py:25`; `criticality_engine.dart:86-112` |
| 4 | **Server and client criticality engines support different operator sets.** Server: `gte/lte/eq/in/contains_any/contains_all`. Client: `eq/neq/gte/lte/gt/lt`. `in`/`contains_*` silently never match on mobile; `neq/gt/lt` are unsaveable server-side. Client `eq` is string-coerced, server `eq` is strict. | `services/criticality.py:16` vs `criticality_engine.dart:56` |
| 5 | **`pos_meta` is not editable through the checklist editor** — it is absent from `ChecklistItemForm.Meta.fields`, contradicting the "edit the catalog without a code change" claim for that one field. | `forms.py:54` vs `README.md:47` |
| 6 | **Deleting a used catalog row returns HTTP 500.** `checklist_delete` has no `ProtectedError` handling, and `PROTECT` guards group→item, item→defect, and item/defect→ItemResult/DefectEntry/DefectTicket. | `admin_views.py:346` |
| 7 | **`CatalogVersion.bump()` is a non-atomic read-modify-write** (`obj.version += 1`, not `F('version') + 1`); concurrent saves can lose a bump. `current()` also performs a `get_or_create` write on read paths. | `models.py:255-265` |
| 8 | **`sync_employee_cadre` never prunes.** Departed employees keep stale `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` rows indefinitely; since `is_admin()` reads `position_id` from this table, a leaver could retain Admin rights. | `sync_employee_cadre.py:29-51` |
| 9 | **`RoleAssignment` / `LineTowerAssignment` soft-deletes are not audited.** `is_active=False` records that a grant ended but not when or by whom; only the grant has `assigned_by`/`assigned_at`. | `models.py:454-456`, `:477-479`; `admin_views.py:157`, `:179` |

Verified consistent in the seed (all references resolve, all 22 questions used) but nothing enforces it, and deleting a question via the editor silently orphans references. | `models.py:323`, `:372`; `admin_views.py:346` |
| 12 | **The seed docstring cites POC files that are absent from this checkout** (`transcoapps/gisdata/clearpoc.html`, `transcoapps/poc_v2.html`). | `seed_checklist_catalog.py:4`; directory listing of `transcoapps/` |
| 13 | The `~1,830-row` snapshot size in `viewing.subordinate_snapshots`' docstring is **unverified against a live DB** from this checkout. Likewise the 67,128-tower figure in `README.md:405`. | `viewing.py:39`; `README.md:405` |
## 6. Data Model — Part 3: Inspections, Tickets, LILO & Migration History

Everything below lives in `line_inspection/models.py`, sections 4 (transactional inspection
data, lines 491–632), 5 (LILO lineage, lines 635–682) and 6 (mobile auth, lines 685–729), plus
the eight migrations in `line_inspection/migrations/`. All of these tables are routed by
`LineInspectionRouter` (`line_inspection/db_router.py`) to the `line_inspection_db` connection,
which is the same PostgreSQL database as `default` but with `search_path=clear`
(`transcoapps/settings.py:159-166`). Every model uses Django's implicit `BigAutoField` `id`
surrogate primary key.

Sections 4 and 5 of this document cover the GIS master data (`Subdivision` / `Line` / `Tower` /
`Substation` / `SapLine`), the checklist catalog (`CatalogVersion` / `ChecklistItemGroup` /
`ChecklistItem` / `Defect` / `FollowUpQuestion` / `CriticalityRule`) and the cadre/role tables.
This section covers what those two produce and consume: the records an inspector actually
creates, the tickets they raise, the LILO lineage that keeps them attached to the right tower,
and the migration ladder that built all of it.

### 6.1 Domain vocabulary used in this section

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Ground Patrolling** | The routine, non-detailed of the two annual inspection cycles. Enum value `ground_patrol`. |
| **PMI** | **P**re-**M**onsoon **I**nspection — the detailed cycle run before the monsoon. Enum value `pmi`. Each tower is meant to be inspected twice a year: one Ground Patrol + one PMI (`line_inspection/models.py:57-63`). |
| **LILO** | **L**oop-**I**n **L**oop-**O**ut. A physical/organisational event in which an existing transmission line is cut and both ends are looped into a newly built substation, splitting one line into two. |
| **Criticality** | Severity of a recorded defect: `minor` / `major` / `critical` (`CRITICALITY_CHOICES`, `models.py:311-315`). |
| **Worst criticality** | The severest criticality across an inspection, widened with two extra states for towers: `none` (never inspected) and `ok` (inspected, no defects) — `WORST_CHOICES`, `models.py:49-55`. |
| **VT / virtual tower** | A `Tower` row with `is_virtual=True`: a second (or third) circuit strung on the *same physical structure* as a real tower. VT rows are never inspected; `_create_inspection` rejects them outright. |
| **`structure_key`** | `'<voltage>:<lat 5dp>:<lng 5dp>'` — groups a real tower and its co-located VT rows into one physical structure. |
| **Jurisdiction vs oversight** | *Jurisdiction* (`jurisdiction.py`) = the towers an employee may **write** to. *Oversight* (`viewing.py`) = the wider, reporting-hierarchy-derived set they may **read**. Inspection creation checks jurisdiction; ticket/inspection lists check oversight. |
| **`client_id`** | A client-generated UUID v4 that acts as the idempotency key for an inspection submit. |
| **checkCred** | The legacy APTRANSCO credential-verification web service used to authenticate the mobile app (`services/checkcred_client.py`). See section 3. |

### 6.2 `Inspection` — the root transactional record

`line_inspection/models.py:495-529`. One row per completed inspection of one real tower by one
employee on one date. There is **no FK to `Line`** — the line is always reached through
`tower.line` / `tower.line_name`, so a LILO that re-parents a tower automatically re-parents its
history.

| Field | Type | Null/blank | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | BigAutoField | — | auto | Surrogate PK. |
| `client_id` | CharField(64) | `null=True, blank=True`, **`unique=True`** | none | Client-generated idempotency key (UUID v4). See §6.2.1. |
| `tower` | FK → `Tower` | not null | — | **`on_delete=PROTECT`**, `related_name='inspections'`. |
| `inspector_employee_id` | CharField(32) | not null | — | Bare SAP employee id. Not a FK — there is no `django.contrib.auth.User` anywhere in this app; identity is always a plain employee-id string. |
| `catalog_version` | PositiveIntegerField | not null | — | Snapshot of `CatalogVersion.current()` at submit time. |
| `date` | DateField | not null | — | The **field date** the inspection is *for* (date only, no time). |
| `inspection_type` | CharField(16), choices | `null=True, blank=True` | none | `ground_patrol` / `pmi`; NULL = unknown cycle. |
| `remarks` | TextField | `blank=True` | `''` | Free-text inspector remarks for the whole inspection. |
| `worst_criticality` | CharField(16), choices `WORST_CHOICES` | not null | `'none'` | Severest criticality across all defect entries; `'ok'` when there were none. Computed server-side. |
| `saved_at` | DateTimeField | `null=True, blank=True` | none | Server-side wall-clock instant the row was written. |
| `created_at` | DateTimeField `auto_now_add` | not null | now | Row-insert timestamp, set by Django, never writable. |
| `inspector_lat` | FloatField | `null=True, blank=True` | none | GPS block — see §6.3. |
| `inspector_lng` | FloatField | `null=True, blank=True` | none | GPS block. |
| `gps_accuracy_m` | FloatField | `null=True, blank=True` | none | GPS block — device-reported horizontal accuracy. |
| `gps_distance_m` | FloatField | `null=True, blank=True` | none | GPS block — **server-recomputed** distance to the tower. |
| `presence_flag` | CharField(16), choices `PRESENCE_FLAG_CHOICES` | `blank=True` (**not** `null=True`) | `''` | GPS block — `''` means "not a GPS-aware submit". |
| `override_reason` | TextField | `blank=True` | `''` | GPS block — mandatory justification when presence failed. |

**Meta:** one index, `models.Index(fields=['tower', 'saved_at'])`. This is the index that makes
`status.latest_inspection_status()` / `latest_inspections()` cheap: they use Postgres
`DISTINCT ON (tower_id)` with `ORDER BY tower_id, -saved_at, -id`, which walks that composite
index directly (`line_inspection/status.py:39-44`).

#### 6.2.1 `client_id` — nullable-unique as the idempotency key

The field is `CharField(max_length=64, unique=True, null=True, blank=True)`. The combination
looks contradictory at first glance but is exactly the right shape:

- **Unique** is what makes the idempotency guarantee real. The application-level check in
  `InspectionCreateView.post` / `LineInspectionSubmitView.post` is a `filter(...).first()`
  lookup, which is racy on its own (two retries in flight simultaneously). The DB-level unique
  index is the backstop that turns the second concurrent insert into an `IntegrityError`
  instead of a silent duplicate.
- **Nullable** is what lets records exist without one. In PostgreSQL a nullable unique column
  permits unlimited `NULL`s (NULL is never equal to NULL), so every historical row, every row
  created by a script, and any future web-side create can leave it empty without colliding.
  The same trick is used for `Line.sap_line` (see section 4).
- `validate_client_id` on both create serializers (`api/serializers.py:146-147`, `191-192`)
  coerces an empty string to `None` — otherwise a client sending `"client_id": ""` twice would
  trip the unique constraint on the *second* submit.

The contract, mirroring the reference Flutter backend the field app was originally written
against: **same `client_id` on retry returns the existing record with HTTP 200; a new
`client_id` creates and returns 201.**

```python
# line_inspection/api/views.py:606-613 (mobile multipart submit)
client_id = data.get('client_id')
if client_id:
    existing = Inspection.objects.filter(client_id=client_id).first()
    if existing:
        return Response(_submit_result(existing), status=status.HTTP_200_OK)
inspection = _create_inspection(request.user.employee_id, data, files=request.FILES)
return Response(_submit_result(inspection), status=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)
```

Why it matters operationally: the Flutter app has a durable offline **outbox** that reuses the
same `client_id` across retries
(`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/services/offline/outbox.dart:32`,
`lib/utils/uuid.dart:8`). A field engineer who submits on a flaky 2G link, gets a timeout after
the server already committed, and retries hours later must not create a second inspection —
and must not lose their photos either. Idempotency on a client-chosen key is the only way to
get that without the client being able to observe the server's response.

#### 6.2.2 `catalog_version`

A plain `PositiveIntegerField` copy of the `CatalogVersion` singleton counter (section 5). The
checklist catalog is deliberately DB-backed and editable by Admins without a code deploy,
because the questionnaire is not finalised — which means the *meaning* of an inspection depends
on which catalog shape produced it. Stamping the version onto the row makes historical records
traceable to that shape.

Resolution order in `_create_inspection` (`api/views.py:488`):
`data.get('catalog_version') or CatalogVersion.current()`.

- The **mobile** serializer declares `catalog_version = serializers.IntegerField(required=False)`
  (`api/serializers.py:177`), and the Flutter app always sends it
  (`lib/services/line_inspection_api.dart:436`) — so a mobile submit records the version the
  *device's cached catalog* was at, which is the honest answer for an offline capture made
  against a possibly-stale catalog.
- The **legacy JSON** serializer `InspectionCreateSerializer` does **not** declare
  `catalog_version` at all (`api/serializers.py:136-147`). DRF's `validated_data` therefore
  never contains it, so that path always falls through to `CatalogVersion.current()`.

#### 6.2.3 Three different times: `date` vs `saved_at` vs `created_at`

These are genuinely three different concepts, and on an offline-first system they routinely
disagree. Getting them confused is the single easiest way to misread this table.

| Field | Kind | Who sets it | Semantics |
|---|---|---|---|
| `date` | `DateField` (no time, no tz) | The client, in the payload | The **field date**: the day the inspector was physically at the tower. This is the reporting date — it is what the register, the cycle filters and any audit consider "when the inspection happened". |
| `saved_at` | `DateTimeField`, nullable | Server, `timezone.now()` inside the create transaction (`api/views.py:482,492`) | **When the server accepted it.** This is the ordering key for "latest inspection" everywhere (`Meta.indexes` is on `(tower, saved_at)`, and `status.py` orders by `-saved_at, -id`). |
| `created_at` | `DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)` | Django, at INSERT | Immutable row-insert audit stamp. Cannot be supplied or overwritten by any caller. |

For an inspection submitted online, all three land on the same moment. They diverge in the case
this system is built for:

> An inspector walks a line on **3 August** with no mobile signal. The capture goes into the
> Flutter outbox. They return to coverage on **7 August** and the outbox drains.
> Result: `date = 2026-08-03` (the real inspection day) while
> `saved_at ≈ created_at ≈ 2026-08-07T10:14Z`.

They also diverge if a row is ever backfilled by script: `saved_at` may be set to the historical
instant while `created_at` records the (much later) import.

Two consequences worth internalising:

1. `saved_at` — not `date` — decides which inspection is "current" for a tower, and it is also
   what `status.bump_tower_cache` compares against (`status.py:72-73`), so a late-arriving
   *older* inspection cannot regress `Tower.last_worst_criticality`. But note the comparison is
   against `saved_at`, and `saved_at` is the *server's* now — so two offline captures of the
   same tower drain in outbox order, not field-date order.
2. `saved_at` is nullable in the schema but is **always** populated by `_create_inspection`
   (it passes `saved_at=now` unconditionally). A NULL `saved_at` therefore only ever appears on
   rows created outside the API — fixtures, tests, or a manual `objects.create()`.

#### 6.2.4 `inspection_type` — and a README discrepancy

`INSPECTION_TYPE_CHOICES` (`models.py:60-63`) is `ground_patrol` / `pmi`. The field is nullable
everywhere it appears (`Inspection.inspection_type`, `Tower.last_inspection_type`), and the
in-code comment explains why: "Nullable everywhere for now — the Flutter app (Phase 4) will
start stamping it; existing rows stay NULL (unknown)." NULL is a real, distinct third state
meaning *we do not know which cycle this was*, not a defaulted `ground_patrol`.

The web dashboard never creates inspections at all (Phase 3 is read-only monitoring), so the
only writer that could populate this is the mobile app.

> **DISCREPANCY — the code contradicts both the README and its own comment.**
> `line_inspection/README.md:269-271` states "`inspection_type` … the Flutter app populates it,
> existing rows stay NULL", and `models.py:504-506` repeats the claim. The backend is ready for
> it: `MobileInspectionCreateSerializer` declares
> `inspection_type = serializers.ChoiceField(choices=['ground_patrol', 'pmi'], required=False, allow_null=True)`
> (`api/serializers.py:179`) and `_create_inspection` passes it straight through
> (`api/views.py:490`).
> **But the Flutter app in this checkout never sends it.** A recursive search for
> `inspection_type` / `inspectionType` / `ground_patrol` / `pmi` across every `.dart` file under
> `Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/` returns **zero matches**, and the submit payload
> built at `lib/services/line_inspection_api.dart:433-446` enumerates its keys explicitly
> (`tower_id`, `inspector_employee_id`, `catalog_version`, `date`, `remarks`, `client_id`,
> `items`, `inspector_lat`, `inspector_lng`, `gps_accuracy_m`, `presence_flag`,
> `override_reason`) with no cycle field among them.
> **Therefore, as the tree stands, every mobile-created `Inspection` has
> `inspection_type = NULL` and every `Tower.last_inspection_type` stays NULL.** The
> Ground-Patrol/PMI cycle filters on the dashboard map, the inspections screen (`?cycle=`) and
> the register (`status.latest_inspections(..., inspection_type=...)`) will match **nothing**
> until the app is taught to send the field. Nothing errors — the feature is simply inert.

#### 6.2.5 `worst_criticality`

Computed entirely server-side, never accepted from the client. After all `DefectEntry` rows are
created, `_create_inspection` folds their final criticalities:

```python
# line_inspection/api/views.py:538-539
inspection.worst_criticality = worst_of(all_criticalities) if all_criticalities else 'ok'
inspection.save(update_fields=['worst_criticality'])
```

`worst_of` (`services/criticality.py:48-56`) ranks against
`CRITICALITY_ORDER = {'none': 0, 'ok': 1, 'minor': 2, 'major': 3, 'critical': 4}` and starts
from `'ok'`. Note the asymmetry that makes the model readable: `'none'` (never inspected) can
only ever appear as a *default* on a `Tower`/`Inspection` row that no create path has touched —
an inspection that was actually submitted is at worst `'ok'`. The same enum and the same
ordering are reused for `Tower.last_worst_criticality`, which is what colours the ~67k markers
on the map without a per-tower subquery.

### 6.3 GPS proof of presence — the policy in full

Phase 4 added a block of six fields plus one module constant. The rationale is stated bluntly in
the model comment (`models.py:65-67`): *"Presence is the utmost criterion for field
inspection"*. A tower inspection that the inspector never physically attended is worthless, and
the historically hard part of running this programme on paper was proving attendance.

```python
# line_inspection/models.py:68-73
PRESENCE_FLAG_CHOICES = [
    ('in_range',     'In range (<=50 m)'),
    ('out_of_range', 'Out of range (overridden)'),
    ('no_fix',       'No GPS fix (overridden)'),
]
PRESENCE_RADIUS_M = 50.0
```

| Field | Type | Source of truth | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `inspector_lat` | Float, null | **Client** | The device fix latitude at submit time. Stored as-sent (it is evidence). |
| `inspector_lng` | Float, null | **Client** | As above. |
| `gps_accuracy_m` | Float, null | **Client** | Device-reported horizontal accuracy. Recorded but **not** gated on — a 200 m-accuracy fix that happens to read in-range is still accepted as `in_range`. |
| `gps_distance_m` | Float, null | **Server** | Recomputed by haversine against `tower.latitude/longitude`. A client-sent distance is never read. |
| `presence_flag` | Char(16), blank | **Server** | Derived, never trusted from the client (see below). |
| `override_reason` | Text, blank | **Client** | Free text. Required and enforced when the flag is not `in_range`. |

All six are nullable/blank so that historical rows and any non-GPS create path stay valid — the
migration that added them (`0008`) is additive precisely for this reason.

#### 6.3.1 Distance is recomputed server-side

```python
# line_inspection/api/views.py:46-53
def _haversine_m(lat1, lng1, lat2, lng2):
    """Great-circle distance in metres between two lat/lng points."""
    r = 6371000.0
    p1, p2 = math.radians(lat1), math.radians(lat2)
    dp = math.radians(lat2 - lat1)
    dl = math.radians(lng2 - lng1)
    a = math.sin(dp / 2) ** 2 + math.cos(p1) * math.cos(p2) * math.sin(dl / 2) ** 2
    return 2 * r * math.asin(min(1.0, math.sqrt(a)))
```

The reference tower coordinates come from `Tower.latitude` / `Tower.longitude`, which are
ArcGIS master data, not anything the client can influence. Crucially, the mobile serializer
does **not even declare** a `gps_distance_m` input field (`api/serializers.py:183-189` accepts
only `inspector_lat`, `inspector_lng`, `gps_accuracy_m`, `presence_flag`, `override_reason`), so
a client-supplied distance is dropped by DRF before the view ever sees it. The client *does*
send `presence_flag`, but the server overwrites it — the value is used only as a signal that
this is a GPS-aware submit (§6.3.3).

The mobile app computes the same distance locally to build its "towers within 50 m" picker
(`lib/screens/li_tabs/inspection_tab.dart:147-153`), but that is UX; the record of truth is the
server's number.

#### 6.3.2 The gate — three flags, one hard radius, one audited escape hatch

```python
# line_inspection/api/views.py:462-480
lat = data.get('inspector_lat')
lng = data.get('inspector_lng')
override_reason = (data.get('override_reason') or '').strip()
gps_aware = lat is not None or lng is not None or bool(data.get('presence_flag'))
distance_m = None
if gps_aware:
    if lat is not None and lng is not None and tower.latitude is not None and tower.longitude is not None:
        distance_m = _haversine_m(lat, lng, tower.latitude, tower.longitude)
    if lat is None or lng is None:
        presence_flag = 'no_fix'
    elif distance_m is not None and distance_m <= PRESENCE_RADIUS_M:
        presence_flag = 'in_range'
    else:
        presence_flag = 'out_of_range'
    if presence_flag != 'in_range' and not override_reason:
        raise ValidationError({'override_reason':
            'An out-of-range or no-GPS inspection requires an override reason (presence is required).'})
else:
    presence_flag = ''
```

Branch by branch:

| Condition | `presence_flag` | `gps_distance_m` | Accepted? |
|---|---|---|---|
| lat **and** lng present, tower has coords, distance ≤ 50.0 m | `in_range` | the number | Always. |
| lat **and** lng present, distance > 50.0 m | `out_of_range` | the number | **Only** with a non-empty `override_reason`; otherwise HTTP 400. |
| lat **and** lng present, but the **tower** has no stored coords | `out_of_range` | `None` | Only with an override reason. Note the fail-**closed** behaviour: a tower with missing ArcGIS coordinates cannot be inspected in-range at all, because `distance_m` stays `None` and the `<= 50` test cannot pass. |
| lat **or** lng missing (no fix) | `no_fix` | `None` | Only with an override reason. |
| Not GPS-aware at all | `''` | `None` | Always — the gate is skipped entirely. |

Design notes:

- **50 m is a hard number, not a tunable setting.** `PRESENCE_RADIUS_M = 50.0` is a module
  constant in `models.py`, imported by `api/views.py:21`. There is no environment variable or
  DB row for it — changing the radius is a code change, deliberately, because it is a
  compliance parameter rather than a deployment parameter.
- **The override is allowed but audited, not blocked.** Refusing out-of-range submits outright
  would be operationally unusable — towers sit in fields with no signal, some ArcGIS
  coordinates are wrong, and a phone can fail to get a fix under a canopy. So the policy is:
  the inspection is accepted, but the row permanently carries *which* failure mode occurred,
  *how far off* they were, and *why they say it was fine*. `override_reason` is
  `.strip()`ped before the emptiness test, so whitespace does not satisfy it.
- **`presence_flag` uses `blank=True` and not `null=True`.** The "not a GPS submit" state is the
  empty string, not NULL. That keeps `presence_flag` a plain non-nullable text column and makes
  filtering (`.exclude(presence_flag='')`) straightforward, at the cost of `''` not being one
  of the declared `choices` — Django's model validators would reject `''` under `full_clean()`,
  but this code path never calls `full_clean()`, so nothing enforces it.
- The GPS block is a *stamp*, not a constraint: nothing in the model layer (no `CheckConstraint`)
  prevents a script from writing `presence_flag='in_range'` with a 900 m `gps_distance_m`. The
  policy lives entirely in `_create_inspection`.

#### 6.3.3 Why the legacy JSON create path is exempt — the `gps_aware` detection

There are two write endpoints, sharing one atomic core:

| Endpoint | View | Serializer | Payload style |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POST /inspection/api/inspections/` | `InspectionCreateView` (`api/views.py:549`) | `InspectionCreateSerializer` | Legacy JSON: `tower`, `item_results[]`, items/defects by **slug key** |
| `POST /inspection/api/line-inspections/` | `LineInspectionSubmitView` (`api/views.py:585`) | `MobileInspectionCreateSerializer` | Mobile multipart: one `payload` JSON field + file parts named by each `photo_key`; `tower_id`, `items[]`, items/defects by **numeric id**; carries the GPS block |

`gps_aware` is true when the payload carries **any** of `inspector_lat`, `inspector_lng`, or a
truthy `presence_flag`. The legacy JSON path can never satisfy that, because
`InspectionCreateSerializer` (`api/serializers.py:136-147`) declares only `client_id`, `tower`,
`date`, `inspection_type`, `remarks`, `item_results` — DRF strips every GPS key out of
`validated_data` before `_create_inspection` runs. The exemption is therefore *structural*,
not a flag someone can flip: a caller on the legacy path could not opt into the gate even by
sending GPS fields, and equally cannot bypass it by pretending to be mobile.

Why exempt it at all? The legacy path predates Phase 4 and exists for the browser/test/script
consumers documented in section 5 of the API; it has no device fix to offer, so gating it would
break the tests and the register-seeding scripts for no safety gain. The consequence is that
`presence_flag=''` reliably identifies "created through a non-GPS path" in the data.

**Residual gap worth knowing:** on the *mobile* endpoint, a client that sends neither
coordinates nor a `presence_flag` also evaluates `gps_aware=False` and skips the gate entirely.
The real Flutter app cannot do this — `presenceFlag` is a required positional value in the app's
submit chain and defaults to `'in_range'`
(`lib/screens/line_inspection_form_screen.dart:45`, `lib/services/offline/offline_actions.dart:60`),
so every mobile submit is GPS-aware — but a hand-rolled client holding a valid `Token` could
omit both and be accepted with `presence_flag=''`.

**Note on the two distance functions.** This app computes geodesic distance in two different
ways on purpose: `_haversine_m` (great-circle, `api/views.py:46`) for the presence gate, and
`lilo_matching.distance_m` (planar/equirectangular, `services/lilo_matching.py:28-36`) for LILO
tower matching. The LILO one is explicitly justified in its docstring as "accurate enough for
matching towers a few metres to a few hundred metres apart"; the presence gate is a compliance
boundary and uses the exact formula. If you ever compare the two numbers, expect sub-centimetre
disagreement at these scales — but they are not interchangeable code.

### 6.4 `ItemResult` — one checklist answer

`line_inspection/models.py:540-554`. One row per checklist item the inspector answered — or per
item *and position*, for positional items.

| Field | Type | Null/blank | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `inspection` | FK → `Inspection` | not null | **`on_delete=CASCADE`**, `related_name='item_results'`. Deleting an inspection takes its answers with it — they have no meaning apart from it. |
| `item` | FK → `ChecklistItem` | not null | **`on_delete=PROTECT`**, `related_name='item_results'`. You cannot delete a catalog item that has been answered. |
| `position` | CharField(32) | `blank=True` | The position within a positional item, e.g. `"Top"` / `"Middle"` / `"Bottom"` / `"Earth wire"`. **`''` (empty string, not NULL) for non-positional items.** |
| `status` | CharField(16), choices | required, no default | See below. |
| `meta` | JSONField | `default=dict, blank=True` | Per-item structured extras keyed by `ChecklistItem.pos_meta['id']`, e.g. `{"insType": "Fog Disc"}`. |
| `photo` | ImageField | `null=True, blank=True` | `upload_to='line_inspection/item_photos/%Y/%m/'`. |

**`ITEM_STATUS_CHOICES`** (`models.py:532-537`) — four states, and the distinction between the
first two is the one people get wrong:

| Value | Label | Means |
|---|---|---|
| `na` | Not applicable | The item **does not apply to this tower**. Structural: e.g. an item whose `applicable_tower_types` excludes this `tower_type`, with `ChecklistItem.na_reason` explaining why. Nothing is expected. |
| `not_provided` | Not available | The item applies in principle, but **the component is not fitted on this tower** — the availability-gated case (`ChecklistItem.is_availability_gated` / `is_position_availability_gated`). Absence is itself the finding. |
| `normal` | Normal | Inspected, nothing wrong. This is the **default state of every item** in the app's exception-based UI: the inspector only touches the items that are defective. |
| `defect` | Defect | One or more `DefectEntry` children hang off this row. |

`status` has **no default** in the model, so an `ItemResult` created without one raises at the
DB level; both input serializers declare it as a required `ChoiceField`.

**The `(inspection, item, position)` unique constraint** (`uniq_itemresult_inspection_item_position`)
is what keeps an inspection internally consistent. It prevents an inspector — or, far more
likely, a retry, a double-tap, or a buggy payload that repeats an item — from recording two
contradictory answers for the same thing in one inspection. Because `position` is `''` rather
than NULL for non-positional items, the constraint **does** bite for them: in PostgreSQL two
NULLs would compare as distinct and the constraint would silently do nothing, whereas two `''`
values collide as intended. That `''`-not-NULL choice is load-bearing, not cosmetic.

Note that the constraint is intra-inspection only: a tower can absolutely have the same item
answered many times across many inspections, which is the whole point of history.

### 6.5 `DefectEntry` — one recorded defect

`line_inspection/models.py:557-568`. Child of `ItemResult`; there is one per defect the
inspector recorded against that item/position.

| Field | Type | Null/blank | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `item_result` | FK → `ItemResult` | not null | **`on_delete=CASCADE`**, `related_name='entries'`. |
| `defect` | FK → `Defect` | not null | **`on_delete=PROTECT`**, `related_name='entries'`. Resolved *scoped to the parent item* (`_resolve_defect(item, ref)` filters `Defect.objects.filter(item=item, ...)`), so a defect key from another item cannot be attached. |
| `answers` | JSONField | `default=dict, blank=True` | The follow-up answers. Shape: `{followUpKey: scalar | [scalar, ...]}`. |
| `suggested_criticality` | CharField(16), choices, `blank=True` | may be `''` | What the **server's rule engine** computed. |
| `criticality` | CharField(16), choices | required | What was actually **recorded** — the inspector's confirmation or override. |
| `note` | TextField | `blank=True` | Inspector's free text about this specific defect. |
| `photo` | ImageField | `null=True, blank=True` | `upload_to='line_inspection/defect_photos/%Y/%m/'`. |
| `created_at` | DateTimeField `auto_now_add` | not null | Row-insert stamp. |

**`answers` shape.** Keys are `FollowUpQuestion.key` values, drawn from the ordered
`Defect.ask` list. Values depend on `FollowUpQuestion.answer_type`: a scalar for
`choice` / `number` / `text`, and a list for `multichoice`. Example for a broken-disc defect:

```json
{ "discCount": 3, "insType": "Fog Disc", "location": ["Top", "Middle"] }
```

Nothing validates the answers against the follow-up definitions on the way in — `answers` is a
`DictField` in both serializers and is written through verbatim. The criticality rule engine
tolerates missing/odd keys by simply not matching (`_rule_matches` returns `False` when the key
is absent, `services/criticality.py:18-19`).

**Why both `suggested_criticality` and `criticality` are stored.** The catalog carries
`CriticalityRule` rows — data-driven replacements for the POC's hardcoded `critRule()` JS, e.g.
*"if `discCount >= 2` then critical"*. On submit the server evaluates them:

```python
# line_inspection/api/views.py:521-527
answers = entry_data.get('answers', {})
suggested = suggest_criticality(defect, answers)
final = entry_data.get('criticality') or suggested
entry = DefectEntry.objects.create(
    item_result=item_result, defect=defect, answers=answers,
    suggested_criticality=suggested, criticality=final, note=entry_data.get('note', ''),
)
```

Storing both makes **disagreement auditable**. If the rules say `critical` and the inspector
recorded `minor`, the row keeps the pair, and a supervisor (or a later query) can find every
case where a human downgraded the machine's suggestion. If only the final value were stored,
that signal would be lost forever, and there would be no way to tell a rule that is
mis-calibrated from an inspector who is under-reporting. It also insulates history from rule
edits: the rules can change tomorrow, but this row still records what the engine said *at the
time*.

Note the precedence in `final = entry_data.get('criticality') or suggested`: the **inspector
wins** when they supply a value; the suggestion is only a fallback. Both `''` and `None` from
the client fall through to the suggestion.

> **Discrepancy (minor).** `MobileDefectEntryInputSerializer` accepts a client-sent
> `suggested_criticality` field (`api/serializers.py:156`), and `README.md:484-486` describes
> criticality as "suggested client-side from `criticality_rules` … and sent
> (`criticality` + `suggested_criticality`) for the server to trust/re-derive". In fact
> `_create_inspection` **ignores** the client's `suggested_criticality` entirely and always
> recomputes it from the DB rules. That is the safer behaviour (the stored suggestion is
> genuinely the server's own), but the accepted-and-discarded input field is dead weight.

### 6.6 `DefectTicket` — the actionable work item

`line_inspection/models.py:582-610`. Auto-raised, one per `DefectEntry`, inside the same
transaction as the inspection. A ticket is the thing an O&M crew closes; the `DefectEntry` is
the immutable observation.

| Field | Type | Null/blank | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `inspection` | FK → `Inspection` | not null | — | **PROTECT**, `related_name='tickets'`. Provenance. |
| `tower` | FK → `Tower` | not null | — | **PROTECT**, `related_name='tickets'`. Denormalized from `inspection.tower` so ticket queries never need a join through `Inspection`. |
| `item` | FK → `ChecklistItem` | not null | — | **PROTECT**, `related_name='tickets'`. |
| `item_label` | CharField(255) | required | — | **Snapshot** of `item.label` at raise time. |
| `position` | CharField(32) | `blank=True` | `''` | Copied from the parent `ItemResult`. |
| `defect` | FK → `Defect` | not null | — | **PROTECT**, `related_name='tickets'`. |
| `defect_label` | CharField(255) | required | — | **Snapshot** of `defect.label` at raise time. |
| `answers` | JSONField | `blank=True` | `{}` | **Snapshot** of the `DefectEntry.answers` dict. |
| `criticality` | CharField(16), choices | required | — | The entry's **final** criticality (not the suggestion). |
| `status` | CharField(16), choices `TICKET_STATUS_CHOICES` | required | `'open'` | `open` / `closed`. |
| `source` | CharField(32), choices `TICKET_SOURCE_CHOICES` | required | `'human_inspection'` | `human_inspection` / `drone_inspection`. |
| `drone_metadata` | JSONField | `null=True, blank=True` | none | Schema-only placeholder. |
| `raised_at` | DateTimeField | not null | — | Set explicitly to the inspection's `now`, **not** `auto_now_add` — so it is exactly equal to the parent inspection's `saved_at`. |
| `raised_by_employee_id` | CharField(32) | not null | — | The inspecting employee. |
| `closed_at` | DateTimeField | `null=True, blank=True` | none | Close workflow. |
| `closed_by_employee_id` | CharField(32) | `blank=True` | `''` | Close workflow. |
| `close_note` | TextField | `blank=True` | `''` | Close workflow. |

**Meta:** `Index(['status', 'criticality'])` — serving the dashboard's default "open tickets by
severity" queries — and `Index(['tower'])` for the per-tower drill-down and the map pop-up.

Creation is a single `bulk_create` at the end of the transaction (`api/views.py:531-540`), so an
inspection with 12 defects issues one INSERT for all 12 tickets.

#### 6.6.1 Label snapshotting — and why

`item_label`, `defect_label` and `answers` are all **copied onto the ticket**, even though the
ticket also holds FKs to `ChecklistItem` and `Defect` from which the labels could be read.
This is intentional denormalisation:

```python
# line_inspection/models.py:586-591
item = models.ForeignKey(ChecklistItem, on_delete=models.PROTECT, related_name='tickets')
item_label = models.CharField(max_length=255)  # snapshotted so tickets stay readable if catalog wording changes
```

The checklist catalog is **editable by Admins at runtime** and is explicitly not finalised —
the whole point of making it DB-backed (section 5) is that field engineers will revise the
wording after using the app. If a ticket rendered its label by dereferencing the FK, then an
Admin rewording item 14 from *"Condition of stub/coping"* to *"Stub & coping — corrosion"*
would silently rewrite the text of every ticket ever raised under the old wording, including
closed ones. Tickets are operational and legal records: what they *said* when they were raised
must not be retroactively edited by an unrelated catalog change. The FKs are kept alongside for
grouping/filtering ("all tickets for item X"), the snapshots for display.

`answers` is snapshotted for the same reason, plus a practical one: it makes the ticket
self-describing without a three-hop join back through `DefectEntry → ItemResult → Inspection`.
`DefectTicketSerializer` exposes it directly (`api/serializers.py:275-277`). Note there is
**no** FK from `DefectTicket` to the `DefectEntry` that spawned it — the snapshot *is* the link,
which is why entry and ticket cannot drift but also cannot be joined programmatically.

#### 6.6.2 `source` and `drone_metadata` — schema-only

`TICKET_SOURCE_CHOICES` is `human_inspection` / `drone_inspection` (`models.py:576-579`).
Everything the code writes today is `source='human_inspection'` — the literal is hardcoded in
`_create_inspection` (`api/views.py:534`).

**No drone ingestion pipeline exists.** A full-tree search for writers of
`source='drone_inspection'` or of `drone_metadata` finds only readers: the rollup aggregation
`drone=Count('id', filter=Q(source='drone_inspection'))` (`dashboard_views.py:204`), the ticket
screen's source filter (`templates/line_inspection/dashboard_tickets.html:31`), the serializer
field, and a test that fabricates both sources (`tests/test_dashboard.py:103`). `drone_metadata`
is `null=True` with no declared shape at all.

The reason this exists as dead schema rather than being deferred: drone inspection is being
built **in parallel** by a separate effort. Reserving the column and the enum value now means
the dashboard, the filters, the serializer and the rollups are already drone-aware, so
integrating the drone pipeline later is an ingestion job that writes rows — not a migration
plus a UI change plus a reporting change. The cost is one nullable JSON column that is
currently always NULL.

#### 6.6.3 Close workflow

`POST /inspection/api/tickets/<pk>/close/` → `DefectTicketCloseView` (`api/views.py:707-729`).

1. 404 if the ticket does not exist.
2. Authorization: `is_admin(employee_id) or jurisdiction.can_edit_tower(employee_id, ticket.tower)`.
   The comment explains the asymmetry — Admins (who hand out jurisdiction in the first place)
   may act on any ticket in their oversight; field inspectors only on towers they personally
   hold jurisdiction over. Failing both raises `PermissionDenied` (403).
3. **Idempotent:** an already-`closed` ticket returns 200 with the current state and is not
   re-stamped, so a retry cannot overwrite the original closer/timestamp.
4. Otherwise: `status='closed'`, `closed_at=timezone.now()`,
   `closed_by_employee_id=<caller>`, `close_note=request.data.get('close_note', 'Attended and rectified')`
   — note the **default close note** when the caller sends none.

There is **no reopen path** anywhere in the codebase. Once closed, a ticket stays closed;
a recurrence produces a fresh ticket from the next inspection.

### 6.7 `SupportRequest` — the dispute / contact-admin channel

`line_inspection/models.py:619-632`. Not part of the inspection tree at all; it exists so a
field engineer can raise a query (a wrong jurisdiction assignment, a wrong tower coordinate, a
catalog item that makes no sense) without leaving the app.

| Field | Type | Null/blank | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `subdivision` | FK → `Subdivision` | `null=True, blank=True` | none | **`on_delete=PROTECT`**, `related_name='support_requests'`. Which subdivision the request concerns; also the scoping key for who can see it. |
| `raised_by_employee_id` | CharField(32) | not null | — | Set server-side from the authenticated identity; read-only in the serializer. |
| `category` | CharField(255) | required | — | Free-form category string — **not** an enum, no choices defined. |
| `subject` | CharField(255) | required | — | Short title. |
| `text` | TextField | required | — | Body. |
| `status` | CharField(16), choices `SUPPORT_STATUS_CHOICES` | required | `'open'` | `open` / `resolved`. |
| `created_at` | DateTimeField `auto_now_add` | not null | now | |
| `response` | TextField | `blank=True` | `''` | The resolver's reply. |
| `resolved_by_employee_id` | CharField(32) | `blank=True` | `''` | |
| `resolved_at` | DateTimeField | `null=True, blank=True` | none | |

No `Meta` — no indexes, no constraints, no ordering.

**Lifecycle.**

- **Create** — `POST /inspection/api/support/` (`SupportRequestListCreateView.create`,
  `api/views.py:760-777`). `raised_by_employee_id` is forced to the caller. There is a
  **content-match dedup** rather than a `client_id`: an existing **open** request from the same
  employee with the identical `subject` **and** `text` returns 200 instead of creating a
  duplicate. This mirrors the reference backend and matches the app's retry semantics — a
  support request has no natural idempotency key, so equality of content is used as a proxy.
  New requests return 201.
- **List** — own requests, unioned with requests raised in any subdivision inside the caller's
  oversight scope (`api/views.py:746-758`), newest first, optional `?subdivision=` filter.
- **Resolve** — `POST /inspection/api/support/<pk>/resolve/` (`api/views.py:780-793`). Sets
  `status='resolved'`, `response=request.data.get('response', 'Done')` (again a hardcoded
  default), `resolved_by_employee_id`, `resolved_at`. Like ticket close, there is no un-resolve.

> **FINDING (authorization gap).** `SupportRequestResolveView` (`line_inspection/api/views.py:780-793`)
> declares only `permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]` and performs **no ownership, admin, or
> oversight check** before resolving. Any authenticated employee — including a field inspector
> with a mobile token — can resolve **any** support request in the system by primary key,
> including ones raised in subdivisions they cannot even see in the list view. Contrast
> `DefectTicketCloseView` immediately above it, which does gate on `is_admin` or
> `can_edit_tower`. This looks like an oversight rather than a decision; the README does not
> mention it.

### 6.8 The `on_delete=PROTECT` policy

The rule (`README.md:282-284`): *"All FKs from transactional models to `Tower`/`Line`/`Inspection`
use `on_delete=PROTECT` — deleting a Tower with Inspections/Tickets raises instead of silently
cascading (a bug present in the original POC)."* Verified against the code — here is every FK in
the app, grouped by behaviour.

| Model.field | Target | `on_delete` | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Inspection.tower` | Tower | **PROTECT** | An inspection is evidence that someone attended a tower. Losing it because a sync or an admin removed the tower row would be data loss with no trace. |
| `ItemResult.item` | ChecklistItem | **PROTECT** | A catalog item that has been answered cannot be deleted — the answers would become uninterpretable. Forces the Admin to retire rather than delete. |
| `DefectEntry.defect` | Defect | **PROTECT** | Same reasoning at the defect level. |
| `DefectTicket.inspection` | Inspection | **PROTECT** | A ticket must always be traceable to the inspection that raised it. |
| `DefectTicket.tower` | Tower | **PROTECT** | |
| `DefectTicket.item` | ChecklistItem | **PROTECT** | |
| `DefectTicket.defect` | Defect | **PROTECT** | |
| `SupportRequest.subdivision` | Subdivision | **PROTECT** | |
| `RoleAssignment.subdivision` | Subdivision | **PROTECT** | Deleting a subdivision must not silently revoke people's jurisdiction. |
| `LineTowerAssignment.from_tower` | Tower | **PROTECT** | The range boundary towers *are* the assignment's definition. |
| `LineTowerAssignment.to_tower` | Tower | **PROTECT** | |
| `ChecklistItem.group` | ChecklistItemGroup | **PROTECT** | |
| `Defect.item` | ChecklistItem | **PROTECT** | |
| `LiloEvent.old_line` | Line | **PROTECT** | The lineage record's whole purpose is naming the pre-LILO line. |
| `LiloTowerRemap.surviving_tower` | Tower | **PROTECT** | The audit row must keep pointing at the tower whose PK was preserved. |
| `ItemResult.inspection` | Inspection | CASCADE | Answers have no meaning without their inspection. |
| `DefectEntry.item_result` | ItemResult | CASCADE | Same, one level down. |
| `CriticalityRule.defect` | Defect | CASCADE | A rule is a property of its defect. |
| `LineTowerAssignment.line` | Line | CASCADE | If the line is gone the range is meaningless — but note this is the one place a `Line` delete can silently remove assignments. |
| `LiloTowerRemap.event` | LiloEvent | CASCADE | Audit rows belong to their event. |
| `Line.subdivision`, `Tower.subdivision`, `Tower.line`, `Substation.subdivision`, `Line.sap_line`, `LiloEvent.split_tower` | various | SET_NULL | GIS/administrative re-parenting must be survivable — a tower whose line disappears becomes an orphan tower, not a deleted tower. |

The practical effect: `tower.delete()` on a tower with any inspection, ticket, or range
assignment raises `django.db.models.ProtectedError`. This is deliberate and is called out as a
**bug fix relative to the original POC**, where the equivalent relations cascaded and a tower
cleanup could quietly wipe inspection history. Note that the routine ArcGIS sync never deletes
anything anyway — rows that vanish upstream are marked `is_active=False`
(`management/commands/sync_gis_towers.py:335-338`) — so PROTECT is a safety net against manual
`delete()` calls and ad-hoc scripts, which is precisely where the POC's data loss came from.

**The one place a delete is genuinely performed** is `lilo_matching.apply_reconcile`, which
calls `new.delete()` on the freshly-created duplicate tower row (`services/lilo_matching.py:185`).
That is safe by construction: the row being deleted was created by the sync moments earlier and
has no inspections, tickets, or assignments — all of those live on the *old* surviving row,
which is the one being kept. The comment on that line explains the ordering: the delete must
happen *before* the survivor adopts the new `arcgis_object_id`, to free the
`(source_layer, arcgis_object_id)` unique constraint.

### 6.9 LILO — Loop-In Loop-Out

#### 6.9.1 What a LILO is, physically

A LILO is a real-world grid reconfiguration. A new substation is built somewhere near an
existing transmission line. Rather than run fresh lines to it, the utility cuts the existing
line at a convenient tower and **loops both cut ends into the new substation** — "loop in, loop
out". Two short spur sections of new towers are built to reach the substation.

Administratively, what was one line (A → C) becomes **two** lines (A → B and B → C, where B is
the new substation). The great majority of the towers are physically untouched — the same steel
in the same ground — but they now belong to a differently-named line.

Frequency and gating: **roughly 20–30 per year across the state**, and the reconcile is
**Super-Admin only** (`@auth.super_admin_required` on both `lilo_home` and `lilo_reconcile`,
`admin_views.py:415,440`; CLI equivalents at `management/commands/lilo_reconcile.py` and
`detect_tower_churn.py`). It is a rare, explicitly-triggered, reviewed operation — never
automatic.

#### 6.9.2 The data problem it causes

The GIS team does not *edit* the line in ArcGIS. They **delete the old line feature and create
new ones.** ArcGIS assigns fresh `OBJECTID`s to every recreated feature, including all the
towers.

Our sync (`sync_gis_towers`) identifies rows by the pair `(source_layer, arcgis_object_id)` —
the unique constraint `uniq_tower_source_object`. So after a LILO:

- Every tower on the affected line arrives with an **unfamiliar** `arcgis_object_id`, and the
  sync **creates brand-new `Tower` rows** with brand-new primary keys.
- The old rows are no longer present upstream, so the sync's staleness pass marks them
  `is_active=False` (it never deletes — `sync_gis_towers.py:335-338`).

The result of a naive sync is a silent catastrophe: **every `Inspection`, `DefectTicket` and
`LineTowerAssignment` still points at the deactivated old `Tower` PKs**, while the map, the
register, the rollups and the mobile app all read the new, empty rows. The towers look like
they have never been inspected. History is not lost from the database — it is *stranded*,
attached to rows nothing displays. And because ~20–30 LILOs happen a year, this would
accumulate quietly.

#### 6.9.3 The solution: coordinates are the tower's true identity

The insight (`models.py:635-644`, `services/lilo_matching.py:1-10`): a physical tower does not
move during a LILO. Its `arcgis_object_id` is an accident of the GIS editing workflow; its
**coordinates** are what it actually is. `tower_number` corroborates (a surviving tower keeps
its number).

So the reconcile does not create a mapping table pointing new PKs at old PKs. It **revives the
survivors in place**:

> The **old** `Tower` row is kept — same primary key — and *adopts* the new row's ArcGIS
> attributes (`arcgis_object_id`, `line`, `line_name`, coordinates, subdivision, raw
> properties…). The duplicate **new** row is deleted. Genuine new loop towers, which match
> nothing, simply stay as the new rows they already are.

Because the PK never changes, **every FK that pointed at it keeps pointing at it**:
`Inspection.tower`, `DefectTicket.tower`, `LineTowerAssignment.from_tower`/`to_tower`, and the
`Tower.last_*` status cache. Nothing needs rewriting. That is why "revive in place" was chosen
over "create new + migrate FKs": there is no partial-failure state where half the history has
moved.

The core of `apply_reconcile` (`services/lilo_matching.py:179-195`):

```python
dist = distance_m(new.latitude, new.longitude, old.latitude, old.longitude)
nm = bool(_norm_number(new.tower_number)) and _norm_number(new.tower_number) == _norm_number(old.tower_number)
method = 'auto' if _is_auto(dist, nm) else 'manual'
old_obj, new_obj = old.arcgis_object_id, new.arcgis_object_id
snapshot = {f: getattr(new, f) for f in _COPY_FIELDS}
new_line_id, new_sub_id = new.line_id, new.subdivision_id
new.delete()  # free (source_layer, object_id) and drop the duplicate BEFORE adopting it
for f in _COPY_FIELDS:
    setattr(old, f, snapshot[f])
old.line_id, old.subdivision_id = new_line_id, new_sub_id
old.is_active = True
if old.latitude is not None and old.longitude is not None:
    old.structure_key = f'{old.voltage}:{old.latitude:.5f}:{old.longitude:.5f}'
old.save()
```

`_COPY_FIELDS` (`lilo_matching.py:139-144`) is the explicit allow-list of 22 attributes copied
from the new row onto the survivor. It deliberately **excludes** `voltage` (unchanged by a
LILO) and the denormalized `last_*` caches and `line_sequence` (recomputed). The whole apply
runs inside `transaction.atomic(using='line_inspection_db')`, and finishes by rebuilding the
tower schedule for each new line via `schedule.assign_line_sequence(line)` — necessary because
the towers' ordering along a now-shorter line has changed.

#### 6.9.4 `LiloEvent`

`line_inspection/models.py:646-659`. One row per recorded LILO — the declaration, created by a
Super Admin *before* the reconcile is reviewed.

| Field | Type | Null/blank | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `old_line` | FK → `Line` | not null | **PROTECT**, `related_name='lilo_events_as_old'`. The pre-LILO line. |
| `new_lines` | M2M → `Line` | `blank=True` | `related_name='lilo_events_as_new'`. The line(s) it became — normally two. |
| `split_tower` | FK → `Tower` | `null=True, blank=True` | **SET_NULL**, `related_name='lilo_split_events'`. The tower at which the line was cut. |
| `lilo_date` | DateField | `null=True, blank=True` | The real-world date of the LILO (may be unknown / not the day it was recorded). |
| `notes` | TextField | `blank=True` | Free text. |
| `performed_by_employee_id` | CharField(32) | not null | The Super Admin who recorded it (`request.session['employee_id']`). |
| `created_at` | DateTimeField `auto_now_add` | not null | When the event was declared. |
| `applied_at` | DateTimeField | `null=True, blank=True` | **NULL = draft, set = the reconcile has been applied.** This is the event's state machine: two states, and it is one-way. |

`__str__` renders `LILO #<pk>: old line <id> (applied|draft)`.

> **`split_tower` is declared but never written.** The LILO creation form
> (`admin_views.py:417-423`) posts only `old_line_id`, `new_line_ids`, `lilo_date` and `notes`;
> nothing anywhere in `line_inspection/` assigns `split_tower`. A full-tree grep finds it only
> in `models.py`, the migration, and the README's field list. It is reserved schema, always
> NULL today. The README lists it as a field without noting that it is unpopulated.

#### 6.9.5 `LiloTowerRemap`

`line_inspection/models.py:669-682`. The per-tower audit trail: exactly one row per decision
made during an apply.

| Field | Type | Null/blank | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `event` | FK → `LiloEvent` | not null | **CASCADE**, `related_name='remaps'`. |
| `surviving_tower` | FK → `Tower` | not null | **PROTECT**, `related_name='lilo_remaps'`. For a match this is the **old** row that was kept (its PK is the point of the whole exercise); for a `new` decision it is the new row itself. |
| `old_object_id` | CharField(64) | `blank=True` | The pre-LILO `arcgis_object_id`. `''` for a `new` decision. |
| `new_object_id` | CharField(64) | `blank=True` | The post-LILO `arcgis_object_id` that was adopted. |
| `distance_m` | FloatField | `null=True, blank=True` | Coordinate distance between the matched pair, rounded to 1 dp. `None` for `new`. |
| `method` | CharField(16), choices | required | How the decision was reached. |
| `created_at` | DateTimeField `auto_now_add` | not null | |

**`LILO_REMAP_METHOD_CHOICES`** (`models.py:662-666`):

| Value | Label | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `auto` | Auto (high-confidence match) | The pair satisfied `_is_auto()` — see the thresholds below. The operator did not need to intervene, though on the web screen they still confirmed the whole page. |
| `manual` | Manual (operator override) | A pair the matcher only *suggested* (or that the operator chose against the suggestion). Recorded distinctly so that later, if a tower's history looks wrong, you can tell whether a human made the call. |
| `new` | New tower (no match) | A genuine new loop tower — no old row corresponds to it. |

Note that `method` is recomputed at **apply** time by `_is_auto(dist, nm)`
(`lilo_matching.py:181`), not copied from the proposal. So if an operator manually pairs two
towers that happen to be 3 m apart, the audit records `auto` — the label describes the
*confidence of the match*, not the *provenance of the click*.

**Both LILO tables are written only by the explicit Super-Admin reconcile.** The routine
`sync_gis_towers` / `arcgis_client` path is completely unmodified and never touches them —
stated in the model docstring (`models.py:641-643`), in `lilo_matching.py:8-9`, and in both
management commands. This separation is the safety property: the nightly sync cannot silently
merge towers.

#### 6.9.6 Matching thresholds and the proposal classification

`services/lilo_matching.py:18-44`:

| Constant | Value | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `AUTO_EXACT_M` | 5.0 m | Near-identical coordinates → auto-accept regardless of tower number. |
| `AUTO_NUMBER_M` | 60.0 m | A moderate coordinate move **with the same `tower_number`** → auto-accept. Absorbs GPS re-survey drift and road-works shifts. |
| `CANDIDATE_M` | 250.0 m | The farthest an old tower may be to even appear as a manual candidate. |
| `CHURN_M` | 30.0 m | Co-location radius used by the undeclared-churn detector. |
| `_M_PER_DEG_LAT` | 110 574.0 | Equirectangular conversion constant. |
| `_M_PER_DEG_LON_EQ` | 111 320.0 | Ditto, scaled by `cos(mean latitude)`. |

`_is_auto(dist, number_match)` = `dist <= 5.0 or (dist <= 60.0 and number_match)`.
`_norm_number` upper-cases and strips all spaces before comparing tower numbers.

`propose_matches(event)` (`lilo_matching.py:61-133`) returns
`{'pairs': [...], 'unmatched_old': [...], 'counts': {...}}`:

- **Old towers** = deactivated towers matching the old line by FK **or** by `line_name`
  (the name fallback catches rows whose `line` FK was already SET_NULL by a Line deactivation).
- **New towers** = active towers on the event's `new_lines`.
- Candidates per new tower are all old towers within `CANDIDATE_M`, sorted
  `(not number_match, distance)` — a same-number candidate is preferred over a merely closer
  one **for the review suggestion**, while auto-acceptance stays purely distance-driven.
- Auto assignment is **greedy, globally nearest first, one-to-one**: every auto-eligible pair
  across all towers is sorted by distance and consumed in order, so no old tower can be claimed
  twice. (The sort key is the distance alone — the comment at `lilo_matching.py:92-93` notes
  this is deliberate, because putting model objects in the tuple would make Python try to
  compare `Tower` instances on a tie and raise.)
- Each pair is then classified `auto` / `review` (a suggestion plus up to 5 alternative
  candidates for the operator) / `new` (nothing within 250 m).
- `unmatched_old` = old towers that no pair references at all — e.g. a tower physically removed
  during the LILO, or renumbered beyond recognition. The operator judges these.

Applying: the **web screen** (`admin_views.py:441-461`) posts a `decision_<new_tower_id>` value
per pair (`match:<old_id>` or `new`), applies all of them, and then sets `applied_at`
unconditionally. The **CLI** (`management/commands/lilo_reconcile.py`) is a dry run by default;
with `--apply` it applies **only** the `auto` and `new` pairs and deliberately leaves
`applied_at` NULL when any `review` pairs remain, so the event stays open for the screen. That
split is why `apply_reconcile` itself does not set `applied_at` — its docstring says so
explicitly.

#### 6.9.7 The churn detector — a safety net for *undeclared* churn

Everything above requires a Super Admin to have *told the system* a LILO happened. The detector
covers the case where nobody did — an unannounced LILO, a re-survey, a road-works relocation, or
any other GIS edit that recreated features.

`detect_churn(line=None)` (`lilo_matching.py:203-236`) is **read-only; it flags only** and never
writes. It finds deactivated towers that

1. carry **inspection history** (`Exists(Inspection.objects.filter(tower=OuterRef('pk')))`) **or**
   an **active range assignment** (`LineTowerAssignment` referencing them as `from_tower` or
   `to_tower`), **and**
2. have a co-located **active** tower of the **same voltage** within `CHURN_M` (30 m).

The spatial search is a cheap indexed bounding box first — `delta = 0.0004` degrees, about a
44 m box — followed by exact distance filtering inside it, so it does not need PostGIS.

Returns `[{'stranded': <Tower>, 'twin': <Tower>, 'distance_m': float}]`. Consumers:

- **Super-Admin home badge** — `context['churn_count'] = len(lm.detect_churn())` (`admin_views.py:46-48`).
- **The LILO screen** — `'churn_flags': lm.detect_churn()` (`admin_views.py:432`), with a
  "Start LILO" link that pre-fills the create form via `?old_line=&new_line=`.
- **CLI** — `python manage.py detect_tower_churn [--line <id>]`.

The logic reads as: *"this deactivated tower has real history, and something active is standing
in exactly the same place — history is about to be stranded."* Condition (1) is what keeps it
quiet: towers that were deactivated and never inspected are not interesting and are not
reported.

Covered by `LiloReconcileTests` in `line_inspection/tests/test_dashboard.py:328-385` —
`test_propose_classifies`, `test_apply_preserves_history` (asserts the inspection still points
at the same PK, the survivor adopted `N3`'s object id, the duplicates are gone, four
`LiloTowerRemap` rows exist with methods `['auto','auto','auto','new']`, and `line_sequence` was
rebuilt), `test_detect_churn`, and `test_lilo_screen_is_super_admin_only` (200 for a
`SuperAdmin`, 403 otherwise).

### 6.10 `MobileAuthToken`

`line_inspection/models.py:700-729`. The Phase 4 mobile session. The full auth flow —
checkCred verification, the `Token` vs `Bearer` scheme split, the dev-login bypass — is
section 3's subject; here is the table itself.

| Field | Type | Null/blank | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `key` | CharField(64), **unique**, `db_index=True` | not null | — | The bearer string. Generated by `MobileAuthToken.generate_key()` = `secrets.token_urlsafe(48)`, which is exactly 64 characters of base64url from 48 random bytes (~288 bits) — it fits the column exactly, with no room to spare. |
| `employee_id` | CharField(32), `db_index=True` | not null | — | Already `zfill(8)`-normalised by checkCred (see the field comment). No FK — identity is a bare employee id throughout this app. |
| `display_name` | CharField(255) | `blank=True` | `''` | Human name from checkCred, falling back to the employee id (`api/views.py:106`). Returned by `/auth/me/` so the app can re-hydrate its header on launch. |
| `created_at` | DateTimeField `auto_now_add` | not null | now | Issue time. |
| `last_used_at` | DateTimeField | `null=True, blank=True` | none | Touched by `MobileTokenAuthentication` **at most once every 5 minutes** (`_touch_after = timedelta(minutes=5)`, `api/authentication.py:45,61-63`) so a busy client does not write a row to the `clear` schema on every request. |
| `expires_at` | DateTimeField | `null=True, blank=True` | `_default_token_expiry()` = now + **30 days** | Long-lived on purpose. |
| `is_active` | BooleanField | not null | `True` | Cleared by `revoke()`. |
| `revoked_at` | DateTimeField | `null=True, blank=True` | none | Set by `revoke()`. |

**Meta:** `Index(['employee_id', 'is_active'])` — for "all live tokens for this employee".

**Behaviour on the model:**

- `is_valid` (property) — `False` if `not is_active`; otherwise `False` only when `expires_at`
  is set and in the past. A NULL `expires_at` therefore means *never expires*.
- `revoke()` — sets `is_active=False` and `revoked_at=now`, saving just those two columns.
  Called by `MobileLogoutView` when `request.auth` is a `MobileAuthToken`.

**Why 30 days and not a short TTL** (`models.py:694-697`): *"Long-lived on purpose — field
engineers may stay offline for days between syncs. Revocation is explicit (logout) or by expiry,
not by a short TTL."* A short-lived token plus refresh would require connectivity to stay logged
in, which is exactly what this app cannot assume. Revocation is instead a DB flag, which is why
the token is DB-backed rather than a self-contained JWT — a JWT cannot be revoked without a
server-side deny-list anyway, so the row *is* the deny-list.

Note that `MobileTokenAuthentication.authenticate` does **not** call `is_valid`; it re-implements
the same two checks inline so it can raise two *different* messages ("Invalid or revoked token."
vs "Token expired — please sign in again."), both as 401 so the Flutter app knows to re-login.

Eight migrations, all in `line_inspection/migrations/`, all generated between 2026-07-21 and
2026-07-23. Note that every file header reads *"Generated by Django 5.0.13"* even though the
project now targets Django 6.0 (`requirements.txt:5`) — the migrations predate the upgrade and
have not been regenerated (nor do they need to be).

| # | File | What it does | Why (the feature it shipped) | Strictly additive? |
