```bash
python manage.py grant_super_admin --employee-id <id> [--notes "<text>"]
```

| Flag | Required | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--employee-id` | **yes** | — | `.strip()`ed. Should be the SAP id in the same zero-padded 8-digit form the login path normalises to (`checkcred_client` / `dev_login` both `zfill(8)` all-numeric ids) — a mismatch here silently produces an id nobody can log in as. |
| `--notes` | no | `''` | Free text recorded on the row, used only on creation |

**Writes.** One `SuperAdmin` row via `get_or_create`. Note `--notes` is passed in
`defaults=`, so it applies **only when the row is created** — re-running with
different notes does not update them.

**Idempotency.** Fully idempotent, non-destructive. Prints
`Granted Super Admin to <id>.` or `<id> is already a Super Admin.` There is no
corresponding `revoke_super_admin` command; removal is a manual DB operation or an
admin-UI action.

**Runtime.** Instant. **Depends on** nothing — it does not validate the employee id
against `EmployeeCadreSnapshot`, so you can grant to an id that does not exist yet.
In practice run it after `sync_employee_cadre` so the person can actually sign in.

---

### 9.3.8 `warm_tower_status`

**Purpose.** Rebuilds the denormalised per-tower inspection-status cache
(`Tower.last_inspection_at`, `Tower.last_worst_criticality`,
`Tower.last_inspection_type`) from the authoritative `Inspection` rows. Those three
columns exist so the map and the dashboards can colour tens of thousands of towers
without a correlated subquery per tower. Day to day the cache is maintained
incrementally by `api.views._create_inspection`; this command is the bulk
backfill and the repair path.

**Usage.** No arguments.

```bash
python manage.py warm_tower_status
```

**Reads.** `Inspection`, using a Postgres-specific `DISTINCT ON` to get the latest
inspection per tower in a single query:

```python
latest = (Inspection.objects.filter(tower_id__in=tower_ids)
          .order_by('tower_id', '-saved_at', '-id')
          .distinct('tower_id')
          .values('tower_id', 'saved_at', 'worst_criticality', 'inspection_type'))
```

The tie-break on `-id` makes the result deterministic when two inspections share a
`saved_at`. "Latest of **any** type" — a PMI does not shadow a later ground patrol
or vice versa.

**Writes.** `bulk_update` of the three cache columns, batch size 500, on towers that
have at least one inspection. Towers with no inspections are not touched — so this
command **cannot clear a stale cache entry** left behind if inspections were deleted.

**Idempotency.** Idempotent and non-destructive.

**Runtime.** Two queries plus a batched update; proportional to the number of
*inspected* towers, not total towers. Fast. On an empty system it short-circuits
with `No inspections found — nothing to warm.`

**When to run.** Once after applying migration 0003 (which introduced the columns),
and any time the map's colouring looks wrong or out of date.

**Failure modes.** `.distinct('tower_id')` is Postgres-only; on any other backend
this raises `NotSupportedError`. That is acceptable here because the project is
Postgres-only by construction.

---

### 9.3.9 `detect_tower_churn`

**Purpose.** A read-only diagnostic for a specific, insidious data-integrity
problem. When upstream ArcGIS reassigns `OBJECTID`s — because a line was rebuilt,
towers were shifted for road works, or an undeclared LILO happened — the old rows
stop appearing in the feed and get soft-deleted, while new rows appear at
essentially the same coordinates. The inspection history stays attached to the
now-invisible old row: *stranded*. This command finds those cases so a human can
decide what to do.

**Usage.**

```bash
python manage.py detect_tower_churn            # whole system
python manage.py detect_tower_churn --line 42  # one line's deactivated towers
```

| Flag | Type | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--line` | `int` | `None` | Scope to a single `Line` primary key. An id that does not exist silently degrades to a whole-system scan, because the lookup uses `.filter(pk=…).first()`. |

**Logic.** `services.lilo_matching.detect_churn(line=...)` looks for towers that are
simultaneously: `is_active=False`, carrying inspection history or an active range
assignment, and within `CHURN_M = 30.0` metres of an *active* tower.

**Writes.** Nothing whatsoever. The docstring is explicit that it "flags only" and
is "never run by the routine ArcGIS sync" — deliberately, because auto-remapping
history on a coordinate coincidence would be far worse than leaving it stranded.

**Output.** Either `No stranded-history towers with co-located active twins found.`
or one line per flag:

```
2 possible churn flag(s):
  stranded T-45 (LINE A) <-> active T-45A (LINE A) · 6.2 m
```

**Idempotency.** Trivially safe — it is a report.

**When to run.** After any large or surprising `sync_gis_towers` run, and as a
periodic hygiene check. What to do with a flag is a human decision: either record a
`LiloEvent` and reconcile it properly (9.3.10), or accept that the history belongs
to a structure that no longer exists.

---

### 9.3.10 `lilo_reconcile`

**Purpose.** Reports — and optionally applies — the tower-identity reconciliation for
a recorded LILO event. When a line is looped in and out of a new substation, the
utility issues a new line with renumbered towers, but most of the physical
structures are the *same steel in the same ground*. This command matches new towers
to old ones so that inspection history, defect tickets and range assignments follow
the structure rather than being lost. It is a Super-Admin operation and is never
triggered by the routine sync.

**Usage.**

```bash
python manage.py lilo_reconcile --event <id>           # dry run (default)
python manage.py lilo_reconcile --event <id> --apply
```

| Flag | Type | Required | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--event` | `int` | **yes** | — | `LiloEvent` primary key. Missing → `CommandError: LiloEvent #N not found.` |
| `--apply` | `store_true` | no | `False` | Apply the AUTO matches and NEW towers immediately. REVIEW pairs are always left alone. |

**Matching thresholds** (`services/lilo_matching.py:22-25`):

| Constant | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `AUTO_EXACT_M` | 5.0 m | Near-identical coordinates → auto-accept |
| `AUTO_NUMBER_M` | 60.0 m | Moved a bit, but **same tower_number** → auto-accept |
| `CANDIDATE_M` | 250.0 m | Beyond this an old tower is not even offered as a manual candidate |
| `CHURN_M` | 30.0 m | (Used by `detect_tower_churn`, not here) |

Each proposed pair is classified `auto`, `review`, or `new` (a genuinely new
structure with no old counterpart). The dry-run output prints the counts and every
pair:

```
LILO #3 — old line 'X': auto=41 review=3 new=7 unmatched_old=2
  [auto  ] new T-12 -> OLD T-12 (2.1m, num_match=True)
  [review] new T-19 -> OLD T-18 (91.4m, num_match=False)
  [new   ] new T-55 -> NEW
(dry run — pass --apply to apply auto/new)
```

**Writes (only with `--apply`).** `lm.apply_reconcile(event, decisions)` performs a
**history-preserving in-place revive**: the surviving old `Tower` row is updated to
the new tower's identity and reactivated, rather than the new row being kept and the
old one discarded — that way every `Inspection`/`DefectTicket` foreign key remains
valid without touching those tables. `LiloTowerRemap` rows record the mapping. If
`review == 0` the event is closed by stamping `LiloEvent.applied_at`; otherwise the
event is left open with a warning and the remaining pairs must be resolved on the
Super-Admin LILO screen (`/inspection/admin/lilo/<pk>/`).

**Destructive?** Yes — `--apply` rewrites tower identity and cannot be undone by
re-running the command. Always run the dry form first and read every `[review]`
line. The dry run is the default precisely because of this.

**Idempotency.** Re-running `--apply` after a full application is a no-op in effect
(the previously matched towers now sit at the new identity, so they classify
differently), but this has not been designed as a resumable operation — treat it as
once per event.

**Depends on** a `LiloEvent` already existing, created through the Super-Admin LILO
screen, with its old and new lines identified.

---

### 9.3.11 `run_sync_scheduler`

**Purpose.** Keeps `sync_gis_towers` and `sync_employee_cadre` refreshed on a repeating
interval without introducing Celery, APScheduler, or any other dependency. The
docstring's rationale: "a plain sleep loop is enough for this and keeps the
dependency list small". It is explicitly *not* meant to run inside the web server
process.

**Usage.**

```bash
python manage.py run_sync_scheduler
python manage.py run_sync_scheduler --gis-interval-minutes 120 --cadre-interval-minutes 60
python manage.py run_sync_scheduler --run-once
```

| Flag | Type | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--gis-interval-minutes` | `int` | `60` | Minimum minutes between `sync_gis_towers` starts |
| `--cadre-interval-minutes` | `int` | `60` | Minimum minutes between `sync_employee_cadre` starts |
| `--run-once` | `store_true` | `False` | Run each sync once and return. Intended for testing and for wrapping in an external scheduler. |

**The loop** (`run_sync_scheduler.py:26-46`). Both `next_*_run` counters start at 0,
so **each sync fires immediately on start-up**, then reschedules to
`now + interval`. `now` is `time.monotonic()`, so the schedule is immune to wall-clock
changes and DST. The sleep is `min(gis_interval, cadre_interval, 60)` seconds —
capped at 60 so the loop wakes at least once a minute and responds promptly to
Ctrl-C. Because `next_run` is computed from the time the iteration *started* rather
than when the sync finished, a sync that overruns its interval simply starts again
on the next tick; there is no overlap risk, since everything is sequential in one
thread.

Each child command runs through `call_command()` in-process and is individually
wrapped:

```python
def _run(self, command_name):
    self.stdout.write(f'[{timezone.now().isoformat()}] running {command_name} ...')
    try:
        call_command(command_name)
    except Exception:
        self.stderr.write(f'{command_name} failed:\n{traceback.format_exc()}')
```

so a failed ArcGIS sync logs a traceback and the loop continues — the scheduler
never dies from a transient upstream outage.

**What it does not do.** It runs the child commands with **no arguments**, so there
is no way to pass `--skip-*` or `--root-employee-id` through it. And it does **not**
run `build_tower_schedule`, `warm_tower_status`, or `map_sap_lines`. If towers churn
upstream, `line_sequence` goes stale until someone runs the schedule builder.

**Destructive?** No, beyond whatever the child commands do.

**Runtime.** Forever, in the foreground, holding a terminal. There is no
daemonisation, no PID file, no log rotation. For production, wrap it — a Windows
Task Scheduler task with "run whether user is logged on or not" and restart-on-
failure, an NSSM service, or systemd on Linux — and redirect stdout/stderr to a
file, because the per-run timestamps it prints are the only operational log.

---

### Part B — Operational runbook

### 9.4 First-time bring-up: empty database → working system

Each step depends on the one before it; the dependency is stated because getting
the order wrong produces confusing, non-obvious symptoms rather than clean errors.

**1. Create the Postgres database and the `clear` schema.**

```sql
CREATE DATABASE aptransco_ai_db;
\c aptransco_ai_db
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS clear;
```

*Why first, and why the schema explicitly:* the `line_inspection_db` connection sets
`search_path=clear` (`transcoapps/settings.py:164`) but nothing in the codebase
issues `CREATE SCHEMA`. No model overrides `db_table` with a schema prefix, and no
migration contains a `RunSQL`. If the schema does not exist, `migrate` fails with
Postgres's "no schema has been selected to create in". Both aliases point at the
*same* physical database; they differ only in search path — Django's own
`auth`/`admin`/`sessions`/`contenttypes` tables live in `public`, the platform
tables in `clear`.

**2. Install dependencies into the virtualenv.**

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

`requirements.txt` (at `transcoapps/requirements.txt`) pins Django ≥6.0 <6.1, DRF,
`psycopg[binary]`, Pillow, requests, openpyxl and pandas, each with a comment saying
which part of the codebase needs it. Do not confuse it with
`Aptransco_TIS-main/aptransco_backend/requirements.txt`, which belongs to the dead
donor project.

**3. Create `.env.local`.**

`transcoapps/.env.local` is read by `_load_local_env()` before any other setting is
evaluated, using `os.environ.setdefault` so real environment variables still win.
The rationale in the docstring is worth repeating: dot-sourcing a shell script only
affects one shell, whereas this works no matter how the process is started — IDE Run
button, task runner, a fresh terminal.

Variables the code actually reads:

| Variable | Read by | Default if unset |
|---|---|---|
| `PG_NAME` | `settings.py:152` | `aptransco_ai_db` |
| `PG_USER` | `settings.py:153` | `postgres` |
| `PG_PASSWORD` | `settings.py:154` | **a hardcoded literal — see the finding below** |
| `PG_HOST` | `settings.py:155` | `localhost` |
| `PG_PORT` | `settings.py:156` | `5432` |
| `EXTRA_ALLOWED_HOSTS` | `settings.py:65` | `''` — comma-separated hostnames/IPs appended to `ALLOWED_HOSTS`, so a developer can add their current Wi-Fi IP without editing settings |
| `ARCGIS_USERNAME`, `ARCGIS_PASSWORD` | `services/arcgis_client.py:16-17` | `''` |
| `SAP_RFC_BASE_URL`, `SAP_RFC_USER`, `SAP_RFC_PASSWORD` | `services/sap_client.py` | base URL defaults to the production RESTAdapter; credentials have no default |
| `SAP_HIERARCHY_ROOT_EMPLOYEE_ID` | `services/sap_client.py` | none — overridable per run with `--root-employee-id` |
| `APTRANSCO_AUTH_URL`, `APTRANSCO_AUTH_USER`, `APTRANSCO_AUTH_PASS` | `services/checkcred_client.py` | URL defaults to the qath gateway; the two credentials are the **app-level** Basic Auth for the gateway itself, not any employee's own password |
| `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN` | `services/dev_login.py:32` | unset — set to exactly `'1'` to arm the dev-login bypass |
| `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD` | `services/dev_login.py:33` | unset — the single shared development password |

The `.env.local` present in this checkout defines exactly five of these:
`APTRANSCO_AUTH_USER`, `APTRANSCO_AUTH_PASS`, `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN`,
`LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD`, `EXTRA_ALLOWED_HOSTS`. Their values are
`<set in .env.local>` and are deliberately not reproduced here. Everything else
(Postgres, ArcGIS, SAP) is currently running on the settings.py defaults, which
means **`sync_gis_towers` and `sync_employee_cadre` cannot succeed in this checkout
as configured** — no ArcGIS or SAP credentials are present.

> **The dev-login bypass — what it actually is.** `services/dev_login.py` is an
> offline stand-in for checkCred, wired in by a four-line delegation at the top of
> `checkcred_client.verify_credentials` (`checkcred_client.py:48-53`). It exists
> because checkCred is unreachable from outside APTRANSCO's network, which would
> otherwise make the whole system un-loggable-into on a developer machine.
> `is_enabled()` requires **all three** of: `settings.DEBUG` true,
> `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN == '1'`, and a non-empty `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD`.
> When armed it verifies the submitted password against that one shared string with
> `hmac.compare_digest`, ignores the employee's real password entirely, and signs in
> **any** `employee_id` that exists in `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` (zero-padded to 8
> digits the same way the real gateway normalises). It logs a `WARNING` on first
> activation and on every sign-in. Since `settings.DEBUG = True` is hardcoded
> (`settings.py:47`), the *only* thing standing between this checkout and a
> shared-password login is the two environment variables — both of which are
> currently set in `.env.local`. Unset `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN` to restore real
> auth; delete the module plus the four-line delegation to remove the feature.

> **Findings — secrets hardcoded in tracked source.** `line_inspection/README.md:355`
> asserts "None of these have hardcoded fallback secrets in code", and
> `README.md:352` says specifically "Never hardcode `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET` as a
> source default". The code contradicts both:
> - `transcoapps/settings.py:220` — `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET` is a literal string.
> - `transcoapps/settings.py:154` — the `PG_PASSWORD` fallback is a real-looking
>   literal password, not a placeholder.
> - `transcoapps/settings.py:44` — `SECRET_KEY` is the checked-in
>   `django-insecure-…` development key.
> - `transcoapps/settings.py:47` — `DEBUG = True` is hardcoded with no environment
>   override.
> None of these values are reproduced in this document. All four must be moved to
> the environment before any deployment outside a developer laptop.

**4. Run migrations — with the explicit database.**

```bash
python manage.py migrate --database=line_inspection_db line_inspection
python manage.py migrate           # Django's own tables into `public` on `default`
```

*Why:* `LineInspectionRouter.allow_migrate` returns `db == 'line_inspection_db'` for
the `line_inspection` app label. A plain `python manage.py migrate line_inspection`
runs against `default`, where the router refuses every operation — but Django still
records the migration as applied in `default`'s `django_migrations` table. The
result is the worst kind of failure: the command reports success, `showmigrations`
looks clean, and the `clear` schema is completely empty. The README calls this out
at line 396-401 and it is accurate. There are eight migrations, `0001_initial`
through `0008_inspection_gps_accuracy_m_inspection_gps_distance_m_and_more`.

**5. Seed the checklist catalog.**

```bash
python manage.py seed_checklist_catalog
```

*Why here:* the catalog is independent of GIS data, and nothing can be inspected
until it exists. Doing it now means the API's catalog endpoint is already valid by
the time the mobile app first connects.

**6. Sync GIS.**

```bash
python manage.py sync_gis_towers
```

*Why after migrations and before everything spatial:* this creates every `Line`,
`Tower`, `Substation` and `Subdivision`. Do **not** pass `--skip-lines` on a fresh
database (see 9.3.2 — towers would land with a null line FK). Watch the
`wrote N/M` lines for skipped batches. Expect minutes.

**7. Build the tower schedule.**

```bash
python manage.py build_tower_schedule
```

*Why immediately after:* `sync_gis_towers` does not set `line_sequence`. Until this
runs, `schedule.line_schedule()` orders by `line_sequence NULLS LAST` and then by
raw `tower_number` string, so the register columns and the mobile tower list come
out in string order (`1, 10, 100, 11, …`) rather than along the line, and range
role assignments — which are defined as "everything whose sequence lies between two
boundary towers" (`models.py:469`) — resolve to nothing.

**8. Sync employee cadre.**

```bash
python manage.py sync_employee_cadre
```

*Why before any login:* `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` is what every eligibility, hierarchy
and jurisdiction check reads, and it is also what the dev-login path resolves
employee ids against. With an empty table, nobody can sign in — the dev path fails
with `No cadre snapshot for employee <id>`, and the real path succeeds at the gateway
but then finds no cadre for authorisation.

**9. Import and map SAP lines.**

```bash
python manage.py import_sap_lines --file "<path to EHT LINES SAP DATA ….XLSX>"
python manage.py map_sap_lines --dry-run
python manage.py map_sap_lines
```

*Why after the GIS sync:* `map_sap_lines` only considers active ArcGIS `Line` rows,
so there must be lines to map. Remember the default file path does not exist in this
checkout (9.3.5) — pass `--file`. This step is optional for a working inspection
system; it only affects SAP cross-referencing.

**10. Grant the first Super Admin.**

```bash
python manage.py grant_super_admin --employee-id 01073093 --notes "initial bootstrap"
```

*Why it must be the CLI:* the admin UI's grant screen is itself gated on being a
Super Admin. Use the zero-padded 8-digit form the login path normalises to.

**11. In-app: grant Admin (Field-EE cadre) positions.**

Sign in at `/inspection/login/` as the Super Admin, then go to
**`/inspection/admin/super/positions/`** (`manage-admins`). A Super Admin designates
which SAP *position ids* count as Admin — the Field EE cadre. Position-based rather
than person-based, so a transfer into the post carries the rights automatically and
the list does not need editing every time someone moves.
`/inspection/admin/super/positions/lookup/<position_id>/` resolves a position id
against the cadre snapshot so you can confirm you have the right one before granting.

**12. In-app: create role assignments.**

Go to **`/inspection/admin/assignments/`** (`role-assignments`) and, per employee,
**`/inspection/admin/assignments/new/<employee_id>/`**. A `RoleAssignment` is what
gives a field user *jurisdiction* — the set of towers they may inspect — scoped
either to whole lines or to a tower range on a line (which is why step 7 must have
run: ranges are expressed in `line_sequence` terms).

Distinguish the two authorisation axes, because they are easy to confuse:
**jurisdiction** is "which towers may I edit / submit for" and comes from a
`RoleAssignment`; **oversight** is "whose work may I see" and is derived from the SAP
reporting hierarchy in `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` (`viewing.oversight_towers` unions the
lines assigned to the viewer *or anyone below them*).

**13. Warm the status cache (only if inspections already exist).**

```bash
python manage.py warm_tower_status
```

On a genuinely fresh system this prints `No inspections found — nothing to warm.`
and is a no-op; run it after restoring a database that has inspection history.

**14. Run the server.**

```bash
python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000
```

Bind `0.0.0.0` (not the default `127.0.0.1`) so a phone on the same network can reach
it, and add your machine's current LAN IP to `EXTRA_ALLOWED_HOSTS` in `.env.local` —
that is exactly what the variable exists for. `ALLOWED_HOSTS` already contains
`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`, the ngrok domains, and `192.168.137.1` (the
Windows Mobile Hotspot default gateway).

**15. Point the Flutter app at it.** See 9.7.

### 9.5 Routine operations

| Cadence | Action |
|---|---|
| Continuous | `run_sync_scheduler` running as a service — refreshes GIS and cadre hourly by default |
| After each GIS sync that changed towers/lines | `build_tower_schedule` (**not** automated — this is the gap in the scheduler) |
| When a new SAP export arrives | `import_sap_lines --file <new export>` then `map_sap_lines --dry-run` then `map_sap_lines` |
| Weekly / after a surprising sync | `detect_tower_churn` |
| Per LILO event | `lilo_reconcile --event <id>` (dry) → resolve reviews on the LILO screen → `--apply` |
| On demand | `warm_tower_status` when dashboard/map numbers look stale |
| Rarely | `seed_checklist_catalog` — only when `ITEMS` in the source changed, and remembering it destroys hand-tuned criticality rules |
| Rarely | `grant_super_admin` for a new administrator |

**Running the scheduler for real.** `run_sync_scheduler` is a foreground process
with no daemonisation of its own. On the Windows host this project runs on, wrap it
in a **Task Scheduler** task configured to run whether the user is logged on or not,
start at boot, and restart on failure, with the action:

```
Program:   C:\...\transcoapps\.venv\Scripts\python.exe
Arguments: manage.py run_sync_scheduler
Start in:  C:\...\transcoapps
```

Redirect output to a file (via a one-line `.cmd` wrapper) — the ISO-timestamped
`running <command> ...` lines and the tracebacks it prints on failure are the only
record you get. On Linux, a systemd unit with `Restart=always` is the equivalent.
The alternative, if you prefer the OS to own the scheduling, is
`run_sync_scheduler --run-once` on a cron/Task-Scheduler trigger — or simply
scheduling `sync_gis_towers`, `build_tower_schedule` and `sync_employee_cadre`
individually, which has the advantage of covering the schedule-builder gap.

### 9.6 Serving the web app in development, and the three network paths

The backend is mounted under `/inspection/` (`transcoapps/urls.py`), so the API base
is **`/inspection/api/`** and the browser UI lives at `/inspection/login/`,
`/inspection/admin/…`, `/inspection/dashboard/…`. Media (inspection photos) is served
by Django itself in development via `static(settings.MEDIA_URL, …)`; in production
that must move behind nginx, as the comment at the bottom of `transcoapps/urls.py`
says.

There are three ways for a phone to reach the backend, and the reason there are
three is corporate TLS interception. The full rationale is in the header comment of
`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/services/api_service.dart`:

1. **ngrok tunnel over the internet (the default).** Run
   `ngrok http 8000 --url=<reserved-domain>` against the running dev server. This
   works from anywhere, including LTE, regardless of what network the phone or the
   dev machine are on. The reserved static domain is baked into `ALLOWED_HOSTS` and
   `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS`, along with wildcard `.ngrok-free.dev` / `.ngrok-free.app`
   entries.

   > **Discrepancy.** `settings.py:53` names the reserved domain
   > `mammal-calamari-create.ngrok-free.dev`, while the Flutter app's compile-time
   > default is `https://mispacked-beamy-noelle.ngrok-free.dev/inspection/api`
   > (`api_service.dart`). They do not match. The wildcard `.ngrok-free.dev` entry in
   > `ALLOWED_HOSTS` means the app's domain is still accepted, and
   > `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` has a matching wildcard, so nothing breaks in practice —
   > but one of the two is stale and the exact-match entries are misleading.

2. **Plain HTTP on the LAN / Windows Mobile Hotspot (the documented corporate
   fallback).** On a network doing SSL inspection — a corporate FortiGate that
   re-signs every HTTPS response with its own CA — HTTPS to ngrok fails with
   `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED: self signed certificate`. The documented workaround is
   to bypass the internet entirely: point the app at the laptop directly over plain
   `http://` on the local network, traffic the firewall never sees. Hence
   `runserver 0.0.0.0:8000`, the `192.168.137.1` entry in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (the
   default gateway address Windows assigns to its Mobile Hotspot), and
   `EXTRA_ALLOWED_HOSTS` for whatever Wi-Fi IP you happen to have today. This is
   plain HTTP by design and only acceptable because the traffic never leaves a
   trusted LAN segment.

3. **HTTPS through the interceptor**, if you must. `lib/services/network_security.dart`
   offers two opt-in mechanisms, both off by default so that a normal build keeps
   fully-verified TLS:
   - **Bundled corporate CA (secure).** Paste the real SSL-inspection root CA into
     `assets/certs/corp_ca.pem` and rebuild; it is *added* to the trust store
     (`setTrustedCertificatesBytes` on a context created `withTrustedRoots: true`),
     so intercepted certificates validate normally. The comment records that on this
     project the CA actually required was `CN=FG6H1FTB22904052, O=Fortinet`, and that
     the dev machine only had an unrelated `CN=support` Fortinet root, which is why
     this path was never made to work. **The file currently in the repo is a
     placeholder containing only instructions**, so the mechanism is inert: `install()`
     checks that the asset starts with `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----` before using it.
   - **`--dart-define=ACCEPT_CORP_MITM=true` (insecure).** Sets
     `badCertificateCallback` to accept an unverifiable certificate **only** for the
     host of the currently-configured backend URL — never a blanket accept-all. It
     prints a loud `debugPrint` warning and the comment says plainly: this disables
     TLS authentication for that host, anyone on-path can read the traffic, "never in
     a build handed to real inspectors".

### 9.7 Building and running the Flutter field app

> **The donor documentation is gone.** Older notes refer to
> `Aptransco_TIS-main/README.md` sections 5-6 and `Aptransco_TIS-main/project.md`.
> Neither file exists in the tree any more — `Aptransco_TIS-main/` now contains only
> `.gitignore`, `aptransco_backend/` (the dead donor Django project) and
> `drone_inspection_app/`. The instructions below are therefore derived from the
> live source (`pubspec.yaml`, `lib/main.dart`, `lib/services/api_service.dart`,
> `lib/services/network_security.dart`) rather than adapted from the donor's text.

The app is `drone_inspection_app` v1.1.0+2, Dart SDK `^3.12.2`, key packages
`http`, `shared_preferences`, `geolocator`, `image_picker`, `flutter_map` +
`latlong2`, `connectivity_plus`, `path_provider`.

```bash
cd Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app
flutter pub get

# Run on an attached device, pointed at a LAN backend
flutter run --dart-define=API_BASE_URL=http://192.168.137.1:8000/inspection/api

# Release APK
flutter build apk --release --dart-define=API_BASE_URL=https://<host>/inspection/api
```

**The base-URL rule.** `ApiService.baseUrl` must end in `/api`. Because this backend
mounts the app under `/inspection/`, the correct value for this backend is
`http://<host>:8000/inspection/api` — **not** `http://<host>:8000/api`. That trailing
segment is the single most common misconfiguration, and it is the one thing the
donor's instructions would get wrong: the donor backend
(`Aptransco_TIS-main/aptransco_backend/`) served its API at the bare `/api` root.

Three layers decide the active URL, most specific first
(`api_service.dart`):

| Priority | Source | Persistence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | In-app override — the **Settings** control on the Line Inspection screen | `SharedPreferences` key `api_base_url_override`; read fresh on every request, so a change takes effect without restarting the app |
| 2 | `--dart-define=API_BASE_URL=…` | Compile-time; shown as the placeholder / reset target in Settings |
| 3 | The ngrok default compiled into the source | — |

The in-app override exists specifically so a field user can flip between the
office/LAN URL and the field/ngrok URL **without a rebuild** — which is what makes
the plain-HTTP-on-LAN fallback practical rather than theoretical.

`main.dart` calls `ApiService.loadBaseUrl()` and then `NetworkSecurity.install()`
before `runApp`, in that order — the TLS override needs to know the configured
backend host to scope its exception to it.

### 9.8 Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `migrate` reports success but the `clear` schema is still empty; `showmigrations` shows everything applied | Migrations were run against `default`, where `LineInspectionRouter.allow_migrate` blocks every operation while Django still records them as applied | `python manage.py migrate --database=line_inspection_db line_inspection`. If the bogus rows were recorded in `default`'s `django_migrations`, delete the `line_inspection` rows there first, or the correct run may be skipped |
| `migrate` errors "no schema has been selected to create in" | The `clear` schema does not exist; nothing in the code creates it | `CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS clear;` on the target database |
| Mobile app suddenly gets **401** on every call | `MobileTokenAuthentication` raises `AuthenticationFailed` for a token that is revoked (`is_active` false) or past `expires_at` (`api/authentication.py:35-60`) | Sign out and back in — `POST /inspection/api/auth/login/` mints a fresh token. Check the `MobileAuthToken` row before assuming a server fault |
| Mobile app cannot reach the backend on corporate Wi-Fi; logs show `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED: self signed certificate` | The corporate firewall is doing TLS interception and re-signing the ngrok certificate with a CA the phone does not trust | Use the in-app **Backend URL** override with plain HTTP on the LAN, e.g. `http://192.168.137.1:8000/inspection/api`, with `runserver 0.0.0.0:8000` and the host IP in `EXTRA_ALLOWED_HOSTS`. Proper fix: bundle the real corporate CA in `assets/certs/corp_ca.pem` and rebuild |
| Backend returns `DisallowedHost` / "Invalid HTTP_HOST header" | The phone is reaching Django by an address not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` | Add the machine's current IP to `EXTRA_ALLOWED_HOSTS` in `.env.local` and restart the server |
| Submit rejected: `{"override_reason": "An out-of-range or no-GPS inspection requires an override reason (presence is required)."}` | The GPS proof-of-presence gate. The server recomputes the distance from the submitted fix to the tower's stored coordinates (never trusting a client-sent distance) and requires it within `PRESENCE_RADIUS_M = 50.0` m (`models.py:73`). Anything else — `out_of_range`, or `no_fix` when lat/lng are absent — demands a typed reason | Get closer to the structure, or supply a genuine `override_reason`. Note the legacy JSON create path sends neither coordinates nor `presence_flag` and is exempt from the gate entirely (`api/views.py:459-478`) |
| Submit rejected: `{"tower": "Virtual (VT) towers are not inspected — inspect the real co-located tower."}` | The tower id is a VT row — a second circuit on a structure, not a structure (`api/views.py:451`) | Submit against the real tower sharing the same `structure_key`. If the app is offering VT towers for capture, the tower list is not filtering `is_virtual=False` |
| Submit rejected with 403 "You don't have jurisdiction over this tower" | No `RoleAssignment` covers that tower for that employee | Create or widen the assignment at `/inspection/admin/assignments/new/<employee_id>/` |
| A user sees **no towers at all** | Either no active `RoleAssignment` (empty jurisdiction), or a range assignment whose bounds resolve to nothing because `line_sequence` is null, or the towers are on a line the assignment does not cover | Check for an active assignment first; then run `build_tower_schedule`; then confirm the towers are `is_active=True` and not `is_virtual` |
| Register renders but the tower columns are in string order (`1, 10, 100, 11`) and range assignments match nothing | `build_tower_schedule` has not been run since the last GIS sync, so `line_sequence` is null and `line_schedule()` falls back to `NULLS LAST` + raw `tower_number` (`schedule.py:123-128`) | `python manage.py build_tower_schedule` |
| Register cells are blank for every tower on a line | Distinct from the above: a blank cell means *no inspection exists* for that tower in the selected cycle (`register._item_cell` returns `kind='blank'` when `inspection is None`). Check the cycle selector — "Pre-Monsoon Inspection (PMI)" shows nothing if only ground patrols have been done | Switch the cycle to "Latest (any cycle)"; confirm inspections exist for that line |
| Map / dashboard shows every tower as uninspected, or stale criticality colours | The `Tower.last_*` denormalised cache is cold or stale. The map and `MobileDashboardView` aggregate purely from those columns (`api/views.py:815-820`), never from `Inspection` | `python manage.py warm_tower_status` |
| Map shows nothing at all | `oversight_towers(..., geocoded_only=True)` drops towers with null lat/lng (`viewing.py:79-93`), and VT and inactive rows are excluded — so a scope with no geocoded real towers renders empty | Verify the GIS sync populated `latitude`/`longitude`; verify the user's oversight scope is non-empty |
| Login fails with `No cadre snapshot for employee <id>` | The dev-login bypass is active and that employee is not in `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` | `python manage.py sync_employee_cadre`, or use an employee id that is already synced |
| Login succeeds for everyone with one shared password | The dev-login bypass is armed: `DEBUG` true **and** `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN=1` **and** `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD` set | Unset `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN` in `.env.local` and restart. Look for the `DEV LOGIN ACTIVE` warning in the server log to confirm |
| Login fails with "Auth service unreachable" | Real checkCred path; the gateway at `APTRANSCO_AUTH_URL` is not reachable from this host, or `APTRANSCO_AUTH_USER`/`APTRANSCO_AUTH_PASS` are missing | Confirm network reach to the gateway; for offline work, arm the dev-login bypass instead |
| `sync_gis_towers` prints `wrote 0/34000 towers` with repeated `batch of 1000 towers failed and was skipped` | The per-chunk writes are erroring — usually schema drift (a migration not applied to `line_inspection_db`) or a dropped connection | Read the first exception text on stderr; re-run migrations with `--database=line_inspection_db` |
| `import_sap_lines` fails with "SAP line file not found" | The default path `BASE_DIR/'EHT LINES SAP DATA 06.07.2026.XLSX'` does not exist in this checkout despite the README calling it "checked-in" | Pass `--file <path>` explicitly |
| `map_sap_lines` matches almost nothing | `import_sap_lines` never ran (no candidates), or naming diverges beyond the 0.75 Jaccard threshold | Check `SapLine` row count; use the SAP↔ArcGIS mapping admin page, which shows ranked suggestions below the auto-accept threshold |
| Hand-entered `insulator_type` / `type_of_earthing` values vanished after a sync | Someone added those names to `update_fields` in `_sync_towers` | Revert `sync_gis_towers.py:269-276`; the values are unrecoverable from ArcGIS because ArcGIS never had them |
| Criticality rules tuned in the admin reverted | `seed_checklist_catalog` was re-run; it deletes and recreates every rule for every seeded defect (`seed_checklist_catalog.py:290`) | Re-apply the edits; treat the seed command as one-time |
| Nobody can access the admin panel | The `SuperAdmin` table is empty | `python manage.py grant_super_admin --employee-id <id>` — this is the only path in, by design |
## 10. Core Domain Logic Modules

Seven small, dependency-light modules sit between `line_inspection/models.py` and every view
(`admin_views.py`, `dashboard_views.py`, `api/views.py`). They contain essentially all of the
system's business rules. None of them import Django views, DRF, or templates; all of them are
directly unit-testable, and `line_inspection/tests/test_dashboard.py` exercises most of them.

| Module | Lines | One-sentence purpose | Read/Write authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| `line_inspection/jurisdiction.py` | 94 | The **own-assignment** scope: what one employee may *inspect and edit* | **Write authority** |
| `line_inspection/viewing.py` | 155 | The **oversight** scope: what one employee may *see*, widened up the reporting tree | Read only |
| `line_inspection/status.py` | 78 | Latest-inspection status per tower + the denormalized `Tower.last_*` cache | Writes 3 cache columns only |
| `line_inspection/schedule.py` | 129 | The "tower schedule" — ordered position of each tower along its line | Writes `line_sequence`/`line_offset_m` |
| `line_inspection/register.py` | 193 | Builds the per-line item×tower **inspection register** matrix + its `.xlsx` export | Pure read |
| `line_inspection/forms.py` | 113 | Django `ModelForm`s for the custom admin panel | n/a |
| `line_inspection/context_processors.py` | 18 | Injects identity/role flags into every rendered template | n/a |

### 10.1 Domain jargon used throughout this section

Defined here once so the rest of the section can be terse.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **cadre** | The SAP employee grade/class. Stored as `EmployeeCadreSnapshot.emp_sub_grp` (e.g. `AE`, `AAE`, `ADE/AEE`, `DE/EE`, `SE`, `CE`). Real SAP codes are *combined and coarse* — `DE/EE` is one code covering both DE and EE — which is exactly why authorization is **not** derived from cadre. |
| **AEE / DEE / EE / SE / CE** | Assistant Executive Engineer → Deputy Executive Engineer → Executive Engineer → Superintending Engineer → Chief Engineer. Ascending field hierarchy. Field inspection is done by AEE/DEE; EEs assign the work; SE/CE monitor. |
| **checkCred** | The legacy APTRANSCO employee-credential HTTP gateway (`services/checkcred_client.py`) that validates `employee_id` + password and returns the identity used as the session key. Not `django.contrib.auth`. |
| **jurisdiction** | The set of lines/towers an employee may **inspect** (capture data on), derived *only* from that employee's own `RoleAssignment` and `LineTowerAssignment` rows. `jurisdiction.py`. |
| **oversight** | The set of lines/towers an employee may **view**, = their own jurisdiction ∪ the jurisdictions of everyone below them in the SAP reporting tree. `viewing.py`. Strictly read-only. |
| **VT / virtual tower** | ArcGIS models a multi-circuit structure as one *real* tower row plus one extra "VT" row per additional circuit, co-located at the same coordinates. `Tower.is_virtual=True`. VT rows are **never inspected or counted**; they exist so each circuit's line has a full column of towers. |
| **structure_key** | `"{voltage}:{lat:.5f}:{lng:.5f}"`-style string assigned by `sync_gis_towers` that groups the real tower and all its co-located VT rows into one *physical structure*. It is the join key for `viewing.circuits_at()` and for the register's VT columns. |
| **CP / SP** | `Tower.cp_sp` — the structure's role in the corridor: **C**utting **P**oint / **S**uspension **P**oint (also `Boom`). Display/QA only; no logic depends on it. |
| **LILO** | *Loop-In Loop-Out* — a line reorganisation in which an existing line is cut and looped into a new substation, producing two or more new lines from one old one. Causes duplicate `tower_number`s along a corridor, which is why `schedule.py` has a branched-line fallback. |
| **Ground Patrol / PMI** | The two annual inspection **cycles**. Ground Patrolling is the routine walk-down; PMI (Pre-Monsoon Inspection) is the detailed one done before the monsoon. `Inspection.inspection_type ∈ {'ground_patrol','pmi', NULL}`. |
| **criticality** | Severity of a defect: `minor` / `major` / `critical`. A tower's *status* adds `ok` (inspected, no defect) and `none` (never inspected) — see `WORST_CHOICES` in `line_inspection/models.py:49`. |
| **line_sequence** | The tower's 1-based ordinal position along its line, computed by `schedule.py` and persisted on `Tower`. The backbone of range assignments and of register column order. |

---

### 10.2 `jurisdiction.py` — the own-assignment (write) scope

The module docstring states its own contract, and it is the single most important paragraph in
the codebase:

```python
"""...This is the *own-assignment* (edit/capture) scope: the REST API write path
(_create_inspection) and can_edit_tower depend on it staying scoped to a single
employee's own assignments. The reporting-hierarchy-widened *oversight* (read)
scope for the Phase 3 dashboard lives in viewing.py and is built on top of
_lines_for_assignments below — never by widening these functions."""
```

Two model tables feed it, and **only** these two:

| Model | Grants | Fields consulted |
|---|---|---|
| `RoleAssignment` (`line_inspection/models.py:448`) | A whole **subdivision** (every active `Line` whose `subdivision` FK points at it) and/or an explicit set of **lines** (M2M) | `employee_id`, `is_active`, `subdivision_id`, `lines` |
| `LineTowerAssignment` (`line_inspection/models.py:465`) | A **from-tower → to-tower stretch** of one line | `employee_id`, `is_active`, `line_id`, `from_tower`, `to_tower` |

#### 10.2.1 `_active_assignments(employee_id) -> QuerySet[RoleAssignment]`

```python
def _active_assignments(employee_id):
    return RoleAssignment.objects.filter(employee_id=employee_id, is_active=True)
```

Lazy queryset, one row per grant. Backed by the composite index
`models.Index(fields=['employee_id', 'is_active'])` declared on `RoleAssignment.Meta`
(`line_inspection/models.py:459`). Note the *soft-delete* discipline: the Roles &
Jurisdiction admin screen never deletes an assignment, it sets `is_active=False`
(`line_inspection/admin_views.py:157`), so the audit trail (`assigned_by_employee_id`,
`assigned_at`) survives revocation.

Private by convention (leading underscore); the only callers are `visible_lines` below.

#### 10.2.2 `_lines_for_assignments(assignments) -> QuerySet[Line]` — the shared union helper

This is the **one place** in the codebase where "a set of RoleAssignments" is turned into
"a set of Lines". It exists as a separate function precisely so that the single-employee
scope (`visible_lines`) and the whole-subtree scope (`viewing.oversight_lines`) cannot drift
apart — a divergence there would be an authorization bug.

```python
def _lines_for_assignments(assignments):
    assignments = list(assignments)
    if not assignments:
        return Line.objects.none()

    subdivision_ids = [a.subdivision_id for a in assignments if a.subdivision_id]
    line_ids = list(
        RoleAssignment.lines.through.objects.filter(roleassignment__in=assignments)
        .values_list('line_id', flat=True)
    )

    if not subdivision_ids and not line_ids:
        return Line.objects.none()

    query = Q(pk__in=[])
    if subdivision_ids:
        query |= Q(subdivision_id__in=subdivision_ids)
    if line_ids:
        query |= Q(pk__in=line_ids)
    return Line.objects.filter(query, is_active=True).distinct()
```

**Signature.** `assignments`: any iterable or queryset of `RoleAssignment`.
**Returns:** a lazy `QuerySet[Line]` (never a list), so callers can chain `.filter(pk=…)`,
`.values_list('id', flat=True)`, `.count()`, `.order_by('name')` without re-running the union.

**Exact queries issued** (three, in order):

1. `list(assignments)` forces evaluation:
   `SELECT … FROM role_assignment WHERE employee_id = … AND is_active = true`
   (or `employee_id IN (…)` for the oversight caller).
2. The M2M through-table, queried **directly** rather than via `a.lines.all()` per row —
   this is the anti-N+1 move. Django auto-generates the through model and exposes it as
   `RoleAssignment.lines.through`:
   `SELECT line_id FROM roleassignment_lines WHERE roleassignment_id IN (…)`.
3. The union itself:
   `SELECT DISTINCT … FROM line WHERE (subdivision_id IN (…) OR id IN (…)) AND is_active = true`.

**Why the subdivision-OR-explicit-lines union at all.** An EE assigning work has two natural
granularities. "You own everything in Vijayawada Rural subdivision" is one row and stays correct
when ArcGIS syncs a *new* line into that subdivision — the grant is by reference, not by
snapshot. "You own these three named lines" is needed when a subdivision is split across
several AEEs. Both must be expressible on the same `RoleAssignment` row (the model allows a
subdivision **and** lines simultaneously), so the resulting line set is a union, not a
choice. `.distinct()` is required because a line can be reached by both branches at once.

**Why `Q(pk__in=[])` is used as the empty seed.** Building an OR chain needs an identity
element. `Q()` (the empty Q) is the identity for **AND**, not OR — `Q() | Q(x=1)` collapses to
*no filter at all*, i.e. **every** row. Using it here would mean "an assignment with neither a
subdivision nor a line grants the whole grid". `Q(pk__in=[])` is instead the identity for OR:
Django's SQL compiler raises `EmptyResultSet` for an `IN ()` lookup, and an `EmptyResultSet`
child inside an `OR` node is simply dropped, so the compiled SQL contains only the real
branches. If *every* branch is empty, the whole `OR` raises `EmptyResultSet` and the queryset
returns nothing **without touching the database**. In one phrase: the empty seed makes the
union **fail-closed**. The explicit `if not subdivision_ids and not line_ids: return
Line.objects.none()` guard above is belt-and-braces for the same case, and additionally saves
constructing the query object.

**Invariants maintained:** result contains only `is_active=True` lines (soft-deleted lines never
grant anything); result is deduplicated; result is empty for an empty input.

**Callers:** `jurisdiction.visible_lines` (`jurisdiction.py:48`) and
`viewing.oversight_lines` (`viewing.py:76`). Nothing else may call it — that is the module
docstring's "never by widening these functions" rule.

#### 10.2.3 `visible_lines(employee_id) -> QuerySet[Line]`

```python
def visible_lines(employee_id):
    return _lines_for_assignments(_active_assignments(employee_id))
```

The active lines granted to **this employee alone**. Lazy queryset.

**Critical subtlety, easy to miss:** `LineTowerAssignment` (ranges) does **not** contribute here.
An employee who holds only a from/to-tower range therefore has `visible_lines() == ∅` while
having a non-empty `visible_towers()`. See §10.6 for the consequences.

**Callers:** `visible_towers`, `can_edit_tower` (both below), and
`line_inspection/tests/test_dashboard.py:67`.

#### 10.2.4 `range_tower_ids(employee_ids) -> set[int]`

```python
def range_tower_ids(employee_ids):
    if isinstance(employee_ids, str):
        employee_ids = [employee_ids]
    ids = set()
    ranges = (LineTowerAssignment.objects
              .filter(employee_id__in=list(employee_ids), is_active=True)
              .select_related('from_tower', 'to_tower'))
    for r in ranges:
        f_seq, t_seq = r.from_tower.line_sequence, r.to_tower.line_sequence
        if f_seq is not None and t_seq is not None:
            lo, hi = sorted((f_seq, t_seq))
            ids.update(Tower.objects.filter(
                line_id=r.line_id, is_active=True, is_virtual=False,
                line_sequence__gte=lo, line_sequence__lte=hi,
            ).values_list('id', flat=True))
        else:
            ids.update({r.from_tower_id, r.to_tower_id})
    return ids
```

**Signature.** Accepts either a single `employee_id` string or any iterable of them — the
`isinstance(employee_ids, str)` normalisation exists so the same function serves the
single-employee jurisdiction path and the multi-employee oversight path (`viewing.py:85`
passes a whole set).

**Returns:** a plain Python `set` of `Tower.id` ints (**not** a queryset), because callers
need to OR it into a larger `Q` object.

**The stretch expansion.** A range is stored as two boundary **Tower FKs**, never as raw
sequence indices. The docstring gives the reason directly: *"boundaries stored as towers, so a
schedule rebuild can't drift the stretch."* `Tower.line_sequence` is recomputed by
`manage.py build_tower_schedule` whenever geometry or the tower set changes; if a range had
been stored as "sequence 40 to sequence 60", a rebuild that inserted one tower would silently
shift 21 towers' worth of accountability onto a different person. Storing the endpoints as
rows means the stretch always re-derives to the physically correct span.

Expansion is therefore: read the two boundary towers' current `line_sequence`, `sorted()` them
(so an Admin picking from-tower after to-tower still gets a valid range), and select every
**real, active** tower on the same line whose sequence is inclusive-between. Query per range
row: `SELECT id FROM tower WHERE line_id = … AND is_active AND NOT is_virtual AND
line_sequence BETWEEN lo AND hi`. `select_related('from_tower','to_tower')` collapses what
would otherwise be two extra queries per range into the initial join.

**The boundary-only fallback.** If either boundary tower has `line_sequence IS NULL` — the
schedule has not been built for that line yet, or the line was skipped as `'empty'` — the
range degenerates to exactly the two boundary tower ids. This is deliberately the *narrowest*
safe interpretation: rather than guessing an order (and possibly granting the whole line), it
grants only what was unambiguously named. It is fail-closed, consistent with `_lines_for_assignments`.
Note the fallback branch does **not** re-check `is_active` / `is_virtual` on the boundaries,
but both consumers (`visible_towers`, `viewing.oversight_towers`) re-apply those filters in
their outer query, so no inactive or VT tower can escape through it.

**Cost note:** one query for the ranges plus **one query per range row**. Acceptable because
ranges are rare (a handful per line at most) and the whole scope is recomputed per request.

**Callers:** `visible_towers`, `can_edit_tower`, `viewing.oversight_towers` (`viewing.py:85`).

#### 10.2.5 `visible_towers(employee_id) -> QuerySet[Tower]`

```python
def visible_towers(employee_id):
    line_ids = list(visible_lines(employee_id).values_list('id', flat=True))
    range_ids = range_tower_ids(employee_id)
    scope = Q(line_id__in=line_ids)
    if range_ids:
        scope |= Q(id__in=range_ids)
    return Tower.objects.filter(scope, is_active=True, is_virtual=False)
```

The real towers this employee may **inspect**: every tower on a whole-line/subdivision grant,
UNION every tower inside a from/to range.

**Returns:** a lazy `QuerySet[Tower]`.

**Invariants:** `is_active=True` (soft-deleted towers vanish from scope) and
`is_virtual=False`. The VT exclusion is enforced here, in `viewing.oversight_towers`, and again
independently at the write boundary — `api/views.py:451` rejects a VT tower with
*"Virtual (VT) towers are not inspected — inspect the real co-located tower."* Three
independent enforcement points for one rule, because a VT inspection would silently
double-count a structure.

Note that `Q(line_id__in=[])` here is *not* fail-open: it is an `IN ()` on a **non-pk** column,
combined with `AND is_active` — Django still raises `EmptyResultSet` for the empty `IN`, so an
employee with no grants at all gets an empty queryset. The `if range_ids:` guard exists so the
common (no-range) case does not construct a second `Q` node.

**Callers:** `api/views.py:628` (the `GET /inspections/?tower=` history filter) and the tests.

#### 10.2.6 `can_edit_tower(employee_id, tower) -> bool`

```python
def can_edit_tower(employee_id, tower):
    if tower.line_id is None:
        return False
    if visible_lines(employee_id).filter(pk=tower.line_id).exists():
        return True
    return tower.id in range_tower_ids(employee_id)
```

**The single write gate of the entire system.** Takes a *materialised* `Tower` instance (not an
id), returns a bool.

Three branches, in cheapest-first order:

| Branch | Condition | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `tower.line_id is None` | `False` | An orphaned tower (its `Line` was soft-deleted and the `SET_NULL` FK fired) belongs to nobody's jurisdiction. Fail-closed. |
| 2 | tower's line ∈ `visible_lines(employee_id)` | `True` | Whole-line / subdivision grant. One `EXISTS` query, no row materialisation. |
| 3 | `tower.id ∈ range_tower_ids(employee_id)` | `True`/`False` | From/to range grant. Only evaluated if branch 2 missed, so the per-range queries are skipped for the common case. |

**Callers (both are write paths):**
- `api/views.py:453` — inside `_create_inspection`, before any row is written. A failure
  raises DRF `PermissionDenied` → HTTP 403 and the whole atomic block never opens.
- `api/views.py:719` — `POST /tickets/<id>/close/`, as `if not is_admin(employee_id) and not
  jurisdiction.can_edit_tower(employee_id, ticket.tower)`. The Admin escape hatch is
  deliberate: the README (`line_inspection/README.md:669`) records this as a *fixed bug* —
  the first implementation checked only the requester's own jurisdiction, which locked Admins
  out of closing tickets on jurisdiction they had themselves assigned to someone else.

---

### 10.3 `viewing.py` — the reporting-hierarchy oversight (read) scope

```python
"""Oversight (viewing) scope for the Phase 3 web dashboard — the reporting-
hierarchy-widened superset of jurisdiction.py's own-assignment scope.
...
Viewing tier is FUNCTIONAL, not grade-based: real SAP cadre codes are coarse/
combined (e.g. 'DE/EE'), so authorization derives from the reporting tree + who
actually holds RoleAssignments. emp_sub_grp is used only for display labels and
the management-dashboard gate (CADRE_LABELS / MANAGEMENT_SUBGRPS)."""
```

The design decision worth internalising: **authorization is derived from the reporting tree and
from who actually holds assignments, never from the cadre code.** SAP's `emp_sub_grp` values are
combined (`DE/EE` covers both DE and EE; `AAE` and `AE` both mean AEE), so a grade-based rule
would be both wrong and unmaintainable. `emp_sub_grp` survives in exactly two places — a display
label and the management-reports gate — and both are cosmetic-to-coarse, never a scope narrowing.

#### 10.3.1 Module constants

```python
CADRE_LABELS = {
    'AAE': 'AEE', 'AE': 'AEE', 'ADE/AEE': 'DEE',
    'DE/EE': 'EE', 'SE': 'SE', 'CE': 'CE',
    'DIRECTOR': 'Director', 'GM': 'GM', 'JMD': 'JMD', 'CMD': 'CMD',
}
MANAGEMENT_SUBGRPS = {'CE', 'DIRECTOR', 'GM', 'JMD', 'CMD'}
```

| Constant | Type | Purpose | Fallback |
|---|---|---|---|
| `CADRE_LABELS` | `dict[str,str]` | Maps raw SAP `emp_sub_grp` → the field-recognised cadre label shown in the header. The mapping was **enumerated from the live synced snapshot**, not invented (comment cites `memory/aptransco-cadre-codes`). Two SAP codes (`AAE`, `AE`) collapse to one label `AEE`; `ADE/AEE` means DEE, `DE/EE` means EE. | Unlisted codes fall back to the raw `emp_sub_grp` string (`display_label`), so a newly-appearing SAP code degrades to showing itself rather than blanking. |
| `MANAGEMENT_SUBGRPS` | `set[str]` | The cadre codes that unlock the zonal/circle/division rollups **and** all-tower scope on `/dashboard/reports/`. Top of the technical cadre only. | Anything else → not management. |

**Note that `SE` is deliberately absent from `MANAGEMENT_SUBGRPS`.** An SE has a wide *oversight*
scope (their whole subtree) but does **not** get the all-tower management rollups — those start
at CE. This is easy to misread from `README.md:307` ("an SE/CE sees their whole circle"), which
is about oversight scope, not about the reports gate; `README.md:311` states the gate correctly.

#### 10.3.2 `subordinate_snapshots(employee_id) -> list[EmployeeCadreSnapshot]`

```python
def subordinate_snapshots(employee_id):
    by_manager = {}
    for emp in EmployeeCadreSnapshot.objects.exclude(reporting_manager_id='').only(
        'employee_id', 'employee_name', 'reporting_manager_id', 'position_text', 'emp_sub_grp'
    ):
        by_manager.setdefault(emp.reporting_manager_id, []).append(emp)

    result, frontier, seen = [], [employee_id], {employee_id}
    while frontier:
        next_frontier = []
        for manager_id in frontier:
            for emp in by_manager.get(manager_id, []):
                if emp.employee_id not in seen:
                    seen.add(emp.employee_id)
                    result.append(emp)
                    next_frontier.append(emp.employee_id)
        frontier = next_frontier
    return result
```

**Returns:** a `list` of `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` model instances in **BFS order** (all direct
reports first, then their reports, …). **The seed employee is NOT included** — the function
answers "who is *below* me", and `visible_employee_ids` is responsible for adding self back.

**Algorithm.** One pass builds `by_manager: dict[manager_id, list[snapshot]]` — an in-memory
adjacency list of the whole org chart. Then a breadth-first walk from the seed, with a `seen`
set. The `seen` set is seeded with `employee_id` itself, which makes the walk immune to two
real hazards in SAP data: an employee listed as their own manager (self-loop), and a
manager/report cycle (A reports to B reports to A) — both would otherwise spin forever.

**Why an in-memory walk instead of a recursive CTE.** The docstring answers this: *"Cheap
in-memory walk over the ~1,830-row snapshot."* The `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` table is the entire
APTRANSCO technical cadre — the README's Phase 1 verification records **1,830 employees**
(`line_inspection/README.md:405-406`; unverified against a live DB from this repo). Loading
1,830 short rows and walking them in Python is a single sequential scan and a few milliseconds;
a `WITH RECURSIVE` CTE would be more code, would be Postgres-dialect SQL embedded in the ORM
layer, and would issue an unbounded-depth recursive query per call for no measurable gain at
this scale. The `.only(...)` projection keeps the loaded row narrow, and
`models.Index(fields=['reporting_manager_id'])` (`line_inspection/models.py:408`) is declared —
though note the query here has no `WHERE reporting_manager_id = …`, so the index is not actually
used by *this* function; it pays off for other lookups.

**`.exclude(reporting_manager_id='')`** drops top-of-tree rows (the field is a
`CharField(blank=True)`, so "no manager" is the empty string, not NULL). Those rows can never
be anyone's subordinate, so excluding them shrinks the dict without changing the result.

**Callers:**
- `viewing.visible_employee_ids` (`viewing.py:66`).
- `admin_views._subordinates` (`line_inspection/admin_views.py:122-126`), which is a
  three-line delegation whose own docstring says *"Single implementation lives in
  viewing.subordinate_snapshots (shared with the Phase 3 oversight scope)"*. It supplies the
  default candidate list on the Roles & Jurisdiction screen: an Admin is shown their own
  reporting-hierarchy subordinates first, with a full-employee search as fallback.

> **Finding — deferred-field N+1 on the Roles screen.** The `.only(...)` list omits
> `emp_sub_grp_desc`, but `templates/line_inspection/role_assignments.html:20` renders
> `{{ row.employee.emp_sub_grp_desc }}`. Every candidate row therefore triggers one extra
> `SELECT` to load the deferred column. Harmless for a handful of direct reports, quadratic-ish
> for an SE with a large subtree. Adding `'emp_sub_grp_desc'` to the `.only()` list fixes it.

#### 10.3.3 `visible_employee_ids(employee_id) -> set[str]`

```python
def visible_employee_ids(employee_id):
    ids = {employee_id}
    ids.update(e.employee_id for e in subordinate_snapshots(employee_id))
    return ids
```

**Returns:** a `set[str]` of employee ids — the seed **plus** the whole subtree.

**Why self is included — the key property.** Because self is in the set, a *leaf* user (nobody
reports to them) gets `visible_employee_ids == {self}`, which makes
`oversight_lines(self) == _lines_for_assignments(own active assignments) == visible_lines(self)`
**exactly**. In other words: **for a field AEE/DEE, the oversight scope and the jurisdiction
scope are the same set.** The two scope systems only diverge for someone who actually has
reports. That is why the mobile app can safely read from `viewing.oversight_*`
(`api/views.py:224-226` comments this explicitly) while still writing through
`jurisdiction.can_edit_tower` — for the field user the two are identical, and for a supervisor
who opens the app the reads widen but the writes do not.

#### 10.3.4 `oversight_lines(employee_id) -> QuerySet[Line]`

```python
def oversight_lines(employee_id):
    assignments = RoleAssignment.objects.filter(
        employee_id__in=visible_employee_ids(employee_id), is_active=True,
    )
    return jurisdiction._lines_for_assignments(assignments)
```

**Returns:** a lazy `QuerySet[Line]` — the union of active lines assigned to the viewer **or**
anyone below them.

Note the shape: **one widened query** (`employee_id IN (…subtree…)`), not N per-subordinate
queries, and then the *same* `_lines_for_assignments` union used by the write scope. This is the
"exists once" guarantee — if the subdivision-or-lines union logic is ever changed, both scopes
change together.

Same caveat as `visible_lines`: **ranges do not contribute lines here either.**

**Callers:** `dashboard_views.map_view:52` (line count tile), `dashboard_views.register_view:141`
(the Register screen's line dropdown **and** its 403 gate), `api/views.py:213`
(`GET /subdivisions/` derives subdivisions from scope lines), `api/views.py:226`
(`GET /lines/`), `api/views.py:292` (`GET /map/lines/` GeoJSON), `api/views.py:751`
(support-request scoping).

#### 10.3.5 `oversight_towers(employee_id, geocoded_only=False) -> QuerySet[Tower]`

```python
def oversight_towers(employee_id, geocoded_only=False):
    scope_ids = visible_employee_ids(employee_id)
    line_ids = list(oversight_lines(employee_id).values_list('id', flat=True))
    range_ids = jurisdiction.range_tower_ids(scope_ids)
    scope = Q(line_id__in=line_ids)
    if range_ids:
        scope |= Q(id__in=range_ids)
    qs = Tower.objects.filter(scope, is_active=True, is_virtual=False)
    if geocoded_only:
        qs = qs.filter(latitude__isnull=False, longitude__isnull=False)
    return qs
```

Structurally the mirror image of `jurisdiction.visible_towers`, but with the subtree-widened
inputs. Returns a lazy `QuerySet[Tower]`; same `is_active` / `is_virtual=False` invariants.

**The `geocoded_only` flag.** Pass `True` **only for the map** — a tower with NULL lat/lng
cannot be placed on a Leaflet layer and would either crash the marker builder or silently
produce a `[null, null]` GeoJSON coordinate. Pass `False` (the default) for **tickets,
inspections and rollups**, which must count *every* tower in scope including the not-yet-geocoded
ones. Getting this backwards would understate pending-inspection counts. Callers that pass
`True`: `dashboard_views.map_view:35`, `api/views.py:330` (`GET /map/towers/`). Everything else
uses the default.

> **Performance finding — repeated subtree walks.** `oversight_towers` calls
> `visible_employee_ids` directly *and* calls `oversight_lines`, which calls
> `visible_employee_ids` again. Each call re-runs `subordinate_snapshots`, i.e. a full scan of
> `EmployeeCadreSnapshot`. So one `oversight_towers()` = **two** full-table walks. A single
> `/dashboard/map/` render calls `oversight_towers` (2) + `cadre_tier` (1) + `oversight_lines`
> (1) = **four** walks of the ~1,830-row table. Nothing is memoised per request. Correct, but a
> per-request cache (or threading `scope_ids` through as an optional argument) would be the
> obvious optimisation.

#### 10.3.6 `circuits_at(tower) -> list[Line]`

```python
def circuits_at(tower):
    if tower.structure_key:
        line_ids = list(
            Tower.objects.filter(structure_key=tower.structure_key, is_active=True, line__isnull=False)
            .values_list('line_id', flat=True).distinct()
        )
    else:
        line_ids = [tower.line_id] if tower.line_id else []
    if not line_ids:
        return []
    return list(Line.objects.filter(id__in=line_ids, is_active=True).order_by('voltage', 'name'))
```

Answers the map pop-up question *"click a tower → which lines/circuits actually run through this
structure?"*. Because ArcGIS models extra circuits as separate co-located VT rows, the tower you
clicked knows only about *its own* circuit; the physical truth lives in the `structure_key`
group.

**Returns:** a materialised `list[Line]` (not a queryset), deduplicated, ordered by
`voltage` then `name`. Empty list when the structure has no key and no line.

Note the query deliberately does **not** filter `is_virtual` — it must include VT rows, since
those are exactly the extra circuits it is looking for. It filters `line__isnull=False` so
orphaned rows contribute no `None` to `line_ids`, and `is_active=True` on both the tower rows
and the resulting lines. Backed by `models.Index(fields=['structure_key'])`
(`line_inspection/models.py:202`).

**Caller:** `api/views.py:394` — `GET /api/towers/<id>/` returns a `circuits` array of
`{id, name, voltage, circuit_type}`. Also covered by `tests/test_dashboard.py:435`.

#### 10.3.7 `_snapshot`, `cadre_tier`, `is_management`, `display_label`

`_snapshot(employee_id)` is a one-line private helper:
`EmployeeCadreSnapshot.objects.filter(employee_id=employee_id).first()` → a model instance or
`None`. Cheap: `employee_id` is `unique=True`, so it is an index lookup.

**`cadre_tier(employee_id) -> str`** — the *functional* viewing tier, one of four strings:

| Return | Condition (evaluated in this order) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `'admin'` | `auth.is_admin(employee_id)` — holds a granted `FieldEECadrePosition`, or is a `SuperAdmin` | Panel-level authority |
| `'none'` | no active `RoleAssignment` anywhere in `visible_employee_ids` | Nothing assigned to them or beneath them |
| `'field_user'` | the set of assignment-holding ids in scope is exactly `{employee_id}` | A leaf inspector |
| `'supervisor'` | otherwise (someone *else* in the subtree holds an assignment) | Has people below them doing the work |

```python
    assigned = set(
        RoleAssignment.objects.filter(employee_id__in=scope_ids, is_active=True)
        .values_list('employee_id', flat=True)
    )
    if not assigned:
        return 'none'
    if assigned == {employee_id}:
        return 'field_user'
    return 'supervisor'
```

The docstring is explicit that this is presentation logic: *"Used only for map framing and the
landing view; never to restrict a viewer below their own jurisdiction."* Nothing branches on
tier to *deny* access — a `'none'` tier still gets an (empty) map, not a 403.

> **Finding — a range-only user is reported as tier `'none'`.** `cadre_tier` inspects
> `RoleAssignment` only; it never consults `LineTowerAssignment`. An AEE who holds *only* a
> from/to-tower stretch has a real, non-empty `visible_towers()` and can capture inspections,
> yet `cadre_tier()` returns `'none'` (and `is_management()` returns `False`). The dashboard
> still shows them their towers — nothing is denied — but the tier label and any UI keyed off
> it are wrong for that employee. Not covered by any test (`FromToRangeTests` at
> `tests/test_dashboard.py:237` exercises the scope functions but not `cadre_tier`).

**`is_management(employee_id) -> bool`** — whether to expose the zonal/circle/division rollups
**and all-tower scope**. `True` for any `SuperAdmin` unconditionally; otherwise `True` iff the
employee's `emp_sub_grp ∈ MANAGEMENT_SUBGRPS`. Consumers:
- `oversight_lines` / `oversight_towers` — **the widening itself**. A management viewer's
  line scope is every active `Line` and their tower scope every active real `Tower`,
  irrespective of who holds a `RoleAssignment`. Because every scoped read in the app goes
  through these two, one predicate now decides the whole scope.
- `dashboard_views.rollup_view:229-240` — gates `/dashboard/reports/` (403 for
  non-management non-admins) and picks the `scope_label` ("All towers (management view)" vs
  "Your oversight scope"). The queryset itself is plain `oversight_towers`.
- `context_processors.identity` / `api/views._identity_profile` → the `Reports` nav link and
  the mobile role hints.
- `SubdivisionListView` (`api/views.py:213`) — `Subdivision.objects.all()`, kept as its own
  branch on purpose: deriving it from `oversight_lines` would drop a subdivision that has no
  active line yet, and the mobile scope picker should still offer it.
- `MobileDashboardView` (`api/views.py:913`) — whether to attach the per-subdivision roll.

> **Fixed — the two halves of the widening used to disagree.** `is_management` widened the
> *tower* scope at three hand-written call sites (`rollup_view`, `MobileDashboardView`,
> `SubdivisionListView`) but never `oversight_lines`/`oversight_towers` themselves. A super
> admin holds no `RoleAssignment` of their own and has nobody below them, so every read that
> went through `viewing.oversight_*` — the mobile `/lines/` list, both map endpoints, tickets,
> inspections, the register, and `map_view`'s own `tower_total`/`line_total` — came back
> **empty**, while the KPI strip and the rollups reported all ~66k towers from the hand-written
> querysets. The app rendered "66k Towers" and "No lines assigned to you yet" in the same frame.
> The widening now lives in `oversight_lines`/`oversight_towers` and the duplicate branches are
> gone, so the two answers cannot drift apart again. Regression tests:
> `DashboardScopeTests.test_management_scope_covers_lines_and_towers_together`,
> `test_super_admin_scope_needs_no_assignment`,
> `test_management_scope_still_excludes_inactive_and_virtual`,
> `test_management_scope_does_not_grant_capture_rights`.

**`display_label(employee_id) -> str`** — `CADRE_LABELS.get(snap.emp_sub_grp, snap.emp_sub_grp or '')`,
or `''` when there is no snapshot row at all. Pure display. Consumers:
`dashboard_views.map_view:48` → rendered next to the map title
(`templates/line_inspection/dashboard_map.html:22`), `context_processors.identity` →
`cadre_label`, and `api/views.py:63` (`cadre` in the mobile profile payload).
