### 10.4 Jurisdiction vs oversight, side by side

| Aspect | `jurisdiction.py` (own-assignment) | `viewing.py` (oversight) |
|---|---|---|
| **Question answered** | "What may *I* inspect and edit?" | "What may *I* look at?" |
| **Employee set** | exactly `{employee_id}` | `{employee_id}` ∪ entire reporting subtree |
| **Source of the subtree** | n/a | `EmployeeCadreSnapshot.reporting_manager_id`, BFS in Python |
| **Line source** | own active `RoleAssignment`s → `_lines_for_assignments` | subtree's active `RoleAssignment`s → **the same** `_lines_for_assignments` |
| **Range source** | `range_tower_ids(employee_id)` | `range_tower_ids(scope_ids)` (whole subtree) |
| **Grants writes?** | **Yes** — `can_edit_tower` is the only write gate | **Never.** No write path calls anything in `viewing.py` |
| **Grants reads?** | Yes (`api/views.py:628`, inspection history) | Yes — every dashboard screen and every map/list API |
| **VT towers** | excluded (`is_virtual=False`) | excluded (`is_virtual=False`) |
| **Inactive rows** | excluded (`is_active=True` on assignments, lines, towers) | same |
| **Return types** | `QuerySet[Line]`, `set[int]`, `QuerySet[Tower]`, `bool` | `list[snapshot]`, `set[str]`, `QuerySet[Line]`, `QuerySet[Tower]`, `list[Line]`, `str`, `bool` |
| **Widening direction** | never widens | widens **up** the tree only (a manager gains their reports' scope; a report never gains their manager's) |
| **For a leaf employee** | `visible_lines` | **identical** to `oversight_lines` |
| **Tests** | `tests/test_dashboard.py:66-69`, `:252-263` | `tests/test_dashboard.py:58-63`, `:265-271` |

### 10.5 Worked example — one SE, two EEs, four AEEs

*(A synthetic org chart, constructed to exercise every branch. The names and ids are
illustrative; the computed results below follow strictly from the code above.)*

**Org chart** (`EmployeeCadreSnapshot` rows):

| employee_id | emp_sub_grp | `display_label` | reporting_manager_id | Admin? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `SE-01` | `SE` | SE | `''` (top) | no |
| `EE-A` | `DE/EE` | EE | `SE-01` | **yes** — position_id granted in `FieldEECadrePosition` |
| `EE-B` | `DE/EE` | EE | `SE-01` | no |
| `AEE-1` | `AE` | AEE | `EE-A` | no |
| `AEE-2` | `AAE` | AEE | `EE-A` | no |
| `AEE-3` | `ADE/AEE` | DEE | `EE-B` | no |
| `AEE-4` | `AE` | AEE | `EE-B` | no |

**GIS data.** Subdivision `SD-North` owns lines `L1` (100 towers, `line_sequence` 1–100), `L2`
(50 towers) and `L3` (30 towers). Subdivision `SD-South` owns `L4` (20 towers) and `L5` (25
towers). All towers real (`is_virtual=False`), all active. 225 towers total.

**Assignments** (created by EE-A / EE-B on the Roles & Jurisdiction screen):

| Employee | Row | Grant |
|---|---|---|
| `AEE-1` | `RoleAssignment(subdivision=SD-North)` | every active line in SD-North → L1, L2, L3 |
| `AEE-2` | `RoleAssignment(lines=[L4])` | L4 only |
| `AEE-3` | `RoleAssignment(lines=[L5])` | L5 only |
| `AEE-4` | `LineTowerAssignment(line=L1, from_tower=T-40, to_tower=T-60)` — **no RoleAssignment at all** | L1 towers with `line_sequence` 40…60 (21 towers) |
| `EE-A`, `EE-B`, `SE-01` | *(none)* | nothing of their own |

#### What each person may EDIT (`jurisdiction.py`)

| Employee | `visible_lines()` | `range_tower_ids()` | `visible_towers()` | `can_edit_tower(L1 T-45)` | `can_edit_tower(L1 T-61)` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `AEE-1` | L1, L2, L3 | ∅ | 180 (all of L1+L2+L3) | **True** (branch 2) | **True** |
| `AEE-2` | L4 | ∅ | 20 | False | False |
| `AEE-3` | L5 | ∅ | 25 | False | False |
| `AEE-4` | **∅** | 21 ids (L1 seq 40–60) | **21** | **True** (branch 3) | **False** — outside the stretch |
| `EE-A` | ∅ | ∅ | **∅** | **False** | **False** |
| `EE-B` | ∅ | ∅ | **∅** | **False** | **False** |
| `SE-01` | ∅ | ∅ | **∅** | **False** | **False** |

Read the bottom three rows carefully: **EE-A, EE-B and SE-01 cannot edit a single tower.** They
assigned the work; they did not take it. This is the whole point of the split, and it is
asserted directly at `tests/test_dashboard.py:67-68`.

Note also `AEE-4`, who has jurisdiction over 21 towers while `visible_lines()` is empty.

#### What each person may SEE (`viewing.py`)

| Employee | `subordinate_snapshots()` (BFS order) | `visible_employee_ids()` | `oversight_lines()` | `oversight_towers()` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `AEE-1` | [] | {AEE-1} | L1, L2, L3 | 180 |
| `AEE-2` | [] | {AEE-2} | L4 | 20 |
| `AEE-3` | [] | {AEE-3} | L5 | 25 |
| `AEE-4` | [] | {AEE-4} | **∅** | **21** (range only) |
| `EE-A` | [AEE-1, AEE-2] | {EE-A, AEE-1, AEE-2} | L1, L2, L3, L4 | 200 |
| `EE-B` | [AEE-3, AEE-4] | {EE-B, AEE-3, AEE-4} | **L5 only** | **46** = L5's 25 **+ 21 on L1** |
| `SE-01` | [EE-A, EE-B, AEE-1, AEE-2, AEE-3, AEE-4] | all 7 | L1…L5 | 225 (everything) |

For the four AEEs, oversight and jurisdiction are **the same sets** — the leaf-equality property
from §10.3.3. For EE-A, EE-B and SE-01, oversight is non-empty while jurisdiction stays empty.

**`EE-B` is the instructive row.** Their oversight *towers* include 21 towers on L1 (inherited
from AEE-4's range), but their oversight *lines* do **not** include L1, because
`oversight_lines` is built from `RoleAssignment` only. Concretely:

- `/dashboard/map/` — EE-B sees 46 tower markers, 21 of which are on L1.
- `/dashboard/register/` — the line dropdown offers **only L5**. If EE-B hand-crafts
  `?line=<L1 id>`, `dashboard_views.register_view:151-154` finds no match in
  `oversight_lines` and returns **403 "That line is outside your jurisdiction."**
- `GET /api/map/lines/` returns one GeoJSON feature (L5), yet `GET /api/map/towers/`
  returns markers on a line that has no feature — the map draws unattached dots.

That asymmetry is a genuine design gap, not a bug in any single function: ranges grant towers
but never grant the line they sit on.

#### Tier, management and labels

| Employee | `cadre_tier()` | `is_management()` | `display_label()` | Sees "Reports" tab? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `AEE-1` | `field_user` | False | `AEE` | no |
| `AEE-2` | `field_user` | False | `AEE` | no |
| `AEE-3` | `field_user` | False | `DEE` | no |
| `AEE-4` | **`none`** (see finding in §10.3.7) | False | `AEE` | no |
| `EE-A` | `admin` (is_admin short-circuits before the assignment check) | False | `EE` | **yes** — via `is_admin`, not `is_management` |
| `EE-B` | `supervisor` (assigned = {AEE-3} ≠ {EE-B}) | False | `EE` | no |
| `SE-01` | `supervisor` | **False** — `SE ∉ MANAGEMENT_SUBGRPS` | `SE` | no |

An SE with a whole circle beneath them still cannot open the management rollups; a CE can.
If `EE-A` opens `/dashboard/reports/`, `rollup_view` admits them (`auth.is_admin`) but scopes
the rollup to **their oversight scope** (200 towers), whereas a CE would get **all** towers.

### 10.6 The security invariant, stated plainly

> **Reads may widen up the reporting tree. Writes never widen.**

Operationally that means:

1. Every write path in the system passes through `jurisdiction.can_edit_tower`
   (`api/views.py:453` for inspection create, `api/views.py:719` for ticket close) — and
   nothing else. There is no second write gate, and no write path imports `viewing`.
2. `viewing.py` may only *widen* by feeding a bigger employee-id set into the **same**
   `_lines_for_assignments` / `range_tower_ids` primitives. It never adds a new grant type,
   never relaxes `is_active`, and never relaxes `is_virtual=False`.
3. Every scoped queryset in the API **starts** from `viewing.oversight_*` and is only ever
   **narrowed** afterwards by client-supplied parameters (`?bbox`, `?line`, `?status`,
   `?subdivision`). The comment at `api/views.py:262-265` states the invariant and
   `tests/test_dashboard.py:137-140` proves it: a forged bounding box covering all of Andhra
   Pradesh returns **zero** features for an employee with no scope.
4. Client-supplied ids are re-checked against scope rather than trusted:
   `dashboard_views.register_view:151` (`lines.filter(pk=line_id)` → 403),
   `dashboard_views.inspections_view:101` (`scope.filter(pk=tower_id)` → out-of-scope page),
   `api/views.py:389` and `:676` (→ 404 "Not found or outside your jurisdiction", which also
   avoids leaking existence).
5. Both empty-set constructions (`Q(pk__in=[])`, the boundary-only range fallback,
   `Line.objects.none()`) are **fail-closed**: a missing or malformed grant yields nothing,
   never everything.

The one place where an *oversight* actor gains a write-ish power is deliberate and narrow:
closing a `DefectTicket` is permitted for **any Admin** (`api/views.py:719`), because the
alternative locked Admins out of tickets on jurisdiction they had assigned to others
(`README.md:669`). That is a status transition on a ticket, not inspection capture.

### 10.7 `status.py` — inspection status and the denormalized tower cache

```python
"""Status = the worst_criticality of a tower's most recent Inspection ('none' if
never inspected). The Tower model carries a denormalized cache
(last_inspection_at / last_worst_criticality / last_inspection_type), maintained
on inspection create by bump_tower_cache() below — the map and rollups read that
cache directly and avoid any per-tower subquery across ~67k towers."""
```

The whole module exists to answer "what colour is this tower?" at two very different scales:
**67,128 towers at once** (map, rollups → read the cache) and **one line's worth at a time**
(register, tests, cache warming → recompute from `Inspection`).

#### 10.7.1 `STATUS_COLORS` and `STATUS_LABELS`

```python
STATUS_COLORS = {
    'none': '#898781',   # grey  — never inspected
    'ok': '#0ca30c',     # green — inspected, no defect
    'minor': '#fab219',  # amber
    'major': '#ec835a',  # orange
    'critical': '#d03b3b',  # red
}
STATUS_LABELS = dict(WORST_CHOICES)
```

`STATUS_COLORS` reproduces the original proof-of-concept's colour coding
(`gisdata/clearpoc.html`) so that map markers, the legend, and the rollup bars are guaranteed to
agree — one dict, no hex codes duplicated in templates. `STATUS_LABELS` derives from
`WORST_CHOICES` (`line_inspection/models.py:49`), giving
`{'none': 'Not inspected', 'ok': 'Normal', 'minor': 'Minor', 'major': 'Major', 'critical': 'Critical'}`.

Consumers: `dashboard_views.map_view:53-54` serialises `STATUS_COLORS` to JSON into
`dashboard_map.html:60` (used for both the legend swatches and the Leaflet `fillColor` at
`dashboard_map.html:73,125`), and passes `STATUS_LABELS` for the status `<select>` and legend
text (`dashboard_map.html:33,51`).

> **Minor finding.** `dashboard_views.register_view:176` also puts `status_colors` in the
> Register template context, but `templates/line_inspection/dashboard_register.html` never
> reads it — the register hard-codes its own criticality chip colours in CSS
> (`.crit-minor/.crit-major/.crit-critical` at `dashboard_register.html:22`), which duplicate
> the three defect colours from `STATUS_COLORS` by hand. If the palette changes, the register
> chips will silently drift.

#### 10.7.2 `latest_inspection_status(tower_ids, inspection_type=None) -> dict[int, str]`

```python
    qs = Inspection.objects.filter(tower_id__in=tower_ids)
    if inspection_type:
        qs = qs.filter(inspection_type=inspection_type)
    rows = (
        qs.order_by('tower_id', '-saved_at', '-id')
        .distinct('tower_id')
        .values_list('tower_id', 'worst_criticality')
    )
    return dict(rows)
```

**Signature/returns.** `tower_ids`: any iterable of ints (normalised with `list()`, empty → `{}`
with no query). Returns `{tower_id: worst_criticality}`. **Towers with no matching inspection
are omitted** — every caller treats a missing key as `'none'` (e.g.
`api/views.py:354`: `status_by_tower.get(row['id'], 'none')`).

**The `DISTINCT ON` dependency.** `.distinct('tower_id')` compiles to Postgres
`SELECT DISTINCT ON (tower_id) …`, which keeps the *first* row per `tower_id` under the
`ORDER BY`. The ordering `tower_id, -saved_at, -id` is therefore load-bearing: `-saved_at`
picks the newest, and `-id` is the deterministic tie-break for two inspections saved in the same
transaction/microsecond. The `models.Index(fields=['tower', 'saved_at'])` on `Inspection`
(`line_inspection/models.py:526`) is what makes it a single index scan instead of a sort.

`DISTINCT ON` **does not exist in SQLite** — Django raises
`NotSupportedError: DISTINCT ON fields is not supported by this database backend`. This is
precisely why the test suite requires a real Postgres test database; the test module header
says so at `line_inspection/tests/test_dashboard.py:4-10`:

```
NOTE ON RUNNING: line_inspection models are routed to the `line_inspection_db`
Postgres connection (the `clear` schema) and the status helper uses Postgres
`DISTINCT ON`, so these tests require a Postgres test database for that
connection — they will not run on the default sqlite alias.
```

**The `inspection_type` filter.** `None` (default) = latest inspection of *any* cycle.
`'ground_patrol'` / `'pmi'` = latest inspection *of that cycle only*, which is the mechanism
behind the twice-yearly cycle view. Because the filter is applied **before** the `DISTINCT ON`,
a tower whose most recent inspection was a PMI still reports its older Ground Patrol result when
`inspection_type='ground_patrol'` is passed — that is the intent, and
`tests/test_dashboard.py:90-92` pins all three cases.

**Caller:** `api/views.py:349`, inside `MapTowerListView` (see §10.7.5).

#### 10.7.3 `latest_inspections(tower_ids, inspection_type=None) -> dict[int, Inspection]`

Same query shape and the same `DISTINCT ON` dependency, but returns the full `Inspection`
objects instead of just the criticality string, with the register's needs prefetched:

```python
    latest = (
        qs.order_by('tower_id', '-saved_at', '-id')
        .distinct('tower_id')
        .prefetch_related('item_results__item', 'item_results__entries__defect')
    )
    return {insp.tower_id: insp for insp in latest}
```

The `prefetch_related` chain loads, in a bounded number of extra queries: every `ItemResult`,
each one's `ChecklistItem`, each one's `DefectEntry` rows, and each entry's `Defect`. Without it
`register._item_cell` would issue several queries per item×tower cell — for a 100-tower line
with 25 checklist items that is 2,500 cells. Follow-up *questions* are not in the chain; the
register loads them once separately into `fu_map` (`register.py:106`).

**Caller:** `register.build_register` (`register.py:104`) — the only one.

#### 10.7.4 `bump_tower_cache(tower, saved_at, worst_criticality, inspection_type) -> None`

```python
def bump_tower_cache(tower, saved_at, worst_criticality, inspection_type):
    if tower.last_inspection_at and saved_at and saved_at < tower.last_inspection_at:
        return
    tower.last_inspection_at = saved_at
    tower.last_worst_criticality = worst_criticality
    tower.last_inspection_type = inspection_type
    tower.save(update_fields=['last_inspection_at', 'last_worst_criticality', 'last_inspection_type'])
```

**Signature.** `tower`: a materialised `Tower` (mutated in place *and* saved). `saved_at`: a
`datetime`. Returns `None`.

**The "advance only if newer" guard.** The mobile app is offline-first: an inspector can capture
on Monday, lose connectivity, and sync on Friday — *after* someone else has already synced a
Wednesday inspection of the same tower. Without the guard the late-arriving Monday row would
**regress** the cache, turning a Wednesday `critical` back into a Monday `ok` on the map. The
guard makes `bump_tower_cache` monotonic in `saved_at`: it is a max-by-timestamp write, not a
last-write-wins write.

Three no-op conditions are worth noting: if `tower.last_inspection_at` is NULL (never inspected)
the guard cannot fire and the cache is set unconditionally; if `saved_at` is falsy the guard also
cannot fire (in practice `_create_inspection` always passes `timezone.now()`); and equal
timestamps overwrite (`<` not `<=`), so a same-instant resubmit takes the newer values.

`update_fields=[…]` limits the UPDATE to the three cache columns — important because the caller
holds a `Tower` loaded possibly minutes earlier, and a full save would clobber any concurrent
ArcGIS-sync writes to the ~40 other columns.

**Caller:** exactly one — `api/views.py:544`, inside `_create_inspection`'s
`transaction.atomic()` block, immediately after the inspection's `worst_criticality` is
computed. The comment there explains the placement: *"advance the tower's denormalized status
cache in the same transaction so the map/rollups reflect this inspection immediately."*
If the transaction rolls back, so does the cache write.

**Bulk repair path:** `manage.py warm_tower_status`
(`line_inspection/management/commands/warm_tower_status.py`) rebuilds all three columns from
`Inspection` with its own inline `DISTINCT ON` query and a `bulk_update` — deliberately *not*
via `bump_tower_cache`, since a rebuild must overwrite unconditionally rather than only advance.
Note it duplicates the `order_by('tower_id','-saved_at','-id').distinct('tower_id')` incantation
instead of reusing `status.latest_inspections`; harmless but a second place to keep in sync.

#### 10.7.5 How per-cycle status is recomputed when a type filter is applied

The denormalized cache stores only the latest inspection **of any type** — there is no
per-cycle cache column. So the moment a user picks "Ground Patrolling" or "PMI" on the map, the
cache becomes unusable and the status must be recomputed from the `Inspection` table. The
branch lives in `MapTowerListView.get` (`api/views.py:345-367`):

```python
        if inspection_type:
            capped_ids = list(qs.values_list('id', flat=True)[:MAX_MAP_TOWERS + 1])
            truncated = len(capped_ids) > MAX_MAP_TOWERS
            capped_ids = capped_ids[:MAX_MAP_TOWERS]
            status_by_tower = tower_status.latest_inspection_status(capped_ids, inspection_type=inspection_type)
            rows = qs.filter(id__in=capped_ids).values(…)
            features = []
            for row in rows:
                st = status_by_tower.get(row['id'], 'none')
                if status_filter and st != status_filter:
                    continue
                features.append(self._feature(row, st))
            return Response({'type': 'FeatureCollection', 'truncated': truncated, 'features': features})
```

Sequence, and why each step is in that order:

1. **Cap first.** Take at most `MAX_MAP_TOWERS + 1` (= 5,001) tower ids from the already
   scope-and-bbox-narrowed queryset; the extra id is how `truncated` is detected without a
   `COUNT(*)`. Capping *before* the status query bounds the `tower_id IN (…)` list.
2. **One `DISTINCT ON` query** for the ≤5,000 towers, filtered to the requested cycle.
3. **Status filter moves to Python.** In the cache path, `?status=` is a SQL filter
   (`qs.filter(last_worst_criticality=status_filter)`, `api/views.py:361`). In the per-cycle
   path it *cannot* be, because the per-cycle status does not exist as a column — so it becomes
   an in-loop `continue`. Consequence worth knowing: with `inspection_type` set, `truncated` is
   computed **before** the status filter, so the cap applies to the pre-filter set and a
   heavily-filtered view can report `truncated: true` while returning few features.
4. Towers absent from `status_by_tower` render as `'none'` (grey) — correct: "never inspected
   *in this cycle*".

The cache path (no `inspection_type`) is the fast default: no `Inspection` touch at all, colour
straight from `Tower.last_worst_criticality`, and the cap applied by slicing the values query.

> **Consistency note across the two "inspected" definitions.** `dashboard_views._rollup:191`
> counts a tower as inspected when `last_inspection_at IS NOT NULL`, whereas
> `api/views.py:300` (the per-line rollup on `/map/lines/`) counts it when
> `last_worst_criticality != 'none'`. These agree for cache rows written by
> `bump_tower_cache`/`warm_tower_status` (both fields are set together), but they are two
> different predicates over the same cache and would diverge if either column were ever
> written alone.

### 10.8 `schedule.py` — the tower schedule (ordered position along a line)

```python
"""Order is derived by projecting each tower's lat/long onto the line's GeoJSON
LineString (distance measured *along* the line), which works for 100% of active
lines. ... Pure Python, no PostGIS: an equirectangular metres approximation about
the line's first vertex is plenty accurate for *ordering* towers along a
~kilometres-long corridor."""
```

**Why a schedule is needed at all.** ArcGIS gives towers a `tower_number`, but those numbers are
not reliably sortable: they can be `'12/1'`, `'A-3'`, `'Boom'`, `'Gantry'`, and after a LILO the
same number can appear twice on one line. Three features depend on a *correct* linear order:
the register's column order, the from/to-tower range picker on the Roles screen, and
`range_tower_ids`'s BETWEEN expansion. So the order is computed once from geometry and persisted
as `Tower.line_sequence`.

**Why no PostGIS.** The project needs *ordering*, not measurement. An equirectangular projection
about the line's first vertex is accurate to well under a metre over a few tens of kilometres at
Andhra Pradesh's latitudes — far more than enough to say which of two towers comes first —
and it removes a heavyweight database extension from the deployment.

| Constant | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `_M_PER_DEG_LAT` | `110_574.0` | metres per degree of latitude (near-constant) |
| `_M_PER_DEG_LON_EQ` | `111_320.0` | metres per degree of longitude **at the equator**; scaled by `cos(lat₀)` |

#### 10.8.1 `tower_sort_key(tower) -> tuple`

```python
def tower_sort_key(tower):
    m = re.match(r'\s*(\d+)', tower.tower_number or '')
    return (0, int(m.group(1)), tower.tower_number or '') if m else (1, 0, tower.tower_number or '')
```

Numeric-prefix-then-string sort. `'12'` → `(0, 12, '12')`; `'12/1'` → `(0, 12, '12/1')`;
`'Boom'` → `(1, 0, 'Boom')`. The leading `0`/`1` discriminator pushes every non-numeric row
(Boom, Gantry — structures that carry no tower number) to the tail rather than interleaving them
by ASCII. Mirrors the original register's sort so the fallback order looks familiar to field
staff. Used only inside `compute_line_order`.

#### 10.8.2 `line_vertices(geometry) -> list[tuple[float,float]]`

Extracts `(lon, lat)` pairs from a GeoJSON `LineString` (`coordinates` = list of positions) or
`MultiLineString` (concatenating every part's positions in order). Returns `[]` for `None`, an
unknown `type`, or empty coordinates, and skips malformed positions
(`isinstance(c, (list, tuple)) and len(c) >= 2`). Note GeoJSON is **lon-first** — the tuples are
`(lon, lat)`, matching how `project_onto_line` is called. Tested at
`tests/test_dashboard.py:193-198`.

#### 10.8.3 `project_onto_line(vertices, lon, lat) -> (along_m, offset_m)`

```python
def project_onto_line(vertices, lon, lat):
    if len(vertices) < 2 or lon is None or lat is None:
        return None, None
    cos_lat0 = math.cos(math.radians(vertices[0][1]))
    pts = [_to_xy(lo, la, cos_lat0) for lo, la in vertices]
    px, py = _to_xy(lon, lat, cos_lat0)

    best_off2, best_along, cum = None, 0.0, 0.0
    for (x1, y1), (x2, y2) in zip(pts, pts[1:]):
        dx, dy = x2 - x1, y2 - y1
        seg2 = dx * dx + dy * dy
        seg_len = math.sqrt(seg2)
        if seg2 == 0.0:
            t, cx, cy = 0.0, x1, y1
        else:
            t = max(0.0, min(1.0, ((px - x1) * dx + (py - y1) * dy) / seg2))
            cx, cy = x1 + t * dx, y1 + t * dy
        off2 = (px - cx) ** 2 + (py - cy) ** 2
        if best_off2 is None or off2 < best_off2:
            best_off2, best_along = off2, cum + t * seg_len
        cum += seg_len
    return best_along, math.sqrt(best_off2)
```

**In plain terms.** Imagine the line drawn on graph paper and the tower as a dot somewhere near
it. Walk along the line from its start, segment by segment. For each straight segment, drop a
perpendicular from the dot onto that segment and note two numbers: how far *off* the segment the
dot is, and how far *along* the whole line you had walked when you reached the foot of that
perpendicular. Keep whichever segment gives the smallest off-distance. The along-distance for
that winning segment is the tower's position in the schedule; the off-distance is a data-quality
signal.

**Returns:** `(along_m, offset_m)` in metres, or `(None, None)` if the line has fewer than 2
vertices or the tower has no coordinates.

Mechanics, term by term:

| Piece | What it does |
|---|---|
| `cos_lat0 = cos(radians(vertices[0][1]))` | The longitude-compression factor at the line's **first vertex**. One shared `lat₀` for the whole line (rather than per-point) keeps the projection a rigid, order-preserving transform. |
| `_to_xy(lon, lat, cos_lat0)` | `(lon · 111320 · cos lat₀, lat · 110574)` — degrees to a local flat metre grid. |
| `t = clamp(((P−A)·(B−A)) / \|B−A\|², 0, 1)` | The classic point-to-segment parameter. The dot product projects P onto the infinite line through AB; dividing by \|B−A\|² normalises it to 0…1 along the segment; the clamp makes the foot fall on the **endpoint** when the perpendicular would land outside — that is what makes it a *segment* projection, and it is what correctly handles towers beyond the ends of the corridor. |
| `seg2 == 0.0` branch | Duplicate consecutive vertices (a zero-length segment) would divide by zero; the segment degenerates to its start point. |
| `off2` compared squared | Avoids a `sqrt` per segment; only the winner is square-rooted at the end. |
| `cum` | Running total of segment lengths — the along-distance to the *start* of the current segment; the winner's along-distance is `cum + t · seg_len`. |

Tested at `tests/test_dashboard.py:200-207`: along-distance strictly increases eastward on a
west→east line, a tower exactly on the line gets ~0 offset, and a 1-vertex line returns
`(None, None)`.

#### 10.8.4 `compute_line_order(line) -> (mode, ordered)`

Computes without writing. `mode ∈ {'geometry', 'fallback', 'empty'}`;
`ordered = [(Tower, offset_m_or_None), …]` in schedule order.

```python
    towers = list(Tower.objects.filter(line=line, is_active=True)
                  .only('id', 'tower_number', 'latitude', 'longitude'))
    if not towers:
        return 'empty', []
    verts = line_vertices(line.geometry)
    dup = any(c > 1 for c in Counter(t.tower_number for t in towers if t.tower_number).values())
    use_geometry = len(verts) >= 2 and not dup
```

Decision table:

| Condition | Mode | Order produced |
|---|---|---|
| No active towers | `'empty'` | `[]` — caller skips the line |
| ≥2 vertices **and** no duplicate `tower_number` **and** ≥1 tower projects | `'geometry'` | Projected towers sorted by `along_m`, then non-geocoded towers appended sorted by `tower_sort_key` with `offset=None` |
| Otherwise | `'fallback'` | All towers sorted by `tower_sort_key`, all offsets `None` |

**The duplicate-`tower_number` branch detection.** `Counter` over the towers' numbers; any count
> 1 means the corridor is **branched** — a Tap or a LILO has produced two physical towers
legitimately carrying the same number on what the database records as one line. On a branched
corridor a single along-line order is *ambiguous* (two towers can project to nearly the same
along-distance on different arms), so geometry is abandoned wholesale in favour of the numeric
sort. Note this check happens **before** projection: the presence of duplicates disqualifies the
line even if the geometry is perfect.

Note the towers query has **no `is_virtual` filter** — VT rows get a `line_sequence` too. That
is required: `register.build_register` orders its columns (real *and* VT) by `line_sequence`,
so a VT row without one would be pushed to the end of the register instead of sitting next to
its co-located real tower.

Towers with NULL coordinates cannot project (`along is None`) and are collected in `missing`;
they are appended **after** all projected towers, ordered among themselves by `tower_sort_key`.
If *no* tower projects, `use_geometry` flips to `False` and the whole line falls back.

#### 10.8.5 `assign_line_sequence(line) -> str`

Computes **and persists** for one line: sets `line_sequence = 1, 2, 3, …` in schedule order and
`line_offset_m = round(offset, 2)` (or `None`), then one `Tower.objects.bulk_update(…,
batch_size=1000)`. Returns the mode string. `line_offset_m` is a QA/branch-detection signal
only — a tower 800 m off its own line's polyline is almost certainly mis-attributed.

**Callers:** `services/lilo_matching.py:199` — after a LILO reconcile, every new line's schedule
is rebuilt, because towers have just been re-parented. The `build_tower_schedule` management
command does **not** call it; it calls `compute_line_order` directly so it can batch the
`bulk_update` across lines (`management/commands/build_tower_schedule.py:29-54`, `BATCH = 1000`,
reporting `N lines ordered by geometry, M by tower_number fallback`).

#### 10.8.6 `line_schedule(line, include_virtual=True) -> list[Tower]`

```python
def line_schedule(line, include_virtual=True):
    qs = Tower.objects.filter(line=line, is_active=True)
    if not include_virtual:
        qs = qs.filter(is_virtual=False)
    return list(qs.order_by(F('line_sequence').asc(nulls_last=True), 'tower_number', 'id'))
```

The read-back. Returns a materialised `list[Tower]`. The three-key ordering is the important
part: `line_sequence` ascending with **`nulls_last=True`** (a line whose schedule was never
built, or a tower added since the last build, sinks to the bottom rather than sorting first as
Postgres would otherwise do for ASC NULLs), then `tower_number` as a stable secondary, then `id`
as a total tie-break so the order is deterministic across requests. Backed by
`models.Index(fields=['line', 'line_sequence'])` (`line_inspection/models.py:203`).

**Callers:**
- `register.build_register` (`register.py:90`) with `include_virtual=True` — the register shows
  every circuit's column.
- `admin_views.line_schedule_json` (`admin_views.py:217`) with `include_virtual=False` — the
  `GET /inspection/admin/line/<id>/schedule/` endpoint backing the from/to range picker, which
  must offer only inspectable (real) towers. Returns
  `{'line': name, 'towers': [{'id','tower_number','cp_sp','line_sequence'}, …]}`.

### 10.9 `register.py` — the line inspection register

```python
"""Line inspection register — the formal patrolling record, a per-line matrix
that mirrors the physical field register (see the "Register" tab in the POCs
poc_v2.html / gisdata/clearpoc.html).

Layout: columns = the towers on one line (each showing its LATEST inspection for
the chosen cycle), rows = metadata (Date / Loc No / Tower type) + checklist items
grouped by component category + a Remarks row."""
```

This is a **digital replica of the paper register** APTRANSCO line staff already keep: one sheet
per line, towers across the top, checklist items down the side. Matching the physical artefact
was a deliberate adoption decision — the output is printable and exportable so it can replace
the paper sheet rather than sit alongside it.

#### 10.9.1 `CYCLE_LABELS`

```python
CYCLE_LABELS = {
    '': 'Latest (any cycle)',
    'ground_patrol': 'Ground Patrolling',
    'pmi': 'Pre-Monsoon Inspection (PMI)',
}
```

An ordered dict driving the cycle `<select>` (`dashboard_register.html:52` iterates
`cycle_labels.items`). Note the key is the **empty string**, not `None` — it is a URL query
value. `build_register` converts it with `inspection_type = cycle or None`. Also reused by the
Inspections screen (`dashboard_views.py:105,117`). `dashboard_views.register_view:143-145`
whitelists the incoming `?cycle=` against exactly `('', 'ground_patrol', 'pmi')` and silently
coerces anything else to `''`.

#### 10.9.2 `build_register(line, cycle='') -> dict`

**Exact returned shape** (pseudo-JSON; `line` is a live `Line` model instance, `date` a
`datetime.date` or `None`):

```jsonc
{
  "line":  <Line instance>,
  "cycle": "" | "ground_patrol" | "pmi",
  "tower_headers": [                       // one per COLUMN, in schedule order
    { "id": 4711,                          // this tower's pk (VT or real)
      "source_id": 4710,                   // pk of the tower the data came from
      "tower_number": "VT 5",              // falls back to str(id) if blank
      "tower_type": "Boom",
      "is_virtual": true,
      "inspected": true,                   // an inspection existed for source_id
      "date": "2026-06-01",                // Inspection.date, or null
      "worst": "major" }                   // Inspection.worst_criticality, or "none"
  ],
  "rows": [                                // in render order, top to bottom
    { "group": null, "sno": 1, "label": "Date of inspection",
      "cells": [ {"kind":"meta","text":"01-06-2026","crit":""}, … ] },
    { "group": null, "sno": 2, "label": "Loc No",        "cells": [ … ] },
    { "group": null, "sno": 3, "label": "Type of tower", "cells": [ … ] },

    { "group_header": "Tower parts" },     // group separator — NO other keys

    { "group": "tower_parts", "sno": 5, "label": "Members bent",
      "cells": [ {"kind":"defect","text":"Top: Bent member (How many: 3 nos)",
                  "crit":"major"}, … ] },
    // … one row per ChecklistItem, groups in sort_order …

    { "group": null, "sno": null, "label": "Remarks",    "cells": [ … ] }
  ]
}
```

Every `cells` array has **exactly** `len(tower_headers)` entries, in the same order — the
template indexes them positionally (`dashboard_register.html:90`, and the mobile one-tower view
at `:130` does `tds[2 + col]`). A consumer must distinguish the two row shapes: a row with
`group_header` is a separator and has no `cells`.

**Step by step:**

1. `inspection_type = cycle or None`; `towers = sched.line_schedule(line, include_virtual=True)`
   — **all** towers on the line, real *and* VT, in schedule order.
2. **VT source resolution** (the rule below), in one extra query.
3. `latest = tower_status.latest_inspections([source ids], inspection_type=…)` — one
   `DISTINCT ON` + prefetch.
4. `fu_map = {q.key: q for q in FollowUpQuestion.objects.all()}` — the whole follow-up catalog
   (22 rows per the README) loaded once, used to turn stored answer keys into readable text.
5. Three meta rows (sno 1/2/3), then, for each `ChecklistItemGroup` ordered by `sort_order`
   (prefetching `items`): a `group_header` row, then one row per item sorted by
   `(sort_order, sno)`. Empty groups are skipped entirely.
6. A trailing Remarks row.

Note the register renders **every** checklist item for **every** tower — it does not consult
`ChecklistItem.applicable_tower_types`. Inapplicability shows up as an `N/A` cell only if the
inspector actually recorded `status='na'`.

> **Small fidelity gap.** The physical register numbers Remarks as row 29 (the README describes
> items at `sno` 4–28 with "Remarks at 29", `README.md:217`). `build_register` appends Remarks
> with `sno=None` (`register.py:144`), so the printed/exported sheet shows a blank S.No there.
> The three meta rows *are* numbered 1–3 to match the paper form.

#### 10.9.3 The VT column rule

```python
    vt_keys = {t.structure_key for t in towers if t.is_virtual and t.structure_key}
    real_id_by_key = {}
    if vt_keys:
        for rt in (Tower.objects.filter(structure_key__in=vt_keys, is_virtual=False, is_active=True)
                   .only('id', 'structure_key')):
            real_id_by_key.setdefault(rt.structure_key, rt.id)

    def source_id(t):
        return t.id if not t.is_virtual else real_id_by_key.get(t.structure_key)
```

**The rule:** a VT tower's column is populated from the inspection of the **co-located real
tower** sharing its `structure_key`.

**Why.** A physical structure carrying a double circuit appears once as a real tower on Ckt-1
and once as a VT row on Ckt-2. The inspector climbs the structure **once** and files **one**
inspection, against the real tower. If the Ckt-2 register read that VT row literally it would
show an entire line as never inspected, and the whole circuit would look like outstanding work.
Sourcing the cells from the real tower makes an inspected *structure* read as inspected on
**every circuit that runs through it** — which is what is physically true and what the field
register has always recorded. Verified end-to-end at `tests/test_dashboard.py:210-234`: a
register built for the VT-carrying circuit shows one column `'VT 5'`, `is_virtual=True`,
`inspected=True`, `worst='major'`, all borrowed from the real tower on the other circuit.

Implementation notes: all VT structure keys are resolved in **one** query (no per-column
lookup); `setdefault` keeps the first real tower found if a key were ever to have several;
`source_id(t)` returns `None` for a VT row with no key or no real twin, and `latest.get(None)`
then yields `None`, so the column simply renders blank. The `if (sid := source_id(t)) is not
None` walrus filter at `register.py:105` keeps `None` out of the `tower_id IN (…)` list.
`is_virtual` is passed through to the header so the UI can badge the column — the template
renders a grey `VT` chip (`dashboard_register.html:76`).

#### 10.9.4 How a cell is computed — `_item_cell(item, inspection, fu_map)`

Returns `{'kind': …, 'text': …, 'crit': …}`. Five kinds, resolved in this exact order:

| # | Condition | `kind` | `text` | `crit` | Rendered as |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `inspection is None` (no inspection for this tower/cycle) | `blank` | `''` | `''` | empty cell |
| 2 | Inspection exists but has **no `ItemResult` for this item** | `blank` | `''` | `''` | empty cell |
| 3 | Any result for this item has `status == 'defect'` | `defect` | joined defect text | `worst_of(crits)` or `'minor'` | criticality chip + text, pink background |
| 4 | The set of statuses is exactly `{'na'}` | `na` | `'N/A'` | `''` | grey, centred |
| 5 | Statuses ⊆ `{'not_provided', 'na'}` (and not all `na`) | `np` | `'Not available'` | `''` | grey, centred |
| 6 | Otherwise (at least one `'normal'`) | `ok` | `'✓'` | `''` | green tick |

Kinds 1 and 2 are both `blank` but mean different things — "the tower was never inspected in
this cycle" vs "it was inspected but this item was left unanswered". The register does not
distinguish them visually; the tower header's `inspected` flag is what tells them apart.

**Positional handling.** `ChecklistItem.positions` is a JSON list such as
`["Top","Middle","Bottom"]` (empty = not positional). When positional, results are sorted by
their index in that list — `order.get(r.position, 99)` sends any unknown position to the end —
so a cell always reads Top-then-Middle-then-Bottom regardless of insertion order. Each defective
position contributes its own segment prefixed `"<position>: "`, and segments are joined with
`' | '`:

```python
    if defect_segs:
        return {'kind': 'defect', 'text': ' | '.join(defect_segs), 'crit': worst_of(crits) if crits else 'minor'}
```

Example text for a positional item with two bad positions:
`"Top: Bent member (How many: 3 nos) | Bottom: Corroded"`.

**Defect text** per position is every `DefectEntry`'s `defect.label`, each optionally followed by
its follow-up answers in parentheses. `_answers_text(answers, fu_map)` renders
`"<question_text>: <value><space><unit>"` joined by `'; '`, looking each key up in `fu_map` and
falling back to the raw key if the question was deleted from the catalog; list answers
(multichoice) are joined with `', '`. If an `ItemResult` is marked `'defect'` but carries no
entries, the text degrades to the literal `'Defect'` and the criticality to `'minor'`.

**Criticality roll-up** uses `services/criticality.worst_of` with
`CRITICALITY_ORDER = {'none':0,'ok':1,'minor':2,'major':3,'critical':4}` — the highest wins.
Note `worst_of` seeds at `'ok'`, so it can never return `'none'` for a non-empty list.

#### 10.9.5 `register_to_xlsx(structure) -> bytes`

Serialises a `build_register()` result to `.xlsx` bytes with **openpyxl** (already a project
dependency — `requirements.txt:10`, `openpyxl>=3.1`). The import is function-local, so openpyxl
is only loaded when someone actually downloads.

Sheet layout (`ws.title = 'Register'`):

| Row | Content |
|---|---|
| 1 | `Line inspection register — <line.name or line.id>` (bold, size 13) |
| 2 | `Voltage: <voltage>    Cycle: <CYCLE_LABELS[cycle] or 'Latest'>` |
| 3 | blank |
| 4 | Header: `S.No`, `Item`, then `T-<tower_number>` per column (whole row bold) |
| 5+ | One row per `rows` entry. A `group_header` row emits its label in column A only, bold+italic. Otherwise `[sno or '', label, *cell texts]`. |

Defect cells are prefixed with the criticality in brackets — `f"[{c['crit'].upper()}] {text}"` —
because Excel has no chip element; that makes the export greppable and sortable. Finishing
touches: column A width 6, column B width 34, `freeze_panes = 'C5'` (keeps the S.No/Item columns
and the four header rows visible while scrolling a 100-tower line), and
`Alignment(vertical='top', wrap_text=True)` on every cell. Returns `buf.getvalue()` from a
`BytesIO` — never touches disk.

**Caller:** `dashboard_views.register_view:157-165`, which streams it as
`application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet` with a filename sanitised by
`re.sub(r'[^A-Za-z0-9]+', '_', line.name)` and suffixed with the cycle. Smoke-tested at
`tests/test_dashboard.py:176-179`.

> **Dead code.** `register._tower_sort_key` (`register.py:29-33`) is defined but never called —
> `build_register` orders columns via `sched.line_schedule`. It is a byte-for-byte duplicate of
> `schedule.tower_sort_key` (`schedule.py:26-30`), left behind when column ordering moved from
> a numeric sort to the geometry-derived schedule. Safe to delete.

### 10.10 `forms.py` — admin-panel ModelForms

Nine form classes, all plain Django `forms.ModelForm` except the last. There is **no
django-admin** in this project (`line_inspection/admin.py` is deliberately empty), so these back
hand-written views and hand-written templates. Eight of the nine render through the single
generic `templates/line_inspection/simple_form.html`.

| Form | Model | Fields | Rendered by (view → URL name) | Template |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `FieldEECadrePositionForm` | `FieldEECadrePosition` | `position_id`, `position_text`, `notes` | `admin_views.manage_admins:72,101` → `manage-admins` (`@super_admin_required`) | `manage_admins.html` |
| `RoleAssignmentForm` | `RoleAssignment` | `employee_id`, `subdivision`, `lines` | `admin_views.role_assignments:146` (POST) and `role_assignment_new:225` (GET) → `role-assignments` / `role-assignment-new` (`@admin_required`) | `role_assignment_form.html` |
| `ChecklistItemGroupForm` | `ChecklistItemGroup` | `key`, `label`, `sort_order` | `admin_views.checklist_item_group_form` → `checklist-group-new/-edit` | `simple_form.html` |
| `ChecklistItemForm` | `ChecklistItem` | `group`, `key`, `sno`, `label`, `sort_order`, `positions`, `is_availability_gated`, `is_position_availability_gated`, `applicable_tower_types`, `na_reason` | `admin_views.checklist_item_form` → `checklist-item-new/-edit` | `simple_form.html` |
| `DefectForm` | `Defect` | `item`, `key`, `label`, `sort_order`, `ask`, `default_criticality` | `admin_views.defect_form` → `checklist-defect-new/-edit` | `simple_form.html` |
| `FollowUpQuestionForm` | `FollowUpQuestion` | `key`, `question_text`, `answer_type`, `options`, `unit`, `placeholder` | `admin_views.followup_question_form` → `checklist-followup-new/-edit` | `simple_form.html` |
| `CriticalityRuleForm` | `CriticalityRule` | `defect`, `follow_up_key`, `operator`, `threshold_value`, `resulting_criticality`, `priority` | `admin_views.criticality_rule_form` → `checklist-rule-new/-edit` | `simple_form.html` |
| `SapLineForm` | `SapLine` | `functional_location`, `description`, `voltage` | `admin_views.sap_mapping:383,406` → `sap-mapping` (`@admin_required`) | `sap_mapping.html` |
| `LineMappingForm` | *(plain `forms.Form`)* | `sap_line` (`ModelChoiceField`, `required=False`) | **nobody** | — |

All five checklist-catalog forms share the same view shape: `get_object_or_404` on edit,
`form.save()`, then **`CatalogVersion.bump()`** and a redirect to `checklist-editor`. The bump is
the important side effect — the singleton version counter is stamped onto every
`Inspection.catalog_version`, so historical inspections stay traceable to the catalog shape that
produced them (`line_inspection/models.py:248-265`). `checklist_delete` bumps too.

> **Finding — `LineMappingForm` is dead code.** Defined at `line_inspection/forms.py:111-112`
> and imported nowhere. The SAP↔ArcGIS mapping screen sets `Line.sap_line` from raw
> `request.POST` values instead (`admin_views.sap_mapping:371-381`). Safe to delete.

#### 10.10.1 Custom widgets, validation and dynamic construction

**`FieldEECadrePositionForm` — read-only `position_text`.**

```python
            'position_text': forms.TextInput(attrs={
                'readonly': 'readonly',
                'placeholder': 'Auto-filled from SAP once you enter a position id',
            }),
```

The comment gives the reason: *"posid/postext are interlinked in SAP — auto-filled by
manage_admins.html's JS via the lookup-position endpoint instead of an Admin typing it by hand."*
The JS at `templates/line_inspection/manage_admins.html:76-95` calls
`GET /inspection/admin/super/positions/lookup/<position_id>/` →
`admin_views.lookup_position` → `sap_client.get_employee_by_position_id`, and fills the field
plus the current holder's name. Making it read-only prevents an Admin from pairing a valid
position id with the wrong description. Note `readonly` is a *client-side* attribute only — a
crafted POST can still set `position_text`; the field is descriptive, not authorizing (the
grant is keyed on `position_id`), so this is cosmetic rather than a security hole.

**`RoleAssignmentForm` — hidden employee, queryset narrowing.**

```python
        widgets = {
            'employee_id': forms.HiddenInput(),
            'lines': forms.SelectMultiple(attrs={'size': 10}),
        }

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.fields['subdivision'].queryset = Subdivision.objects.order_by('name')
        self.fields['lines'].queryset = Line.objects.filter(is_active=True).order_by('name')
```

`employee_id` is hidden because the employee is chosen on the *previous* screen and arrives via
the URL (`role-assignment-new/<employee_id>/`, seeded as `initial=`). The two queryset
overrides in `__init__` are load-bearing and commented as such: both fields are re-rendered by
JS as searchable comboboxes in `role_assignment_form.html`, and *"these querysets are what that
JS treats as the full candidate set, so they must exclude soft-deleted lines and stay
name-sorted for the search UI."* The `lines` queryset is also the **server-side validation set**
— since it is `is_active=True` only, a POST naming a soft-deleted line is rejected by the form,
not silently accepted. `admin_views.role_assignment_new:228-232` serialises the *same*
active-lines query to `lines_json` for the client-side filter, keeping the two in agreement.

Note what the form does **not** set: `role` and `assigned_by_employee_id` are stamped by the
view on `commit=False` (`admin_views.py:149-152`) — `role='FIELD_INSPECTOR'` (the only value in
`ROLE_CHOICES`) and the assigning Admin's session id — so a client cannot forge either. The
M2M requires the explicit `form.save_m2m()` after the deferred save.

**`ChecklistItemForm` — dynamic tower-type choices + comma-string ↔ JSON list.**

```python
    applicable_tower_types = forms.MultipleChoiceField(required=False, widget=forms.CheckboxSelectMultiple)

    def __init__(self, *args, tower_type_choices=(), **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.fields['applicable_tower_types'].choices = [(t, t) for t in tower_type_choices]

    def clean_positions(self):
        raw = self.data.get('positions', '')
        if isinstance(raw, list):
            return raw
        return [p.strip() for p in raw.split(',') if p.strip()]
```

`applicable_tower_types` is a `JSONField` on the model, which would otherwise render as a raw
JSON textarea. It is replaced by a checkbox group whose **choices are built at construction
time** from a keyword-only `tower_type_choices` argument. The view supplies
`_tower_type_choices()` = `sorted({t for t in Tower.objects.values_list('tower_type',
flat=True).distinct() if t})` (`admin_views.py:255-256`) — i.e. the tower types that **actually
exist in the synced ArcGIS data**. The rationale is recorded in `README.md:221-228`: the catalog
was seeded with the POC's placeholder codes `DA/DB/DC/DD`, but real ArcGIS values look like
`"Boom"`; presenting the observed values lets an Admin correct the mismatch through the UI
rather than through a migration. The README also states plainly that this **has not been
corrected yet** — a known open gap.

`clean_positions` converts the free-text `"Top,Middle,Bottom"` input into the JSON list the model
stores, tolerating an already-list value. It reads `self.data` (raw POST) rather than
`self.cleaned_data`, sidestepping the `JSONField`'s own JSON parsing which would reject the
comma string. The round trip back to the text box is done by the view:
`initial = {'positions': ','.join(instance.positions)}` (`admin_views.py:277`), and after
validation the view re-assigns both JSON fields explicitly onto the `commit=False` instance
(`admin_views.py:281-284`).

**`DefectForm.clean_ask` and `FollowUpQuestionForm.clean_options`** use the identical
comma-string ↔ JSON-list pattern, each with a declared `forms.CharField(required=False)`
shadowing the model's `JSONField`:

```python
    ask = forms.CharField(required=False, help_text='Comma-separated FollowUpQuestion keys, in order')
    def clean_ask(self):
        return [k.strip() for k in self.cleaned_data['ask'].split(',') if k.strip()]
```

`Defect.ask` is an **ordered** list of `FollowUpQuestion.key`s driving which follow-ups the
mobile app asks after that defect is selected — hence "in order" in the help text. Neither
`clean_ask` nor `clean_options` validates that the keys exist; a typo produces a defect whose
follow-up silently never renders (and `register._answers_text` falls back to showing the raw
key). A `FollowUpQuestion.objects.filter(key__in=…)` existence check would be a cheap
improvement.

**`CriticalityRuleForm`** adds no cleaning — just a `help_text` on the raw `JSONField`:
*"A plain number or string, e.g. 2 or \"Main leg / corner member\" (JSON — quote text values)."*
The Admin types JSON directly, because the value's type must match the follow-up's answer type
for `services/criticality._coerce_for_compare` to compare correctly.

### 10.11 `context_processors.py` — template identity injection

```python
def identity(request):
    employee_id = request.session.get('employee_id')
    if not employee_id:
        return {}
    return {
        'session_employee_id': employee_id,
        'session_display_name': request.session.get('display_name', employee_id),
        'is_admin': is_admin(employee_id),
        'is_super_admin': is_super_admin(employee_id),
        'is_management': viewing.is_management(employee_id),
        'cadre_label': viewing.display_label(employee_id),
    }
```

Registered at `transcoapps/settings.py:120` as `'line_inspection.context_processors.identity'`,
so it runs for **every** `render()` in the project.

| Key | Type | Source | Templates that read it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `session_employee_id` | `str` | `request.session['employee_id']` (set by `auth.login_view` after checkCred) | `base.html:51,56` — gates the whole topbar/nav block |
| `session_display_name` | `str` | `request.session['display_name']`, defaulting to the employee id | `base.html:52` — `"Name (12345)"` |
| `is_admin` | `bool` | `auth.is_admin` — a granted `FieldEECadrePosition` **or** `SuperAdmin` | `base.html:63,64`, `admin_home.html:20,23` — Reports link, Roles/Checklist/SAP links |
| `is_super_admin` | `bool` | `auth.is_super_admin` — a `SuperAdmin` row | `base.html:69,70`, `admin_home.html:6,23` — Manage Admins link, LILO link, churn banner |
| `is_management` | `bool` | `viewing.is_management` | `base.html:63`, `admin_home.html:20` — the Reports tab, OR'd with `is_admin` |
| `cadre_label` | `str` | `viewing.display_label` | (available everywhere; `dashboard_map.html:22` uses the view-supplied copy) |

**Behaviour when logged out.** Returns `{}` — none of the keys exist. Django templates resolve a
missing variable to the empty string (falsy), so every `{% if %}` above simply fails and the
pre-login pages (`login.html`, `forgot_password.html`, `change_password.html`, which do not even
extend `base.html`) render clean.

**Cost.** Four queries per rendered page: `is_super_admin` (one `SuperAdmin` existence check),
`is_admin` (that check again — `is_admin` calls `is_super_admin` first — plus an
`EmployeeCadreSnapshot` lookup and a `FieldEECadrePosition` existence check),
`is_management` (another `SuperAdmin` check plus a snapshot lookup), and `display_label`
(a third snapshot lookup). All are single-row indexed lookups on tiny tables. The inline comment
justifies including `is_management` here — *"Cheap (one indexed snapshot lookup); the heavier
tier/subtree walk stays in the views"* — which is the right line to draw: `cadre_tier` and
`oversight_*` (which trigger the ~1,830-row subtree walk) are deliberately **not** in the
context processor.

> **Redundancy note.** `dashboard_views.tickets_view:82` also puts `'is_admin':
> auth.is_admin(employee_id)` into its own context. The view dict wins over the context
> processor, so the value is identical and the only cost is one duplicate query. Likewise
> `dashboard_views.map_view:48` re-computes `cadre_label`.

### 10.12 Consolidated findings for this section

| # | Finding | Location | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Ranges grant towers but never grant lines.** `visible_lines` / `oversight_lines` read `RoleAssignment` only, so a range-holder's line is absent from the Register dropdown (403 on direct access) and from `GET /map/lines/`, while its towers appear on the map. | `jurisdiction.py:47`, `viewing.py:70` | Design gap |
| 2 | **`cadre_tier` reports `'none'` for a range-only user.** It inspects `RoleAssignment` only, ignoring `LineTowerAssignment`. Cosmetic (nothing is denied), untested. | `viewing.py:117-136` | Low |
| 3 | **Two full subtree walks per `oversight_towers()` call**, four per `/dashboard/map/` render; no per-request memoisation of `subordinate_snapshots`. | `viewing.py:79-93` | Performance |
| 4 | **Deferred-field N+1** — `subordinate_snapshots`'s `.only()` omits `emp_sub_grp_desc`, which `role_assignments.html:20` renders. | `viewing.py:43-45` | Low |
| 5 | **`register._tower_sort_key` is dead code** and a byte-for-byte duplicate of `schedule.tower_sort_key`. | `register.py:29-33` | Cleanup |
| 6 | **`forms.LineMappingForm` is dead code** — defined, imported nowhere. | `forms.py:111-112` | Cleanup |
| 7 | **`status_colors` is passed to the Register template but never read**; the register hard-codes the same three defect colours in CSS, so the palette can drift. | `dashboard_views.py:176`, `dashboard_register.html:22` | Cleanup |
| 8 | **Two different "inspected" predicates** over the same cache: `last_inspection_at IS NOT NULL` (dashboard rollup) vs `last_worst_criticality != 'none'` (`/map/lines/`). | `dashboard_views.py:191`, `api/views.py:300` | Low |
| 9 | **README says `GET /lines/` and `GET /towers/?line=` are "Jurisdiction-filtered via `jurisdiction.py`"; the code uses `viewing.oversight_*`.** The code is newer and self-documents the change; the README table was not updated. | `README.md:335` vs `api/views.py:226,242` | **README wrong** |
| 10 | **`warm_tower_status` re-implements the `DISTINCT ON` query inline** instead of reusing `status.py`, so the latest-per-tower incantation exists in three places. | `management/commands/warm_tower_status.py:21-26` | Cleanup |
| 11 | **Remarks row carries `sno=None`**, so the exported/printed register shows a blank S.No where the paper form has 29. | `register.py:144` vs `README.md:217` | Cosmetic |
| 12 | **`clean_ask` / `clean_options` do not validate that referenced keys exist**, so a typo in a `Defect.ask` key silently disables the follow-up question. | `forms.py:81-82,92-93` | Low |
## 11. REST API Reference

### 11.1 Mount point and base URL

The API is a plain Django-REST-Framework (DRF) URLconf with no router, no
ViewSets and no versioning prefix. It is reached through a three-level include
chain:

| Level | File | Prefix contributed |
|---|---|---|
| Project URLconf | `transcoapps/urls.py:27` — `path('inspection/', include('line_inspection.urls'))` | `/inspection/` |
| App URLconf | `line_inspection/urls.py:51` — `path('api/', include('line_inspection.api.urls'))` | `api/` |
| API URLconf | `line_inspection/api/urls.py` | the 25 routes below |

**Every endpoint therefore lives under `/inspection/api/`** — e.g.
`GET https://<host>/inspection/api/catalog/`.

Every route in `api/urls.py` ends in a trailing slash and Django's
`APPEND_SLASH` behaviour only redirects safe methods, so a client that posts to
`/inspection/api/line-inspections` (no slash) gets a redirect it will not follow
correctly. **Clients must always send the trailing slash.**

#### The mobile base-URL rule ("must end in `/api`")

The Flutter field app is configured with a single `API_BASE_URL` string
(`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/services/api_service.dart:28`,
overridable at runtime through the in-app *Backend URL* dialog). Every call is
built as `'$_base/<route>/'`. Two hard constraints follow:

1. **The base must include the whole mount path**, i.e.
   `https://<host>/inspection/api` — not `https://<host>/api`. The app's own
   comment (`api_service.dart:24-26`) says exactly this.
2. **The base must end in `/api`**, because photo URLs are derived from it by
   *stripping* that suffix:

   ```dart
   // lib/services/line_inspection_api.dart:91
   static String mediaUrl(String path) {
     final host = _base.replaceAll(RegExp(r'/api/?$'), '');
     return '$host/media/$path';
   }
   ```

   With base `https://h/inspection/api`, `mediaUrl('x.jpg')` yields
   `https://h/inspection/media/x.jpg`. Note that this does **not** match where
   Django actually serves media (`/media/…` at the project root —
   `transcoapps/urls.py:37`). That mismatch is harmless in practice only because
   the API already returns **absolute** photo URLs (see §11.30), so `mediaUrl()`
   is a fallback path the app rarely exercises. It becomes a real bug on any
   endpoint that emits a *relative* photo URL — see the finding in §11.31.

The app's compiled-in default base points at a different ngrok host
(`mispacked-beamy-noelle.ngrok-free.dev`) than the one enumerated in
`transcoapps/settings.py:53` (`mammal-calamari-create.ngrok-free.dev`); both are
accepted because `ALLOWED_HOSTS` also contains the wildcards `.ngrok-free.dev`
and `.ngrok-free.app`. For LAN testing, the developer's Wi-Fi IP is added via
the `EXTRA_ALLOWED_HOSTS` environment variable (`settings.py:65`, comma-separated,
normally set in `.env.local`).

#### Global DRF configuration (there is none)

`transcoapps/settings.py` contains **no `REST_FRAMEWORK` dict**. Everything is
DRF stock defaults, which matters in four concrete ways:

| Default in force | Consequence |
|---|---|
| `DEFAULT_PARSER_CLASSES = [JSONParser, FormParser, MultiPartParser]` | `POST /line-inspections/` gets multipart parsing for free; every write endpoint also accepts `application/json` and `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. |
| `DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES = [JSONRenderer, BrowsableAPIRenderer]` | A browser hitting any endpoint with `Accept: text/html` gets DRF's HTML *browsable API* page. Combined with `DEBUG = True` this is a debugging aid but also an information-disclosure surface in any non-local deployment. |
| `DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS = None`, `PAGE_SIZE = None` | **No endpoint is paginated.** List endpoints return a bare JSON array (never `{count, next, previous, results}`). Size is bounded only by the hand-written slices documented per endpoint (`MAX_LIST = 500`, `MAX_MAP_TOWERS = 5000`, `[:1000]` on tickets) — and `GET /towers/` and `GET /lines/<id>/towers/` have **no cap at all**. |
| `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES = [AllowAny]` | Irrelevant here: every view sets `permission_classes` explicitly. |

DRF's `APIView.as_view()` wraps the view in `csrf_exempt`
(`rest_framework/views.py:150`), so `django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware`
never applies to these routes. See the CSRF finding in §11.31.

### 11.2 Authentication

There is **no `django.contrib.auth.User` anywhere in this application**. Identity
is a bare SAP employee ID string (zero-padded to 8 digits, e.g. `01073093`).
All three DRF authentication classes in `line_inspection/api/authentication.py`
resolve to the same tiny stand-in object:

```python
# line_inspection/api/authentication.py:15
class SimpleIdentity:
    is_authenticated = True
    def __init__(self, employee_id):
        self.employee_id = employee_id
        self.pk = employee_id
```

Views therefore always read `request.user.employee_id`, never
`request.user.id`/`.username`. `IsAuthenticated` works because
`is_authenticated` is hard-coded `True` — the class is only ever instantiated
after a credential has already been verified.

| Class | `Authorization` scheme | Credential source | `request.auth` set to |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MobileTokenAuthentication` | `Token <key>` (case-insensitive prefix match) | `MobileAuthToken` row in the `clear` schema, issued by `POST /auth/login/` | the `MobileAuthToken` instance |
| `SessionEmployeeAuthentication` | none — Django session cookie | `request.session['employee_id']`, written by the web login at `line_inspection/auth.py:36` | `None` |
| `KeycloakBearerAuthentication` | `Bearer <access_token>` | live `GET` to Keycloak's `userinfo` endpoint via `services/keycloak_client.resolve_bearer_token` | the raw access-token string |

#### `AUTH_CLASSES` — the order is load-bearing

```python
# line_inspection/api/views.py:43
AUTH_CLASSES = [MobileTokenAuthentication, SessionEmployeeAuthentication, KeycloakBearerAuthentication]
```

Every authenticated view sets `authentication_classes = AUTH_CLASSES`. Two
things about this list are deliberate and documented in the comment above it
(`views.py:37-42`):

- **Each class declines a header that isn't its scheme**, returning `None`
  rather than raising. `MobileTokenAuthentication` returns `None` unless the
  header starts with `token `; `KeycloakBearerAuthentication` returns `None`
  unless it starts with `bearer `; `SessionEmployeeAuthentication` returns
  `None` unless the session carries an `employee_id`. So the three coexist and
  DRF simply walks the list until one returns a tuple.
- **`MobileTokenAuthentication` is first so that DRF's 401-vs-403 decision uses
  its `authenticate_header()`**, which returns the string `'Token'`. DRF only
  emits `401 Unauthorized` when the *first* authenticator supplies a
  `WWW-Authenticate` header value; otherwise `NotAuthenticated` is downgraded to
  `403 Forbidden`. Neither the session class nor the Keycloak class implements
  `authenticate_header`, so if either were first, an expired mobile token would
  surface as a 403. The Flutter client treats **401 and only 401** as "session
  expired → force re-login" (`line_inspection_api.dart:84` `_guard()` →
  `UnauthorizedException`), which is why the ordering matters.

#### Token lifecycle

`MobileAuthToken` (`line_inspection/models.py:700`):

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| `key` | `secrets.token_urlsafe(48)` — a ~64-char opaque string, unique + indexed |
| `employee_id` | already zero-padded by `checkcred_client` |
| `display_name` | from checkCred's `CNAME`/`NAME1` |
| `expires_at` | defaults to **now + 30 days** (`_default_token_expiry`, `models.py:694`). Deliberately long: "field engineers may stay offline for days between syncs. Revocation is explicit (logout) or by expiry, not by a short TTL." |
| `is_active` / `revoked_at` | set by `.revoke()` on logout |
| `last_used_at` | touched at most once per 5 minutes (`MobileTokenAuthentication._touch_after`) so a busy client does not write a row to the `clear` schema on every request |

Authentication failures inside the token class raise
`exceptions.AuthenticationFailed` (→ 401):

- `Invalid or revoked token.` — no row, or `is_active` is false
- `Token expired — please sign in again.` — `expires_at` in the past

#### The local dev-login bypass (affects `POST /auth/login/`)

`POST /auth/login/` delegates straight to
`services/checkcred_client.verify_credentials`, whose first four lines are an
escape hatch:

```python
# line_inspection/services/checkcred_client.py:51
from . import dev_login
if dev_login.is_enabled():
    return dev_login.verify(user_id, passwd)
```

`services/dev_login.py` requires **all three** guards to hold before it does
anything (`dev_login.py:38`):

1. `settings.DEBUG` is `True`
2. env `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_LOGIN == '1'`
3. env `LINE_INSPECTION_DEV_PASSWORD` is non-empty

When active, it does **not** verify anyone's real password: it compares the
submitted password against that one shared string with `hmac.compare_digest`,
then resolves `user_id.zfill(8)` against `EmployeeCadreSnapshot`. Any employee
already synced into that table can be signed in with the single shared string,
and a `MobileAuthToken` is minted for them exactly as if checkCred had approved.
It logs a `WARNING` on first activation and again on every sign-in. Both env
vars are present in `.env.local` (`<set in .env.local>`); values are never
reproduced here. It exists because checkCred is unreachable from outside
APTRANSCO's network and needs gateway credentials that are not in the checkout,
which would otherwise make the app un-loggable-into on a developer machine.

### 11.3 The two API families and why both exist

`api/urls.py` mixes two generations of endpoint that were built for different
consumers and are kept side by side on purpose.

| | **Legacy JSON API** | **Mobile contract** |
|---|---|---|
| Routes | `inspections/`, `inspections/create/`, plus the shared read routes (`catalog/`, `lines/`, `towers/`, `towers/<id>/`, `map/*`, `tickets*`, `support-requests*`) | `ping/`, `auth/*`, `subdivisions/`, `lines/<id>/towers/`, `line-inspections/`, `line-inspections/list/`, `line-inspections/<pk>/`, `dashboard/` |
| Built for | Phase 1–3: the project's own web dashboard templates (same-origin `fetch`) and end-to-end verification scripts | Phase 4: the Flutter field app (`drone_inspection_app`), re-homed from the donor `Aptransco_TIS-main/aptransco_backend` project |
| Identifies catalog objects by | **slug key** (`ChecklistItem.key`, `Defect.key`) — stable, human-readable, survives a catalog reseed | **numeric primary key** — the app downloads the catalog and echoes back the ids it was given |
| Payload shape | `{tower, item_results:[{item, entries:[{defect,…}]}]}` | `{tower_id, items:[{item_id, entries:[{defect_id,…}]}]}` |
| Transport | `application/json` | `multipart/form-data` with a `payload` JSON text field + photo file parts (plain JSON also accepted) |
| Read scope | `jurisdiction.visible_towers` (own assignments only) for `inspections/` | `viewing.oversight_towers` (reporting-hierarchy widened) |

Both write paths funnel into **one** function, `_create_inspection`
(`api/views.py:439`), which accepts either shape. That is the whole point: the
idempotency contract, VT rejection, auto-ticket creation, `worst_criticality`
rollup and the `Tower.last_*` cache bump exist exactly once and cannot drift
apart. The donor project's endpoints (`Aptransco_TIS-main/aptransco_backend/`)
are the *specification* the mobile family was written against; that backend is
not used at runtime.

### 11.4 The scoping rule: reads are oversight-scoped, writes are jurisdiction-scoped

Two distinct authorization scopes exist, and confusing them is the single
easiest way to introduce a security bug here.

- **Jurisdiction** (`line_inspection/jurisdiction.py`) — the *own-assignment*,
  **edit/capture** scope. `visible_lines(employee_id)` is the union of lines
  granted by that employee's own active `RoleAssignment` rows (whole subdivision
  and/or explicit lines); `visible_towers()` adds towers inside their own
  `LineTowerAssignment` from-tower→to-tower ranges. `can_edit_tower()` is the
  gate.
- **Oversight** (`line_inspection/viewing.py`) — the *read-only*, reporting-
  hierarchy-widened superset. `visible_employee_ids()` is `{self} ∪` every
  subordinate found by a BFS over `EmployeeCadreSnapshot.reporting_manager_id`;
  `oversight_lines()`/`oversight_towers()` then union the assignments of that
  whole subtree. For a leaf field engineer (an **AEE**/**DEE** with no
  subordinates) oversight is *exactly equal to* jurisdiction; for a supervisor
  it is strictly wider. Oversight **never** grants edit rights.

| Operation | Scope function used | Where |
|---|---|---|
| All catalog reads | none (catalog is global) | `CatalogView` |
| `subdivisions/`, `lines/`, `towers/`, `lines/<id>/towers/`, `towers/<id>/`, `map/*`, `line-inspections/list/`, `line-inspections/<pk>/`, `tickets/`, `dashboard/` | `viewing.oversight_*` | throughout `api/views.py` |
| `inspections/` (legacy list) | `jurisdiction.visible_towers` | `views.py:628` — the only read endpoint on the narrow scope |
| **Creating an inspection** (both paths) | `jurisdiction.can_edit_tower` | `views.py:453` |
| Closing a ticket | `jurisdiction.can_edit_tower` **OR** `auth.is_admin` | `views.py:719` |
| Resolving a support request | **nothing beyond `IsAuthenticated`** | `views.py:784` — see finding F-3 |

Additional invariants that hold everywhere:

- **VT rows are never returned or inspected.** A *virtual tower* (VT) is a
  database row representing another circuit strung on the *same physical
  structure* as a real tower, linked by coordinate co-location and grouped by a
  shared `structure_key`. `jurisdiction.visible_towers` and
  `viewing.oversight_towers` both filter `is_virtual=False`, and
  `_create_inspection` rejects a VT tower outright. VTs surface only through
  `viewing.circuits_at()` in `GET /towers/<id>/`.
- **`is_active=True` is always applied** to lines and towers.
- **Client-supplied filters never widen scope.** Every `?line=`, `?bbox=`,
  `?subdivision=`, `?tower=` parameter is applied as an additional `.filter()`
  on a queryset that *already* starts from the scope function.

### 11.5 Standard error shapes

| Situation | Status | Body | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| No credentials at all | `401` | `{"detail": "Authentication credentials were not provided."}` + `WWW-Authenticate: Token` | Produced by `IsAuthenticated` → `NotAuthenticated`, upgraded to 401 by the `AUTH_CLASSES` ordering (§11.2). |
| Bad / revoked / expired `Token` | `401` | `{"detail": "Invalid or revoked token."}` or `{"detail": "Token expired — please sign in again."}` | From `MobileTokenAuthentication`. |
| Bad `Bearer` token | `401` | `{"detail": "<KeycloakClientError message>"}` | e.g. `Invalid or expired Keycloak session: …`. |
| Bad login credentials | `401` | `{"error": "<message>"}` | **Note the key is `error`, not `detail`** — `MobileLoginView` builds this response by hand (`views.py:101`). The Keycloak exchange/refresh views do the same. |
| Serializer validation failure | `400` | `{"<field>": ["<message>", …], …}` — values are **lists** | From `serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True)`. Nested errors mirror the payload structure, e.g. `{"items": [{}, {"status": ["\"bad\" is not a valid choice."]}]}`. |
| `ValidationError` raised inside `_create_inspection` | `400` | `{"<field>": "<message>"}` — values are **plain strings** | DRF does not list-wrap the values of a dict passed directly to `ValidationError`. Integrators must handle *both* the list and the scalar form on the same endpoint. |
| Jurisdiction / permission failure | `403` | `{"detail": "You don't have jurisdiction over this tower."}` | `rest_framework.exceptions.PermissionDenied`. |
| Object not found or out of scope | `404` | `{"error": "…"}` **or** `{"detail": "…"}` | Inconsistent by endpoint: `TowerDetailView`, `DefectTicketCloseView` and `SupportRequestResolveView` use `error`; `MobileInspectionDetailView` uses `detail`. Documented per endpoint below. |
| Wrong HTTP method | `405` | `{"detail": "Method \"GET\" not allowed."}` | e.g. `GET /auth/logout/`. |
| Unparseable body | `400` | `{"detail": "JSON parse error - …"}` | From `JSONParser`. `POST /line-inspections/` intercepts *its own* JSON-in-a-form-field case and returns `{"error": "Invalid payload JSON."}` instead. |
| Unhandled exception | `500` | HTML traceback (because `DEBUG = True`) | Reachable in at least one documented way — the `client_id` race in F-4. |

There is no envelope: successful responses are the resource itself (object or
bare array), never `{"data": …}`.

Paths are relative to `/inspection/api/`. "Scope" names the function the
queryset starts from.

| # | Method | Path | Auth | Scope | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | GET | `health/` | none | — | Liveness probe |
| 2 | GET | `ping/` | none | — | Pre-login reachability probe with server clock |
| 3 | POST | `auth/login/` | none | — | checkCred login → issue `MobileAuthToken` |

| 7 | POST | `auth/keycloak/refresh/` | none | — | OIDC refresh (dormant) |
| 8 | GET | `catalog/` | yes | global | Whole questionnaire catalog, dual-shaped |

(25 URL patterns; `support-requests/` counts twice because it serves GET and
POST.)
