| `dashboard_rollup.html` | Yes | `dashboard_views.rollup_view` (`line_inspection/dashboard_views.py:227`) | Zone/Circle/Division management rollups |

#### The three pre-login templates

`login.html`, `forgot_password.html` and `change_password.html` **deliberately do not extend
`base.html`**. Each is a complete standalone document with its own `<style>` block that re-declares
a trimmed subset of the same `:root` palette. This is intentional and is documented in the app
README's file map ("standalone, no base.html — pre-login"):

- `base.html`'s header and nav are meaningless before a session exists — the identity strip would
  be blank and every nav link would 302 back to the login page.
- The pre-login pages use a completely different layout primitive: `body { height: 100vh; display:
  flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center }` with a single centred `.card`, versus
  `base.html`'s top-bar-plus-`main` document flow.

The cost is triplicated CSS: the palette appears four times in the tree, and a colour change means
editing four files. That is the accepted trade for keeping the pre-login pages self-contained.

All three post to themselves and rely on `{% csrf_token %}`. `change_password.html:29` does an
inelegant but functional error detection — `{% if 'Error' in result %}` — because
`auth.change_password_view` returns one `result` string for both success and failure, prefixing
failures with `Error:`.

### Part B — Admin panel

Every admin screen is mounted under `/inspection/` (`transcoapps/urls.py:27` includes
`line_inspection.urls` at that prefix). URLs below are given in full.

#### B.1 Home — `/inspection/admin/`

| | |
|---|---|
| View | `admin_views.admin_home` (`line_inspection/admin_views.py:38`) |
| URL name | `line_inspection:admin-home` |
| Template | `admin_home.html` |
| Gate | `@auth.login_required` — **any** logged-in employee |

This is the post-login landing page (`auth.login_view` redirects here when no `?next=` is given).
It always shows a "Your dashboard" panel with buttons into Map / Tickets / Inspections (and
Reports if `is_management or is_admin`), and the explicit reminder *"Inspections are captured in
the field mobile app."*

The "Admin overview" counter table is rendered only when `is_admin or is_super_admin`; everyone
else gets the line *"You're logged in as a field user. Contact a Super Admin if you should be
assigning inspection roles."* Counters:

| Row | Source |
|---|---|
| Active towers | `Tower.objects.filter(is_active=True).count()` |
| Active lines | `Line.objects.filter(is_active=True).count()` |
| Active role assignments | `RoleAssignment.objects.filter(is_active=True).count()` |
| Lines unmapped to SAP | `Line.objects.filter(sap_line=None, is_active=True).count()` |
| Checklist catalog version | `CatalogVersion.current()` (`line_inspection/models.py:256`) |

Non-obvious behaviour:

- The five counter queries run **for every visitor**, including field users who will never see the
  table (`line_inspection/admin_views.py:39`). Harmless but wasteful.
- The **churn badge** is Super-Admin-only. `admin_views.py:47` calls
  `lilo_matching.detect_churn()` on every home-page load for a Super Admin and renders a red panel
  with the count plus a "Review LILO" button. `detect_churn()` scans all *deactivated* towers that
  still carry inspection history or an active tower-range assignment, and for each one runs a
  ~44 m bounding-box query for a co-located *active* tower of the same voltage
  (`line_inspection/services/lilo_matching.py:203`). It is a per-tower loop, not a single query —
  on a large stranded set this is the slowest thing on the page. The badge exists as a safety net:
  if an ArcGIS re-sync silently replaced towers (a LILO nobody declared), history would be
  orphaned, and this surfaces it.
- The README's admin-panel table (`line_inspection/README.md:293`) describes Home as *"any logged-in
  employee | Quick counts"* and does **not** mention the churn badge. The code is as described
  above.

#### B.2 Manage Admins — `/inspection/admin/super/positions/`

| | |
|---|---|
| View | `admin_views.manage_admins` (`line_inspection/admin_views.py:57`) |
| Template | `manage_admins.html` |
| Gate | `@auth.super_admin_required` — membership in the `SuperAdmin` table |
| Models | `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` (read), `FieldEECadrePosition` (write) |
| Form | `FieldEECadrePositionForm` (`line_inspection/forms.py:9`) |

**The central design idea: Admin rights are granted to a SAP *position*, never to a person.** A
"position" (`position_id` / `position_text`, e.g. an O&M Executive Engineer posting) is a slot in
the SAP org structure that an individual occupies for a while. `auth.is_admin()`
(`line_inspection/auth.py:79`) resolves `employee_id → EmployeeCadreSnapshot.position_id →
FieldEECadrePosition` on every check, so when the holder is transferred, their successor inherits
Admin rights automatically and the predecessor loses them, with no action by the Super Admin. The
template states this in its lede.

*Cadre* here means the SAP employee-subgroup grade code (`emp_sub_grp`): `AE`/`AAE` → AEE,
`ADE/AEE` → DEE, `DE/EE` → EE, then SE, CE, and the board grades. See
`viewing.CADRE_LABELS` (`line_inspection/viewing.py:25`).

Three sections on the page:

1. **Candidate positions (DE/EE cadre, O&M)** — auto-surfaced. The filter is exactly
   `emp_sub_grp='DE/EE'` **and** `position_text__icontains='O&M'`, excluding blank `position_id`
   (`line_inspection/admin_views.py:83`). A comment there records why: *"Real synced data uses the
   single combined code 'DE/EE' (confirmed against the live sync, not two separate 'DE'/'EE'
   values)."* The rows are then deduplicated by `position_id` via `setdefault`, keeping the first
   row seen in `position_text` order — the `sample_employee` column is therefore "one of the people
   currently in this position", not necessarily the only one.
2. **Currently granted Admins** — every `FieldEECadrePosition` row, each with a Revoke button.
   This is where a manually-added position that failed the DE/EE + O&M filter shows up.
3. **Add by position id (fallback)** — the `FieldEECadrePositionForm`, whose `position_text` widget
   is `readonly` with placeholder *"Auto-filled from SAP once you enter a position id"*.

POST actions (all on the same URL; the view always `redirect`s back, so the browser never re-posts
on refresh — the POST/redirect/GET pattern):

| `action` | Fields read | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `grant` | `position_id`, `position_text` | `FieldEECadrePosition.objects.get_or_create(position_id=…, defaults={'position_text': …})`. Idempotent |
| `revoke` | `position_id` | `FieldEECadrePosition.objects.filter(position_id=…).delete()` — a **hard delete**, no soft-delete flag and no audit row. Both the candidate table and the granted table post this |
| `add_manual` | full `FieldEECadrePositionForm` (`position_id`, `position_text`, `notes`) | `form.save()`. **If the form is invalid the view silently does nothing** — no `messages.error`, and the redirect discards the bound form, so the operator sees the page reload with no explanation |

**The `lookup_position` AJAX endpoint.** `GET /inspection/admin/super/positions/lookup/<position_id>/`
→ `admin_views.lookup_position` (`line_inspection/admin_views.py:107`), also
`@super_admin_required`. It calls `sap_client.get_employee_by_position_id(position_id)` and returns
that dict as JSON, or `{"error": "…"}` with HTTP 400 on `SapClientError`. Its docstring gives the
reason it exists: *"posid/postext are interlinked in SAP, so an Admin only needs to type the
position id; this resolves position_text and the current holder."*

The JS at `manage_admins.html:63` wires it up:

```js
posIdInput.addEventListener('blur', lookup);
posIdInput.addEventListener('keydown', function (e) {
  if (e.key === 'Enter') { e.preventDefault(); lookup(); }   // Enter looks up, never submits
});
```

Two details worth copying elsewhere: it clears `position_text` before every lookup so a stale value
can never be submitted, and it guards against out-of-order responses with a monotonic
`currentRequestId` (`if (requestId !== currentRequestId) return; // a newer lookup superseded this
one`). On success it reports the current holder, or *"Position found (currently vacant)"*.

#### B.3 Roles & Jurisdiction — `/inspection/admin/assignments/`

| | |
|---|---|
| Views | `admin_views.role_assignments` (`line_inspection/admin_views.py:142`), `role_assignment_new` (`:223`), `line_schedule_json` (`:211`) |
| Templates | `role_assignments.html`, `role_assignment_form.html` |
| Gate | `@auth.admin_required` on all three |
| Models | `EmployeeCadreSnapshot` (read), `RoleAssignment`, `LineTowerAssignment`, `Subdivision`, `Line`, `Tower` |
| Form | `RoleAssignmentForm` (`line_inspection/forms.py:24`) |

*Jurisdiction* is the **own-assignment, edit-authority** scope: the lines/subdivisions/tower
ranges a person is personally responsible for. It is distinct from *oversight* (Part C), the
read-only reporting-hierarchy-widened superset. This screen is where jurisdiction is granted.

**The candidate list — how a subject employee is found.** The list at the top of
`role_assignments.html` has two mutually exclusive modes, chosen by the presence of `?q=`:

| Mode | `candidate_source` | Query | Cap |
|---|---|---|---|
| default (no `?q`) | `'hierarchy'` | `_subordinates(session employee_id)` → `viewing.subordinate_snapshots()` — a BFS over `EmployeeCadreSnapshot.reporting_manager_id` returning the Admin's **entire reporting subtree, self excluded** (`line_inspection/viewing.py:36`) | none |
| search (`?q=…`) | `'search'` | `employee_name__icontains` **OR** `employee_id__icontains`, `.distinct()` | 50 |

The heading swaps between "Employees reporting to you" and "Search results", and a "Show my
hierarchy" button appears to clear the search. The design intent is that an EE assigning work
normally only cares about their own AEEs/DEEs, so those are offered with zero typing; the
full-employee search is the escape hatch for the cases the reporting tree gets wrong (secondments,
stale `reporting_manager_id`, vacancies). `admin_views._subordinates` is a two-line wrapper whose
docstring stresses that the subtree walk has exactly one implementation, shared with the Phase 3
oversight scope — so an admin's candidate list and their dashboard scope can never disagree.

**Jurisdiction coverage.** Each candidate row shows a coverage string computed by
`_jurisdiction_coverage` (`line_inspection/admin_views.py:129`):

```
{assigned_lines} / {total_lines_in_subdivisions} lines across {subdivision_count} subdivision(s)
```

where `assigned_lines` = distinct line ids across the employee's active `RoleAssignment`s,
`subdivision_count` = distinct subdivisions on those assignments, and
`total_lines_in_subdivisions` = every `Line` in those subdivisions. The point is to answer "does
this person already have a workload, and how much of their subdivision is covered?" before you add
more. Note the degenerate reading: an employee assigned only *specific lines* and no subdivision
renders as `3 / 0 lines across 0 subdivision(s)`, because the denominator is only populated by
subdivision-level grants. This is an N+1 — two queries per candidate row — which is why the search
mode caps at 50.

The rest of the page is two tables: **Active assignments** (`RoleAssignment` where `is_active`,
with `subdivision`, line count, who assigned it and when) and **Active tower ranges**
(`LineTowerAssignment`, rendered `T-<from> → T-<to>`), each row carrying a Deactivate button
behind a `confirm()`.

POST actions — note that **all four post to `role_assignments`**, including the two forms rendered
on the separate `role_assignment_new` page:

| `action` | Fields | Effect / validation |
|---|---|---|
| `create` | `RoleAssignmentForm` (`employee_id` hidden, `subdivision`, `lines`) | `role` is forced to `'FIELD_INSPECTOR'` server-side (never user-selectable), `assigned_by_employee_id` from the session. `save(commit=False)` → `save()` → `save_m2m()`. Invalid forms produce `messages.error(... form.errors.as_text())` |
| `deactivate` | `assignment_id` | `RoleAssignment.filter(pk=…).update(is_active=False)` — soft delete, history preserved. **Not scoped**: any Admin can deactivate any assignment, including one they did not create |
| `create_range` | `employee_id`, `range_line_id`, `from_tower_id`, `to_tower_id` | All four required. Both towers must belong to the chosen line, checked in one query: `{int(from_id), int(to_id)} <= on_line`. Creates a `LineTowerAssignment` |
| `deactivate_range` | `range_id` | `LineTowerAssignment.filter(pk=…).update(is_active=False)` |

Two subtleties in `create_range`. Because it is a **set** containment test, `from == to` passes and
creates a single-tower range. And the view does **not** require `from` to precede `to` along the
line — that is fine, because `jurisdiction.range_tower_ids` normalises with
`lo, hi = sorted((f_seq, t_seq))` (`line_inspection/jurisdiction.py:66`). Range membership is
resolved by `line_sequence` between the two boundary towers, and boundaries are stored as `Tower`
FKs rather than raw indices *so that rebuilding the tower schedule cannot drift an assigned
stretch* (`line_inspection/models.py:465`).

**`role_assignment_new` — `/inspection/admin/assignments/new/<employee_id>/`.** A pure form
renderer: it 404s on an unknown `employee_id`, builds an unbound `RoleAssignmentForm` with
`initial={'employee_id': …}`, and serialises every active line to `lines_json`:

```python
lines_payload = list(
    Line.objects.filter(is_active=True)
    .order_by('name')
    .values('id', 'name', 'subdivision_id', 'voltage')
)
```

The comment explains the invariant: this is the *"same active-lines queryset the form's 'lines'
field validates against"* (`forms.py:40`), so the client-side picker can never offer a line that
would then fail server validation.

The template's picker is **progressive enhancement over the real Django widgets, not a
replacement**. `{{ form.subdivision }}` and `{{ form.lines }}` are rendered inside
`.real-select-hidden` (1×1px, `opacity:0`, `pointer-events:none`) and remain the elements that
actually submit. The JS (`role_assignment_form.html:133`) reads the subdivision options *out of the
hidden `<select>`* and drives:

- a single-select subdivision combobox with a `— No subdivision —` clear row;
- a multi-select line combobox rendering selected lines as removable chips, with a live
  `N line(s) selected` counter;
- **subdivision-narrowed line search**: picking a subdivision filters the line pool client-side to
  that subdivision, with the label *"showing lines from &lt;subdivision&gt;"* and a
  "— show all subdivisions instead" link to reset (`subdivisionFilterId = null`);
- a 200-row display cap with *"Showing first 200 of N — keep typing to narrow"*, because there are
  on the order of a thousand lines.

Semantics of the two fields (from the labels): subdivision is optional and *"grants every line in
it"*; specific lines are optional and *"grant just these, **in addition to** any subdivision
above"*. They union, they do not override.

**The from/to tower picker and `line_schedule_json`.** The second form on the page assigns a tower
range. Selecting a line fires:

```js
var SCHEDULE_URL = "{% url 'line_inspection:line-schedule-json' 0 %}";
fetch(SCHEDULE_URL.replace('/0/', '/' + id + '/'), { credentials: 'same-origin' })
```

The `reverse()`-with-0-then-string-replace trick appears three times in this codebase (here, the
map's tower detail, and the ticket close) and exists so no URL is ever hard-coded in JS.

`GET /inspection/admin/line/<line_id>/schedule/` → `admin_views.line_schedule_json`
(`line_inspection/admin_views.py:211`) returns:

```json
{"line": "220KV XYZ - ABC", "towers": [
  {"id": 4412, "tower_number": "1", "cp_sp": "CP", "line_sequence": 1}, …]}
```

Three things make this the right data source for the picker:

- It calls `schedule.line_schedule(line, include_virtual=False)`, i.e. towers in **schedule order**
  — the order derived by projecting each tower onto the line's GeoJSON geometry, persisted as
  `Tower.line_sequence` (`line_inspection/schedule.py:122`). A range is a physical stretch of line,
  so the dropdown must be in walking order, not id or alphabetical order.
- **Virtual towers are excluded.** A VT ("virtual tower") is a placeholder row representing a
  circuit that shares a physical structure with another circuit; VTs are never inspected, so they
  cannot be a range boundary.
- `cp_sp` is surfaced in the option label as `T-12 (CP)`. CP/SP = Cut Point / Section Point,
  the operational markers field crews use to describe a stretch.

Both dropdowns start `disabled` with *"— select a line first —"*, show `loading…` during the fetch,
and fall back to `Failed to load` on a network error.

#### B.4 Checklist Catalog editor — `/inspection/admin/checklist/`

| | |
|---|---|
| Views | `checklist_editor` (`line_inspection/admin_views.py:245`) plus five form views and one delete view |
| Templates | `checklist_editor.html` (listing), `simple_form.html` (every create/edit) |
| Gate | `@auth.admin_required` on all seven |

The inspection questionnaire lives in the database, not in code, because — as the page itself
says — *"this questionnaire is not finalised."* The editor is the whole CRUD surface for it.

The listing page renders the catalog as a nested tree: group → items → (inline sub-table) defects →
criticality rules, plus a flat table of follow-up questions at the bottom. It is read-only; every
mutation is a link to `simple_form.html` or an inline POST.

Model shapes surfaced in the listing:

| Level | Columns shown | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `ChecklistItemGroup` | `sort_order`. `label` (`key`) | e.g. "Foundation", "Tower body" |
| `ChecklistItem` | `sno`, `label` (`key`), `positions`, `applicable_tower_types`, availability mode | `positions` = the per-position axis (e.g. `Top,Middle,Bottom`); blank = non-positional. `applicable_tower_types` blank renders as "all tower types". Availability column shows `item-level` when `is_availability_gated`, `per-position` when `is_position_availability_gated`, else `—` |
| `Defect` | `label` (`key`), `ask`, `get_default_criticality_display`, rules | `ask` is an ordered list of `FollowUpQuestion` keys |
| `CriticalityRule` | `follow_up_key <operator> threshold_value → resulting_criticality` | Rendered inline under its defect |
| `FollowUpQuestion` | `key`, `question_text`, `answer_type`, `options`/`unit` | |

The five editor forms (all rendered through `simple_form.html`, all routed
`…/new/` and `…/<pk>/` to the same view):

| Form | Fields | Special handling |
|---|---|---|
| `ChecklistItemGroupForm` | `key`, `label`, `sort_order` | plain |
| `ChecklistItemForm` | `group`, `key`, `sno`, `label`, `sort_order`, `positions`, `is_availability_gated`, `is_position_availability_gated`, `applicable_tower_types`, `na_reason` | `positions` is a comma-separated text input (`"Top,Middle,Bottom (comma-separated, blank = not positional)"`) split in `clean_positions`; `applicable_tower_types` is a `CheckboxSelectMultiple` whose **choices are built at runtime from `DISTINCT Tower.tower_type` in the DB** (`admin_views._tower_type_choices`, `:255`) so the options always match real synced master data instead of a hard-coded enum |
| `DefectForm` | `item`, `key`, `label`, `sort_order`, `ask`, `default_criticality` | `ask` comma-separated → list of follow-up keys, order preserved |
| `FollowUpQuestionForm` | `key`, `question_text`, `answer_type`, `options`, `unit`, `placeholder` | `options` comma-separated → list |
| `CriticalityRuleForm` | `defect`, `follow_up_key`, `operator`, `threshold_value`, `resulting_criticality`, `priority` | `threshold_value` is a JSON field; help text warns *"A plain number or string, e.g. 2 or \"Main leg / corner member\" (JSON — quote text values)."* |

Because `positions` / `applicable_tower_types` / `ask` / `options` are array-typed model fields fed
by plain text inputs, each view does the same dance — `form.save(commit=False)`, copy the cleaned
list onto the instance, then `save()`:

```python
item = form.save(commit=False)
item.positions = form.cleaned_data['positions']
item.applicable_tower_types = form.cleaned_data['applicable_tower_types']
item.save()
CatalogVersion.bump()
```

**`CatalogVersion.bump()` on every save — and every delete.** All five form views and
`checklist_delete` call it (`line_inspection/admin_views.py:266, 285, 305, 323, 338, 355`).
`CatalogVersion` is a singleton row whose docstring states the reason
(`line_inspection/models.py:248`): it is *"stamped onto each Inspection so historical records stay
traceable to the catalog shape that produced them."* The editor page repeats this in the lede:
*"Editing anything here bumps the catalog version so past inspections stay traceable to the shape
they were recorded under."* The version is also what the Flutter app compares against to decide
whether to re-download the catalog. Note that the bump happens only on a **valid** form —
an invalid POST re-renders the form and leaves the version alone, which is correct.

**`checklist_delete`** — `POST /inspection/admin/checklist/delete/<model_name>/<pk>/`
(`line_inspection/admin_views.py:347`). A whitelist maps five slugs to models
(`group`/`item`/`defect`/`followup`/`rule`) so no arbitrary model can be targeted, and the delete
only runs on POST. Unknown slugs and GETs fall through to a silent redirect back to the editor.

Two real gaps here:

- **`CriticalityRule` has no delete button in the UI.** `checklist_editor.html:46` renders only an
  `edit` link for each rule. The `rule` slug is wired in `checklist_delete` and the URL exists, but
  nothing in any template posts to it — deleting a rule requires hand-crafting a request.
- **Deleting a non-empty group/item/defect raises an unhandled `ProtectedError` (HTTP 500).**
  `ChecklistItem.group`, `Defect.item`, `ItemResult.item` and `DefectTicket.item` are all
  `on_delete=PROTECT` (`line_inspection/models.py:281, 319, 542, 586`) — a deliberate choice so
  inspection history can never be silently cascaded away. But `checklist_delete` calls
  `.delete()` with no `try/except`, so pressing "delete" on a group that has items, or on an item
  that has ever been inspected, produces a server error instead of a message. Compare with the SAP
  mapping screen below, which *does* catch its integrity error and explain it. This is an
  inconsistency in error handling, not a data-safety problem — the PROTECT does its job.

#### B.5 SAP ↔ ArcGIS Mapping — `/inspection/admin/sap-mapping/`

| | |
|---|---|
| View | `admin_views.sap_mapping` (`line_inspection/admin_views.py:365`) |
| Template | `sap_mapping.html` |
| Gate | `@auth.admin_required` |
| Models | `Line` (`sap_line` FK), `SapLine` |
| Form | `SapLineForm` (`functional_location`, `description`, `voltage`) |

Two systems name the same transmission line differently: ArcGIS (the GIS master, source of tower
and line geometry) uses one naming convention, SAP PM (the maintenance system) identifies the line
by a *functional location* code with a free-text description. `Line.sap_line` is a
`OneToOneField(SapLine, on_delete=SET_NULL)` (`line_inspection/models.py:110`) — one ArcGIS line
maps to at most one SAP line and vice versa. This screen is where that correspondence is curated.

The page header reports `{{ matched_count }} mapped, {{ unmatched_count }} unmapped` and states
the policy: *"Auto-map writes only high-confidence matches — review the rest below."*

The table lists up to 300 active lines (optionally narrowed by `?q=` on `name__icontains`), each
with its current mapping as a green `pill-ok` (functional location + description) or a red
`pill-bad` "unmapped", ranked suggestions, and a `<select>` of every `SapLine` for a manual set.

**Ranked suggestions.** Computed only for lines that are still unmapped
(`admin_views.py:397`) — there is no point suggesting alternatives for a line an operator has
already decided:

```python
suggestions = [] if line.sap_line_id else find_best_matches(line, all_sap_lines, top_n=3)
```

`services.sap_matching.find_best_matches` returns up to three `(SapLine, score, reason)` tuples
sorted best-first, dropping anything scoring 0; the template renders them as
`<functional_location> — <description> (<reason>, <score to 2dp>)`. `reason` is a short string
explaining *why* it matched, which is what lets an operator accept or reject at a glance. Note the
cost model: this is an in-Python cross product of (up to 300 lines) × (all SAP lines) executed on
every page render.

POST actions:

| `action` | Effect |
|---|---|
| `auto_map` | `call_command('map_sap_lines')` — runs the management command **synchronously inside the request**. There is no job queue; a large catalog means a long-running request. Always reports success |
| `set_mapping` | Sets `line.sap_line_id` to the posted value (or `None` for "— unmapped —") and saves just that column |
| `add_sap_line` | `SapLineForm.save()` for a SAP line that the import missed. Like `manage_admins`, an invalid form fails silently |

**The friendly unique-constraint handling** is the notable piece of this view
(`line_inspection/admin_views.py:376`):

```python
try:
    # Atomic so a unique-violation rolls back cleanly instead of
    # leaving the connection in an aborted-transaction state.
    with transaction.atomic(using='line_inspection_db'):
        line.save(update_fields=['sap_line'])
    messages.success(request, f'Updated mapping for {line.name}.')
except IntegrityError:
    messages.error(request, 'That SAP line is already mapped to another ArcGIS line — clear the existing mapping first.')
```

Two things are going on. Because `sap_line` is one-to-one, re-using a SAP line raises
`IntegrityError` — and the operator gets a sentence telling them exactly what to do instead of a
500 page. And the `transaction.atomic(using='line_inspection_db')` wrapper is not decoration: in
PostgreSQL an integrity error aborts the enclosing transaction, and without a savepoint the
connection would refuse every subsequent query in the request (including the ones needed to render
the redirect target). The explicit `using=` names this app's database because the project runs a
multi-database router (`line_inspection/db_router.py`).

#### B.6 LILO — `/inspection/admin/lilo/` and `/inspection/admin/lilo/<pk>/`

| | |
|---|---|
| Views | `admin_views.lilo_home` (`line_inspection/admin_views.py:416`), `lilo_reconcile` (`:441`) |
| Templates | `lilo.html`, `lilo_reconcile.html` |
| Gate | `@auth.super_admin_required` on both |
| Models | `LiloEvent` (with `new_lines` M2M), `Line`, `Tower` |
| Service | `services/lilo_matching.py` (`detect_churn`, `propose_matches`, `apply_reconcile`) |

**LILO = Loop-In Loop-Out.** When a new substation is built next to an existing transmission line,
the line is cut and both ends are looped into the new substation. One line becomes two, most of the
physical towers are untouched, but in the GIS master they are re-attributed to the new line names
and re-issued with new object ids. Naively re-syncing would deactivate every old tower and create
new rows — orphaning years of inspection history for towers that never moved. This screen exists to
prevent that, and it is deliberately manual: *"Rare event; nothing here runs automatically."*

**`lilo_home`** shows three blocks:

1. **Possible undeclared churn** (only when `detect_churn()` returns anything) — the same safety-net
   detector behind the admin-home badge. Each flag renders as
   `Stranded T-<n> (<line>) ↔ active T-<n> (<line>) · <distance> m` with a "Start LILO" link that
   deep-links back to this page as `?old_line=<id>&new_line=<id>`; those two params become
   `prefill_old` / `prefill_new` and pre-select the two dropdowns via JS.
2. **Record a LILO** — a plain POST form (`action=create_lilo`): old line (single select), new
   lines (multi-select, *"Ctrl/Cmd-click for two"*), optional date, free-text notes. On submit the
   view creates the `LiloEvent`, sets the `new_lines` M2M, stamps
   `performed_by_employee_id` from the session, and **redirects straight to the reconcile page**
   with the message *"LILO #N recorded — review the tower reconcile."*
3. **LILO events** — the 50 most recent events with a `Draft` / `Applied <date>` pill, and a button
   labelled "Reconcile" or "View" depending on `applied_at`.

Both dropdowns are populated client-side from a `<script type="application/json">` payload of all
active lines, the same pattern as the assignment form.

**`lilo_reconcile`** is the decision screen. On GET it calls `lm.propose_matches(event)`, which
returns `{'pairs': [...], 'unmatched_old': [...], 'counts': {...}}`. Each pair carries
`new_tower`, a suggested `old_tower` (or `None`), `distance_m`, `number_match`, a `method`, and a
ranked `candidates` list (`line_inspection/services/lilo_matching.py:61`):

| `method` | Meaning | What the UI renders |
|---|---|---|
| `auto` | High confidence (nearest-first greedy one-to-one on distance) | A 2-option select pre-selected to "Re-link to OLD T-n (Dm)", with "Mark as NEW tower" as the override |
| `review` | Ambiguous — operator must confirm | One option per candidate (`T-n (Dm[, #match])`), first pre-selected, plus "Mark as NEW tower". Candidates are ordered *same-tower-number first, then nearest*, because a surviving tower normally keeps its number through a LILO |
| `new` | Genuinely a new loop tower | A single locked option "NEW tower (no match)" |

A summary panel shows the four counts (`auto` / `review` / `new` / `unmatched_old`) colour-coded
green / dark-yellow / blue, with a legend sentence in the lede. Old towers with no proposal are
listed separately with the explanation that they *"stay deactivated; their history is retained."*

POST `action=apply` (`line_inspection/admin_views.py:443`):

```python
proposal = lm.propose_matches(event)          # recomputed, not trusted from the form
decisions = {}
for pair in proposal['pairs']:
    val = request.POST.get(f'decision_{pair["new_tower"].id}', '')
    if val.startswith('match:'):  decisions[nid] = int(val.split(':', 1)[1])
    elif val == 'new':            decisions[nid] = None
summary = lm.apply_reconcile(event, decisions)
```

Non-obvious behaviour worth knowing:

- The proposal is **recomputed server-side on apply** and the submitted `decision_<id>` values are
  only consulted for tower ids that appear in the fresh proposal. That is the right security
  posture (you cannot inject an arbitrary tower id), but it means a master-data change between
  render and submit silently drops decisions for towers that disappeared, and leaves towers that
  newly appeared out of `decisions` entirely.
- Any `decision_` value that is neither `match:<id>` nor `new` is skipped rather than defaulted.
- After apply, `applied_at` is stamped and the page becomes read-only: the selects are replaced by
  plain text (`→ T-n` or `new`) and the Apply button disappears (`lilo_reconcile.html:43, 74`).
- The success message reports `"{matched} tower(s) re-linked (history preserved), {new} new."`
- The Apply button is behind a `confirm()` spelling out the consequence.

### Part C — Field-engineer / oversight dashboard (read-only)

**No inspection capture happens on the web, ever.** There is no form anywhere in
`dashboard_views.py` or its templates that creates an `Inspection`, an `ItemResult`, or a
`DefectEntry`. Capture is the exclusive job of the Flutter field app, which posts to
`/inspection/api/line-inspections/`. `dashboard_views.py:1` states it outright — *"Phase 3
field-engineer / oversight web dashboard — read-only. No inspection capture here (that is the
Flutter app, Phase 4)"* — and `admin_home.html` and `dashboard_inspections.html` both repeat it to
the user. The **single** state-changing action on the whole dashboard is closing a defect ticket.

Every dashboard screen is scoped by **oversight**, not jurisdiction. The distinction is the most
important concept in this part of the system (`line_inspection/viewing.py:1`):

- **Jurisdiction** (`jurisdiction.py`) — an employee's *own* active `RoleAssignment`s and tower
  ranges. This is the **edit/capture authority** the REST API write path enforces.
- **Oversight** (`viewing.py`) — jurisdiction *widened up the reporting hierarchy*: your own towers
  **plus every tower assigned to anyone below you in the reporting tree**. An EE sees their AEEs',
  an SE sees their whole circle. Oversight is **read-only and never grants edit rights.**

`viewing.oversight_towers()` returns active, **non-virtual** towers on any oversight line, unioned
with tower-range ids, optionally filtered to geocoded rows for the map
(`line_inspection/viewing.py:79`). The viewing *tier* (`viewing.cadre_tier`) is functional, not
grade-based — `admin` / `supervisor` / `field_user` / `none` — because real SAP cadre codes are
coarse and combined; grade codes are used only for display labels and the management gate.

#### C.1 Map — `/inspection/dashboard/map/`

| | |
|---|---|
| View | `dashboard_views.map_view` (`line_inspection/dashboard_views.py:33`) |
| Template | `dashboard_map.html` |
| Gate | `@auth.login_required` — any logged-in employee |

The server does very little: it computes the scope's bounding box and four counters, then hands
Leaflet everything it needs as JSON.

| Context key | Value |
|---|---|
| `tier`, `cadre_label` | `viewing.cadre_tier()` / `viewing.display_label()` (the grey text next to the H1) |
| `tower_total`, `inspected_total`, `pending_total`, `line_total` | Toolbar stats. "Inspected" = `last_inspection_at__isnull=False` on the denormalized Tower cache |
| `status_colors_json` | `json.dumps(status.STATUS_COLORS)` |
| `status_labels` | `status.STATUS_LABELS` = `dict(WORST_CHOICES)`, drives the filter `<select>` and the legend |
| `ap_center_json`, `ap_zoom` | `[15.8497, 78.0661]` @ z8 — the Andhra Pradesh default, chosen to match `gisapp`'s `map_data` centre |
| `bounds_json` | `{min_lat,max_lat,min_lng,max_lng}` aggregated over the scope, or `null` |

**Status colour scheme** — the single source is `status.STATUS_COLORS`
(`line_inspection/status.py:16`), whose comment records the reason: *"POC colour coding
(gisdata/clearpoc.html). Single source so map/legend/rollup match."* Status is the
`worst_criticality` of the tower's most recent inspection.

| Key | Label (`WORST_CHOICES`) | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| `none` | Not inspected | `#898781` (grey) |
| `ok` | Normal | `#0ca30c` (green) |
| `minor` | Minor | `#fab219` (amber) |
| `major` | Major | `#ec835a` (orange) |
| `critical` | Critical | `#d03b3b` (red) |

The legend dots are coloured **from that JSON at runtime** rather than in CSS
(`document.querySelectorAll('.legend .dot')…el.style.background = STATUS_COLORS[el.dataset.status]`),
so adding a criticality level in Python needs no template change.

Client-side behaviour (`dashboard_map.html:58`):

1. **Base layer** — OpenStreetMap raster tiles, `maxZoom: 19`.
2. **Initial framing** — `map.fitBounds(BOUNDS, {padding:[30,30]})` when the scope has any geocoded
   towers, otherwise `setView(AP_CENTER, AP_ZOOM)`. An empty scope also shows a panel: *"No towers
   are assigned within your jurisdiction yet. Ask your Admin to assign lines/subdivisions to you."*
3. **Line overview — loaded exactly once**, unconditionally, from
   `GET /inspection/api/map/lines/` as a GeoJSON `FeatureCollection`. Lines are small (≤1,212 in
   scope) so this is cheap. Stroke colour comes from a hard-coded voltage map in the template —
   `{'132kV': '#2a78d6', '220kV': '#7a3fb0', '400kV': '#c0392b'}`, weight 2, opacity 0.7 — and each
   line binds a popup with name, voltage and `Inspected X / Y towers` (a rollup the API computes
   from the denormalized tower cache, no `Inspection` join). Clicking a line calls
   `loadTowers(lineId)`, which loads **all** of that line's towers regardless of zoom and
   `fitBounds` to them with `maxZoom: 15`.
4. **Zoom-gated bbox tower loading.** `TOWER_ZOOM_MIN = 12`. On every `moveend`,
   `loadTowersByBbox()` runs: below zoom 12 it clears the layer and shows *"Zoom in to load
   individual towers."*; at or above 12 it builds
   `bbox=<west>,<south>,<east>,<north>` and fetches `GET /inspection/api/map/towers/`. This is the
   whole reason the map is usable at all — the tower table is on the order of tens of thousands of
   rows and is never sent wholesale. The API caps the response at `MAX_MAP_TOWERS` and sets a
   `truncated` flag, which the hint line surfaces as *"Showing first N towers — zoom in to see the
   rest."* versus *"N towers shown."*
5. **Clustering** — `L.markerClusterGroup({ disableClusteringAtZoom: 16, chunkedLoading: true })`.
   Clusters below z16, individual markers above; `chunkedLoading` keeps the UI responsive while
   thousands of markers are added. Markers are `L.circleMarker` (radius 6, dark outline, fill =
   `STATUS_COLORS[status]`), not image pins — no sprite assets to host.
6. **Filters.** Two `<select>`s in the toolbar, both wired to `loadTowersByBbox`:
   - **Status** — the five `STATUS_LABELS` keys, sent as `?status=`.
   - **Cycle** — `ground_patrol` ("Ground Patrolling") or `pmi` ("Pre-Monsoon (PMI)"), sent as
     `?inspection_type=`. Each tower is inspected twice a year on these two cycles; **PMI** is the
     detailed pre-monsoon inspection, ground patrolling is the routine walk-down. When a cycle is
     given, the API recomputes per-cycle status from the `Inspection` table instead of reading the
     denormalized cache (`line_inspection/api/views.py:345`).
   - Both filters affect **towers only** — the line overview layer keeps its original styling and
     is never refetched. And because a filter change calls `loadTowersByBbox`, it discards a
     line-click selection and reverts to the current viewport.
7. **Tower pop-up.** Rendered in two stages. Immediately: tower number, tower type · voltage,
   status, and a **"View history" deep-link** to `/inspection/dashboard/inspections/?tower=<id>`,
   plus a `loading circuits…` placeholder. Then on `popupopen` it fetches
   `GET /inspection/api/towers/<id>/` and rewrites the popup with:

   ```
   ──────────────────────────
   Circuits on this structure:
   220KV A–B (220kV, D/C)
   132KV C–D (132kV, S/C)
   <tower_ckts_conductor>
   ```

   That circuits list is the payoff of the **`structure_key`** design: one physical steel structure
   can carry several circuits, each modelled as a separate `Tower` row on a different `Line`
   (the extra ones flagged `is_virtual`). `viewing.circuits_at()` resolves every active line
   sharing the structure key (`line_inspection/viewing.py:96`), so clicking one tower answers "what
   else runs through this structure?" — critical before planning a shutdown. The fetch is lazy
   (only on popup open) so a screen of 500 markers costs zero extra requests.

All fetches use `credentials: 'same-origin'`, which works because
`SessionEmployeeAuthentication` (`line_inspection/api/authentication.py:26`) is one of the three
DRF auth classes and reads `request.session['employee_id']` directly. Every error path is a bare
`.catch(function () {})` — failures are silent, with no user-visible error state.

#### C.2 Tickets — `/inspection/dashboard/tickets/`

| | |
|---|---|
| View | `dashboard_views.tickets_view` (`line_inspection/dashboard_views.py:63`) |
| Template | `dashboard_tickets.html` |
| Gate | `@auth.login_required` |

`DefectTicket`s whose tower is in the viewer's oversight scope, newest-raised first, **capped at
500 with no pagination**. Three GET filters, each an auto-submitting `<select>`
(`onchange="this.form.submit()"` — no JS file needed):

| Param | Values |
|---|---|
| `status` | `open` / `closed` |
| `source` | `human_inspection` / `drone_inspection` |
| `criticality` | `critical` / `major` / `minor` |

The `source` split is structural: the system is designed to ingest drone-derived defects alongside
human field inspections, and every rollup keeps the two apart. Columns: raised timestamp, tower
number, `tower.line_name` (denormalized on Tower — no join), item label + optional position with
the defect label beneath, criticality (colour-coded), source (a pill), status pill, and the action
cell.

**The one write action on the dashboard.** Every *open* ticket row gets a "Close" button. Clicking
it `prompt()`s for a closing note pre-filled with `Attended and rectified`, then POSTs JSON
`{"close_note": …}` to `/inspection/api/tickets/<id>/close/` and, on success, rewrites the row's
status cell to a green "Closed" pill and removes the button — no page reload.

Authorization is enforced entirely server-side (`line_inspection/api/views.py:719`):

```python
# Admins (who assign jurisdiction to others) can act on any ticket in
# their oversight, not just towers they personally hold jurisdiction
# over; field inspectors can only close their own jurisdiction's tickets.
if not is_admin(employee_id) and not jurisdiction.can_edit_tower(employee_id, ticket.tower):
    raise PermissionDenied("You don't have jurisdiction over this ticket's tower.")
```

Note the deliberate asymmetry: viewing is by *oversight*, but closing is by *jurisdiction* (or
Admin). A supervisor can see a subordinate's tickets and cannot close them unless they are an
Admin. The template does not attempt to predict this — it renders the button for everyone and
relies on the server, showing `alert('Could not close this ticket — you may not have permission.')`
on failure and re-enabling the button. The view does pass `is_admin` into the context
(`dashboard_views.py:82`) but **the template never uses it**; it is dead context.

Two further notes. Closing is idempotent — an already-closed ticket returns 200 with the serialized
ticket rather than erroring. And the POST carries **no CSRF token**: it succeeds because
`SessionEmployeeAuthentication` is a custom `BaseAuthentication` subclass, not DRF's
`SessionAuthentication`, so DRF's CSRF enforcement never runs. That is a cookie-authenticated
state-changing endpoint with no CSRF protection — worth flagging to whoever hardens this for
production.

#### C.3 Inspections — `/inspection/dashboard/inspections/`

| | |
|---|---|
| View | `dashboard_views.inspections_view` (`line_inspection/dashboard_views.py:88`) |
| Template | `dashboard_inspections.html` |
| Gate | `@auth.login_required` |

One view, one template, **three render modes** selected by the `detail` / `out_of_scope` context
flags:

**Mode 1 — scope list (no `?tower`).** The latest 500 inspections across the viewer's oversight
scope, `-saved_at`, each annotated with `defect_count=Count('item_results__entries')`. Columns:
date (+ save time beneath), tower number **linking to `?tower=<id>`**, line name, cycle, inspector
employee id, worst criticality (colour-coded), defect count. Header text restates the read-only
contract.

**Mode 2 — per-tower history (`?tower=<id>`).** The scope check comes first:
`scope.filter(pk=tower_id)…first()`. Note this is the *oversight* queryset, so the check both
resolves the tower and authorizes it in one query. Then every inspection for that tower,
newest-first, with `item_results__item` and `item_results__entries__defect` prefetched, optionally
narrowed by `?cycle=`.

Each inspection renders as an HTML `<details>` element — **native disclosure widgets, zero
JavaScript**. The first one is `open` by default. The `<summary>` line carries date, a cycle pill,
`by <inspector_employee_id>`, and right-aligned the worst criticality and `N defect(s)` (via the
`pluralize` filter). Expanding reveals optional remarks and a four-column table of every item
result:

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| Item | `r.item.label` |
| Position | `r.position` or `—` (positional items only) |
| Status | `get_status_display` + a `photo` link when `r.photo` is set (opens `r.photo.url` in a new tab) |
| Defect detail | One line per `DefectEntry`: criticality (colour-coded) — defect label, then the follow-up `answers` dict rendered `key: value, …`, then the free-text `note`, then a `photo` link |

Rows whose `status == 'defect'` get a pale red background (`.defect-row`).

**Mode 3 — out of scope.** If `?tower=` names a tower outside the oversight scope, the view
re-renders the same template with `out_of_scope=True`, producing a panel — *"That tower isn't
within your jurisdiction."* with a link back. **Note this is a 200, not a 403**, unlike the
register screen which returns a real `HttpResponseForbidden` for the equivalent situation. The two
screens are inconsistent; neither leaks data.

The `?cycle=` filter is whitelisted server-side to `''` / `ground_patrol` / `pmi` (anything else
is coerced to `''`) and is rendered from `register.CYCLE_LABELS`, so the three options read
`Latest (any cycle)` / `Ground Patrolling` / `Pre-Monsoon Inspection (PMI)`. In detail mode the
cycle form carries the tower id in a hidden input so switching cycle preserves the tower.

#### C.4 Register — `/inspection/dashboard/register/`

| | |
|---|---|
| View | `dashboard_views.register_view` (`line_inspection/dashboard_views.py:135`) |
| Template | `dashboard_register.html` |
| Gate | `@auth.login_required` |
| Builder | `register.build_register()` / `register.register_to_xlsx()` (`line_inspection/register.py`) |

The *line inspection register* is the formal patrolling record APTRANSCO keeps on paper: a matrix
whose columns are the towers of one line and whose rows are the checklist items. This screen is a
digital replica of that sheet, built to look enough like the paper form that a field engineer
recognises it.

Two selectors, both auto-submitting: **Line** (only lines in the viewer's oversight scope, listed
`name (voltage)`) and **Cycle** (`register.CYCLE_LABELS`). With a line chosen, two action buttons
appear: **🖨 Print** (`window.print()`) and **⬇ Excel** (a link to `?line=…&cycle=…&format=xlsx`).

The structure returned by `build_register()` and consumed by the template:

| Piece | Content |
|---|---|
| `tower_headers[]` | Per column: `id`, `source_id`, `tower_number`, `tower_type`, `is_virtual`, `inspected`, `date`, `worst` |
| `rows[]` | Three metadata rows (`Date of inspection`, `Loc No`, `Type of tower`), then per checklist group a `{group_header}` row followed by one row per item, then a final `Remarks` row |
| `rows[].cells[].kind` | `blank` / `na` ("N/A") / `np` ("Not available") / `ok` (✓) / `defect` / `meta` |

Rendering specifics:

- Columns include **all** towers on the line, real **and virtual**, in schedule order. VT columns
  are badged with a grey `VT` chip in the header, and a tower header that was never inspected gets
  the `.dim` class.
- A VT column's data comes from the **co-located real tower** sharing its `structure_key`
  (`register.py:92`) — so an inspected structure reads as inspected on every circuit that runs
  through it, which is what the paper register does implicitly.
- Defect cells show a coloured criticality chip (`MINOR` amber / `MAJOR` orange / `CRITICAL` red)
  followed by the defect text including follow-up answers.
- The first two columns (`S.No`, `Item`) are `position: sticky` with explicit `left: 0` / `left:
  42px` offsets, and the `<thead>` is sticky-top, so the matrix stays readable while scrolling
  horizontally inside `.register-scroll` (`overflow-x: auto`).

**Print.** A `@media print` block hides the top bar, nav, toolbar and the mobile view, removes the
`main` padding and the scroll container's border, **un-stickies the frozen columns** (sticky
positioning breaks pagination), and drops the font to 10px — so Ctrl-P yields something close to
the paper register.

**Excel.** `?format=xlsx` short-circuits before rendering and streams
`register.register_to_xlsx(structure)` with content type
`application/vnd.openxmlformats-…spreadsheetml.sheet`. The filename is sanitised from the line name
with `re.sub(r'[^A-Za-z0-9]+', '_', …)` — e.g. `register_220KV_A_B_pmi.xlsx` — because line names
contain slashes and spaces. The workbook freezes panes at `C5` and prefixes defect cells with
`[CRITICAL]`-style tags since colour chips do not survive the export.

**The 403.** The line id is validated against the oversight-scoped queryset, and the comment says
why (`dashboard_views.py:153`): *"Never trust the line id — it must be within the viewer's scope."*
An out-of-scope id returns `HttpResponseForbidden('That line is outside your jurisdiction.')`.
Two wrinkles: the message says "jurisdiction" although the scope actually applied is *oversight*
(wider), and the response is a bare text 403 with no styling or navigation.

**Mobile one-tower-at-a-time.** Below 820px the wide matrix is hidden and `.register-mobile` is
shown: a tower `<select>` (each option `T-<n>` with a ✓ when inspected) plus a two-column table.
The JS does no data fetching — it **reads the already-rendered desktop DOM table** and clones one
column:

```js
var tds = tr.children;               // 0=S.No, 1=Item, 2..=towers
var label = tds[1].textContent.trim();
var cell  = tds[2 + col];
```

So the desktop table is always in the HTML (merely `display:none`), and the mobile view is a pure
client-side projection of it. Group-header rows are re-emitted as full-width rows. Cheap, but it
means the whole matrix is always sent to a phone.

#### C.5 Reports / rollups — `/inspection/dashboard/reports/`

| | |
|---|---|
| View | `dashboard_views.rollup_view` (`line_inspection/dashboard_views.py:227`) |
| Template | `dashboard_rollup.html` |
| Gate | `@auth.login_required` **plus** an in-view management check |

The gate (`dashboard_views.py:229`):

```python
is_mgmt = viewing.is_management(employee_id)
if not (is_mgmt or auth.is_admin(employee_id)):
    return HttpResponseForbidden('The management reports are restricted to admins and management cadre.')
```

`viewing.is_management()` is true for any Super Admin, or for a holder of a top-cadre
`emp_sub_grp` in `MANAGEMENT_SUBGRPS = {'CE', 'DIRECTOR', 'GM', 'JMD', 'CMD'}`
(`line_inspection/viewing.py:33`). The nav tab uses the same predicate via the context processor,
so the tab is hidden for anyone who would get the 403.

**Scope depends on which side of the gate you came in on** — but the branch is no longer here.
`tower_qs` is always `viewing.oversight_towers(employee_id)`, which applies the `is_management`
widening itself; `is_mgmt` survives in this view only to pick the label (`dashboard_views.py:238`):

| Viewer | `tower_qs` resolves to | `scope_label` |
|---|---|---|
| Management (or Super Admin) | every active real tower in the system | "All towers (management view)" |
| Admin, not management | their reporting-subtree oversight scope | "Your oversight scope" |

`?level=` selects the aggregation field from `ROLLUP_LEVELS = ['zone', 'circle', 'division']`
(default and fallback `zone`) — the APTRANSCO geographic org hierarchy, denormalized directly onto
`Tower`. The template renders the three levels as a button switch with the active one primary.

`_rollup()` (`dashboard_views.py:181`) does the aggregation in **two queries, no `Inspection`
join** — the docstring notes it reads *"all from the denormalized Tower cache and the DefectTicket
table"* and is deliberately factored out so *"a future mobile JSON endpoint can share it"*:

| Column | Source |
|---|---|
| Towers | `Count('id')` per group |
| Inspected | `Count(filter=last_inspection_at__isnull=False)` |
| Coverage | rendered as a bar via `{% widthratio r.inspected r.total 100 %}` |
| Pending | `total - inspected` |
| Minor / Major / Critical | `Count(filter=last_worst_criticality=…)` |
| Open tickets | `Count(filter=status='open')`, with critical-open in parentheses in red |
| Human / Drone | `Count(filter=source='human_inspection')` / `'drone_inspection'` |

Ticket counts come from a second query grouped on `tower__<field>` and are merged into the tower
rows in Python by group key; a group with towers but no tickets falls back to zeros. Groups with a
null/blank geo field render as `(unspecified)`. A totals panel above the table sums towers,
inspected, pending and open tickets across all rows. Minor cosmetic note: when a group has
`total == 0`, `widthratio` yields an empty string and the bar's inline `width:` is invalid — the
browser ignores it, so the bar simply renders empty.

The **human-vs-drone split** is present here (and in the ticket filters) because drone inspection
is a planned second capture channel: management needs to see how much of the defect load each
channel is producing, per zone.

### CDN assets and air-gapped deployment

Exactly **one** template loads anything from the network, `dashboard_map.html:5`:

| Asset | URL |
|---|---|
| Leaflet CSS | `https://unpkg.com/leaflet@1.9.4/dist/leaflet.css` |
| MarkerCluster CSS | `https://unpkg.com/leaflet.markercluster@1.5.3/dist/MarkerCluster.css` |
| MarkerCluster default theme | `https://unpkg.com/leaflet.markercluster@1.5.3/dist/MarkerCluster.Default.css` |
| Leaflet JS | `https://unpkg.com/leaflet@1.9.4/dist/leaflet.js` |
| MarkerCluster JS | `https://unpkg.com/leaflet.markercluster@1.5.3/dist/leaflet.markercluster.js` |
| Map tiles | `https://{s}.tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` |

None of them carry Subresource Integrity hashes, and none are pinned to anything stronger than a
semver-exact unpkg path.

Every other template — all 17 of them, including the whole admin panel and four of the five
dashboard screens — is fully self-contained and works with no external network at all.

For an **air-gapped or offline deployment** (a realistic scenario for a utility control room), the
map is the only casualty, and it fails hard: with no Leaflet, `L.map('map')` throws, the IIFE dies,
and the page shows an empty bordered box with the toolbar and legend still rendered. Remediating it
means:

1. Vendoring `leaflet` and `leaflet.markercluster` (CSS, JS, and MarkerCluster's images) into a
   static directory — **which does not exist yet**. `line_inspection/static/` is absent and no
   template does `{% load static %}`, so this is the first Django-static usage in the app and needs
   `STATIC_ROOT`/`collectstatic` to be verified.
2. Replacing the OpenStreetMap `tileLayer` URL with an internal tile server or a WMS the utility
   already runs — the `L.tileLayer(...)` call at `dashboard_map.html:77` is the only place a tile
   URL appears.
3. Nothing else. There are no web fonts, no icon fonts, no analytics, and no other third-party
   scripts anywhere in the tree.

### Discrepancies between the code and `line_inspection/README.md`

The README is unusually good, but the following statements in it do not match the code as it
stands. **The code is authoritative.**

| README | Reality |
|---|---|
| `README.md:288` — *"Login: `/inspection/login/` -> redirects to Keycloak -> `/inspection/auth/callback/` sets `request.session['employee_id']`"* | There is **no** `auth/callback/` route in `line_inspection/urls.py`, and `auth.login_view` (`line_inspection/auth.py:27`) renders a real employee-id/password form validated against checkCred. Keycloak is built but dormant. The README's own changelog (`README.md:70`) records the change — the admin-panel section header was never updated |
| `README.md:293` — Home = *"any logged-in employee \| Quick counts"* | Correct on the gate, but incomplete: non-admins see no counters at all (the table is behind `is_admin or is_super_admin` in `admin_home.html:23`), and Super Admins additionally get a LILO churn badge the table does not mention |
| `README.md:296` — Checklist Catalog *"CRUD for groups/items/defects/follow-up questions/criticality rules"* | The **D** is incomplete: no template renders a delete control for a `CriticalityRule`, and deleting a group/item/defect that has protected children raises an unhandled `ProtectedError` rather than a message (see B.4) |
| `README.md:324` — *"Two DRF authentication classes … `SessionEmployeeAuthentication` … and `KeycloakBearerAuthentication`"* | There are **three**: `AUTH_CLASSES = [MobileTokenAuthentication, SessionEmployeeAuthentication, KeycloakBearerAuthentication]` (`line_inspection/api/views.py:43`). Only the session class matters for these templates |
| `README.md:162` — template inventory | Accurate as far as it goes, but does not mention `simple_form.html`, the shared shell behind all five catalog editors |
## 13. Flutter Field App — Architecture & Screens

The field app is the data-capture half of the platform: the Django web app
(`line_inspection/`) owns the questionnaire catalog, the jurisdiction rules and the
reporting; this app is what an inspector carries to a transmission tower, and it is the
**only** place a tower inspection is ever created. Everything in this section is read from
`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/`.

Two subsystems are deliberately excluded here and covered in section 14: the offline layer
(`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/services/offline/` — `LocalStore`,
`OutboxStore`, `SyncEngine`, `ConnectivityService`, `OfflineActions`, `OfflineDownloader`,
`CachedTileProvider`, `li_cache_keys.dart`) and the HTTP client
(`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/services/line_inspection_api.dart`). They are
referenced by name below where a screen calls into them.

### 13.1 App identity, version, and the misleading package name

| Property | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Pub package name | `drone_inspection_app` | `Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/pubspec.yaml:1` |
| pubspec description | "APTRANSCO drone inspection data collection app with offline upload queue support." | `pubspec.yaml:2` |
| Version | `1.1.0+2` (versionName `1.1.0`, versionCode `2`) | `pubspec.yaml:19` |
| Dart SDK constraint | `^3.12.2` | `pubspec.yaml:22` |
| `publish_to` | `'none'` (private package, never goes to pub.dev) | `pubspec.yaml:5` |
| MaterialApp title | `Aptransco TIS` | `Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/main.dart:62` |
| Android app label | `Aptransco TIS` | `Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:7` |
| iOS display name | `Aptransco TIS` | `Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/ios/Runner/Info.plist:16` |
| Flutter channel/revision | `stable`, `ad70ec4617166f1c38e5d2bfd388af71fda14f06` | `Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/.metadata` |
| Lints | `package:flutter_lints/flutter.yaml`, no rules overridden | `Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/analysis_options.yaml` |

**Why "drone".** The project began as a drone-imagery upload tool; the product it is today is
a *manual, on-foot transmission-line inspection* app (TIS = Transmission Inspection System).
The Dart package name, the Android `applicationId`, the Kotlin package and the pubspec
description were never renamed, because renaming a pub package breaks every `package:`
import, and renaming the `applicationId` would make the new build a different app on the
Play Store / on inspectors' phones (no upgrade path, no data migration). Everything the user
sees says "APTRANSCO / Line Inspection". Only the build metadata still says "drone".

Historical fossils of the same kind, worth recognising so they are not mistaken for live
features:

- `ApiService`'s doc comment refers to "the old map-flow's data/inspection endpoints; those
  screens have been removed" (`.../lib/services/api_service.dart:5-8`).
- `TileLayer.userAgentPackageName` is still `com.aptransco.data_collection`
  (`.../lib/screens/li_tabs/home_tab.dart:297`, `.../lib/screens/li_tabs/inspection_tab.dart:199`).
- `li_asset.dart`'s header explains the `Li` class prefix exists to avoid colliding with
  "the legacy `TransmissionLine` / `TowerLocation` models used by the older upload flow" —
  those legacy models no longer exist in the tree.
- Two bundled JSON data files (see 13.2) are leftovers of the offline-only POC.

### 13.2 Dependencies, asset and tooling configuration

#### Runtime dependencies

| Package | Constraint | What it does in THIS app |
|---|---|---|
| `flutter` | sdk | Framework. Material 3 (`useMaterial3: true`), light theme only. |
| `image_picker` | `^1.1.2` | The only photo source. `_pickPhoto()` in the inspection form offers camera or gallery and returns a `File`; images are downscaled at capture (`imageQuality: 85`, `maxWidth/maxHeight: 1600`) so a 12 MP phone photo does not blow up the offline outbox or a 2G upload. |
| `http` | `^1.2.2` | Every backend call in `line_inspection_api.dart` (`http.get/post`, and `MultipartRequest` for the inspection submit). No Dio, no interceptors — auth headers are merged manually per call. |
| `shared_preferences` | `^2.3.2` | Three distinct uses: the backend base-URL override (`api_base_url_override`), the persisted session (`li_session_v1`), and the whole offline `LocalStore` / `OutboxStore` (see §14). |
| `connectivity_plus` | `^6.0.5` | Backs `ConnectivityService`, which exposes an `online` `ValueNotifier` consumed by `SyncStatusBar` and by the cache-through read core. |
| `flutter_map` | `^7.0.2` | The Home overview map and the Inspect tab's near-me map. Chosen over Google Maps because it needs no API key, no Play-Services dependency, and lets tiles be served from a local disk cache when the phone is offline. |
| `latlong2` | `^0.9.1` | `LatLng` value type used by `flutter_map`, by `LocationService.distanceTo`, and by the presence gate. |
| `cached_network_image` | `^3.4.1` | `LiPhotoThumbnail.network` uses `CachedNetworkImageProvider` so a server photo viewed once stays viewable with no signal. |
| `cupertino_icons` | `^1.0.8` | Standard Flutter template dependency. No Cupertino widget is used anywhere in `lib/`; effectively unused. |
| `geolocator` | `^14.0.3` | The presence gate. Service-enabled check, runtime permission, one-shot `getCurrentPosition`, a 5 m-filtered `getPositionStream`, and `Geolocator.distanceBetween` (haversine) for the 50 m / 500 m radii. |
| `path_provider` | `^2.1.6` | Durable app-documents directory for staged inspection photos and the map-tile cache (§14). |
| `path` | `^1.9.1` | Filename/extension joining for the same. |
| `flutter_map_cancellable_tile_provider` | `^3.0.2` | Base class for `CachedTileProvider` (§14): cancels in-flight tile HTTP requests when a tile scrolls out of view, which matters badly on a metered/flaky field connection. |

### 13.3 Startup sequence — `lib/main.dart` line by line

`Aptransco_TIS-main/drone_inspection_app/lib/main.dart:12-27`:

```dart
Future<void> main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  await ApiService.loadBaseUrl();
  await AuthStore.instance.load();
  await NetworkSecurity.install();
  await LocalStore.instance.init();
  await OutboxStore.instance.init();
  await ConnectivityService.instance.init();
  SyncEngine.instance.start();
  runApp(const AptranscoApp());
}
```

Every step is awaited, and the order is load-bearing:

| # | Call | Site | Why it must be here |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized()` | `main.dart:13` | All of the following touch platform channels (SharedPreferences, rootBundle, path_provider, connectivity). Without the binding they throw. |
| 1 | `ApiService.loadBaseUrl()` | `main.dart:16` | Reads the `api_base_url_override` pref into a static. Must precede **everything** network-shaped: step 3 pins its insecure-cert exemption to `Uri.parse(ApiService.baseUrl).host`, and steps 5-7 can issue requests. If it ran later, the first requests would silently go to the compile-time ngrok default even though the inspector had pointed the app at the LAN. |
| 2 | `AuthStore.instance.load()` | `main.dart:17` | Rehydrates `LiSession` from `li_session_v1`. Must precede the first screen because `WelcomeScreen._enter()` branches on `AuthStore.instance.isLoggedIn` **synchronously**, and must precede any request because `LineInspectionApi._auth` reads the token synchronously per call. |
| 3 | `NetworkSecurity.install()` | `main.dart:18` | Sets `HttpOverrides.global`. `HttpOverrides` only affects `HttpClient`s created *after* it is installed, so it must be in place before the first `http` call. Needs step 1's base URL (see above). |
| 4 | `LocalStore.instance.init()` | `main.dart:22` | The on-device cache + media staging directory. Everything below writes into it. |
| 5 | `OutboxStore.instance.init()` | `main.dart:23` | Rehydrates the durable queue of unsent changes from disk. Must come after `LocalStore` (shared storage) and before `SyncEngine`, which immediately wants to know how many ops are pending. |
| 6 | `ConnectivityService.instance.init()` | `main.dart:24` | Seeds the `online` `ValueNotifier` with the current state and subscribes to changes. `SyncEngine` listens to it, and the cache-through read core consults it on every GET — so a wrong initial value would make the first screen either needlessly offline or needlessly hang. |
| 7 | `SyncEngine.instance.start()` | `main.dart:25` | **Not awaited** — deliberately. Draining the outbox can take minutes over a bad link; blocking `runApp` on it would leave the user staring at the native splash. It is fire-and-forget and publishes progress through `SyncEngine.instance.status` / `.dataRevision`, which the UI subscribes to. |
| 8 | `runApp(const AptranscoApp())` | `main.dart:26` | First frame. |

The net effect is that by the time any widget builds, the app knows *which* backend, *who*
is signed in, *how* to trust TLS, *what* is cached, *what* is queued, and *whether* there is
a network — so no screen has to handle a "not initialised yet" state.

#### The resume hook

`_AptranscoAppState` mixes in `WidgetsBindingObserver`
(`main.dart:36-57`), registers itself in `initState`, removes itself in `dispose`, and:

```dart
@override
void didChangeAppLifecycleState(AppLifecycleState state) {
  if (state == AppLifecycleState.resumed) {
    SyncEngine.instance.onResume();
  }
}
```

The rationale (quoted in the comment) is that an inspector typically walks out of coverage,
records several inspections, pockets the phone, and later comes back into signal — the
app returning to the foreground is the single most reliable moment to re-probe the network
and flush the queue, and it costs nothing when there is nothing to send.

#### STALE COMMENT — flag

`main.dart:66-68` still says:

```dart
// The branded welcome screen is the opening screen; its "Get Started"
// continues into the hub. (Sign-in is still disabled — the hub boots with
// a default Head-Office session.)
```

**Both claims are false in the current code.**
1. There is no "Get Started" button. `WelcomeScreen` is a timed splash — a 1,100 ms
   `AnimationController` whose completion listener navigates (`welcome_screen.dart:30-41`).
   No user interaction exists on that screen at all.
2. Sign-in is *not* disabled and there is no default Head-Office session. `_enter()`
   (`welcome_screen.dart:50-64`) reads `AuthStore.instance.isLoggedIn` and pushes
   `LineInspectionHubScreen(session: session!)` only when a stored token exists; otherwise it
   pushes `const LineInspectionLoginScreen()`, which posts real credentials to
   `POST /auth/login/` (checkCred-verified). `welcome_screen.dart:9-11`'s own doc comment
   states the correct behaviour, so the two comments in the repo contradict each other. The
   code, and `welcome_screen.dart`'s comment, are right; `main.dart:66-68` is stale.


**Why a ticker and not a `Timer`.** The comment at `welcome_screen.dart:27-29` is explicit:
one `AnimationController` both drives the fade (`Interval(0.0, 0.45)`) and, on
`AnimationStatus.completed`, performs the navigation. In `flutter_test`, `tester.pump()`
advances the test clock and therefore the ticker deterministically; a bare `Timer` would
require real wall-clock waits or `FakeAsync` plumbing and would make the smoke test flaky.
The transition itself is a 400 ms `FadeTransition` via `PageRouteBuilder`.

### 13.5 `LiSession` — `lib/models/li_session.dart`

The signed-in user, in full. The header comment records the design shift that matters:
identity and role "now come from the backend login (`POST /auth/login/`, checkCred-verified)
rather than a free-text picker" — *checkCred* being APTRANSCO's central credential-checking
gateway that the Django side calls (see the auth section of this document).

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `employeeId` | `String` | required | APTRANSCO employee number. The server resolves this to a cadre + jurisdiction; the app only displays it and stamps it on inspections/tickets/support requests. |
| `token` | `String` | required | The DB-backed mobile auth token. **Empty string = signed out** — this is the app's only definition of "logged in". |
| `displayName` | `String` | `''` | Human name from the cadre snapshot. Parsed but, as of this build, never rendered — the scope strip shows `employeeId · jurisdictionLabel` instead. |
| `isAdmin` | `bool` | `false` | Server-declared admin. |
| `isManagement` | `bool` | `false` | Server-declared management/HQ user. |
| `cadre` | `String` | `''` | Display label for the grade, e.g. `AEE`, `EE`. Used as the first half of `jurisdictionLabel`. |
| `tier` | `String` | `''` | `'field_user' \| 'supervisor' \| 'admin' \| 'none'`. Parsed and persisted but **never branched on** anywhere in `lib/` — all role gating uses `isManagementOrAdmin`. |
| `subdivisionId` | `int?` | `null` | *Local* scope hint only. |
| `subdivisionName` | `String?` | `null` | Ditto, for display. |

**The authority note is the important part.** `li_session.dart:14-16`: "Optional local scope
hint for list filtering (a subdivision the user chose to focus on). **Server-side
jurisdiction is authoritative regardless.**" The subdivision fields are passed as a
`?subdivision=` query parameter to narrow lists (Tickets, Support); they cannot *widen*
anything, because every endpoint independently filters by the jurisdiction the token
resolves to. A tampered client that sends someone else's subdivision id simply gets a
narrower (or empty) result set, never a broader one. Nothing in the app ever *sets* these
fields — `copyWith` is the only writer and it is never called in `lib/`, so in practice
`subdivisionId`/`subdivisionName` are always `null` and `scopeSubdivisionId` always returns
`null`. The mechanism exists for a subdivision picker that has not been built.

Members:

| Member | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `LiSession.fromLogin(Map j, {required String token})` | Reads `employee_id`, `display_name`, `is_admin`, `is_management`, `cadre`, `tier` — the **snake_case** wire shape of `/auth/login/` and `/auth/me/`. Takes `token` separately because the login screen pulls it out of the same body first (`login_screen.dart:50`). Never populates the subdivision fields. |
| `toJson()` / `fromJson()` | The **camelCase** persistence shape for SharedPreferences (`employeeId`, `isAdmin`, `subdivisionId`, …). The two shapes are intentionally different: `fromLogin` parses the server contract, `fromJson` parses the app's own storage, so a server field rename cannot corrupt stored sessions and vice versa. Every field is null-tolerant (`as String? ?? ''`), so an older stored blob still loads. |
| `copyWith({subdivisionId, subdivisionName})` | Only these two are settable — identity and role can never be locally mutated. Unused today. |
| `isManagementOrAdmin` | `isAdmin \|\| isManagement`. Drives exactly two things: whether the **Inspect** tab exists (`hub_screen.dart:28`) and whether **Resolve** appears on a support request (`support_tab.dart:332`). |
| `scopeSubdivisionId` | Alias for `subdivisionId`, "null = no local filter". |
| `jurisdictionLabel` | `cadre` if non-empty, else `'Admin'` when `isAdmin`, else `'Field'`; then `' — <subdivisionName>'` appended when set. Shown in the hub's scope strip. |

### 13.6 `AuthStore` — `lib/services/auth_store.dart`

An eager singleton (`AuthStore._()` + `static final instance`).

| Member | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `_sessionKey` | `'li_session_v1'` — versioned, so a future incompatible session shape can use `_v2` and simply ignore the old blob rather than crash-looping on a bad parse. |
| `load()` | Called once from `main()`. `jsonDecode` of the stored string into `LiSession.fromJson`. Wrapped in a bare `try/catch (_)` whose comment is "no session → signed out": a corrupted blob degrades to the login screen instead of bricking the app. |
| `save(LiSession)` | **Purges the previous employee's on-device data first** when the incoming `employeeId` differs from the stored one (`LocalStore.purgeUserData()`, §14.3) — this is the one funnel every sign-in goes through, and sign-out alone does not cover a force-kill or a shared device. Compares ids, not sessions, so the scope picker's `copyWith` re-save keeps the warmed cache. Then sets the in-memory session, then best-effort persists. Order matters — if the disk write fails the user is still signed in for this run. |
| `session` / `token` | Synchronous getters. The whole point of loading once at startup is that `LineInspectionApi` can read the token synchronously on every call without an `await`. |
| `isLoggedIn` | `(_session?.token ?? '').isNotEmpty`. A session object with an empty token counts as signed out. |
| `authHeaders()` | `{}` when signed out, else `{'Authorization': 'Token <token>'}`. Returning an **empty map rather than null** is what lets call sites write `{...jsonHeaders, ..._auth}` unconditionally. |
| `clear()` | Nulls the in-memory session, **purges the cache and offline photos** (`LocalStore.purgeUserData()`), and removes the pref. Called by the hub's sign-out flow *after* `LineInspectionApi.logout()`. |

**The `Token <key>` scheme.** This is DRF's classic token header, not `Bearer`. The Django
side registers `MobileTokenAuthentication` first in the authentication class list precisely
so a bad/revoked/expired token yields 401 rather than falling through to anonymous. So
`Authorization: Token <token>` is the single credential on every mobile request.

**Sign-out** (`hub_screen.dart:39-59`): a confirm dialog ("You will need your employee ID and
password to sign in again"), then `LineInspectionApi.logout()` (best-effort server-side
revoke, swallowed on failure — `line_inspection_api.dart:75-81`), then
`AuthStore.instance.clear()` — which now also purges the cache and offline photos (§14.3) — then
`SyncEngine.instance.kick()` to recount the queue against its new owner scope so the status bar
stops advertising this employee's pending changes, then
`pushAndRemoveUntil(LineInspectionLoginScreen, (r) => false)` so no authenticated route survives in
the stack. `CacheWarmer.instance.stop()` runs *first*, before the session goes away, so a pass in
flight cannot keep pulling the outgoing employee's jurisdiction.

The sign-in side mirrors it (`line_inspection_login_screen.dart`): `AuthStore.instance.save()` is
awaited **before** the hub is built — otherwise its tabs paint from the old jurisdiction on their
first frame — and then `SyncEngine.instance.kick()` picks up anything this employee left queued on
this device.

#### FINDING — the documented 401 → re-login path is not wired up

`line_inspection_api.dart:16-22` declares:

```dart
/// Thrown when the backend rejects the auth token (401). The app clears the
/// session and returns the user to the login screen.
class UnauthorizedException implements Exception { ... }
```

and `_guard()` (`line_inspection_api.dart:83-85`) throws it on any 401. The web app's
`line_inspection/README.md` changelog likewise claims the app has "real login + token
transport on every request (**401 → re-login**)".

Grepping the whole `lib/` tree, `UnauthorizedException` appears **only** in its own
declaration and in `_guard`. **Nothing catches it.** A 401 therefore propagates into whatever
tab issued the call and is rendered by `liErrorState()` as the raw string "Session expired —
please sign in again." with a **Retry** button that will fail identically forever. The
session is never cleared and the user is never routed to the login screen; the only escape
is the manual Sign-out button. The README and the doc comment describe an intended behaviour
that the code does not implement.

### 13.7 The hub shell — `lib/screens/line_inspection_hub_screen.dart`

A `StatelessWidget` holding a `DefaultTabController`. Structure:

- **AppBar** (`toolbarHeight: 64`, `kCardBg` on `kInk`): the tower mark (`kLogoMark`, 34 px,
  placed directly on the white bar — the comment notes a white badge "would vanish"),
  a two-line title (`APTRANSCO` / `Line Inspection`), then two actions: a `dns_outlined`
  icon opening `editBackendUrl()` and a `logout` icon.
- **Scope strip** (`AppBar.bottom`, 32 px): an apartment icon for management/admin or a
  person-pin for field users, then `'<employeeId>  ·  <jurisdictionLabel>'`. This exists so
  the inspector can always see *whose* jurisdiction the data below is scoped to — a recurring
  source of confusion when a supervisor and an AEE look at the same screen.
- **Body**: `SyncStatusBar` pinned above an `Expanded(TabBarView(...))`, so the offline/queued
  banner is visible on every tab rather than per-tab.
- **Bottom navigation**: the `TabBar` itself, moved to `bottomNavigationBar`. Its colours are
  overridden locally (`labelColor: kBrandPrimary`, `unselectedLabelColor: kInkFaint`) because
  the shared `tabBarTheme` in `li_theme.dart` is tuned white-on-dark for the brand gradient
  this bar used to sit on. The active tab is marked with a 2.5 px hairline along the **top**
  edge (`Border(top: ...)` as the indicator) — pointing at the content, not the usual
  underline.

`_changeServer()` shows a snackbar after a change ("reopen the tab or search again to
reload") because nothing re-fetches automatically when the base URL changes.

**Tab-visibility rule** (`hub_screen.dart:22-28`): "Home is where a field engineer works…
The separate Inspect tab (a nearby-towers shortlist over the same gate) would be redundant
for them, so it is shown only to supervisors and admins." Both `_tabs` and the `TabBarView`
children apply the same `if (_showInspectTab)` so the two lists stay index-aligned.

### 13.8 The five tabs

#### 13.8.1 Home — `lib/screens/li_tabs/home_tab.dart` (551 lines)

*(551 lines as checked out — this file is being actively edited, so treat line counts as approximate.)*

**What the user sees.** A full-bleed `FlutterMap` of every tower on every line assigned to
them, each a `TowerDot` coloured by criticality (grey `kCritColor['none']` = not yet
inspected). Floating on top: a four-cell KPI strip at the top, a column of map controls down
the right edge, and a pill-shaped "Offline area" button bottom-left.

**Data load** (`_load()`, `home_tab.dart:74-120`):

1. `LineInspectionApi.searchLines('')` — the empty search returns *the caller's assigned
   lines*, jurisdiction-scoped server-side.
2. For each line, concurrently (`Future.wait`): `towersForLine(l.id)` and
   `loadInspections(line: l.id)`. Each is individually `.catchError((_) => <T>[])` — the
   comment explains why: "Tolerate a single line failing (e.g. not yet cached offline) — show
   the rest rather than failing the whole map."
3. `loadDashboard()` in its own `try/catch` that swallows everything, so the map still
   renders when only the KPI endpoint is down.
4. All three are cache-through (§14), so the whole tab works offline once "Download my area"
   has run.

| Endpoint (relative to the `/api` base) | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `GET /lines/?search=` | the user's assigned lines |
| `GET /lines/<id>/towers/` | tower list + coordinates per line |
| `GET /line-inspections/list/?line=<id>` | summaries, for the per-tower colour |
| `GET /dashboard/` | the KPI strip |

**KPI strip** (`_kpiStrip`): `Towers` (`dash.towerTotal`, falling back to the loaded tower
count), `Inspected`, `Coverage %`, `Open` — each showing `—` when the dashboard call failed.

**Map behaviour.**
- Two tile sets, toggled by a layer button: OSM standard
